text: The May evening was transparent and apple-green, as Seven Gulls Harbour reflected the clouds from the golden west amidst its gently darkened banks. On the sand-bar, the ocean uttered an uncanny mournfulness, melancholic despite the spring, yet a cunning, merry breeze whistled down the crimson harbour road where the cozy, motherly form of Miss Winifred traveled toward the village of Glen St. Agnes. Legally, Miss Winifred was Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, a status she had held for thirteen years, though even now she was called Miss Winifred by more people than called her Mrs. Kerr. Her former name remained cherished by her longtime companions, with a single contemptuous exception. Tabitha Pratt, who served as the gray, austere, and loyal servant to the Carrow household at Hollowmere, seized every chance to address her as “Mrs. Ambrose Kerr,” using the most devastating and deliberate stress, as though implying “You desired to be a Mrs., so a Mrs. you will certainly be to the absolute extreme where I am concerned.”

Ascending toward Hollowmere, Miss Winifred went to visit Dr. and Mrs. Carrow, who had recently returned from Europe. Their trip had lasted three months, as they had departed in February for the purpose of attending a renowned medical congress in London; furthermore, during the time they were gone, particular events had occurred in the Glen that Miss Winifred was eager to talk about. A new family had settled in the manse, for instance. And what a family they were! Walking at a quick pace, Miss Winifred shook her head about them repeatedly.

As they were seated on the large porch at Hollowmere, taking pleasure in the twilight's magic, the sweet calls of drowsy robins piping amidst the dusk-bound maples, and the flutter of a wind-blown cluster of daffodils swaying near the lawn's aged, soft red brick wall, Tabitha Pratt and the Nell Harcourt of bygone times observed her approaching.

Hands gathered around her knee, Nell sat upon the steps, appearing, within the gentle twilight, as youthful as it is fitting for a mother of numerous children to seem; and her lovely gray-green eyes, which looked along the harbour road, remained as filled with endless glimmer and reverie as always. Resting behind her inside the hammock, Tessa Carrow lay curled, a plump, rotund little child of six years who was the youngest among the Hollowmere children. Her hair was red and curly, and her hazel eyes were currently shut tight in the amusing, crinkled manner that Tessa constantly fell asleep in.

Harcourt, whom the family “Who’s Who” referred to as “the little brown boy,” lay sleeping held in Tabitha’s arms. His hair was brown, his eyes were brown, and his skin was brown, featuring extremely rosy cheeks, and Tabitha cherished him above all others. Nell suffered a prolonged, severe illness following his delivery, prompting Tabitha to care for the infant as a mother with an intense affection that had not been awakened by any of her other beloved children. Indeed, Dr. Carrow had stated that his survival would have been impossible without her.

“Mrs. Dr. dear, I brought him into this world every bit as much as you,” Tabitha was accustomed to remarking. “The baby belongs to me every bit as much as he belongs to you.” Furthermore, Harcourt would invariably race to Tabitha whenever he needed his bruises kissed better, to be swayed into slumber, and to be shielded from earned beatings. Every one of the remaining Carrow offspring had been dutifully thrashed by Tabitha whenever she believed their spiritual well-being required it, yet Harcourt was spared her hand, nor would she permit his own mother to strike him. On one occasion when Dr. Carrow inflicted a spanking upon him, Tabitha reacted with furious rage.
“Sweet Mrs. Dr., that fellow would whip a seraph, he surely would,” she had asserted with venom; and for many weeks, she refused to bake a pie for the unfortunate doctor.

She had brought Harcourt along to her brother’s residence while his mother and father were away, whereas every other child had departed for Brierley, granting her three glorious months with him entirely on her own. Even so, Tabitha was delighted to return to Hollowmere and be surrounded by all her beloved ones once more. Hollowmere constituted her universe, a realm where her authority was absolute. Even Nell rarely disputed her judgments, which deeply irritated Mrs. Agatha Sowerby of Grey Shutters, who dismal-fashion informed Nell, on every occasion she went to Seven Gulls, “you are letting Tabitha get to be entirely too much of a boss and will live to rue it.”
“Winifred Tolley is walking up the harbour road right now, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked. “She will be arriving here to dump three months’ worth of gossip upon us.”

“I hope so,” said Nell, embracing her knees. “I’m dying for Glen St. Agnes gossip, Tabitha. I hope Miss Winifred can inform me about all that has taken place during our absence—everything—who has been born, or married, or drunk; who has died, or departed, or arrived, or fought, or lost a cow, or found a beau. It’s so wonderful to be back home with all the beloved Glen folks, and I want to hear everything about them. Why, I recall wondering, while I was strolling through Westminster Abbey which of her two particular suitors Millicent Drew would ultimately marry. Do you know, Tabitha, I have a terrible feeling that I love gossip.”

“Well, of course, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha admitted, “any proper woman enjoys listening to the news. I myself am somewhat interested in Millicent Drew’s situation. I was never had by a beau, let alone two, and it does not bother me now, because being an old maid fails to hurt once you grow accustomed to it. To me, Millicent’s hair constantly appears as though she swept it up using a broom. Nevertheless, the men appear not to mind it.”
“Only her attractive, charming, sarcastic, small face is visible to them, Tabitha.”

“That could indeed be true, Mrs. Dr. dear. It is stated in the Good Book that favor is deceitful and beauty is vain, yet I would not have objected to discovering that personally, had it been so destined. Undoubtedly, every one of us will be beautiful once we become angels, but what benefit will that bring us at that point? Turning to the subject of gossip, though, it is reportedly said that over harbour, poor Mrs. Pettifer Miller attempted to hang herself last week.”
“Oh, Tabitha!”

“Compose yourself, Mrs. Dr. dear. Her attempt failed. Yet I cannot truly fault her for attempting it, since the man she married is a dreadful person. Nevertheless, she acted quite foolishly in considering hanging herself, which would only make room for him to wed a different woman. Had I found myself in her situation, Mrs. Dr. dear, my approach would have been to badger him until he attempted to hang himself rather than me. This is not to say that I approve of anyone hanging themselves in any situation, Mrs. Dr. dear.”
“Anyway, what is wrong with Pettifer Miller?” Nell asked with impatience. “He constantly forces somebody into taking drastic measures.”

“Indeed, a few individuals label it religion whereas others term it cussedness, asking your forgiveness, Mrs. Dr. dear, for employing such phrasing. It appears they are unable to discern which one applies regarding Pettifer. On certain days he snaps at everyone owing to his belief that he is predestined for everlasting damnation. On other days, however, he claims he remains indifferent and proceeds to become intoxicated. In my personal view, his mind lacks soundness, given that no members of that Miller family line possessed sound minds. His grandfather lost his sanity. He believed large black spiders encircled him. They crept across his body and drifted through the atmosphere around him. It is my wish that I never become mad, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I doubt I shall, since such behavior is not characteristic of the Bakers. Nevertheless, should a supreme Providence ordain it, I pray it does not manifest as large black spiders, because I detest those creatures. Regarding Mrs. Miller, I remain uncertain if she truly merits sympathy or not. Certain people claim she wedded Pettifer solely to anger Richard Taylor, which strikes me as an exceedingly strange motive for wedlock. Yet, naturally, I lack the authority to evaluate marital matters, Mrs. Dr. dear. Look, Winifred Tolley stands by the gate, meaning I shall place this dear brown infant upon his mattress and retrieve my knitting.”
“Where are the other children?” inquired Miss Winifred, once the initial welcomes—warm from her, ecstatic from Nell, and stately from Tabitha—had concluded.

“Harcourt has gone to bed, while Kit, Edmund, and the twins have gone down to Fern Hollow, which they cherish so much,” Nell stated. “You are aware that they only returned this afternoon, and as soon as supper ended, they hurried off to the valley without delay. To them, it is the most adored place in the world. In their hearts, not even the maple grove can compete with it.”

“I worry that they are overly fond of it,” Tabitha remarked with a sullen expression. “Young Kit mentioned on one occasion that he preferred going to Fern Hollow over heaven upon his death, which was an inappropriate comment.”
“I guess they enjoyed themselves immensely in Brierley?” Miss Winifred remarked.
“Immense. Thirza certainly spoils them to an awful degree. Kit, especially, is incapable of doing wrong as far as she is concerned.”

“Miss Abernethy must be an old woman at this point,” remarked Miss Winifred, retrieving her knitting in order to keep pace with Tabitha. It was Miss Winifred’s belief that a woman with busy hands maintained an upper hand compared to one whose hands remained idle.
“Thirza has reached the age of eighty-five,” sighing, Nell stated. “Snow-white is the color of her hair. Yet, peculiarly, her vision is superior to what it used to be at sixty.”

“Oh, my sweet, it truly pleases me that everyone has returned. My solitude was terrible. However, life in the Glen was far from boring, you can trust that. Regarding affairs of the church, a spring this thrilling has never occurred during my life. My dear Nell, a pastor has finally been secured by us.”
“The Reverend John Knox Ashdown, Mrs. Dr. dear,” said Tabitha, who was determined that Miss Winifred would not recount the entirety of the news.
“Is he nice?” Nell inquired with interest.
A sigh came from Miss Winifred, while a groan was uttered by Tabitha.

“Yes, he’s pleasant enough if that were the only thing,” remarked the first speaker. “He is extremely pleasant—and extremely learned—and extremely spiritual. But, oh Nell dearie, he lacks common sense!
“What name did you give him, in that case?”

“Well, without a doubt, he is the finest preacher our Glen St. Agnes church has ever possessed,” declared Miss Winifred, shifting her approach slightly. “I imagine his failure to secure a town call stems from his being so dreamy and preoccupied. Take my word for it, his trial sermon was truly extraordinary. Everyone lost their minds over it—and his appearance.”

“He possesses great attractiveness, Mrs. Dr. dear, and after taking everything into account, I truly enjoy observing a handsome man standing in the pulpit,” interrupted Tabitha, believing she ought to make her presence felt once more.

“Furthermore,” Miss Winifred remarked, “we wanted to be settled soon. Also, Mr. Ashdown was the initial applicant about whom everyone was of one mind. Everyone else faced an objection from someone. Calling Mr. Folsom was mentioned as a possibility. He preached well, too, yet for some reason his look didn't appeal to folks. His complexion was too dark, and his hair was too sleek.”
“Mrs. Dr. dear, he truly resembled nothing so much as a huge black tomcat,” Tabitha declared. “Every Sunday, I simply couldn’t tolerate a person like that preaching.”

“Then Mr. Rogers arrived and he resembled a chip in porridge—doing neither harm nor good,” Miss Winifred continued. “However, had he preached like Peter and Cedric it would have availed him nothing, since that was the day old Caleb Ramsay’s sheep wandered into church and uttered a loud ‘ba-a-a’ precisely as he declared his text. Everyone laughed, and poor Rogers stood no chance following that. Some believed we should call Mr. Stewart, as he was so well educated. He had the ability to read the New Testament in five languages.”
“However, I am doubtful that this gave him any greater certainty than anyone else of reaching heaven,” Tabitha cut in.

“The majority of us were displeased with how he delivered it,” Miss Winifred stated, paying no attention to Tabitha. “It was as if he spoke using grunts, in a manner of speaking. Furthermore, Mr. Arnett possessed no ability to preach whatsoever. On top of that, he selected nearly the most terrible text for candidating that exists within the Bible—‘Curse ye Meroz.’”

“Each time an idea eluded him, he used to hit the Bible and scream with immense bitterness, ‘Curse ye Meroz.’ That day, poor Meroz was cursed completely, no matter who he might have been, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha said.

“A minister who is candidating must exercise extreme caution regarding his choice of text,” Miss Winifred remarked gravely. “In my opinion, Mr. Pierson would have received the call had his selection of a text been otherwise. However, his fate was sealed the moment he declared ‘I will lift my eyes to the hills’. Everyone smiled, because everybody was aware that those two Hill sisters from Harbour Head had been pursuing every sole minister visiting the Glen over the past fifteen years. Furthermore, the family of Mr. Newman was simply too big.”

“He resided alongside my brother-in-law, James Clow,” Tabitha remarked. “‘What is the number of children you have?’ I inquired of him. ‘Nine boys, plus a sister corresponding to every one of them,’ he answered. ‘Eighteen!’ I exclaimed. ‘My goodness, such a large family!’ And following that, he chuckled repeatedly. However, I remain unaware of the reason, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I feel sure that eighteen children would prove excessive for any manse.”

“He possessed merely ten children, Tabitha,” Miss Winifred clarified, exhibiting a scornful endurance. “And ten well-behaved children would not cause much more damage to the manse and congregation than the four who reside there at present. Although I would not claim, Nell dearie, that they are that terrible, either. They appeal to me—they appeal to everyone. One cannot avoid liking them. They would turn out to be truly pleasant little beings if somebody were present to manage their conduct and instruct them in what is appropriate and correct. As an example, the instructor at school claims they are exemplary children. At home, however, they are completely untamed.”
“What about Mrs. Ashdown?” Nell inquired.

“Mrs. Ashdown does not exist. The problem lies right there. A widower is what Mr. Ashdown is. Four years have passed since his wife passed away. Had that been known to us, I do not believe we would have extended an invitation to him, because a widower causes even more difficulty in a congregation than a bachelor. However, people heard him mention his children, so every one of us assumed a mother existed as well. Yet upon their arrival, no one was present except old Aunt Martha, which is what they name her. I think she is a cousin to the mother of Mr. Ashdown, who brought her into his home so she would not end up in the poorhouse. Her age is seventy-five, and she is nearly blind, extremely hard of hearing, and quite ill-tempered.”
“And an exceedingly bad cook, Mrs. Dr. dear.”

“Regarding a manse, she is the absolute poorest choice of manager,” Miss Winifred declared with bitterness. “Because he claims it would injure Aunt Martha’s feelings, Mr. Ashdown refuses to hire a different housekeeper. My dear Nell, you must trust me that the manse’s condition is utterly dreadful. A heavy layer of dust covers everything, and not a single item can ever be found where it belongs. Yet, prior to their arrival, we had applied such lovely new paint and wallpaper throughout the entire place.”
“You mention there are four children?” inquired Nell, whose heart was already starting to nurture them.

“Indeed. They ascend precisely in the manner of stairway steps. Gerald is the eldest. He has reached twelve years of age and people refer to him as Tobias. He is a bright lad. Grace has reached eleven. She proves to be an outright tomboy, though I have to admit she remains as lovely as a image.”

“She has the appearance of an angel, yet she is a total terror when it comes to mischief, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha stated with gravity. “One evening last week I happened to be at the manse, and Mrs. James Millison was present as well. She had carried up a dozen eggs and a small pail of milk to them—an extremely small pail, Mrs. Dr. dear. Grace accepted the items and dashed right down to the cellar with them. Close to the foot of the steps her toe caught, causing her to tumble down the remaining distance, along with the milk, the eggs, and everything else. You can picture the outcome, Mrs. Dr. dear. Nevertheless, that girl came back up in laughter. ‘I don’t know whether I’m myself or a custard pie,’ she said. And Mrs. James Millison became extremely furious. She declared that she would not bring a single other item to the manse if it was going to be thrown away and ruined in such a manner.”

“Maria Millison never harmed herself carrying items to the manse,” Miss Winifred sniffed. “She merely brought them that evening to justify her inquisitiveness. Yet poor Grace continually finds herself in trouble. She displays such carelessness and impulsiveness.”
“I am just the same, and I shall certainly take a liking to your Grace,” Nell declared with conviction.
“She possesses plenty of spirit—and I truly am fond of spirit, Mrs. Dr. dear,” acknowledged Tabitha.

“She has a certain charm,” Miss Winifred admitted. “Whenever you come across her, she is laughing, and in some way you are always moved to laugh as well. Even during church services, she fails to remain solemn. Ida, who is ten, is an endearing little girl—lacking beauty, yet endearing. Then there is nine-year-old Thomas Carlyle. Going by the name of Rupert, he possesses an absolute obsession with gathering toads, bugs, and frogs to carry inside the home.”

“I guess he was to blame for the deceased rat that was sitting upon a chair in the parlour during the afternoon Mrs. Hollis visited. It startled her,” stated Tabitha, “and I am not surprised, because manse parlours are not locations for deceased rats. Certainly it might have been the cat that deposited it there. He is as filled with the old Nick as he could possibly be packed, Mrs. Dr. dear. A manse cat ought to at minimum appear dignified, in my view, regardless of what he actually is. However, I have never beheld such a dissolute-appearing creature. Furthermore, he paces across the ridgepole of the manse nearly every night when the sun sets, Mrs. Dr. dear, and swishes his tail, and that is not appropriate.”

“Their terrible attire is the hardest part,” Miss Winifred sighed. “They have gone to school without shoes ever since the snow melted. You are aware, Nell dearie, that manse children should not behave that way—particularly with the Methodist minister’s little girl constantly wearing those lovely buttoned boots. I also truly wish that the old Methodist graveyard was not their playground.”
“When it is directly adjacent to the manse, the appeal is strong,” Nell remarked. “Playing in graveyards has always struck me as something that would be wonderful.”
“Oh, no, you did not, Mrs. Dr. dear,” uttered loyal Tabitha, who was resolved to defend Nell from her own actions. “You possess an excess of sound judgment and propriety.”
“For what reason did they build that manse next to the graveyard to begin with?” Nell inquired. “Because their lawn is so tiny, they have nowhere else to play besides in the graveyard.”

“It was an error,” confessed Miss Winifred. “However, they obtained the whole thing at a low price. Furthermore, no other kids from the manse ever considered using that area for recreation. Mr. Ashdown ought to forbid it. Nevertheless, whenever he is present, his face is constantly hidden behind a book. He engages in endless reading, or paces around his study lost in a fantasy. Up until now he has remembered to attend church on Sundays, yet he failed to remember the prayer-meeting on two occasions, requiring one of the elders to travel to the manse to prompt him. Additionally, Fanny Cooper’s wedding slipped his mind. They called him using the ‘phone, whereupon he hurried directly over in his current state, wearing nothing different, carpet slippers included. A person would not care if the Methodists refrained from laughing so much over the matter. Still, a single consolation exists—no one can fault his sermons. Take my word for it, he becomes alert once he stands in the pulpit. Meanwhile, the Methodist minister is completely unable to preach—or so I am informed. I have avoided listening to him, I am glad to say.”
Although her contempt for men had softened slightly after she wed, Miss Winifred maintained a completely uncharitable disdain for Methodists. A sly smile crossed Tabitha's face.
“It is being reported, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, that the Methodists and Presbyterians are considering a union,” she said.

“Indeed, my only desire is to be buried in the ground should such a thing ever occur,” replied Miss Winifred. “There will be no dealings or business between the Methodists and me, and Mr. Ashdown ought to realize that staying away from them would be wise for him as well. In my opinion, his friendliness with them goes much too far. To prove my point, attending the silver-wedding feast at the Jacob Drews’ led him straight into a troublesome situation.”
“What was that?”

“Mrs. Drew requested that he carve the roast goose—because Jacob Drew was neither willing nor able to carve. Anyhow, Mr. Ashdown took on the task, and while doing so he struck it right off the platter straight into the lap of Mrs. Coyle, who happened to be seated beside him. Then he simply remarked in a dreamy way, ‘Mrs. Coyle, will you kindly return me that goose?’ Mrs. Coyle ‘returned’ it, as submissive as Moses, though she surely was enraged, since she was wearing her new silk dress. To make matters worse, she was a Methodist.”

“However, in my opinion, that surpasses her being a Presbyterian,” Tabitha chimed in. “Had she belonged to the Presbyterians, she would, in all probability, have departed from the church, and losing our members is something we cannot afford. Furthermore, Mrs. Coyle is unpopular within her own congregation on account of putting on such grand airs, meaning the Methodists will likely feel somewhat satisfied that Mr. Ashdown ruined her dress.”

“The point is, he turned himself into a laughingstock, and I, for my part, am not fond of seeing my minister turned into a laughingstock before the Methodists,” Miss Winifred stated rigidly. “Had he possessed a wife, it would never have occurred.”
“Even if he possessed twelve wives, I fail to understand how that could have stopped Mrs. Drew from consuming her tough old gander for the marriage banquet,” Tabitha asserted stubbornly.
“That was done by her husband, so they say,” Miss Winifred said. “A domineering, stingy, conceited creature is Jacob Drew.”

“And folks do claim he and his wife hate each other—which doesn't strike me as the right manner for a wedded couple to behave. Though, naturally, I lack any experience in that area,” Tabitha said, tossing her head. “And I don't attribute every fault to the men. Mrs. Drew possesses plenty of meanness herself. People say the sole item she was ever seen to give for free was a butter crock crafted from cream containing a fallen rat. She donated it to a church gathering. The rat remained undiscovered by anyone until later.”

“Luckily, every individual the Ashdowns have angered up to this point is a Methodist,” Miss Winifred said. “That Tobias attended the Methodist prayer-meeting a single evening approximately two weeks back and took a seat next to aged William Marsh, who stood up in his customary way and bore witness accompanied by terrible groans. ‘Do you feel any better now?’ Tobias murmured softly once William was seated again. Unfortunate Tobias intended to show empathy, yet Mr. Marsh believed he was being rude and is enraged with him. Naturally, Tobias ought not to have been at a Methodist prayer-meeting whatsoever. Nevertheless, they venture wherever they please.”

“I hope Mrs. Hector Twiss of the Harbour Head will not be offended by them,” said Tabitha. “It is my understanding that she is quite a touchy woman, though she has great wealth and contributes the highest amount toward the salary. According to what I have heard, she claims the Ashdowns are the most poorly raised children she has ever encountered.”
“All that you utter persuades me increasingly that the Ashdowns pertain to the lineage that is acquainted with Joseph,” declared Mistress Nell with firmness.

“Ultimately, they actually do,” Miss Winifred conceded. “And that makes up for everything. Regardless, we have them in our care now and we simply have to manage as well as possible for them and defend them against the Methodists. Well, I imagine I ought to be heading down harbour. Ambrose will be back home shortly—he traveled over-harbour to-day—and expecting his supper, as men do. I regret that I haven’t met the rest of the children. And where might the doctor be?”

“Over at the Harbour Head. It was merely three days ago that we returned, yet throughout this period he has passed no more than three hours sleeping in his own bed and consumed a total of two meals at home.”

“Indeed, anyone who has been ill over the past six weeks has been anticipating his return—and I cannot fault them. When the doctor from over the harbour wed the undertaker’s daughter in Kettlebridge, folks grew distrustful of him. The appearance of it was bad. You and the doctor ought to visit us shortly and share everything about your journey. I imagine your time was wonderful.”

“We had,” concurred Nell. “Years of dreams were fulfilled by it. Very lovely and very wonderful is the old world. However, we have returned extremely satisfied with our own country. Miss Winifred, Canada is the world’s finest country.”
“That was never in question,” Miss Winifred remarked with a sense of self-satisfaction.

“And ancient P.E.I. is the most charming province within it, with Seven Gulls being the most charming location in P.E.I.,” chuckled Nell, gazing with deep affection across the sunset brilliance of the valley, the port, and the gulf. She gestured toward the scene. “I observed nothing that surpassed the beauty of that while in Europe, Miss Winifred. Is it necessary for you to depart? The youngsters will regret not seeing you.”
“They need to visit me before long. Let them know that there are always doughnuts in the jar.”

“Oh, during the evening meal they discussed making a raid on your place. Their departure will be shortly; however, returning to their studies requires their attention at present. Furthermore, the twins intend to begin studying music.”
“I hope it wasn't from the Methodist minister’s wife?” Miss Winifred asked with concern.
“No—from Clementine Ainslie. I went up yesterday evening so that she and I could arrange it. She is such a pretty girl!”
“Clementine manages effectively. She is no longer as youthful as she used to be.”
“She struck me as quite delightful. As you are aware, I have never actually known her well. The place where they live is so remote, and I have rarely spotted her anywhere besides at church.”

“Clementine Ainslie has always been liked by people, even if she isn't understood by them,” Miss Winifred remarked, entirely unaware that her words were a great compliment to the charm of Clementine. “In a manner of speaking, Harriet has constantly suppressed her. She has dominated her, but she has nevertheless spoiled her in various respects. You are aware that Clementine was engaged at one time—to young Martin Crawford. The Magdalens was where his ship was wrecked, resulting in the drowning of the whole crew. Clementine was merely a child—no more than seventeen. Afterwards, though, she was never quite the same. Ever since the death of their mother, Harriet and she have remained very much at home. They do not reach their own church at Kettlebridge very frequently, and it is my understanding that Harriet dissents from attending a Presbyterian church with any frequency. I will grant her this much, she never sets foot in the Methodist one. Strong Episcopalians have always made up that family of Ainslies. Harriet and Clementine possess a fair amount of wealth. Music lessons do not actually have to be given by Clementine. Her doing so is simply because it pleases her. You know, Lorna is a distant relative of theirs. Will the Treleavens be visiting the harbour during this summer?”

“No. Japan is where they are traveling, and their absence will likely last a year. The background for Adrian’s new novel needs to be Japanese. Since the time we departed from the dear old House of Dreams, this coming summer marks the initial one in which it will have no occupants.”

“Adrian Treleaven ought to discover plenty to author in Canada rather than pulling his wife and his blameless offspring away to a pagan land such as Japan,” complained Miss Winifred. “The Life Book was his finest piece of writing, and he collected the information for it right here in Seven Gulls.”

“He received the majority of that from Captain Saul, as you are aware. Moreover, his collection was gathered from every corner of the globe. Nevertheless, I consider all of Adrian’s books to be charming.”

“Oh, regarding their extent, they are decent enough. It is my rule to peruse each one he produces, even if I have constantly maintained, my dear Nell, that perusing fiction represents an ungodly misuse of hours. Rest assured, I am going to compose a letter informing him about my view on this Japanese affair. Is it his wish for Damaris and Julian to be turned into heathens?”

Following that impossible riddle, Miss Winifred left. Tessa was placed in bed by Tabitha, while Nell remained on the steps of the veranda beneath the young stars, indulging in her persistent fantasies and discovering once more for the hundredth joyful instance the magnificent brilliance and luster of a moonrise over Seven Gulls Harbour.

During the day, playing amid the lush, quiet verdure and shadows of the large maple grove situated between Hollowmere and the Glen St. Agnes pond suited the Carrow children very much; however, when it came to night-time fun, no spot surpassed the small valley lying behind the maple grove. To them, it served as an enchanted kingdom of wonder. On one occasion, while gazing out of the attic windows at Hollowmere through the haze and wake of a summer thunderstorm, they had observed a magnificent rainbow spanning over their cherished location, with one of its ends appearing to plunge directly into the place where a bend of the pond extended into the valley's bottom end.
“We should name it Fern Hollow,” Edmund remarked with joy, and from that moment onward, Fern Hollow became its name.

Beyond Fern Hollow, the gales could be boisterous and rollicking. In this spot, the breeze invariably moved with gentleness. Small, twisting, enchanted tracks coursed to and fro across spruce roots that moss cushioned. Scattered throughout the valley, blending with the dark spruces, were wild cherry trees that would turn misty white when in bloom. Originating from the Glen village, a tiny stream filled with amber waters flowed through the area. The homes of the village stood at a comfortably distant range; just at the top part of the valley was a small, dilapidated, abandoned cottage, known as “the old Bailey house.” No one had lived in it for numerous years, yet an embankment covered in grass encircled it, and contained within was an ancient garden in which the Hollowmere children were able to discover violets, daisies, and June lilies still flowering when the time came. As for the remainder, the garden was smothered in caraway that, during the moonshine of summer evenings, billowed and surged like silver seas.

To the south, the pond was situated, and past it, the ripe landscape faded into purple forests, except where an isolated, ancient gray farmhouse situated on a lofty hill overlooked both the glen and the harbour. A particular untamed woodland quality and seclusion characterized Fern Hollow, regardless of how close it was to the village, making the children of Hollowmere fond of it.

Dear, friendly hollows filled the valley, and their most cherished spot was the biggest one among them. On this specific night, they had gathered in this place. A grove of young spruces stood within this hollow, surrounding a small, grassy glade at its center that opened onto the stream's bank. Alongside the stream grew a silver birch-tree, a young and remarkably straight growth that Edmund had dubbed the “White Lady.” Within this glade as well stood the “Tree Lovers,” the name Edmund gave to a spruce and maple growing in such close proximity that their branches were inextricably tangled together. Kit had suspended an old strand of sleigh-bells, which he received from the Glen blacksmith, upon the Tree Lovers, and each passing breeze elicited unexpected, magical tinkling sounds from it.
“It is so wonderful returning here!” Bess remarked. “When all is said and done, not a single one of the Brierley locations can truly compare to Fern Hollow.”

Even so, they held the Brierley locations in high regard. Going to Grey Shutters was constantly viewed as a wonderful delight. Aunt Thirza treated them very kindly, as did Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, who occupied her remaining years in crafting cotton-warp quilts for when Nell’s daughters required a “setting-out.” Furthermore, delightful companions were present there—“Uncle” Robin’s children along with “Aunt” Isolde’s children. They were acquainted with every location their mother had treasured so deeply during her youth at former Grey Shutters—the lengthy Linger Lane, which possessed pink hedges when wild roses bloomed, the perpetually tidy yard, featuring its willows and poplars, the Nymph’s Well, clear and beautiful just like in the past, the Lake of Glassy Waters, and Reedmere. The twins occupied their mother’s former porch-gable room, and Aunt Thirza was accustomed to entering after dark, whenever she believed they had fallen asleep, to gaze at them fondly. Nevertheless, everyone was aware that she cherished Kit most of all.

Kit was currently very busy frying a batch of little trout that he had recently taken from the pond. A ring of red stones surrounding a burning fire formed his stove, while his cooking gear comprised a flattened old tin can and a fork that retained just a single tine. Even so, splendid dishes had previously been cooked in this manner.

Kit was the offspring who belonged to the House of Dreams. Every other child had come into the world at Hollowmere. His red hair curled just like his mother’s, while his open hazel eyes resembled his father’s; his fine nose was inherited from his mother, and his father gave him a steady, humorous mouth. Furthermore, he was the sole member of the family whose ears were pleasant enough to satisfy Tabitha. Nevertheless, a continuous quarrel existed between him and Tabitha, owing to her refusal to stop addressing him as Little Kit. Thirteen-year-old Kit considered this intolerable. Mother possessed better judgment.
“On the day he turned eight, he had exclaimed with indignation, “Mother, I’m not little any more. I’m awful big.””
With a sigh, a laugh, and another sigh, Mother ceased to address him as Little Kit ever again—or at least, never within his earshot.

He had always been, as he was still, a dependable and solid little fellow. Promises were something he never broke. Speech did not come from him in great amounts. Though his teachers failed to see brilliance in him, his scholastic abilities were solid and well-rounded. Taking matters on trust was not his way; instead, he preferred to personally test the accuracy of any assertion. On one occasion, Tabitha had warned him that contacting a frost-covered latch with his tongue would cause all its skin to be ripped away. Immediately, Kit had proceeded to do so, “just to see if it was so.” The result proved to him that it was “so,” leaving him to endure a painful tongue for a number of days. Even so, Kit did not mind the pain when it served the cause of science. Through continual observation and testing, he acquired much information, and his vast acquaintance with their small environment struck his brothers and sisters as truly remarkable. Kit was always aware of the locations of the earliest and most mature berries, the places where the initial light-colored violets timidly awoke from their cold season of rest, and the exact count of blue eggs inside any specified robin’s nest within the maple grove. Reading fortunes using daisy petals, extracting honey from red clovers, and digging out various kinds of eatable roots along the pond's edge were all things he could do, whereas Tabitha lived in constant dread that the entire group would end up poisoned. He possessed knowledge of the locations containing the most superior spruce-gum, which appeared as light amber lumps upon the lichen-covered bark, he was aware of the spots where nuts clustered most densely within the beechwoods surrounding the Harbour Head, and he knew the finest locations for trout fishing higher up the streams. Any call made by a wild bird or animal in Seven Gulls could be imitated by him, and from spring until autumn, he was familiar with the home of every wild flower.

Beside Edmund Carrow lay a book of poetry as he sat beneath the White Lady, yet reading was not what occupied him. His large, magnificent eyes were filled with delight as he looked first at the willows shrouded in emerald mist beside the pond, and then toward Fern Hollow, where a drift of clouds, resembling small silver sheep driven by the breeze, passed overhead. Extraordinary indeed were the eyes of Edmund. From within their deep gray recesses, the collective happiness, grief, mirth, devotion, and longing of numerous buried ancestors seemed to gaze forth.

In terms of appearance, Edmund was a “hop out of kin.” No recognized family member looked like him. Featuring well-shaped features and straight black hair, he was easily the most handsome among the children of Hollowmere. Yet he possessed the exact same intense love of beauty and lively imagination as his mother. Winter’s frost, spring’s invitation, summer’s dream, and autumn’s glamour every one held great meaning for Edmund.

At school, an institution where Kit held the status of a chieftain, Edmund enjoyed little esteem. Because he never engaged in fights and rarely participated in the school's sports, choosing instead to isolate himself in secluded spots to read books—most notably “po’try books”—he was considered to be “girly” and milk-soppish. Edmund adored the poets and spent hours engrossed in their writings from the moment he learned to read. Their melody—the melody of the immortals—interwove itself into his developing soul. It was Edmund's cherished desire to become a poet himself one day. Such an achievement was possible. Edmund took as his pattern a certain Uncle Cedric—a title granted out of courtesy—who currently resided in that enigma of a place known as “the States.” Uncle Cedric had formerly been a young student in Brierley, and at present, people everywhere read his poetry. Nevertheless, the Glen schoolboys remained unaware of Edmund’s ambitions, nor would they have been much awed had they known. Even with his deficiency in physical strength, he nevertheless extracted a degree of reluctant admiration through his ability for “talking book talk.” No pupil in Glen St. Agnes school possessed his manner of speech. He “sounded like a preacher,” a boy remarked; consequently, he was usually left in peace rather than being targeted, unlike the majority of boys who were thought to abhor or dread fighting.

The Hollowmere twins, who were ten years old, broke twin tradition because they did not look the slightest bit similar. Nell, whom everyone called Bess, possessed great beauty, featuring silky nut-brown hair alongside velvety nut-brown eyes. She was a exceptionally blithe, dainty little maiden—a teacher of hers had remarked that she was Carrow by name and blithe by nature. Her mother derived much satisfaction from her completely faultless complexion.
“It brings me such joy to have a single daughter capable of wearing pink,” Mrs. Carrow was accustomed to exclaiming with delight.

A strong resemblance to her mother was evident in Isolde Carrow, called Izzy, who possessed hair of a red hue and eyes of gray-green that invariably gleamed with a distinct shine and radiance when twilight fell. This reason, perhaps, explained why her father favoured her most. Close companions were found in her and Edmund; he would recite his self-authored poetry solely to Izzy, making her the single individual aware that he was quietly laboring on an epic poem, one that bore a marked similarity to “Marmion” in particular aspects, though not in all. From Bess included, she guarded every one of his confidences, while sharing all of her own with him.
“Will those fish not be cooked shortly, Kit?” asked Bess, inhaling the aroma with her delicate nose. “I am made extremely hungry by the scent.”
“They are almost prepared,” stated Kit, as he deftly flipped one over. “Fetch the plates and the bread, girls. Wake up, Edmund.”

“What a glow the air has this evening,” Edmund remarked in a daydreaming way. It was not that fried trout was something he looked down on at all; nevertheless, nourishment for the spirit was invariably the top priority for Edmund. “The angel of flowers has traveled across the earth today, summoning the blossoms. Those blue wings of his are visible to me on that hill near the forest.”
“Every angel wing that ever met my sight was white,” Bess remarked.
“The angels of the flowers are not. A pale, misty blue describes them, exactly like the valley's haze. Oh, my desire to fly is so strong. Glorious it must be.”
“Occasionally, a person flies when dreaming,” Izzy remarked.

“It isn't precisely flying that I dream about,” Edmund remarked. “Instead, my frequent dream is that I simply lift off the earth and hover above the hedges and the trees. The feeling is wonderful—and my thought is invariably, ‘Unlike every previous time, this is no dream. It's actually happening’—and then I awaken anyway, which is devastating.”
“Make haste, Bess,” Kit instructed.

Bess had brought out the banquet-board—which was a literal board in addition to being a figurative one—from which a great deal of feasts, seasoned in a manner no food was anywhere else, had been consumed in Fern Hollow. By supporting it upon a pair of big, moss-covered stones, it was transformed into a table. The tablecloth was provided by newspapers, and the dishes were supplied by handleless cups and cracked plates taken from the items Tabitha had discarded. Bess produced salt and bread from a tin box hidden within the root of a spruce tree. Adam’s ale of unequaled clarity was furnished by the brook. As for what remained, a particular sauce, made from a mixture of young appetite and fresh air, imparted a heavenly taste to all of it. Sitting within Fern Hollow, soaked in a half-amethyst, half-gold twilight, filled with the scents of woodsy plants growing in their spring vigor and balsam-fir, surrounded everywhere by the pale stars of wild strawberry blossoms, and listening to the tinkling of bells and the soughing of the wind in the rustling tree tops while eating dry bread and fried trout, constituted an experience that the powerful individuals of the world could have envied them for.
“Sit in,” requested Bess, when Kit set his hissing metal plate of fish upon the table. “Kit, you are the one to offer grace.”
“Frying the trout was my job,” complained Kit, who disliked giving thanks before meals. “Let Edmund recite it, since he enjoys reciting grace. Also, make it brief, Walt, because I am famished.”
Yet no blessing, whether brief or extended, was uttered by Edmund at that moment. An event broke in upon them.
“Who is descending from the manse hill?” asked Izzy.

Aunt Martha could be—and indeed was—an exceedingly bad housekeeper, just as the Rev. John Knox Ashdown could be—and indeed was—an exceptionally absent-minded, lenient man. Nevertheless, nobody could deny that the manse of Glen St. Agnes possessed an exceedingly cozy and endearing quality, notwithstanding its clutter. It was felt even by the discerning housewives of the Glen, whose opinions were unwittingly softened as a result. This appeal might have stemmed partly from fortuitous details—the lush vines wrapping around its gray, weatherboarded walls, the welcoming acacias and balm-of-gileads surrounding it with the familiarity of long-time friends, and the lovely vistas of sand-dunes and harbour visible from its forward windows. Yet those features had also existed during the era of Mr. Ashdown’s predecessor, a time when the manse was the most proper, orderly, and gloomy dwelling in the Glen. Consequently, a great deal of the merit belonged to the character of its current occupants. An aura of mirth and fellowship enveloped the place; its doors remained constantly unlatched; and the internal and external realms met. In the Glen St. Agnes manse, love served as the sole rule.

According to the members of his flock, Mr. Ashdown indulged his offspring too much. It was quite probable that he was guilty of this. What remains beyond doubt is that he lacked the heart to reprimand them. “They have no mother,” he was accustomed to remark softly to himself, uttering a sigh whenever an exceptionally blatant misdeed was brought inescapably to his attention. Yet he remained ignorant of most of their misconduct. He was a member of the class of visionaries. Although his study's windows faced the cemetery, while he walked back and forth across the floor, pondering profoundly upon the eternal nature of the spirit, he failed entirely to notice Tobias and Rupert joyously playing leap-frog across the horizontal monuments in that resting place of deceased Methodists. Mr. Ashdown experienced sporadic, sharp epiphanies that his sons and daughters lacked the physical and moral care they had received prior to his wife's passing, and he maintained an ever-present, faint awareness that the residence and food diverged greatly under Aunt Martha’s care compared to their quality during Cecilia’s lifetime. Otherwise, his existence transpired amid volumes of literature and theoretical concepts; consequently, even though his garments were rarely swept clean of dust, and even though the women of the Glen deduced, owing to the alabaster-like paleness of his chiseled face and delicate hands, that he was perpetually undernourished, he did not lead a miserable life.

Should a cemetery ever deserve to be deemed a happy location, the ancient Methodist cemetery located in Glen St. Agnes could perhaps be designated as such. On the opposite side of the Methodist church lay the modern cemetery, which was an orderly, correct, and gloomy area; nevertheless, the ancient one had been abandoned for such a duration to the benevolent and merciful care of Nature that it was rendered exceedingly agreeable.

A stone and sod embankment, crowned with a gray and rickety fence, enclosed three of its sides. Beyond this wall stood a line of lofty fir trees bearing dense, fragrant branches. Constructed by the initial inhabitants of the Glen, the embankment was ancient enough to possess beauty, as mosses and verdant plants sprouted from its cracks, violets bloomed purple at its foot during the initial days of spring, and asters alongside golden-rod created a fall splendor within its nooks. Small ferns gathered closely together among its rocks, while an expansive bracken shot up in places.

No fence or dyke existed on the eastern side. In that direction, the graveyard wandered into a young fir plantation, constantly creeping closer to the graves and darkening to the east into a dense wood. The air was perpetually filled with the sea’s harp-like voices, alongside the music of ancient gray trees, while the bird choruses in the elms encircling the two churches sang of life rather than death on spring mornings. The old graveyard was loved by the Ashdown children.

Over the caved-in burial sites, mint, “garden-spruce,” and ivy with blue eyes proliferated wildly. Beside the fir forest, in the sandy nook, blueberry shrubs developed in great abundance. The changing styles of headstones across three generations could be observed in that place, beginning with the level, rectangular, red sandstone flags belonging to early pioneers, progressing through the era of clutching hands and weeping willows, up to the most recent horrors consisting of covered urns and towering “monuments.” A particular example of this last style, which was the largest and most hideous in the burial ground, honored the remembrance of an individual named Hector Twiss, who was born into the Methodist faith but had married a Presbyterian woman from the Fairlie family. She had forced his conversion to Presbyterianism and forced him to strictly adhere to Presbyterian ways throughout his entire life. However, upon his death, she lacked the courage to condemn him to an isolated plot in the cross-harbor Presbyterian cemetery. His relatives were all interred within the Methodist graveyard; consequently, Hector Twiss returned to his own kin in demise, and his surviving wife found comfort in putting up a stone that proved more expensive than what any Methodist could pay for. The Ashdown children despised this marker, though they did not quite understand the reason, yet they adored the ancient, level, bench-shaped slabs that had high weeds sprouting wildly around them. For one reason, those offered pleasant places to sit. Every one of them was seated upon a single slab at that moment. Tobias, having grown weary of playing leap frog, was making music with a jew’s-harp. Rupert was intently studying an unusual insect he had come across; Ida was attempting to fashion a garment for a doll, and Grace, supporting her weight backward on her thin brown wrists, was moving her unclothed feet in an energetic rhythm to the jew’s-harp.

Tobias possessed the dark hair and expansive dark eyes of his father, though his own eyes sparkled rather than appeared visionary. Grace, who was born after him, carried her loveliness with the casual radiance of a blossom. Her eyes were golden-brown, her ringlets were golden-brown, and her cheeks were deep red. Her frequent laughter displeased her father’s flock, and she had outraged elderly Mrs. Taylor, who was the melancholic widow of multiple deceased spouses, when she pertly asserted—and right in the church-porch no less—“The world isn’t a vale of tears, Mrs. Taylor. It’s a world of laughter.”

Young, visionary Ida rarely giggled. No wild curls appeared in her plaits of limp, pitch-black hair, and a hint of longing and sadness rested within her slanted, deep-blue eyes. Her lips possessed a habit of parting above her minute ivory teeth, and now and then a bashful, thoughtful grin spread across her delicate features. Far more touchy regarding the views of others than Grace, she felt a troubling awareness that their lifestyle was somehow flawed. She desired to fix things, yet lacked the knowledge to do so. On occasion she wiped the dust from the furnishings—though she located the rag very rarely since its location changed constantly. Furthermore, whenever the garment brush could be located she attempted to clean her father’s finest clothing on Saturdays, and on one occasion attached an absent button using thick white yarn. As Mr. Ashdown attended chapel the following morning, each woman present spotted that button, disrupting the harmony of the Ladies’ Aid for a month or more.

Rupert possessed his deceased mother’s unafraid, straightforward, luminous, dark-blue eyes, as well as her golden-glinted brown hair. The hidden ways of insects were known to him, and he held a kind of brotherhood with beetles and bees. Ida always avoided sitting close to him since she could never tell what weird beast he might have hidden on his person. Because Rupert had once brought a juvenile garter snake into bed, Tobias declined to share a bed with him; consequently, Rupert occupied his old crib, where he could not extend his legs because it was too brief, and shared his sleep with odd companions. When Aunt Martha smoothed the blankets of that bed, it was probably fortunate that her sight was failing. On the whole, they formed a merry, endearing small group, and Cecilia Ashdown’s heart surely suffered a terrible pang as she confronted the certainty of her departure from them.
“If you happened to be a Methodist, in what place would you prefer your burial to be?” Grace inquired brightly.
An intriguing area of conjecture was revealed by this.

“Options are limited because the location is crowded,” Tobias remarked. “I suppose I would prefer the corner beside the street. That way, I would be able to listen to the passing teams and the conversations of the people.”
“That small depression beneath the weeping birch would suit me,” Ida remarked. “Birds gather so frequently in that birch, and their morning songs are wonderfully exuberant.”
“I would choose the Porter plot containing the large number of buried children, since I enjoy plenty of companionship,” Grace remarked. “Where would you go, Rupert?”
“I would prefer to forgo burial entirely,” Rupert remarked, “yet were it required, the ant-bed would be my choice, since ants prove terribly fascinating.”

“How extraordinarily good everyone interred in this place must have been,” remarked Ida, having spent time studying the eulogistic old tombstone inscriptions. “Not one wicked person appears to lie within this entire cemetery. It seems Methodists are superior to Presbyterians, when all is said and done.”
“Perhaps bad people are buried by the Methodists in the same manner as cats,” Rupert suggested. “It could be that they do not take the trouble of bringing them to the graveyard whatsoever.”

“Nonsense,” Grace remarked. “Ida, the individuals interred in this place were no superior to anyone else. However, once a person has died, you are required to speak only favorably about him, otherwise his ghost will return to haunt you. That was imparted to me by Aunt Martha. When I queried father regarding its accuracy, his gaze simply passed right through me as he murmured, ‘True? True? What is truth? What is truth, O jesting Pilate?’ Based on his response, I decided it was bound to be true.”
“I wonder whether Mr. Hector Twiss would return to haunt me if I tossed a rock at the urn resting upon his gravestone,” Tobias said.

“Mrs. Twiss would,” Grace giggled. “She simply observes us in church the way a cat observes mice. This past Sunday I pulled a face at her nephew, who pulled one back at me, and her glare was quite something to behold. I bet she cuffed his ears once they left. Mrs. Ambrose Kerr informed me that we must not displease her under any circumstances, otherwise I would have pulled a face at her as well!”

“People claim that Kit Carrow made a face at her a single time and she refused to see his father from then on, even during the period her husband was on his deathbed,” Tobias remarked. “I am curious about the nature of the Carrow gang.”

“Their appearance appealed to me,” Grace remarked. When the Carrow young ones had come that afternoon, the manse kids had been present at the station. “Kit’s appearance was particularly pleasing to me.”
“Tobias mentioned, “It’s said at school that Edmund is a sissy.”
“I doubt that,” stated Ida, who had considered Edmund quite good-looking.

“At any rate, he composes poetry. Bertie Shakespeare Drew informed me that he earned the award provided by the teacher the previous year for composing a verse. Bertie’s mother believed he ought to have received the award owing to his name, yet Bertie stated he was unable to compose poetry for the life of him, regardless of his name.”

“It seems likely that we’ll become familiar with them the moment they start attending school,” Grace pondered. “My wish is that the girls prove pleasant. The majority of the girls in this area do not appeal to me. Slow and dull describes even the pleasant ones. However, the Carrow twins appear cheerful. My impression was that twins invariably resembled each other, yet these two do not. The one with red hair strikes me as the pleasantest.”

“I approved of the way their mother looked,” Ida remarked, uttering a brief sigh. Ida felt jealous of every child who had a mother. Her own mother had passed away when she was merely six, yet within her spirit she guarded invaluable recollections—similar to precious gems—of morning play and dusk hugs, of a gentle tone, affectionate eyes, and a laugh that was unmatched in its sweetness and merriment.
“People claim that she is different from everyone else,” Tobias remarked.
“Grace mentioned that, according to Mrs. Elliot, the reason was her failure to ever truly reach adulthood.”
“Mrs. Kerr is not as tall as she is.”
“Indeed, indeed, yet she is like that on the interior—according to Mrs. Elliot, Mrs. Carrow simply remained a young girl on the inside.”
“What is that scent?” Rupert cut in, taking a breath through his nose.

Every one of them caught the scent at this point. Rising through the unmoving night air, a delightfully appealing fragrance drifted upward from the small, wooded hollow beneath the hill where the manse stood.
“Hearing that gives me an appetite,” Tobias remarked.
“For our evening meal, we had nothing but bread and molasses, and for our mid-day meal, we had the exact same thing cold,” Ida said mournfully.

It was Aunt Martha’s custom to boil a big piece of mutton at the beginning of the week and present it daily, unheated and fatty, for as long as any remained. Grace, during a flash of creativity, had assigned to this the title of “ditto”, and it was constantly called by that name in the manse.
“Let us head over to find the source of that odor,” Tobias suggested.

Every one of them leaped to their feet, romped across the grass with the uninhibited energy of newborn pups, scrambled over a barrier, and rushed down the moss-covered incline, led by the appetizing aroma that continuously intensified. After a short period, they reached the innermost sanctuary of Fern Hollow out of breath, at the precise moment when the Carrow children were on the verge of offering grace and consuming their meal.
They stopped in a hesitant manner. Ida regretted their sudden haste, yet Izzy Carrow could handle that situation just as easily as any other. Displaying a friendly smile, she advanced toward them.
“I believe I recognize you,” she uttered. “You are from the manse, aren’t you?”
Dimples creasing her face, Grace gave a nod.
“Having caught the scent of your trout being prepared, we were curious about it.”
“Sit yourself down so you can assist us in eating them,” Izzy said.
“Perhaps you do not possess extra for your own needs,” Tobias remarked, gazing with craving upon the metal dish.
“We have plenty—three for each of us,” Kit stated. “Take a seat.”

Without further formality, the entire group took their seats upon moss-covered rocks. Long and joyful was that banquet. If Bess and Izzy had been aware of what Grace and Ida were fully conscious of—namely, that a pair of little mice resided within Rupert’s coat pocket—they would likely have perished from fright. However, because they remained unaware, no harm befell them. What better place exists for people to become truly familiar with one another than around a dining table? By the time the final trout was eaten, the kids from the manse and the kids from Hollowmere had become devoted companions and confederates. It felt as though their acquaintance had lasted forever and would endure indefinitely. The lineage of Joseph acknowledged its own kind.

The pasts of their brief lives were recounted by them. Brierley and Grey Shutters, Fern Hollow lore, and the small home beside the harbour coast where Kit came into the world were made known to the manse children. Juneford, the former home of the Ashdowns prior to their arrival at the Glen, along with Ida’s cherished doll possessing a single eye and Grace’s tamed rooster, were told to the Hollowmere children.
It irked Grace that others mocked her habit of stroking a rooster. Her fondness for the Carrows stemmed from their unhesitating acceptance of it.

“In my opinion, a fine-looking rooster such as Adam makes a pet that is every bit as pleasant as a cat or dog,” she remarked. “No one would think it strange if he were a canary. Furthermore, I raised him starting when he was a tiny, small, yellow chick. He was given to me by Mrs. Johnson at Juneford. His brothers and sisters had all been slain by a weasel. I named him for her spouse. Dolls and cats never appealed to me. Cats have too much slyness, while dolls lack life.”
“Who resides in that home far up in that direction?” Tobias inquired.
“The Miss Ainslies—Clementine and Harriet,” Bess replied. “Music lessons from Miss Clementine will be taken by Izzy and me this summer.”

With an affection too mild to be jealousy, Ida looked upon the fortunate twins. Ah, if only music lessons were possible for her! That desire remained a secret dream of her quiet young existence. Nevertheless, the idea was never entertained by anyone.

“Miss Clementine is exceptionally sweet and her clothes are always so pretty,” Izzy remarked. “The shade of her hair matches fresh molasses taffy,” she added longingly—because Izzy, following the example of her mother, had never accepted her own reddish locks.
“Miss Harriet is also someone I like,” Bess said. “When she attended church, she would constantly hand out candies to me. Izzy, however, fears her.”

“She possesses such dark brows alongside that immensely deep voice of hers,” Izzy remarked. “Oh, Julian Treleaven was so terrified of her during his early years! According to Mother, Miss Harriet chanced to be present, seated directly in back of them, on the very first Sunday that Mrs. Treleaven took him to church. And as soon as Julian set eyes on her, he simply shrieked repeatedly to the point where Mrs. Treleaven was forced to lift him up and take him outside.”
“Who is Mrs. Treleaven?” Ida inquired with wonder.

“Oh, the Treleavens aren't residents here. They merely arrive during the summer months. Furthermore, they will not be visiting this summer. Their residence is in that small cottage far, far down along the harbour coast, which used to be my father and mother's home. I would love for you to behold Damaris Treleaven. She resembles a painting.”

“Mrs. Treleaven is someone I have heard of,” Grace interrupted. “It was Bertie Shakespeare Drew who mentioned her to me. A deceased man was her husband for fourteen years, after which he returned to life.”

“Nonsense,” Bess remarked. “It does not happen like that in the slightest. Bertie Shakespeare is incapable of getting a single detail right. The entire account is known to me and I will share it with you eventually, though not at present, as it is excessively lengthy and we must head back home. Mother disapproves of our being outdoors at a late hour on damp evenings such as these.”

No one gave any thought to whether the minister's children remained in the moisture or had come indoors. Aunt Martha had retired to her bed by that time, and the minister remained far too engrossed in his thoughts regarding the soul's immortality to recall that the physical frame was mortal. Nonetheless, they also returned to their dwelling, carrying thoughts of approaching happy moments within their minds.

“Fern Hollow strikes me as being even more pleasant than the cemetery,” Ida remarked. “And those precious Carrows are simply wonderful to me. Being able to care for folks is so delightful, given how frequently it’s impossible. It was stated by Father in his sermon this past Sunday that our love should extend to all people. Yet how is that achievable? In what way could anyone feel love for Mrs. Hector Twiss?”
“Oh, father merely uttered that from the pulpit,” Grace said lightly. “He possesses too much judgment to actually believe it elsewhere.”

Except for Kit, who stole off briefly on an isolated journey to a distant section of Fern Hollow, the Carrow youngsters walked up to Hollowmere. Mayflowers bloomed in that location, and Kit always remembered to bring his mother a bunch of them for as long as they remained.

She squeezed herself with joy and performed a hornpipe atop the bench tombstone belonging to old Hezekiah Pollock, greatly horrifying a pair of elderly maidens who chanced to drive by at the exact moment Grace balanced on a single foot around the marker, shaking her remaining foot along with her arms up in the air.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “What else could one anticipate from the household of a widower?” the second elderly spinster moaned. Thereupon, both of them wagged their heads.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The Ashdowns were outside in the damp morning air early on Saturday, enjoying a wonderful awareness of their day off. They never possessed any duties on a holiday. Even though Bess and Izzy Carrow were required to perform specific chores around the house on Saturday mornings, the daughters of the manse possessed the freedom to wander from dawn until nightfall if they desired. Grace enjoyed this, but Ida experienced a hidden, painful shame over the fact that they were never taught any skills. Cooking, sewing, and knitting were manageable for the remaining girls in her school class; only she was a small dunce.

text: It was proposed by Tobias that they embark on an exploration; consequently, they made their way unhurriedly across the fir grove, collecting Rupert as they went, who was kneeling within the wet grass to examine his beloved ants. Past the grove, they emerged into the pasture field belonging to Mr. Taylor, which was dotted throughout with the pale remnants of dandelions; situated in a distant corner stood an ancient, dilapidated barn, in which Mr. Taylor occasionally kept his extra harvest of hay, though it served no additional function whatsoever. To that place the Ashdown children marched, and they searched around the lower level for a number of minutes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “What was that?” Ida abruptly murmured.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The group paid attention. From the hayloft overhead, a soft yet clear rustling sound emerged. A glance passed between the Ashdowns.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “An object is present up in that location,” Grace whispered softly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I will go up to find out what is there,” Tobias said with determination.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, please refrain,” Ida implored, grasping his arm.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I’m departing.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Then we will all go along, as well,” Grace stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: All four of them scaled the rickety ladder; while Tobias and Grace were entirely fearless, Ida was drained of color by terror, and Rupert mused somewhat distantly about whether they might discover a bat in the loft above. He desperately wished to observe a bat during the daytime.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: As soon as they descended from the ladder, the source of the rustling sound became visible to them, and the vision left them speechless for a short time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Folded up within a small nook in the hay, a girl appeared to have only recently woken up. As her eyes fell upon them, she rose to her feet, appearing somewhat unsteady, and inside the brilliant sunshine pouring through the cobweb-covered window at her back, her slender, sun-browned face was revealed to be extremely pale beneath its brownness. Pairings of limp, heavy, flaxen-colored braids hung on her, and her eyes were most unusual—“white eyes,” as they appeared to the manse children, while her gaze toward them was part rebellious, part sorrowful. Their shade of blue was actually so faint that an appearance of near-whiteness was created, particularly in comparison to the thin black circle that bordered each iris. Wearing neither shoes nor head covering, she was dressed in an old, threadbare, frayed tartan garment that was far too brief and constricted for her frame. Regarding her age, her shriveled small face made it possible for her to be nearly any number of years old, though her stature appeared to place her around twelve.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Who are you?” inquired Tobias.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The girl cast her eyes around, appearing to search for a path to flee. Following that, she appeared to surrender, letting out a slight tremble of hopelessness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “My name is Mary Stubbs,” she declared.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Where did you arrive from?” Tobias asked further.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary, rather than answering, abruptly dropped or collapsed onto the hay and started weeping. Grace immediately threw herself down at her side, wrapping her arm around the slender, trembling shoulders.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You cease troubling her,” she ordered Tobias. She subsequently embraced the waif. “Don’t weep, dear. Simply inform us what is wrong. We are friends.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “My hunger is—so—terrible,” cried Mary. “Since Thursday morning, nothing has passed my lips, ‘save for some brook water from outside.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The kids from the manse stared at one another, filled with horror. Grace jumped to her feet.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You come straight up to the manse and have a bite to eat prior to saying another word.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary drew back.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh—I am unable to. What reaction will your pa and ma have? Additionally, I would be sent back by them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “We are without a mother, and you will not be a concern to father. Aunt Martha will not care either. Come along, I tell you.” Grace struck her foot against the ground with impatience. Could this strange girl be determined to die of hunger practically on their doorstep?

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary gave in. Her weakness was such that descending the ladder was a great struggle, yet somehow she was assisted down, across the field, and into the kitchen of the manse. Aunt Martha, busy with her Saturday cooking chores, paid her no attention. Grace and Ida rushed to the pantry and searched it thoroughly for whatever food was inside—a bit of “ditto,” bread, butter, milk, and a pie of questionable quality. Mary Stubbs devoured the nourishment eagerly and without complaint, while the children of the manse gathered around to observe her. Tobias observed that her mouth was pretty and her teeth were very nice, even, and white. Grace concluded, with hidden dread, that Mary wore nothing at all beneath that tattered, bleached dress. Ida felt complete compassion, Rupert experienced entertained astonishment, and every one of them was filled with curiosity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Now step out to the churchyard and inform us concerning yourself,” commanded Grace, as Mary’s hunger began to diminish. Mary was by this time entirely willing. Her innate liveliness had been renewed by the meal, which set free her tongue that was not at all disinclined to speak.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You won’t tell your pa or anybody if I tell you?” she demanded, once she had taken her seat atop the gravestone of Mr. Pollock. Facing her on a different stone, the children from the manse formed a row. Flavor, secrecy, and excitement were present here. An event had taken place.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “No, we shall not.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Cross your hearts?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Cross our hearts.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Indeed, I have escaped. Mrs. Grimble was housing me across the harbor. Are you acquainted with Mrs. Grimble?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “No.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Well, knowing her isn't something you want. An awful woman is what she is. My, I hate her so much! I was worked to death by her and she refused to give me half enough to eat, plus ‘most every day she used to larrup me. Look a-here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary turned up the tattered sleeves she wore, revealing her bony arms alongside slender hands that were cracked and sore from the cold. Dark bruises covered them completely. A shudder passed through the manse children. Deep anger brought a bright red flush to Grace's face. Ida's eyes, blue in color, brimmed with tears.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “On Wednesday night, she hit me using a stick,” Mary said, uncaringly. “That happened because I permitted the cow to knock a milk pail over. How could I have known the stupid old cow would kick?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Her audience experienced a sensation that was not entirely disagreeable. Although they would not think of employing such questionable terms themselves, hearing another person utter them—especially a girl—was quite stimulating. Without a doubt, this Mary Stubbs was a fascinating individual.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You running away isn’t something I blame you for,” Grace said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, her beating me wasn't the reason I took off. Getting beaten was just a normal part of my everyday life. It happened so often I was completely accustomed to it. No, my plan to run away had been set for seven days because it came to my attention that Mrs. Grimble intended to lease her land, relocate her home to Kettlebridge, and hand me over to one of her cousins up near Port Marlow. That was something I refused to put up with. Her character was far nastier than Mrs. Grimble’s. During the previous summer, Mrs. Grimble let her have me for thirty days, and I would prefer the devil's own company.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The second sensation occurred, yet Ida appeared uncertain.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “So I resolved to clear out. I possessed seventy cents I had put aside, which Mrs. John Crawford bestowed on me back in the spring because I planted potatoes on her behalf. Mrs. Grimble was unaware of it. She happened to be away calling on her cousin at the time I planted them. My plan was to slip up here to the Glen, purchase a ticket bound for Port Marlow, and attempt to find employment in that place. I am a hard worker, I can assure you. There is not one lazy bone anywhere in my body. Therefore, I took off Thursday morning before Mrs. Grimble had risen and made my way on foot to the Glen—a distance of six miles. But upon arriving at the station, I discovered that my money was lost. I don't know how—I don't know where. At any rate, it had vanished. I was at a loss for what to do. Had I returned to old Lady Grimble, she would have skinning me alive. Consequently, I departed and concealed myself inside that old barn.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “And what are you going to do at this point?” Tobias inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I am uncertain. It seems I must return and accept the consequences. My ability to endure it has likely improved now that I have eaten something.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Yet, hidden beneath the bold exterior, terror lingered in the eyes of Mary. Moving swiftly from the first headstone to the next, Ida wrapped an arm around Mary.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Refrain from returning. Merely remain here alongside us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, Mrs. Grimble’ll track me down,” Mary stated. “She’s probably searching for me already. Provided your family doesn't object, I guess I could remain right here until she discovers my location. Thinking I could run away was completely foolish of me. Even a weasel couldn't escape her. However, my misery was just so great.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary had a tremble in her voice, yet she felt embarrassment over revealing her frailty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “For the past four years, my existence has been worse than a dog’s,” she declared in a tone of defiance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Has it been four years that you’ve spent with Mrs. Grimble?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Yip. I was eight years old when she removed me from the asylum located in Hopetown.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Mrs. Carrow originated from that very location,” Grace blurted out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “For two years, I remained in the asylum, having been placed in that institution at six years old. My mother had hanged herself, while my father had slit his own throat.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Holy cats! Why?” asked Tobias.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Alcohol,” Mary stated concisely.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “And you do not have any relatives?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “There isn’t a single one that I’m aware of. However, there had to be some at one time. I received my names from six of them. Mary Martha Lucilla Vane Ball Stubbs is my complete name. Is it possible to top that? A wealthy man was my grandfather. It’s my bet that his wealth exceeded your grandfather’s. Yet it was all guzzled away by pa, and ma contributed her share as well. Furthermore, they were accustomed to striking me. Goodness, I’ve received so many thrashings that I somewhat enjoy it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary jerked her head back. Sensing that the children from the manse felt pity toward her because of her numerous lashings, she rejected their pity. What she desired was their envy. She glanced around herself with a cheerful air. Since the lethargy brought on by hunger had vanished from them, her unusual eyes sparkled with brightness.
