It was her intention to demonstrate to those youths precisely how important a figure she truly was.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I have been ill a tremendous amount,” she declared boastfully. “Only a few children would be able to survive all that I survived. Scarlet fever, measles, ersipelas, mumps, whooping cough, and pewmonia have all afflicted me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Have you ever been sick to the point of death?” Ida inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I am not certain,” Mary uttered with hesitation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Naturally she was not,” mocked Tobias. “You perish when you are terminally ill.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, well, I didn't actually pass away,” Mary stated, “yet I was extremely close to it on one occasion. My death was assumed by them, and my preparation for burial was underway when I suddenly revived.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “How does it feel when someone is half dead?” Tobias inquired with curiosity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “As if it were nothing. Days went by before I realized it. It happened during my bout of pewmonia. Mrs. Grimble refused to call a doctor—stating she had no intention of incurring that kind of cost for a home girl. Nursing me with poultices, old Aunt Christina MacAllister was the one who cared for me. She brought me back to health. Yet at times I wish the remaining half of me had simply died to end it all. My situation would have been better.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I guess you would if you were to go to heaven,” Grace said, with a good deal of doubt.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Well, where else can one possibly go?” Mary asked, sounding bewildered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You know, hell exists,” whispered Ida, drawing Mary close to soften the impact of the grim thought.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “What is that, Hell?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Indeed, the devil makes his home there,” Tobias declared. “He is familiar to you—you made mention of him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, certainly, but I was unaware that he possessed a residence anywhere. My belief was that he merely wandered about. When he was living, Mr. Grimble would bring up hell. He was forever advising people to travel to that location. I assumed it was a certain spot across in New Brunswick, which was his place of origin.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “An atrocious location is hell,” Grace declared, experiencing the theatrical pleasure arising from the narration of terrible matters. “Upon dying, wicked individuals travel to that realm where they undergo eternal combustion in flames.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Who gave you that information?” Mary asked, unable to believe it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “It is located within the Bible. Furthermore, Mr. Isaac Crothers at Juneford informed us of it as well during Sunday School. Being an elder alongside a pillar of the church, he possessed complete knowledge regarding it. However, there is no need for you to be anxious. Provided that you behave well, your destination will be heaven, whereas if your behavior is bad, my assumption is that hell would be your preferred destination.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I wouldn’t,” Mary stated emphatically. “Regardless of how wicked I was I wouldn’t wish to be burned over and over. I am aware of how it feels. A red hot poker was picked up by me once by mistake. What is required of one to be good?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You have to attend church and Sunday School, read the Bible, say your prayers every night, and donate to missions,” Ida stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “That seems like a tall request,” Mary remarked. “Is there anything more?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You are required to pray to God for pardon regarding the transgressions you have done.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “However, I have not ever com—committed a single one,” Mary stated. “In any case, what constitutes a sin?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, Mary, it is impossible that you haven't. All people do. Was there never a time you uttered a falsehood?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Quantities of them,” Mary stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Such a terrible sin,” Ida stated with gravity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Are you saying,” Mary asked, “that committing a falsehood occasionally would cause me to be damned? Truly, I was forced to. Had I not uttered an untruth to Mr. Grimble on one occasion, he would have shattered all the bones in my frame. Spoken falsehoods have spared me numerous beatings, I assure you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Ida let out a sigh. Resolving such an abundance of problems was beyond her capabilities. The thought of receiving a harsh flogging made her tremble. It was quite probable that she would have been dishonest as well. She held Mary’s small, rough hand in a tight grip.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Do you have no other dress besides that one?” inquired Grace, a person whose cheerful temperament declined to brood over unpleasant matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I only wore this dress since it had no value,” exclaimed Mary with a blush. “My garments had been purchased by Mrs. Grimble, and I refused to owe her for a single thing. Furthermore, I am truthful. Had I intended to flee, I had no intention of taking any of her possessions that possessed real worth. Once I am grown, I shall own a blue sating dress. Your personal attire does not appear particularly fashionable. I assumed the offspring of ministers were perpetually clad in fine clothes.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: That Mary possessed a temper and had sensitive spots was obvious. Nevertheless, her strange, wild allure enchanted everyone. That afternoon, she was brought to Fern Hollow and presented to the Carrows as “a friend of ours from over-harbour who is visiting us.” The Carrows received her without question, possibly owing to the fact that she appeared reasonably respectable by then. Following dinner—during which Aunt Martha had muttered and Mr. Ashdown had remained half-unconscious while contemplating his Sunday sermon—Grace had persuaded Mary to wear one of her dresses, along with various other garments. Her hair being tidily braided, Mary proved acceptable enough. Because she was familiar with a number of novel and thrilling games, and because her speech was not without zest, she made a satisfactory playmate. Indeed, a few of her remarks caused Bess and Izzy to view her somewhat suspiciously. Although they were uncertain about how their mother would have viewed her, they were entirely certain of Tabitha’s opinion. Still, since she was a guest at the manse, she had to be fine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: As the time for sleep arrived, deciding where Mary ought to lie down presented a difficulty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “You know we are unable to place her in the guest room,” Grace remarked to Ida in a state of perplexity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “There isn’t anything in my head,” Mary exclaimed, sounding hurt.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, I did not intend to imply that,” Grace objected. “Everything in the spare room is in complete disarray. A large hole was chewed into the feather tick by mice so they could build a nest inside it. It remained completely undiscovered by us until Aunt Martha assigned the room to the Rev. Mr. Fisher from Port Marlow when he stayed overnight last week. It did not take him long to discover it. Consequently, father was forced to surrender his own bed to him and spend the night on the study lounge instead. According to Aunt Martha, she has not yet found the time required to repair the bed in the spare room; therefore, it remains unusable for anyone to sleep in, regardless of how clean their head might be. Furthermore, our room is extremely tiny, and the bed itself is so small that there is no space for you to share it with us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “If a quilt could be lent to me, returning to the old barn’s hay for the evening is fine with me,” Mary remarked pragmatically. “Although last night possessed a bit of a chill, I have slept in worse places, setting that aside.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, no, no, you must not do that,” Ida said. “Grace, I have conceived a scheme. Do you recall that small trestle bed located in the garret room, which has the old mattress upon it that was left there by the previous minister? Let us carry the bedclothes from the spare room upstairs and prepare Mary a bed on it. Mary, you will not object to sleeping in the garret, will you? It is situated directly over our room.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Any place will work for me. Lord knows, I have not possessed a respectable location for sleeping during my entire existence. My sleeping spot was situated in the loft above the kitchen at Mrs. Grimble’s. Rain seeped through the roof throughout the summer, and snow blew inside during the winter. A straw tick placed on the floor served as my bed. You will not catch me being the least bit particular regarding my sleeping quarters.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: The attic of the parsonage was an elongated, low-ceilinged, dim room, featuring a partition at one gable end. In this section, a bed was prepared for Mary with the refined hemstitched sheets and needleworked coverlet that Cecilia Ashdown had formerly crafted with such pride for her guest room, and which had managed to endure the erratic laundering of Aunt Martha. After the good nights were spoken, quiet descended upon the parsonage. Ida was on the verge of drifting off when a noise from the chamber directly overhead caused her to sit upright abruptly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Listen, Grace—Mary’s crying,” she murmured in a low voice. Grace made no answer, having fallen asleep already. Ida stepped from the bed, moving in her small white gown along the hallway and ascending the garret steps. Her approach was loudly announced by the creaking floorboards, and upon arriving at the corner room, she found complete, moonlit quiet, with the trestle bed displaying merely a mound at its center.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Mary,” Ida murmured.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: No reply was made.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Ida moved quietly near the bed and tugged on the coverlet. “Mary, I know you are crying. I heard you. Are you lonesome?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary unexpectedly came into sight, yet she uttered no words.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Allow me to join you in there. I feel cold,” uttered Ida, who was trembling in the brisk draft, because the small attic window stood unclosed, letting in the sharp nocturnal air from the north shore.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Mary shifted her position, allowing Ida to nestle close beside her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “At present you will not be lonely. It was wrong of us to leave you in this place by yourself on that initial evening.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “I didn’t feel lonely,” Mary sniffled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Why were you weeping at that moment, in that case?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, as I sat by myself in this place, my mind simply started dwelling on matters. My thoughts turned to the necessity of returning to Mrs. Grimble—along with receiving a beating because I ran off—and—and—and facing damnation in hell on account of lying. The whole business distressed me terribly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, Mary,” Ida uttered, deeply upset. “I am sure God will not condemn you to hell for telling falsehoods when you were unaware that it was bad. He would not be able to. After all, He is compassionate and benevolent. Naturally, now that you realize it is wrong, you must not say any more.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “What will happen to me if I am not allowed to tell lies?” Mary asked, sobbing. “You fail to comprehend. You are completely ignorant about it. You possess a home and a gentle father—even if I feel he is only half-present. Regardless, he does not beat you, and you receive sufficient food, such as it is—even though your old aunt is clueless regarding cookery. Indeed, today marks the very first time in my memory that I have felt as if I had eaten enough. Throughout my whole life, I have been battered around, save for those two years spent at the asylum. I was not beaten there and it proved tolerable, even if the matron was ill-tempered. She constantly appeared prepared to bite my head off a nail. However, Mrs. Grimble is an absolute nightmare, that is her true nature, and the mere thought of returning to her leaves me utterly terrified.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “It is possible that you will not be required to do so. It is possible that we can discover a means of escape. May we both pray that God prevents you from being forced to return to Mrs. Grimble. Mary, do you offer up your prayers?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, yes, I always repeat an old verse ‘fore I get in bed,” Mary said casually. “Though I never considered requesting any specific thing. No one on this earth ever concerned themselves with me, so I didn’t think God would either. Because you’re the daughter of a minister, He may take greater pains for you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “He would go to just as much effort on your behalf, Mary, I am certain,” Ida declared. “The identity of your parents is irrelevant. Simply make your request to Him—and I shall do so as well.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Very well,” Mary assented. “There’s no harm in it, even if it yields little benefit. Were you as acquainted with Mrs. Grimble as I am, you’d doubt that God would desire to interfere with her. Regardless, I’ll weep no further over this. It’s vastly superior to yesterday evening down inside that ancient barn, where mice were scurrying around. Observe the Seven Gulls light. Isn’t it lovely?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “We are only able to view it from this particular window,” Ida stated. “Watching it brings me so much joy.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Is that so? Me as well. From the loft at Grimble, I was able to spot it, and it offered me my sole consolation. Whenever I was aching all over after getting beaten, watching it allowed me to ignore the painful spots. My thoughts would turn to the vessels journeying farther and farther from it, and I desired to be aboard one, traveling to a distant place as well—far from all of this. During winter evenings when its light was absent, I simply experienced true loneliness. Tell me, Ida, why are all of you people so good to me given that I am merely an outsider?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Because being so is correct. We are instructed by the Bible to show kindness toward everyone.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Is that so? Well, it seems to me that the majority of people do not care about it very much. I cannot recall a single person ever treating me with kindness previously—upon my life, I cannot. Tell me, Ida, are not those wall shadows lovely? They appear exactly like a group of tiny fluttery birds. And listen, Ida, I am fond of all your family as well as those Carrow boys and Izzy, but I am not fond of that Bess. She behaves in a arrogant manner.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, no, Mary, pride isn't in her nature at all,” Ida stated with enthusiasm. “Not even a little.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Do not inform me. Whoever carries her head in that manner possesses pride. I dislike her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “She is greatly liked by all of us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, I guess you prefer her to me?” Mary asked with jealousy. “Is that true?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Well, Mary—she has been known to us for weeks, whereas you have only been known to us for a few hours,” Ida faltered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Then it is true that she is your favorite?” Mary asked furiously. “Very well! Feel whatever you want for her. It makes no difference to me. I do not need you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: She threw her body hard up against the garret wall, causing a loud bang.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Oh, Mary,” uttered Ida, sliding a gentle arm across Mary’s rigid back, “do not speak in such a way. I really like you a great deal. And you cause me to feel terribly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: There was no reply. Soon after, Ida sobbed. Immediately, Mary turned back around and wrapped Ida in a tight embrace.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: “Silence,” she commanded. “There is no need to weep about my words. My speech was as cruel as the devil himself. It would serve me right to be flayed—when all of you treat me so well. It seems to me you would prefer anybody else over me. Every beating I ever received was fully deserved. Be quiet, now. Should your tears continue, I will head straight to the harbour clad only in this night-dress and end my life in the water.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: Because of this frightening warning, Ida swallowed her weeping. With the lace trim from the spare-room pillow, Mary dried her tears, and the two girls nestled together once more, one granting pardon and the other receiving it, with peace re-established, observing the shadows cast by the vine leaves upon the wall in the moonlight until sleep overtook them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER V. THE ADVENT OF MARY STUBBS
text: And down in the study, Rev. John Ashdown paced the room, his eyes bright and his expression entranced as he developed his sermon for the next day, completely unaware that beneath his roof resided a small, desperate spirit, tripping through obscurity and unknowingness, overwhelmed by fear and encircled by obstacles far too immense for it to handle in its unbalanced conflict against a vast, uncaring world.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: The children of the manse brought Mary Stubbs to church alongside them on the following day. Initially, Mary resisted the suggestion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Wasn’t church over-harbour where you went?” Ida asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “You bet. Mrs. Grimble didn't bother with church very often, but I attended on all the Sundays I was allowed away. Going to a place where I was able to rest for a bit made me extremely grateful. However, wearing this worn-out, tattered dress prevents me from going to church.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Grace solved this problem when she proposed to lend her second best dress.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Two buttons have come missing and it has lost some color, yet I suppose it will serve,”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “In just a moment, I will attach the buttons,” Mary remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Not on Sunday,” Ida said, appalled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Of course. A better deed fits a better day. Just provide me with a thread and needle, and turn your eyes away in case you get squeamish.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Mary’s attire was finished off with Grace’s footwear for school, along with a worn black cap made of velvet that had formerly belonged to Cecilia Ashdown, whereupon to church she proceeded. Her demeanor was entirely ordinary, and even if a few people questioned the identity of the threadbare young girl accompanying the manse children, she failed to draw significant notice. With external propriety, she paid attention to the sermon and participated vigorously in the hymn-singing. It seemed that her voice was distinct and powerful, and her ear for music was good.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “His blood can make the violets clean,” Mary sang out cheerfully. Turning around abruptly, Mrs. Jimmy Milgrave, who sat in the pew directly ahead of the manse pew, scrutinized the youngster from head to foot. Purely out of an excess of mischief, Mary thrust her tongue out at Mrs. Milgrave, deeply shocking Ida.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “I was unable to prevent myself,” she stated following the service. “Why did she have to gaze at me in that way? Such conduct! I am pleased that I thrust my tongue out at her. I would have preferred to thrust it out even more. Look, I noticed Rob MacAllister from over-harbour present. I am curious whether he will inform Mrs. Grimble about my behavior.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: However, Mrs. Grimble failed to show up, and the children ceased looking for her after a couple of days had passed. Mary seemingly became a permanent resident at the manse. Nevertheless, she declined to attend school alongside the rest of them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “No. My schooling is done,” she replied, upon Grace’s encouragement for her to attend. “For four winters after I arrived at Mrs. Grimble’s, I attended school, and I have no desire for more. Being constantly scolded because my homework was incomplete has made me thoroughly fed up. There was no time for me to complete homework.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Our teacher won’t scold you. He is extremely kind,” Grace said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Well, I am not attending. Reading, writing, and computing as far as fractions are within my ability. Nothing more is desired by me. You guys may depart, whereas I will remain here. There is no need for you to fear that I will commit theft. My honesty is sworn to.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Mary occupied her time by tidying the manse while the remaining household members were at school. A short time later, the residence had been transformed. She swept the floors, removed dust from the furniture, and arranged all items neatly. She repaired the mattress cover in the spare room, attached buttons that were absent, mended garments skillfully, and even entered the study carrying a dustpan and broom to instruct Mr. Ashdown to leave while she organized the room. However, Aunt Martha would not permit her to meddle with a single area. Although Aunt Martha was potentially hard of hearing, partially sight-impaired, and quite infantile, she remained determined to retain sole control over the food supply, notwithstanding every trick and tactic Mary employed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “I could assure you that you would eat good food if old Martha allowed me to prepare it,” she expressed to the children of the manse with resentment. “You would not face any more ‘ditto’—and lumpy porridge along with blue milk would be gone as well. Where does she put all the cream?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “She offers it to the feline. After all, he belongs to her,” Grace remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “I wish I could drown her,” Mary cried with resentment. “Cats are completely useless to me anyway. Their origin is the devil. Look at their eyes and you’ll know it’s true. Oh well, I guess if old Martha refuses, she refuses. Still, seeing fine food wasted makes me furious.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Upon the conclusion of classes, Fern Hollow was their customary destination. Mary declined to partake in games within the cemetery. She maintained that specters frightened her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Ghosts do not exist,” Kit Carrow asserted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Oh, isn’t there?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Have you ever laid eyes on one?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Hundreds of ‘em,” Mary answered without delay.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “What are they like?” Rupert asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Terrible-looking. Clothed entirely in white with skellington heads and hands,” stated Mary.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “What did you do?” Ida inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Flee as fast as you can,” Mary instructed. Immediately afterward, her gaze met Edmund’s, and her face turned red. Edmund intimidated Mary quite a bit. Indeed, she confessed to the young women at the manse that she felt uneasy under his gaze.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “When I gaze into them,” she said, “the lies I’ve ever spoken come to mind, and I regret telling them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Mary favored Kit above all others. She felt profoundly delighted and honored when he led her up to the Hollowmere attic to display the collection of oddities that Captain Saul Garrick had willed to him. Furthermore, by demonstrating enthusiasm for Rupert’s ants and beetles, she completely captured his affections. There was no denying that Mary fared somewhat better in the company of the boys than she did with the girls. On the second day, she engaged in a fierce quarrel with Bess Carrow.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Your mother is a witch,” she informed Bess disdainfully. “Red-haired women are always witches.” Subsequently, Grace and she argued regarding the rooster. Mary claimed that its tail lacked length. Grace crossly fired back that she supposed God knew the proper length to fashion a rooster’s tail. Because of this, they remained in a state of not “speaking” for one day. Mary handled the hairless, single-eyed doll belonging to Ida with thoughtfulness; however, when Ida displayed her second cherished possession—an illustration depicting an angel bearing an infant, likely toward heaven, Mary stated that to her, it appeared excessively similar to a ghost. Ida slipped off to her chamber and wept regarding this, yet Mary searched for her until she found her, embraced her remorsefully, and begged for pardon. Nobody was able to sustain a feud with Mary for extended periods—not even Bess, who possessed a tendency to harbor resentment and failed to fully pardon the offense against her mother. Mary possessed a merry demeanor. She possessed the ability to narrate, and indeed narrated, the most spine-tingling ghost tales. Without question, the seances at Fern Hollow grew more thrilling once Mary arrived. She acquired the skill to perform on the jew’s-harp and before long outshone Tobias.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “I have not yet encountered a single thing I could not accomplish once I set my intention upon it,” she asserted. Mary rarely missed an opportunity to boast about herself. She instructed them in creating “blow-bags” from the heavy foliage of the “live-forever” that grew abundantly in the former Bailey garden, she introduced them to the delicious nature of the “sours” found within the crevices of the cemetery wall, and using her lengthy, pliable fingers, she was able to project the most extraordinary shadow art upon the walls. Furthermore, whenever the group gathered gum in Fern Hollow, Mary invariably acquired “the biggest chew” and boasted regarding it. At certain moments she was despised by them, while at other moments she was adored by them. Yet under all circumstances she proved captivating to them. Consequently, they yielded rather passively to her leadership, and after two weeks had passed, they felt as though she had constantly been in their presence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Mrs. Grimble not coming to find me is the strangest occurrence,” remarked Mary. “I am unable to comprehend it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “It is possible she will not concern herself with you whatsoever,” remarked Ida. “That way, remaining here indefinitely is an option for you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “This dwelling is scarcely large enough to hold old Martha and myself,” Mary stated gloomily. “Having plenty of food is certainly wonderful—I used to ponder what that felt like—yet I am fussy regarding my meals. Furthermore, Mrs. Grimble has yet to arrive here. She surely has a punishment prepared for me. During the day I hardly dwell on it, but listen, girls, when I am up in that attic during the night, my mind keeps racing about it, to the point where I nearly desire her to appear and finish it. I am not sure if a single thorough thrashing could be any worse than the many I have endured in my thoughts since I fled. Have any among you ever been beaten?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Certainly not,” Grace declared with indignation. “Father would not ever act in that manner.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “You have no idea you exist,” Mary uttered, sighing with a mixture of jealousy and dominance. “You are unaware of the things I survived. And I assume the Carrows were spared a beating as well?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “No-o-o, I suppose not. However, my belief is that they received spankings occasionally during their childhood.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Being spanked is no big deal,” Mary declared scornfully. “Had my family merely spanked me, I would have considered it affection. Ah well, the world lacks fairness. Taking my fair portion of beatings wouldn’t bother me, yet I have received far too many.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “Mary, speaking that word is wrong,” Ida said in a tone of rebuke. “You gave me your word that you would refrain from using it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “G’way,” Mary answered. “If you were aware of a few of the expressions I might utter if I chose, you would not create this much of a commotion about darn. Furthermore, you are well aware that I have not uttered a single lie since my arrival here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “What of all the spectres you mentioned seeing?” Grace inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: Mary turned red.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VI. MARY STAYS AT THE MANSE
text: “That was diff’runt,” she declared with defiance. “I was aware that you wouldn't fall for those tall tales, and I never meant for you to. Yet I truly did spot a strange thing a certain evening while I was going by the over-harbour graveyard, as sure as you're alive. Whether 'twas a ghost or Sandy Crawford’s old white nag I'm not certain, but its appearance was blamed queer and I'm telling you I took off at an incredible speed.”

Tessa Carrow made her way with pride, and maybe a slight touch of primness, along the primary “street” of the Glen before ascending the manse hill, cautiously bearing a tiny basket filled with early strawberries that Tabitha had nurtured into mouth-watering perfection inside a sunlit corner of Hollowmere. Instructions had been given to Tessa by Tabitha that she must hand over the basket to no one other than Aunt Martha or Mr. Ashdown, and Tessa, feeling immense pride in being given this task, was determined to follow those directions precisely.

Tabitha had clad her finely in a pale, stiffened, and worked frock, accompanied by a blue sash and slippers covered in beads. Her lengthy reddish ringlets were smooth and shaped, and Tabitha had permitted her to wear her finest hat, as a gesture of respect toward the manse. It was a rather intricate creation, in which the preference of Tabitha had exerted greater influence than that of Nell, and the little spirit of Tessa exulted in its magnificence of silk, lace, and blossoms. She felt extremely mindful of her hat, and I fear she marched proudly up the manse hill. That proud march, or the hat, or the two together, annoyed Mary Stubbs, who was swinging upon the gate of the lawn. Furthermore, the mood of Mary was rather agitated at that moment. Aunt Martha had denied her permission to scrape the potatoes and had commanded her to leave the kitchen.

“Yah! You’ll carry the potatoes to the table with pieces of skin hanging off them and only half cooked as usual! My, but going to your funeral will be wonderful,” Mary shrieked. Leaving the kitchen, she slammed the door with such force that even Aunt Martha heard the sound, while Mr. Ashdown felt the tremor in his study, vaguely suspecting a minor earthquake had occurred. After that, he resumed writing his sermon.
Mary glided away from the gate to face the immaculate young woman from Hollowmere.
“What’s in that basket?” she asked forcefully, attempting to grab it from me.
Tessa put up a struggle, lisping, “Mithter Ashdown is supposed to have it.”
“Hand it over to me so that I can hand it over to him,” Mary stated.
“No. Thuthan told me that Mithter Mer’dith or Aunt Martha were the only ones I should hand it to,” Tessa maintained.
Mary eyed her sourly.

“You imagine you are special, do you not, completely attired like a plaything! Observe me. My clothing is entirely tattered and I am indifferent! I would prefer being in tatters to being a miniature doll. Return to your home and instruct them to place you inside a display cabinet. Observe me—observe me—observe me!”

Mary performed a frantic dance encircling the appalled and confused Tessa, tossing her tattered skirt and shouting “Look at me—look at me” to the point that unfortunate Tessa became lightheaded. However, when Tessa attempted to sidestep in the direction of the gate, Mary sprang upon her once more.

“Hand that basket over to me,” she demanded, making a face. Mary had perfected the skill of “making faces.” She was able to distort her features into an exceedingly bizarre and uncanny expression, from which her unusual, glowing, pale eyes shone to eerie effect.
“I won’t,” Tessa gasped, terrified yet resolute. “You let me go, Mary Vanth.”

Mary released her hold for a moment and surveyed her surroundings. Right within the entrance stood a modest “flake,” where six sizable codfish were in the process of drying. A member of Mr. Ashdown’s congregation had given them to him on a certain day, maybe instead of the contribution he was expected to contribute toward the salary but failed to. Mr. Ashdown had expressed his gratitude to the man and subsequently completely wiped the fish from his mind, and they would have quickly rotted if the untiring Mary had not readied them for the drying process and constructed the “flake” with her own hands to dry them on.

An evil idea struck Mary. Rushing over to the “flake,” she grabbed the biggest fish on it—an enormous, flat specimen that was almost the size of her own body. Shouting loudly, she charged at the frightened Tessa while waving her strange weapon. Tessa lost her nerve. Being beaten with a dried codfish was an unprecedented ordeal that Tessa was unable to confront. Screaming, she let go of her basket and ran away. The lovely berries, which Tabitha had picked with such care for the minister, spilled in a pink stream across the dusty road, getting crushed beneath the running feet of both the chaser and the chased. Mary was no longer thinking about the basket or what it held. Her sole focus was the joy of scaring Tessa Carrow as she had never been scared before. She intended to show her not to act superior just because she wore fancy garments.

Tessa hurried rapidly down the slope and down the road. Fear gave speed to her steps, allowing her to stay barely in front of Mary, who was slowed down a bit by her laughing, although she possessed sufficient wind to let out periodically terrifying yells while she hurried, waving her codfish around. Along the Glen street they rushed, as all the people rushed to their windows and gates so they could watch them. Mary sensed that she was causing a huge stir, which gave her pleasure. Tessa, unable to see due to her fright and deprived of air, believed she was incapable of continuing to run. Within a moment that dreadful girl was going to reach her with the codfish. Just then the unfortunate small child tripped and collapsed inside the puddle of mud located where the street ended, right when Miss Winifred emerged from Carter Flagg’s shop.

Miss Winifred understood everything immediately. Mary did as well. Halting abruptly in her wild dash, Mary spun about prior to any words from Miss Winifred, fleeing upward with the same speed she had used coming down. Although Miss Winifred’s mouth set in a threatening line, she recognized the futility of trying to pursue her. Consequently, she lifted the miserable, crying, untidy Tessa in her arms and brought her back to the house. Tessa was devastated. Not only were her hat, dress, and slippers destroyed, but a severe blow had also been dealt to her six-year-old pride.
As her face grew pale from anger, Tabitha listened to the tale recounted by Miss Winifred regarding what Mary Stubbs had done.
“Oh, the hussy—oh, the littly hussy!” she declared, while taking Tessa off to be cleansed and consoled.
“Nell dearie, this thing has gone far enough,” Miss Winifred stated resolutely. “We must do something. Who is the creature staying at the manse, and from where does she come?”

“It was my understanding that she was a young girl from over-harbour visiting the manse,” replied Nell, seeing how funny the codfish pursuit had been while privately believing that Tessa possessed too much vanity and required a few lessons.

“I am acquainted with every family from across the harbour who attends our church, and that little devil isn't part of any of them,” Miss Winifred countered. “She is practically dressed in rags, and on the occasions she attends church, she puts on Grace Ashdown’s cast-off garments. A mystery exists here, and I intend to get to the bottom of it, because it appears no one else has any intention of doing so. It is my belief that she was behind their antics in Warren Mead’s spruce bush recently. Have you heard about them scaring his mother so badly she had a fit?”
“No. I was aware that Hugh was summoned to her presence, yet the nature of the issue remained unknown to me.”

“Well, you are aware that her heart is weak. And last week, on a particular day when she was by herself on the veranda, the most terrible screams of ‘murder’ and ‘help’ reached her from the bush—truly horrific noises, Nell dearie. Right away, her heart failed. Warren listened to them too from the barn, going directly to the bush to see what was happening, where he discovered every one of the manse children perched on a downed tree, shouting ‘murder’ as loudly as they could. They explained to him that it was merely a game and they assumed nobody would catch the sound. They were simply pretending to be an Indian ambush. Returning to the house, Warren discovered his unfortunate mother out cold on the veranda.”
Tabitha, who was back, gave a scornful sniff.

“It is my belief that she was nowhere near losing consciousness, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, and you can rely on that. Amelia Warren’s bad heart has been brought to my attention for a period of forty years. It was already a problem when her age was twenty. Making a spectacle and calling the physician brings her pleasure, and she will use any pretext.”
“Hugh did not consider her illness particularly severe, in my opinion,” Nell stated.

“Ah, that might indeed be true,” Miss Winifred remarked. “However, the situation has generated an immense amount of gossip, and the fact that the Meads are Methodists renders it even more terrible. What will happen to those kids? At times, the thought of them keeps me awake during the night, my dear Nell. I genuinely doubt whether they even receive sufficient food, since their father is so absorbed in his reveries that he rarely recalls his own appetite, and that slothful elderly woman fails to cook proper meals. They are simply roaming without restraint, and with the school term ending, their behavior will become even more untamed.”

“Indeed, they enjoy happy moments,” Nell remarked, chuckling as she remembered several events from Fern Hollow that she had heard about. “Furthermore, each one of them is courageous, open, faithful, and honest.”

“What you say is correct, my dear Nell, and considering every bit of the discord in the congregation that was caused by the previous minister’s two gossiping, dishonest children, I am disposed to forgive many things about the Ashdowns.”

“All things considered, Mrs. Dr. dear, those kids are quite lovely,” Tabitha remarked. “I shall grant that they possess an abundance of original sin, yet perhaps that is for the best, since without it they could be ruined by being too sweet. I must insist, however, that playing inside a cemetery is simply unsuitable for them.”

“However, their games are actually rather subdued in that spot,” Nell offered in defense. “Unlike in other places, they refrain from racing about and shouting. Occasionally, such shrieks float up to this place from Fern Hollow! Even so, I imagine my own little ones contribute bravely to the racket. According to Kit, they engaged in a mock fight there yesterday evening and were forced to ‘roar’ on their own, given their lack of cannons for making noise. Kit is currently going through that phase when every boy yearns to become a soldier.”

“Thank goodness, he will definitely not become a soldier,” Miss Winifred stated. “Our boys going off to that conflict in South Africa was something I never supported. However, that is finished, and another event like it is improbable. The world seems to be gaining sense, in my view. Regarding the Ashdowns, my opinion has often been expressed and I repeat it now: everything would be fine if a wife were present for Mr. Ashdown.”
“I have been informed that he visited the Kirks on two occasions during the previous week,” Tabitha remarked.

“Well,” Miss Winifred uttered reflectively, “usually, I am against a clergyman finding a wife among his flock. Most times, it ruins him. However, it wouldn't cause any trouble here, because Elizabeth Kirk is beloved by all, and no one else desires the task of becoming a stepmother to those children. The Hill sisters shrink from it, too. They have not been seen setting snares for Mr. Ashdown. Should he merely realize it, Elizabeth would prove a fine spouse to him. Yet the issue remains that she is genuinely plain, and, my dear Nell, Mr. Ashdown, despite his dreaminess, appreciates an attractive female, just as men do. Trust me, he is not quite so heavenly minded regarding that matter.”

“Elizabeth Kirk is an extremely pleasant individual, but it is indeed rumored that individuals have almost perished from the cold in her mother’s guest bed previously, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha stated ominously. “If I believed I possessed any standing to voice an idea regarding so serious a subject as a clergyman’s wedding I would state that I believe Sarah, Elizabeth’s cousin across the harbor, would prove a superior spouse to Mr. Ashdown.”
“Indeed, Sarah Kirk belongs to the Methodists,” stated Miss Winifred, in a manner quite like Tabitha had proposed a Hottentot to be the wife at the manse.
“Were she to wed Mr. Ashdown, she would probably become a Presbyterian,” Tabitha snapped back.
Miss Winifred gave a shake of her head. It was clear that for her, being a Methodist once meant remaining a Methodist forever.

“Sarah Kirk cannot be considered at all,” she asserted with certainty. “Emmeline Drew is equally impossible—even if the entire Drew family is attempting to bring about the marriage. They are quite literally flinging poor Emmeline in his direction, while he remains completely unaware of what they are doing.”

“I have to concede that Emmeline Drew lacks any drive,” Tabitha remarked. “Mrs. Dr. dear, she belongs to that class of women who would place a hot-water bottle inside your bed during a sweltering dog-night, and subsequently feel offended when you failed to show gratitude. Furthermore, her mother managed a home quite poorly. Were you ever told the tale regarding her dishcloth? On a certain day, she misplaced her dishcloth. However, she discovered it on the following day. Indeed, Mrs. Dr. dear, it was located by her right in the dinner-table goose, blended into the stuffing. Is it your opinion that a minister’s mother-in-law ought to be a woman of that sort? It is not mine. Nevertheless, fixing little Kit’s trousers would surely be a superior use of my time than spreading rumors regarding those who live near me. They were ripped by him in a truly disgraceful manner yesterday evening in Fern Hollow.”
“Where is Edmund?” Nell asked.

“I am afraid he is planning some mischief, Mrs. Dr. dear. Up in the attic, he is putting words into an exercise book. Furthermore, the teacher informs me that his arithmetic performance was not up to standard this term. The cause of this is all too clear to me. Instead of practicing his sums, he spent his time composing foolish verses. Mrs. Dr. dear, I fear the boy will end up as a poet.”
“At present, Tabitha, he has become a poet.”

“Indeed, your composure is remarkable, dear Mrs. Dr. Assuming one possesses the fortitude, I imagine that is the finest approach. A relative of mine, an uncle, started out as a poet and ultimately became a vagrant. My family felt immense embarrassment on his account.”
“It appears you hold a rather low opinion of poets, Tabitha,” Nell said with a laugh.
“Who does that, Mrs. Dr. dear?” Tabitha inquired, truly amazed.
“How about Shakespeare and Milton? As well as the poets in the Bible?”

“It is said to me that Milton failed to live peaceably with his wife, and Shakespeare was merely decent on occasion. Regarding the Bible, naturally matters were otherwise during those holy times—even if I have always held a low view of King David, regardless of what anyone says. Writing poetry has never brought about any benefit in my experience, and I trust and petition that that precious boy will leave the inclination behind. Should he fail to do so—it remains for us to observe what a cod-liver oil emulsion can accomplish.”

The following day, Miss Winifred paid a visit to the manse and interrogated Mary, who, as a youth possessing notable shrewdness and perception, recounted her experience in a straightforward and honest manner, completely devoid of swagger or grievances. Although Miss Winifred formed a more positive impression than she had anticipated, she considered it her obligation to maintain a stern demeanor.

“Do you believe,” she asked in a stern tone, “that you displayed your thankfulness to this household, which has treated you with excessive kindness, when you insulted and pursued one of their small companions in the manner you did yesterday?”

“Listen, I behaved in a terribly unkind way,” Mary readily confessed. “I have no idea what came over me. The old fool appeared to be such a convenient target. However, I felt deeply regretful—to be completely truthful, I wept over it in bed yesterday evening. Ask Ida if that isn’t true. I refused to inform her of the reason since I felt embarrassed, which led to her crying as well, out of fear that my feelings had been injured by someone. Goodness, I hardly possess any feelings that are worth mentioning. The thing that troubles me is the reason Mrs. Grimble hasn't come searching for me. That behavior is unusual for her.”

Although Miss Winifred found the situation somewhat strange, she simply gave Mary a stern warning against making any additional assumptions regarding the minister’s codfish, after which she departed to share the updates at Hollowmere.

“Should the youngster's tale prove accurate, it is an issue that must be investigated,” declared she. “Trust me, I possess a bit of knowledge regarding that Grimble woman. Ambrose was once quite familiar with her during his time residing over-harbour. I recall listening to him remark last summer concerning her and an orphan under her care—in all probability this selfsame Mary-creature. He mentioned that an individual informed him she was pushing the youngster to the point of exhaustion while failing to properly feed and clothe her. You are aware, Nell dearie, that my rule has perpetually been to avoid interacting or interfering with those over-harbour people. However, I am going to dispatch Ambrose across the water tomorrow so he may ascertain the truth of the matter if possible. Following that, I will converse with the clergyman. Do not forget, Nell dearie, that the Ashdowns discovered this young girl in a state of actual starvation inside James Taylor’s former hay barn. She had remained in that place the entire night, frozen, famished, and solitary. Meanwhile, we were resting comfortably in our beds having eaten hearty evening meals.”

“The poor little thing,” Nell said, visualizing a cold, hungry, and solitary child like her own precious babies under those conditions. “Miss Winifred, if she has suffered ill-treatment, she cannot be returned to a place like that. I was formerly an orphan in an almost identical predicament.”

“The Hopetown asylum people will need to be consulted by us,” Miss Winifred said. “She cannot remain at the manse, regardless. Those poor children could acquire dear knows what from her. Swearing is something she has been known to do, as I understand. Just consider her staying there for two entire weeks without Mr Ashdown ever realizing it! A family is something a man of that sort has no business possessing. He should be a monk, why, Nell dearie.”
Miss Winifred returned to Hollowmere two nights afterward.

“Nothing could be more astonishing!” declared she. “The exact morning following the flight of this Mary-creature, Mrs. Grimble was discovered deceased in her bed. For years her heart had been frail, and the physician had cautioned her that death could occur at any moment. Nobody was present in the home, since she had dismissed her hired laborer. The following day, certain neighbors discovered her body. It appears they noticed the child was missing, but they assumed Mrs. Grimble had dispatched her to her cousin close to Port Marlow, just as she had stated her intention to do. Because the cousin failed to attend the funeral, no one ever learned that Mary was not residing with her. Ambrose asserts that the individuals he conversed with recounted details regarding Mrs. Grimble’s treatment of this Mary that caused his blood to simmer. As you are aware, learning that a child has been mistreated throws Ambrose into an absolute rage. According to them, she thrashed her without pity for the slightest flaw or error. A few people spoke of contacting the asylum officials, yet what is everyone’s responsibility belongs to no one, and no action was ever taken.”

“I regret that the Grimble individual has died,” Tabitha declared vehemently. “It would please me to travel across the harbour to express my outrage to her. Denying a child food and striking them, my dear Mrs. Dr.! Naturally, I support proper disciplinary spanking, but nothing beyond that. Furthermore, what will happen to this unfortunate child at present, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr?”

“I imagine we have no choice but to return her to Hopetown,” Miss Winifred remarked. “It seems to me that all the folks in this vicinity desiring a child from the home already possess one. Tomorrow I will consult with Mr. Ashdown and express my views regarding this entire matter.”

“And beyond a doubt she is going to, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked, once Miss Winifred had left. “There is nothing she would hesitate to do, not even shingling the church spire if the notion struck her. Yet I am unable to comprehend how even Winifred Tolley is capable of speaking to a minister in that manner. A person would suppose he was merely an ordinary individual.”

Once Miss Winifred departed, Bess Carrow unbent herself out of the hammock in which she had been learning her lessons and stole off toward Fern Hollow. The rest had arrived beforehand. Kit and Tobias were pitching quoits using aged horseshoes obtained from the Glen blacksmith. Rupert was tracking ants upon a sunlit mound. Edmund, reclining on his belly amid the ferns, was reading out loud to Mary and Izzy and Grace and Ida out of an amazing volume of myths containing enchanting tales about Prester John and the Wandering Jew, dowsing rods and men with tails, about Schamir, the rock-splitting worm that unlocked the path to golden riches, about Fortunate Isles and swan-maidens. Discovering that William Tell and Gelert were likewise myths dealt a severe blow to Edmund; while he would lie awake the entire coming night because of the tale of Bishop Hatto; yet he cherished the legends of the Pied Piper and the San Greal above the rest. He recited them in a gripping manner, as the bells on the Tree Lovers chimed in the summer breeze and the chill of the twilight shadows drifted over the valley.
“Tell me, aren’t those fascinating falsehoods?” expressed Mary appreciatively once Edmund was done reading the book.
“Those are not untruths,” Izzy remarked with indignation.
“Are you saying those are actually true?” Mary inquired with disbelief.
“No—not quite. They resemble those spectral tales you tell. While they lacked truth—you never anticipated our belief in them, which meant they were not falsehoods.”

“The story regarding the divining rod isn't a lie, at any rate,” Mary said. “Old Jake Crawford from over-harbour is able to use it. People fetch him from all over whenever they need a well dug. Furthermore, I think I am acquainted with the Wandering Jew.”
“Oh, Mary,” Ida uttered, filled with awe.

“I really do—as true as your being alive. A certain elderly man was at Mrs. Grimble’s on a single day during the previous autumn. He appeared sufficiently aged to be any age at all. She happened to be questioning him concerning cedar posts, inquiring whether he believed they would endure for long. And he replied, ‘Last well? They’ll last a thousand years. I know, for I’ve tried them twice.’ Well, if his age reached two thousand years, who else could he be except your Wandering Jew?”
“I do not think the Wandering Jew would have anything to do with someone such as Mrs. Grimble,” Grace stated with conviction.

“The tale of the Pied Piper is a favorite of mine,” Izzy remarked, “as well as mother's. My heart always aches for that unfortunate small lame boy who failed to stay abreast of the rest and was locked outside the mountain. His disappointment must have been immense. For the remainder of his days, I imagine he would spend his time pondering the marvelous spectacle he had lost out on and longing to have gained entry alongside the others.”

“However, his mother must have felt such joy,” Ida remarked in a low voice. “I believe the fact that he could not walk properly had grieved her for her entire life. She might have even wept over it at times. Yet she would not feel sorrowful any longer—not ever. His lameness would bring her happiness, as it prevented her from losing him.”

“One day,” Edmund uttered in a dreamy manner, gazing far off into the heavens, “the Pied Piper is going to arrive over that hill up there and travel down Fern Hollow, playing his pipe in a merry and sweet fashion. And I am going to pursue him—pursue him down to the coast—down to the ocean—far from all of you. I do not believe I will desire to depart—Kit is going to desire to depart—it is going to be quite an adventure—yet I will not. But I will be forced to—the melody is going to call and call and call to me to the point where I have to pursue.”

“We’ll all go,” exclaimed Izzy, becoming ignited by the spark of Edmund’s imagination, and nearly convinced that she was able to glimpse the derisive, receding outline of the mystical piper at the distant, shadowy extremity of the dale.

“No. Here is where you will sit and wait,” Edmund declared, the unusual fascination radiating from his large, magnificent eyes. “You will await our return. Yet our coming back is uncertain—because so long as the Piper continues playing, we are unable to return. Around the globe he might pipe us. Even so, you will remain sitting right here, waiting—and waiting.”

“Oh, hush,” Mary said, trembling. “Edmund Carrow, stop looking like that. You make me uneasy. Are you trying to make me cry? I could easily picture that terrible old Piper walking off, with you boys going after him, while we girls stay behind here waiting by ourselves. I don't know the reason—I was never given to weeping—yet the moment you begin your talking, I am always brought to the verge of tears.”

Edmund beamed with a sense of victory. Exercising this influence over his associates—manipulating their emotions, stirring their anxieties, electrifying their spirits—brought him pleasure. It fed a certain theatrical impulse within his nature. Beneath his satisfaction, however, lay a strange, slight shiver of an inexplicable terror. The Pied Piper had felt remarkably genuine to him—just as though the swaying drape concealing what was to come had been briefly parted in the starlight-dappled twilight of Fern Hollow, bestowing upon him a faint vision of the future.
Rupert, who approached their circle to deliver an account of the events occurring in the kingdom of ants, restored everyone to the world of reality.

“Insects are awfully fascinating,” Mary cried out, pleased to get away from the gloomy Piper’s spell. “That mound in the cemetery was observed by Rupert and myself for the whole of Saturday afternoon. I had no idea insects possessed so much to them. Listen, but those tiny creatures sure are feisty—a few of them seem to launch an attack for no apparent cause, as far as we were able to tell. And a few of them lack any courage. Becoming so frightened, they merely curled themselves into a sphere and permitted the rest of the bugs to strike them. They refused to defend themselves whatsoever. A few of them show laziness and refuse to labor. Their loafing was witnessed by us. And a single ant perished from sorrow because a different ant was slain—refused to labor—refused to consume food—simply perished—that happened, truly to Go—oodness.”

A stunned hush hung over the room. That Mary had not intended to utter “goodness” was obvious to all. The looks Grace and Izzy traded would have been worthy of Miss Winifred herself. Rupert and Edmund appeared uneasy, while the lip of Ida quivered.
Mary shifted in distress.

“I didn't mean to let that escape—I really didn't, upon my—that is, as sure as you're alive, and I choked back part of it. It appears to me that you people in these parts are terribly easily offended. If only you could have listened to the Wileys during one of their arguments.”
“Ladies abstain from speaking in that manner,” Grace remarked, adopting an unusually proper tone.
“It’s not right,” Ida murmured.
“A lady I am not,” Mary stated. “What opportunity have I ever been given to be a lady? However, provided I can prevent it, I will not repeat that statement. My word on it to you.”
“Furthermore,” Ida remarked, “you cannot anticipate that your prayers will be answered by God if you use His name irreverently, Mary.”
“I don’t expect Him to answer them anyway,” declared Mary, who lacked faith. “For a week I’ve been requesting Him to resolve this Grimble matter, yet He hasn’t accomplished anything. I plan to quit.”
It was at this moment that Bess, out of breath, came.

“Oh, Mary, I have information to give you. Mrs. Kerr was across the harbour and what do you suppose she discovered? Mrs. Grimble has passed away—her lifeless body was discovered in bed the day following your flight. Consequently, you will not ever need to return to her.”
“Dead!” Mary uttered, completely stunned. A shiver then passed through her.
“Do you think my praying was involved in that somehow?” she begged Ida to answer. “If it was, I will not pray ever again for the rest of my life. Why, she could return and haunt me.”
“No, no, Mary,” Ida said in a comforting way, “it had not. Why, Mrs. Grimble’s death occurred long prior to your ever starting to pray concerning it whatsoever.”

“Indeed,” remarked Mary as she overcame her fright. “However, I must say it startled me. I would hate to imagine that my prayers caused someone's death. Her passing never entered my mind while I prayed. She did not appear to be someone on the verge of death. Was anything said about me by Mrs. Kerr?”
“She mentioned that it was probable you would need to return to the asylum.”
“I suspected that,” Mary said despondently. “And after that they will assign me to another place—probably to a person who is exactly like Mrs. Grimble. Oh well, I guess I can endure it. I am strong.”
“I’m going to pray that you won’t have to go back,” Ida murmured under her breath, while she and Mary traveled on foot back to the manse.

“You may act however you wish,” Mary stated with conviction, “nevertheless I promise I will not. This prayer matter frightens me thoroughly. Look at the outcome. Had Mrs. Grimble passed away once I began to pray, my actions would have caused it.”
“Oh, no, it wouldn’t,” Ida said. “I wish I were able to explain things better—I know father could, Mary, if you’d talk to him.”

“Catch me! I do not understand your father at all, and that is all there is to it. In the middle of the day, he passes right by without noticing me. While I am not arrogant, I am not a door-mat, either!”

“Oh, Mary, father simply acts like that. We are also invisible to him during the majority of the time. His mind is occupied with profound thoughts, nothing more. And my prayers will ask God to retain you in Seven Gulls—for the reason that you appeal to me, Mary.”

“Very well. Just do not allow me to learn about any additional folks perishing because of it,” Mary stated. “I would enjoy remaining in Seven Gulls very much. I am fond of it, as well as the harbour and the light house—plus you and the Carrows. You are my sole friends in my entire life, and departing from you would be terrible to me.”

Miss Winifred held a conversation with Mr. Ashdown that resulted in quite a surprise for that preoccupied man. Without much deference, she drew his attention to how he had failed in his obligations by permitting a street child such as Mary Stubbs to enter his household and mingle with his offspring while remaining completely ignorant of her background.

“Of course, I’m not claiming that a great deal of damage has been brought about,” she finished. “When everything is taken into account, this Mary-creature cannot really be considered wicked. Having interrogated the Carrows as well as your own offspring, I have gathered that no serious complaints can be raised regarding the girl, apart from her use of slang and unpolished expression. Nevertheless, consider the possible outcome had her character resembled certain home children within our acquaintance. You are personally aware of the things that unfortunate youngster at the Saul Flaggs’ instructed and imparted to the Flagg offspring.”
Mr. Ashdown was indeed aware, and he felt genuine shock regarding how careless he had been about the situation.
“However, what can we do, Mrs. Kerr?” he inquired in a helpless manner. “Turning the poor child away is impossible. Caring for her is something that must be done.”

“Certainly. Writing to the Hopetown authorities immediately would be best. In the meantime, I guess she may just as well remain in this place for a couple of extra days until a response from them reaches us. However, stay alert, Mr. Ashdown.”

Tabitha’s death from horror would have occurred right there had Miss Winifred’s admonishment of a clergyman reached her ears. Miss Winifred, however, left filled with a heated sense of fulfillment regarding a performed duty, and when evening arrived, Mr. Ashdown requested that Mary join him inside his study. Looking truly dreadful from terror, Mary complied. Yet the impoverished, beaten little life she led received an unexpected turn. The gentleman who inspired such profound dread in her proved to be the most compassionate, softest spirit she had ever encountered. Mary discovered herself spilling every single one of her woes to him prior to realizing what was occurring, while getting back an amount of compassion and delicate comprehension that she had possessed no ability to conceive. When Mary exited the study, her countenance and eyes were transformed to such a degree that Ida scarcely recognized her.

“When he finally wakes up, your father is all right,” she stated, giving a sniff that almost became a sob. “It is a shame he is not awake more frequently. He told me Mrs. Grimble’s death was not my fault, but he said I ought to attempt to recall her positive traits instead of her negative ones. I do not know what positive traits she possessed, except perhaps maintaining a tidy home and producing superior butter. I am certain I nearly scrubbed my arms to exhaustion on her aged kitchen floor with its knots. However, whatever your father tells me from now on is the law for me.”

In the days that came after, Mary turned out to be quite an uninteresting associate, nevertheless. She admitted to Ida that her hatred of returning to the asylum grew the more she contemplated it. Ida strained her little mind to find any method to prevent this from happening, yet it was Bess Carrow who provided assistance by making a rather shocking proposal.

“Mrs. Kerr could perhaps take Mary on her own. Her home is extremely large, and Mr. Kerr constantly desires that she employ assistance. That would be an absolutely wonderful location for Mary. However, it would require her to conduct herself properly.”
“Oh, Bess, is it possible that Mrs. Kerr might accept her?”

“Asking her would not cause any trouble,” Bess remarked. Initially, Ida felt incapable of doing so. Her shyness was so intense that requesting a favor from anyone caused her extreme distress. Furthermore, the active, vigorous Mrs. Kerr intimidated her greatly. Although she held her in high regard and thoroughly appreciated visiting her home, going there to request that she take in Mary Stubbs appeared so exceedingly bold that it frightened Ida’s fearful nature.

As soon as the Hopetown authorities sent a letter to Mr. Ashdown requesting that Mary be dispatched to them immediately, Mary wept until she fell asleep in the manse attic that evening, which inspired Ida to discover a desperate bravery. On the following evening, she quietly departed from the manse and headed toward the harbour road. Deep within Fern Hollow, she caught the sound of cheerful laughter, yet her path did not lead in that direction. She looked exceedingly pale and was intensely resolute—so focused, in fact, that she paid no attention to the individuals she passed—and old Mrs. Stanley Flagg became rather offended, remarking that Ida Ashdown would turn out to be just as preoccupied as her father once she reached adulthood.

Situated mid-way between the Glen and Seven Gulls Point, Miss Winifred's home possessed a tone of pleasing greenish gray, into which its initial bright green color had softened. Ambrose Kerr had surrounded the dwelling with planted trees, a spruce hedge, and an established rose garden. Compared to its state in past years, the residence had become entirely transformed. Visiting the location was a favorite activity for both the manse children and the Hollowmere children. Traversing the ancient harbour road offered a lovely stroll, which invariably concluded with an abundantly stocked cooky jar.

Way down upon the beach, the foggy ocean was gently washing against the shore. A trio of large vessels was gliding through the port like huge white seabirds. Up the waterway, a schooner was making its approach. Splendid hues, delicate sounds, and an odd enchantment enveloped the realm of Seven Gulls, a place where all people ought to have been joyful. Nevertheless, as Ida went through the entrance to Miss Winifred’s property, her limbs had nearly given out on her.

On the veranda, Miss Winifred was by herself. Mr. Kerr’s presence had been hoped for by Ida. Encouragement would have been found in his being there, because he was so twinkly, hearty, and big. Sitting upon the little stool that Miss Winifred carried outside, she attempted to consume the doughnut that Miss Winifred handed to her. Although it lodged in her throat, she swallowed frantically so Miss Winifred would not take offense. Speech was impossible for her; pallor remained on her face; and Miss Winifred decided that the child was experiencing some distress because her large, dark-blue eyes appeared so piteous.
“What are you thinking about, dearie?” she inquired. “It is obvious that something is troubling you.”
A desperate gulp was how Ida downed the final piece of doughnut.
“Mrs. Kerr, will you not accept Mary Stubbs?” she asked in a pleading manner.
Miss Winifred gave a blank look.
“Keep Mary Stubbs? Is taking her what you mean by that, for me?”

“Yes—keep her—adopt her,” Ida said eagerly, taking heart once the ice had been broken. “Oh, Mrs. Kerr, please do. Returning to the asylum is not what she wants—she cries every night over it. Being sent to another hard place frightens her so much. And she is so smart—nothing exists that she cannot do. I know taking her is something you would not regret.”
“Such a thing had never crossed my mind,” Miss Winifred stated, feeling somewhat helpless.
“Will you not consider it?” begged Ida.

“However, my dear, help is not something I desire. The labor in this place is completely within my own capacity to manage. Furthermore, had I actually required assistance, having a home girl is something I never imagined appealing to me.”
The brightness faded from the eyes of Ida. Her lips quivered. Rejoining her stool, she sat down, transformed into a pitiable small emblem of letdown, and started weeping.

“Don’t—dearie—don’t,” Miss Winifred cried out in upset, as she was completely unable to endure causing pain to a youngster. “I am not refusing to accept her—yet the notion is so novel that it has simply thrown me into confusion. I need time to reflect upon it.”
“Mary is remarkably clever,” Ida repeated.
“Humph! That’s what I’ve been told. I’ve been told she uses profanity, as well. Is it correct?”
“I haven’t ever actually heard her use curse words,” Ida admitted, feeling uneasy. “However, I fear she is capable of it.”
“I trust what you say! Is accuracy in her words a constant thing?”
“Unless she is fearful of being beaten, I believe she does.”
“And all the same, you wish for me to accept her!”
“Any person must adopt her,” Ida wept. “Any person must care for her, Mrs. Kerr.”

“It is true. Doing it might be my responsibility, after all,” Miss Winifred remarked, sighing. “Anyway, I must discuss the matter with Mr. Kerr. Therefore, refrain from mentioning it for the time being. Have another doughnut, my dear.”
Ida accepted the item and consumed it, displaying a improved appetite.

“Doughnuts are a great favorite of mine,” she admitted “They are never made by Aunt Martha. Miss Tabitha at Hollowmere bakes them, though, and she occasionally allows us a full plate in Fern Hollow. Are you aware of my course of action when a craving for doughnuts strikes and none are available, Mrs. Kerr?”
“No, my dear. What is it?”

“I retrieve my mother’s former cookbook to peruse the recipe for doughnuts, as well as the additional recipes. Their descriptions are delightful. This is my habitual reaction whenever hunger strikes me, particularly following a dinner of the same old thing. Subsequent to that, I peruse the recipes for fried chicken alongside the ones for roast goose. My mother possessed the ability to prepare every one of those delicious dishes.”

“If Mr. Ashdown fails to find a wife, those manse children are going to starve to death eventually,” Miss Winifred said to her spouse in a state of indignation once Ida had left. “Yet he will not—so how do we handle this? Furthermore, Ambrose, do we accept this Mary-creature?”
“Yes, take her,” Ambrose said briefly.
“That is typical of a man,” his wife stated in despair. “‘Take her’—as though nothing else mattered. Trust me, there are one hundred matters to take into account.”
“Take her—and we will think about them later, Winifred,” her spouse uttered.
Ultimately, Miss Winifred brought her along and went upstairs to inform the Hollowmere inhabitants of her choice prior to anything else.

“How wonderful!” Nell exclaimed with joy. “Miss Winifred, I was wishing you’d decide to do just that. My desire is for that unfortunate youngster to find a fine home. At one time, I too was an orphan girl without a home, exactly as she is.”

“I fail to believe that this Mary-creature is or ever will resemble you to any great extent,” Miss Winifred gloomily answered back. “She is a feline of a different shade. However, she remains a human being possessing an immortal soul that requires saving. Having put my hand to the plough, trust me, I possess a shorter catechism along with a fine-toothed comb and intend to perform my obligation toward her.”
The information was taken in by Mary with a subdued sense of gratification.
“This is a greater piece of fortune than I had anticipated,” she remarked.
“You’ll need to watch your step around Mrs. Kerr,” Bess stated.
“Indeed, that lies within my power,” snapped Mary. “My understanding of proper conduct when I desire it matches yours precisely, Bess Carrow.”
“It is not right for you to speak vulgarly, Mary, as you are aware,” Ida remarked with concern.

“I reckon the thought would scare her to death,” Mary chuckled, her pale eyes glimmering with mischievous delight at the notion. “You can rest easy, Ida, though. From now on, I will be the picture of innocence. I shall be on my absolute best behavior.”
“Or utter falsehoods,” Grace chimed in.
“Not even to escape being whipped?” Mary begged.
“Izzy declared, “At no time will Mrs. Kerr give you a whipping—at no time.”

“Won’t she?” Mary asked in a doubtful tone. “Should I ever end up in a spot where I am not beaten, I will certainly consider it heaven. There will be no danger of my lying at that point. I am not partial to telling them—I would prefer not to, if given the choice.”

A picnic was held in Fern Hollow to celebrate Mary prior to her leaving the manse the following day, and when night came, each child of the manse presented her with a memento chosen from their small collection of cherished possessions. Rupert presented his Noah’s ark to her, whereas Tobias handed over his second best jew’s-harp. Grace provided a small hairbrush that featured a mirror embedded in its rear, an item Mary had forever viewed as truly marvelous. Ida wavered in deciding between a worn beaded purse and a vibrant illustration showing Daniel in the lion’s den, ultimately letting Mary select whichever she preferred. Mary truly longed for the beaded purse, yet understanding how much Ida cherished it, she said,
“Hand over Daniel. I’d rather take that one since I have a fondness for lions. Although I do wish Daniel had been devoured by them. The story would have been far more thrilling.”
When it was time for bed, Mary persuaded Ida to share her sleep.

“This is the final time,” she remarked, “and rain is falling this evening, and I detest resting up in that room by myself in the rain because of the cemetery. On pleasant evenings I do not care, but during a night such as this the only thing visible to me is the rain falling over those aged white tombstones, while the wind about the windowpane sounds like those deceased individuals attempting to enter and weeping because they fail.”
“Rainy nights are to my liking,” stated Ida, as they lay snuggled beside one another inside the small attic room, “and the Carrow girls enjoy them too.”

“When I am nowhere near cemeteries, I do not care about them,” Mary remarked. “Were I by myself in this place, my loneliness would cause me to weep uncontrollably. The thought of departing from everyone makes me feel terribly miserable.”
“I feel certain Mrs. Kerr will permit you to visit and play in Fern Hollow very frequently,” Ida stated. “And Mary, you are going to be a well-behaved girl, aren’t you?”
“Oh, I’ll try,” Mary sighed. “But being good—on the inside, I mean, and not just the outside—will not be as simple for me as it is for you. My relations were much greater scalawags than yours.”
“Your people were bound to possess a few positive traits alongside their negative ones, however,” Ida reasoned. “It is those you ought to fulfill, ignoring their shortcomings.”

“I do not think they possessed a single redeeming virtue,” Mary remarked morosely. “I was never told about any. My grandfather possessed wealth, yet people claim he was a scoundrel. No, I must simply make my own way and try to succeed as well as possible.”
“And God will assist you, as you are aware, Mary, should you request it of Him.”
“I am not certain of that.”
“Oh, Mary. You are aware that we prayed to God to provide a home for you, and He granted it.”
“I fail to comprehend how He was involved,” Mary answered back. “You were the one who suggested it to Mrs. Kerr.”
“Yet it was placed within her heart by God to adopt you. Had He not done so, no amount of my urging her would have achieved anything.”

“Well, you could be right about that,” conceded Mary. “Listen to me, I don't hold a grudge against God, Ida. I am prepared to grant Him an opportunity. However, truly, I feel He resembles your father immensely—simply distracted and ignoring a person nearly all the time, yet occasionally snapping to attention out of nowhere and proving exceptionally nice and caring and wise.”
“Oh, Mary, no!” Ida cried out in horror. “God is not at all like father—I mean He is a thousand times kinder and better.”
“Provided He is as fine as your father He will suit me,” Mary said. “While your father was speaking with me I had the feeling that I could not ever be wicked again.”
