“It would be better if you spoke with father regarding Him,” Ida sighed. “His ability to explain everything far surpasses mine.”

Mary gave her word, “Well, I shall do that very thing, the moment he awakens again. When he conversed with me in the study during that evening, he made me understand completely that Mrs. Grimble was not killed by my prayers. My thoughts have been untroubled from then on, though I remain extremely careful regarding prayer. It strikes me that relying on the old verse is the most secure approach. Look here, Ida, it appears to my way of thinking that were a person required to pray to someone, choosing the devil would be preferable to choosing God. Since God possesses goodness, as you claim at any rate, He is not going to cause you damage, whereas based on everything I am able to gather, the devil requires soothing. It strikes me as logical to speak to him, ‘Kind devil, I ask that you do not entice me. I request that you simply let me be.’ Wouldn't you agree?”
“Oh, no, no, Mary. I feel certain that praying to the devil couldn’t be proper. Furthermore, it would be useless since he is evil. Doing so might rile him up, making him even worse.”

“Well, regarding this issue of God,” Mary stated obstinately, “because the two of us are unable to resolve it, discussing it further is pointless until an opportunity arises for us to learn the truth about it. Until that time, I will manage as well as I am able by myself.”
“Our mother would be able to inform us about all of it if she were still living,” Ida remarked, sighing.

“I wish she hadn’t died,” Mary remarked. “I am at a loss as to what will happen to you children after my passing. Regardless, make an effort to maintain some neatness in the home. It is disgraceful how folk gossip regarding its condition. Furthermore, before you realize it, another wife will be taken by your father, placing you all in a less favored position.”
Ida felt a sudden shock. Never had the thought occurred to her that her father might remarry. Disliking the notion, she remained still, overwhelmed by the cold feeling it brought.

“Stepmothers are terrible beings,” Mary continued. “If I were to inform you about everything I know concerning them, I could freeze your blood. A stepmother belonged to the Wilson children, who lived across the road from Grimble’s. To them, she behaved just as horribly as Mrs. Grimble behaved to me. If a stepmother comes into your life, it will be dreadful.”
“I feel certain we shall not,” Ida remarked with a quiver in her voice. “Papa will never take another wife.”

“I anticipate he will be driven into it,” Mary remarked somberly. “Every single maiden in the colony is pursuing him. They are impossible to outwit. Furthermore, the trouble with stepmothers is their habit of turning your father against you. Your importance to him would completely disappear. His support would invariably go to her and her offspring. You see, she would convince him of your total wickedness.”
“Mary, I wish you hadn’t shared this with me,” Ida exclaimed. “It fills me with such unhappiness.”

“My intention was merely to give you a warning,” Mary remarked, sounding somewhat contrite. “To be sure, your father is so preoccupied that he may not even consider taking another wife. Still, being ready for it is preferable.”

A considerable time after Mary was sleeping peacefully, little Ida remained awake, tears causing her eyes to sting. Oh, how terrible it would prove if her father were to marry a person who caused him to hate her along with Tobias, Grace, and Rupert! It was impossible for her to endure it—simply impossible!

Mary had refrained from putting any such venom as Miss Winifred had dreaded into the manse children’s thoughts. Nevertheless, with the finest motives, she had definitely managed to cause a bit of trouble. She slept without dreams, however, as Ida remained awake and rain came down while the wind moaned about the aged gray manse. Meanwhile, the Rev. John Ashdown completely neglected to retire for the night owing to his absorption in reading a biography of St. Augustine. Dawn was gray by the time he completed it and proceeded upstairs, grappling with the issues of two millenniums past. Finding the door to the girls’ chamber open, he observed Grace fast asleep, flushed and lovely. He pondered where Ida could be. It crossed his mind that she might have gone across to “stay all night” alongside the Carrow girls. She engaged in this now and then, considering it a splendid pleasure. John Ashdown uttered a sigh. It seemed to him that where Ida was should not be an unknown matter to him. Cecelia would have exercised superior care over her than that.

If Cecelia remained by his side even now! What beauty and cheerfulness she used to possess! The ancient manse located at Juneford had resounded so greatly with her singing! Then she departed with such suddenness, carrying off her mirth and melodies while leaving hush behind—departing so abruptly that his sense of astonishment had never fully faded. How was it possible for her, who was so gorgeous and lively, to pass away?

John Ashdown had never given genuine thought to marrying again. His affection for his wife had been so profound that he felt it impossible to ever love another woman. He entertained a faint notion that Grace would soon reach an age where she could step into her mother’s role. In the meantime, he had to manage as well as possible by himself. Sighing, he proceeded to his bedroom, in which the bed remained unmade. Aunt Martha had overlooked it, whereas Mary had abstained from making it out of fear, as Aunt Martha had instructed her not to interfere with anything in the minister’s chamber. Nevertheless, Mr. Ashdown failed to observe its unmade state. St. Augustine occupied his final thoughts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Ugh,” Grace said, shivering as she sat up in bed. “It’s raining. A rainy Sunday is something I truly hate. Even if the weather is fine, Sunday is dull enough.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Sunday should not be boring for us,” Ida remarked in a slumberous voice, attempting to gather her sleepy thoughts while feeling an uncomfortable certainty that they had slept past the proper time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “However, it is true that we do,” Grace admitted openly. “Mary Stubbs claims that the majority of Sundays prove so boring she feels like hanging herself.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Sunday should be more to our liking than it is to Mary Stubbs,” Ida remarked with regret. “The minister is our father.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I desire for us to be the offspring of a blacksmith,” declared Grace with irritation, searching for her stockings. “People would not anticipate superior behavior from us in that case. Simply observe these openings at my heels. They were completely repaired by Mary prior to her departure, yet their condition is just as terrible currently. Rise from bed, Ida. Preparing the morning meal by myself is impossible for me. Oh, my goodness. My desire is for father and Tobias to return home. It would not be expected that father’s absence would be felt so deeply—his presence is scarce even when he resides here. Even so, it feels as though all has disappeared. Checking on Aunt Martha requires me to dash over briefly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Has she improved at all?” Ida inquired upon Grace’s return.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “No, she isn’t,” I was answered. “She continues to groan with the pain. It might be best if Dr. Carrow were informed. However, she refuses—she has never used a doctor in all her days and will not start at this time. Her belief is that doctors merely make a living through the poisoning of folks. Is that what you think they do?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “No, naturally not,” Ida said, feeling offended. “Dr. Carrow would certainly never poison anyone, I’m positive.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Well, once breakfast is over, Aunt Martha’s back will need another rubbing. It would be better if the flannels aren't heated as much as they were yesterday.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Grace chuckled as she recalled the event. Poor Aunt Martha had almost had the skin boiled off her back by them. A sigh escaped Ida. The exact warmth that flannels ought to have for an aching back would have been known by Mary Stubbs. Everything was known by Mary. Nothing was known by them. And except through harsh experience—for which, on this occasion, the unlucky Aunt Martha had suffered the consequences—how were they to gain knowledge?

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: The previous Monday, Mr. Ashdown had departed for Nova Scotia accompanied by Tobias to pass his brief holiday. On Wednesday, Aunt Martha was abruptly stricken by a repeated and cryptic sickness that she invariably referred to as “the misery,” a condition that was fairly sure to strike her whenever it was least convenient. Rising from her bed was impossible for her, as every motion produced severe pain. Having a doctor was something she unyieldingly declined. The meals were prepared, and her needs attended to, by Grace and Ida. It is preferable to say as little as possible regarding those meals—though their quality was not significantly inferior to what Aunt Martha had produced. Numerous women residing in the village would have gladly assisted, yet Aunt Martha declined to allow anyone to learn of her predicament.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Until I can manage to move about, you have to keep struggling,” she moaned. “Blessedly, John is absent. Cold boiled meat and bread exist in abundance, and attempting to prepare porridge is something you can try.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: The girls had attempted it themselves, yet until now they achieved little success. On day one it proved excessively thin. On the following day it was so dense that slicing it was possible. Furthermore, it was scorched on both days.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I despise porridge,” Grace remarked with venom. “Whenever I possess my own home, I will not permit even one speck of porridge inside.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “In that case, how will your children manage?” Ida inquired. “Unless children eat porridge, they fail to grow. Everyone agrees on that point.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “They will need to manage without it or remain small,” Grace countered with obstinacy. “Ida, come and mix this while the table is being set by me. Should I abandon it briefly, the awful mixture is going to scorch. The time is nine thirty. Our arrival at Sunday School is going to be late.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Nobody has walked by up to now,” Ida remarked. “It is doubtful that a lot of people will be about. Look at the way it is raining. Also, since there is no sermon, people will not travel from far away to deliver the children.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Rupert should be called by you,” Grace said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: As it turned out, Rupert was suffering from a sore throat, brought on by becoming soaked in the Fern Hollow marsh the evening before as he chased dragon-flies. Returning home with soaked boots and stockings, he had remained sitting in them for the rest of the evening. Because he was unable to consume breakfast, Grace forced him to return to bed. Leaving the table untouched, she and Ida departed for Sunday School. Upon their arrival, the school room was completely empty, nor did anyone else show up. Having waited until eleven o'clock, they subsequently returned home.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “It appears there is no one present at the Methodist Sunday School, either,” Ida remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I’m glad,” Grace said. “I’d hate to think the Methodists had a better record for attending Sunday School on rainy Sundays than the Presbyterians. However, there is no sermon at their Church to-day, either, so it is probable that their Sunday School takes place in the afternoon.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Ida cleaned the plates, handling them rather well, because Mary Stubbs had taught her that much. Grace gave the floor a rough sweep and prepared the dinner potatoes by peeling them, slicing her finger as she did so.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “If only our evening meal consisted of something other than ditto,” Ida uttered with a sigh. “My weariness of it is complete. What ditto is remains unknown to the Carrow children. Furthermore, pudding is something we are always without. According to Bess, Tabitha’s swooning would occur if Sunday arrived without pudding. Grace, what keeps us from being like everyone else?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I have no desire to resemble everyone else,” Grace chuckled while binding her cut finger. “Being me suits me better, as it is far more engaging. Jessie Drew manages a home as capably as her mother does, yet would you wish to share her lack of intelligence?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “However, our home is not as it should be. That is what Mary Stubbs claims. According to her, folks remark upon how cluttered it is.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: An idea struck Grace.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “We will tidy up everything,” she exclaimed. “Tomorrow we will start immediately. Since Aunt Martha is bedridden and unable to meddle with our plans, this is a truly great opportunity. By the time father returns, we will render it completely beautiful and spotless, exactly as it appeared when Mary left. Sweeping, dusting, and washing windows are tasks anybody can perform. Folks will no longer have reason to gossip about us. Kit Carrow claims that merely old cats gossip, yet the things they say injure us just as deeply as anyone else's words.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I hope the weather is good tomorrow,” Ida remarked, full of excitement. “Oh, Grace, being completely washed and resembling everyone else is going to be wonderful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “It is my hope that Aunt Martha’s unhappiness continues into tomorrow,” Grace remarked. “If it fails to do so, not a solitary thing will be accomplished by us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: What Grace amicably desired came to pass. On the following day, Aunt Martha remained too unwell to get out of bed. Rupert likewise continued to be ill and was persuaded without difficulty to remain in bed. How ill the child actually was remained completely unknown to both Grace and Ida; a physician would have been summoned immediately by an attentive mother; however, a mother was absent, and poor little Rupert, possessing a sore throat, a throbbing head, and flushed cheeks, wrapped himself within his tangled bedcoverings and endured his distress in solitude, deriving a degree of solace from a little green lizard kept inside the pocket of his worn nighty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Summer sunlight saturated the world once the rain had stopped. House-cleaning was ideal on such a matchless day, so Grace and Ida set about their tasks with light hearts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “The parlour and the dining-room will be cleaned by us,” Grace said. “Meddling with the study would not do, and the upstairs does not matter much. Taking all things out is the first step.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Consequently, every single thing was removed. The lawn and the veranda held the stacked furniture, and rugs were cheerfully hung over the fence of the Methodist graveyard. A frenzy of sweeping came next, accompanied by Ida’s effort to dust, whereas Grace cleaned the dining-room windows, shattering a single pane and splitting two others during the task. Ida looked uncertainly at the streaky outcome.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Somehow, they fail to look proper,” she remarked. “Only gleaming and sparkling are the windows belonging to Tabitha and Mrs. Kerr.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “It doesn't matter. The sunlight passes through them all the same,” Grace remarked bright-heartedly. “With all the soap and water I’ve applied, they have to be sanitary, which is what matters most. Since it has gone past eleven, I am going to clean up this spillage on the floor so we can head outdoors. You can remove dust from the furniture while I beat the rugs. I plan on doing that in the graveyard. Flying dust shouldn't be scattered across the lawn.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Shaking the rugs brought pleasure to Grace. Flapping and snapping the rugs while standing atop the gravestone of Hezekiah Pollock gave her genuine enjoyment. Naturally, Elder Abraham Clow along with his wife appeared to stare at her with stern displeasure as they drove by in their roomy, two-seated buggy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Is that not an awful vision?” Elder Abraham asked with gravity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “If my own eyes had not witnessed it, I never would have given it credit,” Mrs. Elder Abraham stated with even greater gravity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: Grace enthusiastically brandished a welcome mat toward the Clow group. She was untroubled by the lack of response from the elder and his spouse. It was common knowledge that Elder Abraham had not been seen smiling even once in the fourteen years since his appointment as Sunday School Superintendent. However, the failure of Posy and Adella Clow to return her wave caused her pain. Posy and Adella were dear to Grace. Aside from the Carrows, she considered them her closest schoolmates, and she invariably assisted Adella with arithmetic. Here was a fine example of gratitude. She was snubbed by her companions simply for beating carpets in an ancient cemetery in which, according to Mary Stubbs, nobody alive had been interred for ages. Grace turned abruptly and moved to the veranda, discovering Ida there, deeply upset because the Clow sisters had ignored her greeting as well.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “I guess they are angry about something,” Grace remarked. “Maybe they are envious since we spend so much time playing with the Carrows in Fern Hollow. Well, she can just wait until the school term begins and Adella needs me to demonstrate how her arithmetic should be done! Then we will get even. Come along, let us return the items inside. I am completely exhausted, and I doubt the rooms are going to appear significantly improved compared to before we began—even though I beat out pecks of dust over in the graveyard. House-cleaning is something I despise.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: By the time the exhausted girls completed the two rooms, the hour was two o’clock. After having a dismal bite in the kitchen, they planned to do the dishes right away. Grace, however, chanced to lift a new story-book that Izzy Carrow had loaned her, becoming oblivious to everything around her until the sun went down. Carrying a cup of strong, unpleasant tea up to Rupert, Ida discovered that he was sleeping; consequently, she curled up on Tobias’s bed and likewise drifted off to sleep. In the meantime, a strange tale circulated across Glen St. Agnes, leading people to inquire of one another in all seriousness what ought to be done about those manse youngsters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Believe me, that cannot be laughed at anymore,” Miss Winifred said to her husband, sighing deeply. “At the beginning, I was unable to believe it. Ottilie Drew came back from the Methodist Sunday School this afternoon with the tale, and I merely mocked it. However, Mrs. Elder Abraham states that she together with the Elder witnessed it themselves.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “What did you see?” Ambrose inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Grace and Ida Ashdown did not go to Sunday School this morning so they could clean the house,” Miss Winifred said, speaking in tones of despair. “Elder Abraham saw them shaking rugs in the Methodist graveyard as he walked home from church, where he had remained to organize the library books. I will never be able to look a Methodist in the face again. Imagine the scandal this will cause!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: An uproar it most certainly caused, becoming increasingly disgraceful as the news traveled, before those over the harbour learned that not merely had the manse children tidied up and hung a laundry load out on the Sabbath, but they had finished off with a graveyard picnic during the afternoon just as the Methodist Sunday School was taking place. The solitary home that stayed happily unaware of the awful event was the manse itself; rain fell once more on the day Grace and Ida lovingly assumed was Tuesday; it poured for the following three days; no one visited the manse; the inhabitants of the manse did not go anywhere; they could have picked their way across the foggy Fern Hollow to Hollowmere, yet every member of the Carrow family, except Tabitha and the doctor, had gone to Brierley on a trip.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Our bread has run out,” Grace remarked, “and the ditto is finished as well. What are we going to do if Aunt Martha fails to improve shortly?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Some bread can be purchased by us in the village, and the codfish that Mary dried is available,” stated Ida. “However, the method for cooking it is unknown to us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: “Oh, that’s easy,” Grace laughed. “You merely boil it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE
text: They certainly boiled it; however, because soaking it first failed to cross their minds, its saltiness made it inedible. Although intense hunger afflicted them that evening, the next day brought an end to their hardships. The sun shone on the earth again; Rupert had recovered, and Aunt Martha’s distress departed just as abruptly as its arrival; famine was driven off when the butcher visited the manse. Above everything else, the Carrows came back to their house, and when evening arrived, they, alongside Mary Stubbs and the manse children, gathered again for a sunset meeting in Fern Hollow, in which daisy blossoms floated above the grass similar to dew spirits and fairy-like chimes echoed from the bells on the Tree Lovers within the fragrant twilight.

“Well, you kids have gone and done it now,” Mary said upon meeting them in the Valley. In Hollowmere above, Miss Winifred engaged in an anguished conference alongside Nell and Tabitha, a discussion Mary wished would endure, because a full fortnight had passed since she had last been permitted to make merry with her friends in the beloved rainbow valley.
“Done what?” asked all of them except Edmund, who was lost in his usual reverie.

“I am referring to you youngsters from the manse,” Mary declared. “Your actions were simply terrible. Nothing in the world could have made me do something like that, even though I was not raised in a manse—was not raised anywhere at all—just grew up.”
“What have we done?” Grace asked with a blank expression.

“Finished! Asking would be a wise move! People are saying the most dreadful things. It has likely destroyed your father's standing among these churchgoers. The poor man will certainly never overcome this disgrace! Everyone holds him responsible, which is completely unjust. However, justice does not exist in this life. Each of you should feel deep shame.”
“What have we done?” Ida inquired once more, filled with despair. Grace remained silent, yet her eyes shone with a golden-brown disdain directed at Mary.
“Oh, stop acting like you are innocent,” Mary stated scathingly. “All of us are aware of what you did.”
“I do not,” put in Kit Carrow crossly. “Mary Stubbs, do not let me see you make Ida cry. What is it you are talking about?”

“I guess you are unaware, as you have only recently returned from up west,” Mary said, her tone slightly muted. Kit was continually able to handle her. “However, you can be sure that all the other people are fully aware.”
“Is aware of what?”
“Last Sunday, Grace and Ida didn't go to Sunday School and instead did housecleaning.”
“We didn’t,” Grace and Ida shouted, vehemently denying it.
Mary cast a disdainful glance in their direction.

“Given how you reprimanded me for not telling the truth, I didn’t think you would deny it,” she said. “Why claim you didn’t? It’s common knowledge that you did. Elder Clow and his wife were witnesses. A few folks claim the church will split because of it, though I wouldn’t go to that extreme. You are a fine pair.”
Bess Carrow rose to her feet and wrapped her arms about the bewildered Grace and Ida.

“When you were dying of hunger inside Mr. Taylor’s barn, Mary Stubbs, they had the kindness to welcome you, offer you food, and provide you with clothes,” she remarked. “I have to observe that you show great gratitude.”

“I am thankful,” Mary replied. “You would realize it had you listened to me defending Mr. Ashdown no matter what. My tongue has been blistered from speaking on his behalf this week. Over and over, I have stated that he should not be faulted because his children tidyed up on Sunday. He was not there—and they were well aware.”
“However, we failed to do so,” Ida objected. “The day we tidied the home was Monday. Isn't that right, Grace?”

“Naturally it was,” Grace stated, her eyes flashing. “Despite the rain, we attended Sunday School—and nobody appeared—not even Elder Abraham, regardless of his remarks concerning fair-weather Christians.”

“Saturday brought rain,” Mary stated. “The weather on Sunday turned exceedingly lovely. Toothache kept me from attending Sunday School, though all the others were present and witnessed every bit of your belongings displayed across the lawn. Furthermore, Elder Abraham and Mrs. Elder Abraham observed you beating rugs within the cemetery.”
Taking a seat in the middle of the daisies, Ida started weeping.
“Listen to me,” declared Kit with determination, “we have to get to the bottom of this. A blunder has been made by someone. Grace, Sunday had good weather. What made you think Saturday was Sunday?”

“Prayer-meeting occurred on Thursday night,” Grace exclaimed, “and Adam went into the soup-pot on Friday because he was pursued by Aunt Martha’s cat, which ruined our meal; and a snake was in the cellar on Saturday, but Rupert retrieved it using a forked stick to take it outside, and it rained on Sunday. There now!”

“Prayer-meeting occurred on Wednesday night,” Mary remarked. “Elder Baxter was supposed to lead, but he was unable to make Thursday night, so it got moved to Wednesday. Your count was simply off by one day, Grace Ashdown, and you actually performed labor on Sunday.”
All at once, Grace erupted in a fit of laughing.
“I guess we did. What a laugh!”
“For your father, it’s hardly a joke,” Mary remarked with bitterness.
“Once everyone realizes that it was merely an error, everything will be fine,” Grace remarked casually. “A simple explanation will suffice.”

“You can clarify until you are blue in the gills,” Mary stated, “yet a falsehood of that nature will journey more quickly and wider than you ever could. I HAVE witnessed a greater portion of the world than you, and I am aware. Furthermore, a great deal of people will refuse to accept that it was an accident.”
“They shall should I inform them,” Grace declared.
“You cannot inform everyone,” Mary stated. “No, I am telling you that you have brought shame upon your father.”

Although Ida's night was ruined by this gloomy thought, Grace declined to be distressed. Furthermore, she possessed a scheme that was going to set all things to rights. Consequently, she placed the previous time and its error out of her mind and yielded completely to the pleasure of the current moment. Kit departed in order to angle, while Edmund emerged from his musings and went on to portray the forests of paradise. Mary paid close attention and paid attention with deference. In spite of her dread of Edmund, she delighted in his "book talk." A charming feeling was forever bestowed upon her by it. Edmund's reading of his Coleridge had occurred on that day, and he depicted a paradise in which
“There existed gardens radiant with winding streams where numerous incense-bearing trees produced blossoms, and there existed forests as old as the hills surrounding bright patches of vegetation.”
“I was unaware that heaven contained any woods,” Mary uttered, drawing a deep breath. “My belief was that it consisted entirely of streets—and streets—and streets.”
“Naturally, trees exist there,” Bess remarked. “Since Mother is unable to exist without woods and neither am I, what purpose would entering heaven serve if trees were absent?”

“There are cities, too,” the young dreamer said, “magnificent cities—hued exactly as the sunset, having sapphire towers along with rainbow domes. Gold and diamonds are used to build them—entire streets made of diamonds, glittering such as the sun. Within the squares exist crystal fountains kissed by the light, and the asphodel blooms everywhere—the celestial flower.”

“Fancy!” Mary exclaimed. “After seeing Port Marlow’s main street one time, I considered it truly grand, though I imagine heaven makes it look like nothing. Well, your description makes it all seem magnificent, yet won't it also be rather boring?”
“Oh, I suppose we are able to enjoy ourselves a bit whenever the angels aren't looking,” Grace remarked easily.
“Heaven is all fun,” Izzy declared.
“It is not written in the Bible,” exclaimed Mary, whose extensive Sunday afternoon Bible reading under Miss Winifred’s supervision led her to regard herself as a true expert on the text.
“Mother says the language of the Bible is figurative,” Bess said.
“Is it false, then?” Mary asked with a sense of hope.
“No—not precisely—however my impression is that it signifies heaven will mirror whatever you wish for it to be.”

“I want it to be exactly like Fern Hollow,” Mary remarked, “where I can chatter and mess around with all of you children. I am satisfied with that. Regardless, entering heaven is impossible until our lives end, and even that is uncertain, so why fret over it? Kit has arrived holding a catch of trout, and frying them is now my responsibility.”
“Since we belong to the minister’s family, we should possess a greater knowledge of heaven than Edmund,” remarked Ida, while they made their way back home on that evening.
“We have the exact same knowledge, yet Edmund possesses imagination,” Grace remarked. “According to Mrs. Kerr, this trait comes from his mother.”
“It’s such a shame we got the day wrong regarding Sunday,” Ida said with a sigh.
“Do not be anxious about it. I have devised an excellent scheme for clarifying things so that all will understand,” Grace said. “Only hold off until tomorrow evening.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: The Rev. Dr. Cooper delivered his sermon at Glen St. Agnes the following night, filling the Presbyterian Church with an immense gathering of folks from both close by and distant places. Renowned as a highly gifted orator, the Reverend Doctor presented an exceedingly erudite and powerful message, adhering to the age-old proverb which suggests a preacher ought to pack his finest garments for urban trips and his finest homilies for rural ones. Nevertheless, as the congregation returned to their houses that evening, Dr. Cooper’s sermon was not the subject of their conversation. Every bit of it had slipped their minds entirely.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Dr. Cooper finished his speech with an impassioned plea, cleared the sweat from his large forehead, uttered “Let us pray” in his renowned manner, and proceeded to offer the prayer. A brief moment of silence followed. The congregation of Glen St. Agnes church preserved the former custom of collecting the offering following the sermon rather than prior to it—primarily for the reason that this recent practice had been taken up by the Methodists first, and neither Miss Winifred nor Elder Clow would consent to imitate a path the Methodists had forged. Being responsible for passing the plates, Charles Baxter and Thomas Fairlie were just about to stand up. Having pulled out the sheet music for her anthem, the organist waited while the choir cleared its collective throat. All at once, Grace Ashdown stood up in the manse pew, stepped onto the pulpit platform, and turned toward the astonished crowd.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Miss Winifred started to stand up from her place before seating herself once more. Because her pew was positioned near the rear, she realized that whatever action or statement Grace intended to make would already be halfway accomplished or uttered prior to her arrival. Creating a scene any more embarrassing than necessary served no purpose. Directing a pained look toward Mrs. Dr. Carrow, followed by a second toward Deacon Warren belonging to the Methodist Church, Miss Winifred surrendered to the inevitability of yet another scandal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Provided that the youngster was merely clothed in a respectable manner,” her soul lamented.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Grace, after spilling ink on her fine frock, had calmly changed into a washed-out pink print garment from earlier days. A diagonal tear in her skirt had been mended using red embroidery thread, and the bottom edge had been unstitched, revealing a vivid band of original pink along the hemline. However, Grace was giving no thought to her attire whatsoever. A sudden wave of anxiety washed over her. An act that appeared simple in her mind proved quite difficult in truth. Facing that entire collection of fixed, inquiring glances, Grace almost lost her nerve. The illumination was so intense, the quietude so terrifying. It struck her that she might be unable to utter a sound after all. Yet she had to—it was imperative to free her father from doubt. Except—the speech refused to form.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: From the manse pew, the small, pearl-pure face of Ida gleamed up at her in a beseeching manner. The Carrow children were completely astonished. Farther back beneath the gallery, Grace noticed the sweet graciousness present in the smile of Miss Clementine Ainslie, as well as the amusement displayed in that of Miss Harriet. Yet none of these things provided her with aid. It was Bertie Shakespeare Drew who rescued the circumstance. Bertie Shakespeare was seated in the gallery's front row, and he pulled a mockingly scornful face at Grace. Grace immediately pulled an appalling face right back at him, and because of her rage at being made faces at by Bertie Shakespeare, she lost her stage fright. Locating her voice, she spoke aloud both distinctly and courageously.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “I need to make something clear,” she stated, “and I wish to do it right away so everyone who listened to the previous story can hear this one. A rumor is going around that Ida and I remained at home this past Sunday to clean the house rather than attending Sunday School. It is true that we did—however, it was not our intention. The days of the week became confused in our minds. The blame lies entirely with Elder Baxter”—a reaction occurred in the pew belonging to Baxter—“since he proceeded to shift the prayer-meeting over to Wednesday evening, causing us to mistake Thursday for Friday and so forth, until Saturday seemed to us like Sunday. Rupert was bedridden with illness, as was Aunt Martha, meaning neither of them could set us straight. During all that rain on Saturday, we traveled to Sunday School, but not a soul arrived. After that, we decided we would perform our housecleaning on Monday to halt the gossip of old cats regarding the filthy state of the manse”—a broad reaction rippled throughout the whole church—“and that is what we accomplished. The reason I shook out the rugs inside the Methodist graveyard was that it offered a handy spot, not owing to any desire on my part to show disrespect toward the deceased. The departed aren't the ones who raised a commotion about this matter—the living ones are. Furthermore, it is unfair for a single one of you to fault my father regarding this, since he was out of town and unaware, and regardless, we believed the day to be Monday. He happens to be the finest father who ever existed anywhere, and our love for him fills our whole hearts.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Grace’s confidence drained away as she broke into a sob. Hurrying down the stairs, she darted through the church’s side entrance. Outside, she found solace in the welcoming, star-filled summer evening, which eased the pain in her eyes and neck. A sense of great joy washed over her. The terrible clarification had been made at last, meaning all the people were aware that her father held no responsibility and that Ida and she had not been so sinful as to consciously perform housework on a Sunday.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Worshippers exchanged empty looks within the church, yet Thomas Fairlie stood and strode toward the altar with a rigid expression. He had a plain obligation; even if the heavens collapsed, the gathering of offerings had to proceed. It indeed took place; the anthem was performed by the choir, who felt a gloomy certainty that their song lacked any spark, while Dr. Cooper announced the final hymn and offered the blessing with much less enthusiasm than he typically displayed. A sense of comedy possessed the Reverend Doctor, who found himself amused by Grace’s actions. Furthermore, John Ashdown enjoyed widespread recognition among Presbyterian groups.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: The following afternoon brought Mr. Ashdown back home, yet Grace managed to shock Glen St. Agnes once more prior to his arrival. Following the pressure and seriousness of Sunday evening, a rebound left her particularly brimming with what Miss Winifred would have termed “devilment” on Monday. Because of this, she challenged Edmund Carrow to travel down Main Street atop a pig, as she herself mounted a second one.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: The pair of swine being referred to were two long, lean beasts, believed to be owned by the father of Bertie Shakespeare Drew, that had been lingering along the edge of the road near the parsonage for about fourteen days. Although Edmund had no desire to mount a pig through Glen St. Agnes, he was bound to execute any challenge Grace Ashdown set before him. Down the slope and through the settlement they rushed, Grace doubled over in hysterics atop her frightened mount, while Edmund turned bright red with humiliation. They bolted past the clergyman himself, who was just returning from the depot; because he was slightly more alert and less preoccupied than was typical—a result of chatting on the railway carriage with Miss Winifred, who invariably aroused his attention for a short while—he observed the pair, deciding he truly ought to address Grace regarding the matter and inform her that this behavior was improper. However, the minor event had slipped his mind by the moment he arrived at his residence. They swept past Mrs. Hector Twiss, who let out a scream of dismay, and they swept past Miss Clementine Ainslie, who chuckled and uttered a sigh. Ultimately, right before the swine darted into the rear yard of Bertie Shakespeare Drew, never to come out of it again because the trauma to their nervous systems was so severe—Grace and Edmund leaped down, at the exact moment Dr. and Mrs. Carrow sped past in their carriage.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Thus you raise your young men,” stated Hugh with pretended seriousness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Maybe I indulge them slightly,” Nell remarked remorsefully, “however, oh, Hugh, whenever my mind returns to my early years prior to arriving at Grey Shutters, I lack the resolve to enforce rigid discipline. How desperate I felt for affection and amusement—a neglected young slavey who was denied any opportunity to enjoy herself! Their moments spent alongside the manse children are truly delightful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “What about the poor pigs?” Hugh asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Nell attempted to appear serious, but she was unsuccessful.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Is it your genuine belief that it caused them pain?” she asked. “My impression is that nothing has the power to injure those creatures. Throughout this summer, they have acted as the local nuisance, yet the Drews refuse to confine them. Nevertheless, I shall speak with Edmund—provided I manage to suppress my laughter while doing so.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: That evening, Miss Winifred traveled to Hollowmere so she could vent her emotions regarding Sunday night. Upon arrival, she was amazed to discover that Nell failed to see Grace’s conduct from quite the same perspective as her own.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “It seemed to me that her going up in front of those churchgoers to make her confession held a certain courage and sadness,” she stated. “One could tell she was terrified out of her wits—and still, she was determined to vindicate her father. I adored her because of that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Oh, naturally, the unfortunate girl had good intentions,” Miss Winifred sighed, “yet even so, it was an awful deed, which creates a greater stir than the Sabbath house-cleaning. That incident had started to fade, but this event has revived the whole matter. Clementine Ainslie shares your perspective—when departing from the church yesterday evening, she remarked that Grace’s action was brave, though it likewise filled her with pity for the girl. Miss Harriet viewed the entire affair as an amusing jest, stating that she had not enjoyed herself so much at church in years. Naturally, it matters little to them—being Episcopalians. However, we Presbyterians are affected by it. Furthermore, numerous hotel guests attended that evening, alongside dozens of Methodists. Mrs. Leander Crawford wept because of her deep distress. And Mrs. Hector Twiss declared that the young minx deserved a spanking.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “In church, Mrs. Leander Crawford constantly weeps,” Tabitha remarked scornfully. “Any moving word from the minister brings her to tears. However, Mrs. Dr. dear, her signature rarely appears on a subscription list. Crying costs less. One time she attempted to converse with me regarding Aunt Martha’s filthy housekeeping; and I felt like replying, ‘Mrs. Leander Crawford, everybody is aware that you have been observed stirring up cakes inside the kitchen wash-pan!’ Nevertheless, Mrs. Dr. dear, I refrained from saying it, since my self-respect is too great for me to demean myself by disputing with someone like her. Yet, if I were inclined to spread rumors, I could reveal far worse matters concerning Mrs. Leander Crawford. Furthermore, regarding Mrs. Hector Twiss, had she uttered those words to me, Mrs. Dr. dear, do you realize what my response would have been? My reply would have been, ‘Mrs. Twiss, I do not question that spanking Grace would please you, but neither in this world nor in the one to come will you ever be afforded the opportunity to spank the daughter of a minister.’”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Had poor Grace merely been dressed decently,” Miss Winifred lamented once more, “it would not have turned out entirely that terrible. However, standing on the platform there, she looked dreadful in that dress.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Mrs. Dr. dear, it was clean, nevertheless,” Tabitha stated. “Cleanliness is a trait of these children. Mrs. Dr. dear, they might possess a great deal of heedlessness and recklessness, a point I do not deny, yet washing behind their ears is something they never fail to do.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Imagine Grace failing to remember which day Sunday was,” Miss Winifred insisted. “Mark my words, she will become every bit as irresponsible and foolish as her father. I assume Rupert would have possessed more sense had he not been ill. The nature of his ailment escapes me, yet it seems highly probable that he had consumed the blueberries growing within the cemetery. It is no surprise they caused him to be unwell. Were I a Methodist, I would attempt to maintain the graveyard in a tidy state at the very least.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “It is my belief that Rupert merely consumed the sours growing upon the dyke,” Tabitha remarked with optimism. “It seems unlikely to me that a minister’s child would consume blueberries which sprouted from the burial places of deceased folks. Eating items that developed on the dyke, Mrs. Dr. dear, wouldn't be quite so awful, as you know.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “The initial part of yesterday evening’s display that was most awful was the expression Grace directed toward a person in the audience prior to commencing,” Miss Winifred stated. “Elder Clow asserts that she directed it toward him. Furthermore, was it brought to your attention that she was observed astride a pig during the day?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “I spotted her. Edmund accompanied her. I offered him a slight—a quite slight—reprimand regarding the matter. He said little, yet he conveyed to me that the notion was his own and that Grace bore no fault.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “I do not not believe that, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha exclaimed, fully defensive. “Edmund merely acts like that—assuming the fault personally. Yet you are just as aware as I am, Mrs. Dr. dear, that the sweet child would not ever conceive of sitting atop a pig, though he may compose poetry.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Oh, the idea was certainly born inside the mind of Grace Ashdown,” declared Miss Winifred. “And I cannot claim to regret that those elderly pigs belonging to Amos Drew finally received what they deserved for a change. However, it was the child of the minister!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “And the doctor’s son!” Nell uttered, copying the manner of Miss Winifred. After that, she giggled. “Dear Miss Winifred, they are merely small children. Besides, you are aware that they have not performed a single evil act so far—they are simply thoughtless and rash—just as I used to be. They will become serious and grave—just as I have.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: Miss Winifred joined in the laughter, as well.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “At certain moments, Nell dearie, I can tell from your eyes that your serious manner is worn like a piece of clothing and you are actually desperate to act reckless and youthful once more. Well, my spirits are lifted. For some reason, a conversation with you constantly produces that result in me. Currently, whenever I pay a visit to Barbara Samson, the outcome is entirely reversed. I am made to feel by her that all things are amiss and shall forever remain so. Yet naturally, spending a whole lifetime with a husband such as Joe Samson would not prove to be particularly uplifting.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “It is quite a peculiar thought that, despite all the opportunities she had, she ended up marrying Joe Samson,” Tabitha observed. “During her youth, she was greatly pursued. She would brag to me about having twenty-one suitors along with Mr. Pethick.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “In what line was Mr. Pethick?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “Indeed, he functioned as a kind of follower, Mrs. Dr. dear, though calling him a suitor would not be quite accurate. His intentions were not genuine, as a matter of fact. Twenty-one suitors—and myself having never possessed a single one! However, Barbara traversed the forest and selected the twisted branch in the end. Even so, it is claimed that her spouse is capable of preparing superior baking powder biscuits than she is, and she invariably asks him to prepare them whenever guests arrive for tea.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “That brings to my mind that tomorrow guests are arriving at my place for tea, so I have to return home to make my bread dough,” Miss Winifred remarked. “Mary mentioned she was capable of making it, and I do not question that she could. Nevertheless, for as long as I am alive and active and existing, I mix my own bread dough, you can be sure of that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “How is Mary doing?” inquired Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XII. AN EXPLANATION AND A DARE
text: “I can’t complain about Mary,” Miss Winifred remarked somewhat sullenly. “Her frame is gaining weight, plus she is tidy and polite—even if she possesses more depth than I am able to comprehend. She is a cunning creature. Take my word for it, even a millennium of digging wouldn't allow you to reach the depths of that girl's thoughts! When it comes to labor, I have never witnessed anyone her equal. She devours it. Mrs. Grimble might have treated her with cruelty, yet people have no reason to claim she forced Mary to labor. Mary is a natural-born laborer. On occasion, I ponder whether her legs or her tongue will exhaust itself first. Lately, my own workload isn't sufficient to prevent me from causing trouble. The commencement of school will bring me genuine joy, because it means I will once more have tasks to occupy me. Mary has no desire to attend school, yet I took a firm stance and declared that her attendance was mandatory. I will refuse to let the Methodists claim I denied her an education while I relaxed lazily.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: A small, reliable spring, which was perpetually freezing cold and completely clear, sat within a specific hollow concealed by birches in the bottom corner of Fern Hollow close to the marsh. Its presence was not known by very many people. Naturally, the children from the manse and Hollowmere were aware of it, just as they were aware of all other details concerning the enchanted valley. Now and then they visited the spot for a drink, and it served as an ancient romantic fountain in numerous games they played. Nell was aware of it and cherished it since it somehow brought to mind the cherished Nymph’s Well located at Grey Shutters. Clementine Ainslie was aware of it; it served as her romantic fountain as well. Eighteen years previously, during a spring twilight, she had been seated behind it when young Martin Crawford hesitantly confessed his intense, youthful affection. She had murmured her own hidden feelings back to him, and beside the untamed forest spring, they exchanged kisses and vows. They never gathered beside it again—Martin embarked on his deadly journey shortly afterward; nevertheless, Clementine Ainslie perpetually considered it a holy place, sanctified by that timeless moment of adolescence and romance. Every time she went near the spot, she detoured to share a quiet rendezvous with a bygone dream—a dream whose agony had vanished long ago, retaining merely its lingering sweetness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: The spring was concealed from view. One could walk by it within ten feet and not divine that it was there. Almost over it had fallen a large old pine sixty years ago. Nothing remained of that tree except a rotting trunk from which a dense growth of ferns emerged, creating a green canopy and a delicate barrier over the water. Next to it stood a maple with an strangely knotted and bent trunk that crawled along the earth briefly prior to rising skyward, thus shaping an unusual place to sit; and a ribbon of light smoke-blue asters had been draped around the depression by September.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: John Ashdown, while traveling back home from several pastoral calls near the Harbour head one evening by way of the cross-lots road through Fern Hollow, veered off to take a drink from the small spring. Just a short time prior, Edmund Carrow had pointed it out to him one afternoon, and they had engaged in an extended conversation while sitting on the maple bench. Beneath his entire shy and distant exterior, John Ashdown possessed a boyish heart. In his younger years, people had referred to him as Jack, although no resident of Glen St. Agnes would have ever credited such a thing. Edmund and he had drawn close to one another and conversed without restraint. Mr. Ashdown gained entry to certain locked and holy recesses of the youth’s spirit into which not even Izzy had ever peered. Starting from that warm moment, they were destined to be close companions, and Edmund realized he would not be intimidated by the clergyman ever again.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Prior to this, I didn't think one could genuinely come to know a clergyman,” he remarked to his mother that evening.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: John Ashdown took a drink from his thin white hand, which possessed a steel grip that invariably startled those who did not know it, and subsequently took a seat upon the maple bench. He felt no urge to return home quickly; the location was lovely, and he experienced mental exhaustion following a series of somewhat dull discussions with numerous kind yet foolish individuals. A rising moon appeared. At his exact location, Fern Hollow was haunted by the wind and watched over by stars alone, though joyous sounds of young people's voices and laughter drifted from its distant upper reach.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: The pale loveliness of the asters under the moon, the shimmer of the tiny spring, the gentle hum of the stream, and the swaying elegance of the brackens all cast a spell around John Ashdown. Church anxieties and religious dilemmas faded from his mind; the decades melted off him; he returned to being a youth studying theology, and the June roses were blossoming crimson and sweet-smelling upon the dusky, regal hair of his Cecilia. He remained seated and mused just like a youth. Then, during this favorable juncture, Clementine Ainslie left the small trail and paused next to him in that perilous, charm-casting spot. John Ashdown rose to his feet when she approached and looked upon her—truly looked upon her—for the initial time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: On one or two occasions, he had come across her at his church and absently shaken her hand, just as he did with whoever he chanced to meet while walking down the aisle. Because the Ainslies belonged to the Episcopalian faith and were affiliated with a church in Kettlebridge, he had never run into her anywhere else, and there had never been a reason to visit them. Prior to this evening, had somebody inquired of John Ashdown regarding the appearance of Clementine Ainslie, he would have been completely unable to say. Yet, as she was revealed to him in the enchanting moonlight beside the spring, he was destined never to erase the memory of her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: She definitely bore no resemblance whatsoever to Cecilia, the person who had continually represented his standard for female loveliness. While Cecilia had been petite, dark-haired, and full of life, Clementine Ainslie was imposing in height, light-complexioned, and serene; nevertheless, John Ashdown believed that a woman of such beauty had never before crossed his path.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: No hat covered her head, where her golden hair— hair possessing a warm gold hue described by Izzy Carrow as the shade of “molasses taffy”— sat fastened in smooth, tight braids; she possessed big, serene, blue eyes that constantly appeared to be brimming with goodwill, a lofty pale brow, and a exquisitely formed countenance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: People invariably referred to Clementine Ainslie as a “sweet woman.” Her sweetness was so profound that not even her aristocratic, dignified demeanour ever caused her to be branded as “stuck-up,” a label that anyone else residing in Glen St. Agnes would have certainly received. Through life’s experiences, she had learned how to show bravery, exercise patience, express love, and grant forgiveness. Her eyes had followed the vessel carrying her beloved as it departed Seven Gulls Harbour, gliding into the setting sun. Nevertheless, despite her prolonged watch, she never beheld its return voyage. That prolonged waiting stripped the girlhood from her gaze, but she retained her youthful essence to an extraordinary extent. This was possibly owing to her constant retention of that feeling of joyful wonder toward existence that the majority of us abandon during our early years—a disposition that not merely imparted a youthful quality to Clementine herself, but also cast a delightful aura of youth over the mind of anybody engaged in conversation with her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Her beauty surprised John Ashdown, just as finding him there caught Clementine off guard. Finding a person beside that secluded spring had never crossed her mind, particularly not the hermit who lived at the Glen St. Agnes manse. The large stack of volumes she was bringing back from the Glen lending library nearly slipped from her arms, whereupon she uttered one of those minor untruths that even the most virtuous women occasionally resort to in order to hide her embarrassment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I—I came for a drink,” she said, faltering slightly, replying to the solemn “good evening, Miss Ainslie” from Mr. Ashdown. She considered herself to be an unforgivable idiot, wishing she could give herself a shake. However, John Ashdown lacked vanity and recognized that an unexpected encounter with old Elder Clow would probably have startled her just as greatly. Because her embarrassment made him comfortable, he ceased being timid; moreover, in the moonlight, even the most bashful man can occasionally be fairly bold.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Allow me to fetch a cup for you,” he remarked with a smile. Nearby, a fractured blue cup lacking a handle was hidden beneath the maple by the Fern Hollow children, had he merely been aware of it; however, he was unaware, which led him to walk over to a birch-tree and peel off a piece of its white bark. Skillfully shaping this into a triangular container, he drew water from the spring and presented it to Clementine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Clementine accepted it and consumed all of it as a penalty for her lie, because she felt no thirst whatsoever, and consuming a rather substantial cup of water without being thirsty is a bit of a trial. Nevertheless, Clementine would come to cherish the recollection of that drink. During later years, she felt that it possessed a sacred quality. This might have been due to the actions of the minister upon receiving the returned cup from her. Bending down once more, he replenished the container and partook of it himself. His mouth touched the exact spot where Clementine had placed her own lips purely by chance, a fact of which Clementine was aware. Even so, the moment held a strange meaning for her. Both of them had partaken from the identical cup. A fleeting memory returned to her of an aged aunt who often remarked that if two individuals shared a drink like this, their future destinies would be connected in one way or another, be it for benefit or harm.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: With hesitation, John Ashdown gripped the cup. Unsure of how to handle the object, he considered throwing it as the sensible course of action, yet an odd reluctance stopped him from doing so. Reaching toward him, Clementine extended her hand to take it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Would you allow me to keep it?” she asked. “You fashioned it with such skill. I have not witnessed a person craft a birch cup in that manner since my young brother was accustomed to making them many years in the past—prior to his death.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “During my youth while camping out one summer, I picked up the skill to construct them from an old hunter,” remarked Mr. Ashdown. “Allow me to hold your books, Miss Ainslie.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Surprised into telling a second untruth, Clementine stated that they were actually light. However, the minister claimed them from her with a rather authoritative manner, and the pair departed side by side. Never before had Clementine remained beside the valley spring without her thoughts turning to Martin Crawford. The secret rendezvous had been severed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: A small side trail curved around the swamp before climbing the lengthy, forested height where Clementine made her home at the summit. Past that, amid the timber, the light of the moon was visible gleaming over the flat, warm-weather pastures. Nevertheless, the small trail remained dark and constricted. It was tightly hemmed in by trees, which are never entirely as welcoming to people once night arrives compared to when it is day. They retreat into themselves, separate from us. Their whispers and schemes are made in secret. Should they extend an arm toward us, its contact feels unwelcoming and hesitant. Individuals strolling among trees when it is dark invariably pull toward one another by impulse and without intending to, forging a physical and psychological pact facing particular foreign forces encircling them. As the two strolled, John Ashdown felt the fabric of Clementine’s gown brush against him. Even a distracted clergyman—who remained a youthful man despite his solid conviction that his romantic days were behind him—could not fail to feel the appeal of the darkness, the trail, and his fellow traveler.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: It is not entirely safe to assume that our time with life is over. Just when we believe our story has concluded, destiny often turns the page to reveal an additional chapter. These two individuals both believed their hearts were permanently attached to days gone by; nevertheless, each of them enjoyed their stroll up the hill immensely. Clementine considered the Glen pastor to be far less timid and mute than people had claimed. He appeared to experience no trouble conversing in a relaxed and open manner. Housewives in the Glen would have been astonished if they had listened to him. Yet a great number of Glen housewives spoke solely of rumor and how much eggs cost, and John Ashdown had no concern for such things. He spoke with Clementine about literature, music, global events, and a portion of his own past, discovering that she had the ability to comprehend and reply. Clementine, as it turned out, owned a volume that Mr. Ashdown had not perused and desired to read. She volunteered to give him the loan of it, and upon their arrival at the old hill residence, he stepped inside to retrieve it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: The dwelling was an aged grey building covered in vines, with the living room lamp shining through them in a welcoming way. It overlooked the Glen, past the moonlit harbour that gleamed like silver, towards the sandhills and the lamenting sea. They entered across a garden where the scent of roses seemed perpetually present, despite the absence of blooming roses. A cluster of lilies stood by the entrance, a line of asters bordered both sides of the wide path, and a delicate network of firs topped the hill crest behind the home.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “The entire world is right at your threshold in this place,” stated John Ashdown, taking a deep draft of air. “Such a vista—such a perspective! Now and then I feel suffocated down in the Glen. Air is available to breathe up here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “To-night is calm,” Clementine said with a laugh. “Your breath would be blown away if a wind were blowing. Up in this spot, we receive ‘a’ the airts the wind can blow’. Rather than the Harbour, Seven Gulls ought to be the name of this place.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I am fond of wind,” he remarked. “To my mind, a day lacking wind appears lifeless. I am aroused by a windy day.” He uttered a self-aware laugh. “A tranquil day causes me to slip into reveries. You are certainly aware of my repute, Miss Ainslie. Should I fail to acknowledge you at our subsequent encounter, do not attribute it to ill breeding. Kindly realize that it stems merely from preoccupation, pardon me—and address me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Harriet Ainslie was located in the sitting room as they entered. Placing her spectacles upon the volume she was in the middle of reading, she observed them with astonishment mixed with a different emotion. Nevertheless, she warmly shook hands with Mr. Ashdown, who took a seat and conversed with her while Clementine searched for his book.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: A decade older than Clementine, Harriet Ainslie bore so little resemblance to her that their sisterhood seemed scarcely credible. Dark and large of build, she possessed black hair, bushy black eyebrows, and eyes that matched the transparent, slaty blue of gulf waters during a northerly breeze. Although her expression appeared somewhat severe and off-putting, her true disposition was quite cheerful, marked by a robust, bubbling laugh and a rich, smooth, agreeable voice that carried a hint of male quality. On an earlier occasion, she had observed to Clementine that she would genuinely enjoy conversing with that Presbyterian minister at the Glen, aiming to test whether he could muster anything to say to a female if backed into a corner. Having found her opportunity at present, she engaged him regarding global affairs. Being an avid reader, Miss Harriet had recently finished consuming a volume concerning the Kaiser of Germany, and she requested that Mr. Ashdown share his thoughts about him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “A perilous person,” he replied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I take your word for it!” agreed Miss Harriet. “Pay attention to what I say, Mr. Ashdown, because that person will end up in a battle eventually. He craves it. He will cause an absolute sensation.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I scarcely believe he would aimlessly provoke a major conflict, if that is what you are implying,” Mr. Ashdown remarked. “The time for such behavior has passed.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “God bless you, no, it has not,” Harriet boomed. “Not a day passes without people and countries acting foolishly and resorting to fighting. We are not that close to the millennium, Mr. Ashdown, a fact you realize just as well as I. Regarding this Kaiser, pay attention to what I say, he will cause a great deal of difficulty”—and with her slender digit, Miss Harriet jabbed her book forcefully. “Indeed, unless he is stopped early on, he will cause difficulty. It will happen in our lifetime—both you and I will witness it, Mr. Ashdown. And who will stop him? England ought to, yet she will not. Who will stop him? Answer me that, Mr. Ashdown.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Although Mr. Ashdown was unable to inform her, they engaged in a conversation regarding German militarism that continued well past the time Clementine located the volume. Clementine remained silent, sitting instead in a small rocking chair behind Harriet while thoughtfully petting a prominent black cat. John Ashdown pursued large game in Europe alongside Harriet, yet his gaze fell upon Clementine more frequently than upon Harriet, an observation that Harriet did not miss. Following Clementine’s departure to accompany him to the doorway and her subsequent return, Harriet stood up and stared at her with an air of accusation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Clementine Ainslie, it seems to me that man intends to court you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Clementine trembled. She felt as though Harriet’s words were a physical strike. They stripped away all the charm of the enjoyable evening. Nevertheless, she refused to allow Harriet to perceive how much she was wounded by it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Rubbish,” she uttered, giving a chuckle that sounded slightly forced. “Harriet, you imagine a suitor for me behind every tree. Why, he disclosed everything regarding his wife to me this evening—what she meant to him—how devoid of meaning the world became after she died.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Well, he might court in that manner,” Harriet replied. “I gather that men employ all sorts of methods. However, Clementine, remember what you promised.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I have no cause to either put it out of my mind or keep it in mind,” Clementine remarked, somewhat tiredly. “Harriet, you do not remember that I am an old maid. My being yet youthful and flourishing and perilous is nothing more than your sisterly fantasy. Mr. Ashdown simply desires to be a friend—should he even desire that much. Long prior to his return to the manse, he will have forgotten the two of us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “I do not mind if you are friendly with him,” admitted Harriet, “however, keep in mind that it cannot exceed friendship. Widowers always make me suspicious. Romantic notions regarding friendship are not typical for them. Business is what they are likely to mean. Regarding this Presbyterian man, why is he considered shy by people? Absent-minded he might be, yet he is not the least bit shy—his absent-mindedness was so great that he neglected to bid me goodnight as you began walking to the door alongside him. Furthermore, he possesses intelligence. Very few men in these parts are capable of speaking sensibly to a person. The evening was enjoyable to me. Seeing him again would not bother me. Nonetheless, Clementine, remember—no philandering, no philandering.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Harriet frequently cautioned Clementine against flirting whenever she merely conversed for five minutes with any eligible man aged between eighteen and eighty. The admonition had constantly provoked genuine laughter from her in the past. On this occasion, far from entertaining her, it caused her slight irritation. Who harbored any desire to philander?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Harriet, stop being so silly,” she remarked with an unusual sharpness while grabbing her lamp. Leaving without bidding goodnight, she ascended the stairs.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: Harriet, expressing doubt, shook her head while her gaze fell upon the black cat.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: “Why is she in such a bad mood, St. Laurence?” she inquired. “I have always been told, Laurence, that you only yell when you are struck. However, Saint, she gave her word—she gave her word, and members of our family, the Ainslies, never break a promise. Therefore, Laurence, his desire to flirt will be of no consequence. She gave her word. I will not be anxious.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL
text: In her room upstairs, Clementine remained seated for a lengthy period, gazing through the window past the garden bathed in moonlight toward the gleaming, far-off harbour. A indistinct feeling of distress and restlessness washed over her. All at once, she grew weary of faded dreams. Meanwhile, out in the garden, a brief, sudden gust of wind dispersed the petals of the final red rose. Summer had ended—autumn had arrived.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: John Ashdown set off on a unhurried walk toward home. Shortly after starting, his thoughts lingered briefly on Clementine, yet as he arrived at Fern Hollow, she had completely slipped his mind, replaced by contemplation over an aspect of German theology that Harriet had mentioned. Unaware of his surroundings, he traversed Fern Hollow. German theology proved far too compelling for the beauty of Fern Hollow to hold any sway over him. Arriving at the manse, he headed into his study and removed a massive book from the shelf so he could determine whether he or Harriet had held the correct view. He stayed absorbed in its complex arguments until the sun rose, uncovered a fresh line of inquiry, and chased it with relentless determination throughout the following week, entirely detached from society, his congregation, and his relatives. He engrossed himself in reading day and night; whenever Ida was not present to pull him away, he neglected to eat his meals; thoughts of Clementine or Harriet never crossed his mind again. Across the harbor, elderly Mrs. Ambrose became gravely ill and summoned him, yet the note remained ignored upon his desk, collecting dust. Though Mrs. Ambrose pulled through, she never pardoned his absence. A youthful bride and groom arrived at the manse seeking to wed, and Mr. Ashdown performed the ceremony with untidy hair, clad in carpet slippers and a washed-out dressing gown. Indeed, he commenced by reciting the burial rites for their benefit, progressing to the words “ashes to ashes and dust to dust” prior to faintly sensing that an error had occurred.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Dear me,” he remarked in a distracted manner, “that is peculiar—extremely peculiar.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Filled with anxiety, the bride started weeping, while the bridegroom, who felt not even a bit of nervousness, chuckled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “If you please, sir, my belief is that you are burying us rather than marrying us,” he remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Pardon me,” Mr. Ashdown said, as though it was of little consequence. He found the marriage ceremony in the book and finished it, yet for all the days that followed, the bride felt as if she had not been truly wedded.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Once more, he overlooked his prayer-meeting—yet that was of no consequence, since the night was rain-soaked and no one appeared. He could have overlooked his Sunday service as well had Mrs. Hector Twiss not prevented it. On Saturday afternoon, Aunt Martha entered and informed him that Mrs. Twiss was waiting in the parlour to speak with him. A sigh escaped Mr. Ashdown. Within the congregation of Glen St. Agnes church, Mrs. Twiss was the sole woman he thoroughly disliked. Regrettably, she possessed the greatest wealth, and Mr. Ashdown had been cautioned by his board of managers not to displease her. The subject of his stipend was a worldly affair that Mr. Ashdown rarely pondered; the managers, however, were more realistic. Furthermore, they possessed shrewdness. Avoidance of any talk of money did not prevent them from successfully implanting an idea in Mr. Ashdown’s thoughts that Mrs. Twiss must not be angered. Had this not been done, he probably would have dismissed her completely from his memory the moment Aunt Martha departed. Because of this situation, he folded over the page of his Ewald, feeling irritated, and walked across the hallway into the parlour.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Mrs. Twiss sat upon the couch, surveying her surroundings with a expression of disdainful rejection.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: How disgraceful that room was! No curtains hung at the window. Grace and Ida had removed them the previous day for court trains in a play they were putting on and neglected to hang them back up, a fact Mrs. Twiss was unaware of, yet her condemnation of those windows could not have been more intense had she known. Cracked and torn blinds hung there. Crooked pictures adorned the walls; rugs sat askew; faded flowers filled the vases; dust gathered in piles—actual piles.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “What are we coming to?” was the question Mrs. Twiss posed to herself, after which she pursed her unlovely lips.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: As she walked through the hall, Tobias and Rupert were yelling and sliding down the banisters. Unaware of her presence, they kept on yelling and sliding, which Mrs. Twiss felt sure they were doing deliberately. Grace’s pet rooster strolled through the hall, paused in the parlour doorway, and gazed at her. Disliking her appearance, it refrained from entering. Mrs. Twiss let out a disdainful sniff. It was a fine manse, to be sure, in which roosters walked around the halls and stared people down.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Shoo, there,” Mrs. Twiss commanded, thrusting her changeable-silk, flounced parasol in his direction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Adam was shooed away. Because he was an intelligent rooster, and since Mrs. Twiss had personally snapped the necks of a great deal of roosters over her fifty years, she appeared to be surrounded by the aura of an executioner. As the minister entered, Adam hurried through the hall.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
