text: Footwear consisting of slippers and a dressing gown were still worn by Mr. Ashdown, whose dark hair still hung in unkempt locks across his high forehead. Nevertheless, he possessed the appearance of the gentleman he was; whereas Mrs. Hector Twiss, dressed in her silk gown, beplumed bonnet, kid gloves, and gold chain, appeared to be the vulgar, coarse-souled woman she was. The hostility of each other's personality was felt by both of them. While Mr. Ashdown recoiled, Mrs. Twiss prepared herself for battle. Her purpose in coming to the manse was to suggest a particular matter to the minister, a suggestion she intended to make without delay. She was about to bestow upon him a favor—a major favor—and informing him of it as quickly as possible was ideal. Having pondered it throughout the entire summer, she had finally reached a resolution. In the opinion of Mrs. Twiss, this was the only thing that counted. Whenever she settled on something, settled it remained. No one else was entitled to an opinion on the subject. Such had perpetually been her stance. Upon resolving to wed Hector Twiss, she wedded him, and that concluded the affair. The way it occurred was something Hector had never understood, but what difference did that make? Likewise in this instance—Mrs. Twiss had organized every detail to her own contentment. It was now merely a matter of notifying Mr. Ashdown.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Could you close that door, if you don't mind?” requested Mrs. Twiss, loosening her lips just a bit to speak, though her tone was harsh. “There is something crucial I must discuss, which is impossible with all that noise coming from the hallway.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Submissively, Mr. Ashdown closed the door. Following that, he took a seat in front of Mrs. Twiss. He remained partially oblivious to her presence. The points made by Ewald were still being contested within his thoughts. This distance was detected by Mrs. Twiss, and it irritated her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “In a belligerent tone, she declared, “Mr. Ashdown, I am here to inform you of my choice to adopt Ida.””

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “To—adopt—Ida!” blankly staring at her, Mr. Ashdown failed entirely to comprehend.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Indeed. My mind has been on this matter for a while now. Ever since my husband passed away, the thought of taking in a child has frequently crossed my mind. However, finding a fitting one appeared to be quite difficult. There are hardly any children that I would desire to bring into my household. Taking a home child—most likely some slum outcast—is something I would never consider. Furthermore, almost no other sort of child is ever available. Last autumn, a harbour fisherman passed away and left behind six children. An attempt was made to persuade me to take one, yet I quickly let them know that I entertained no thought of adopting such rubbish. A horse was stolen by their grandfather. On top of that, every one of them was a boy, whereas I desired a female child—a calm, dutiful girl whom I could raise to become a lady. Ida will fit my needs perfectly. Provided she receives proper care, she would be a pleasant child—completely unlike Grace. Adopting Grace is something I would not contemplate for a moment. However, I will adopt Ida and provide her with a fine home and raising, Mr. Ashdown, and provided her conduct is good, my entire fortune will be willed to her upon my death. In any event, not a single penny of it will go to any of my own family members; my mind is firmly made up about that. In truth, the thought of irritating them inspired my desire to take in a child as much as any other reason at the start. Ida will receive fine clothing, education, and instruction, Mr. Ashdown, and I will see that she gets lessons in music and painting, caring for her as though she were my very own.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: By this moment, Mr. Ashdown had become fully awake. A pale blush appeared on his pallid cheek, while a perilous gleam shone in his handsome dark eyes. Could this female, whose coarseness and awareness of wealth seeped from every part of her, really be requesting that he bestow Ida upon her—his precious, small, yearning Ida who possessed the very same dark-blue eyes as Cecilia—the youngster whom her expiring mother had hugged to her chest when the remaining youngsters had been escorted crying out of the chamber. Cecilia had held tightly to her infant right up to the moment when the doors of death had closed between them. Across the small dark head, her gaze had met her husband's.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Look after her well, John,” she had begged. “She is extremely small—and easily hurt. The rest are able to battle for themselves—however, she will be wounded by the world. Oh, John, I am uncertain how you and she will manage. The two of you require me to such a degree. Nevertheless, hold her near to you—hold her near to you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Except for a handful of unerasable phrases meant solely for him, these had been practically her final statements. Yet Mrs. Twiss had unfeelingly declared that she planned to remove this very child from his care. Straightening his posture, he gazed at Mrs. Twiss. Regardless of his tattered slippers and threadbare dressing gown, an aspect of his presence compelled Mrs. Twiss to experience a slight touch of that former veneration for “the cloth” instilled in her youth. Ultimately, a distinct aura of sacredness surrounded a clergyman, even one who was impoverished, impractical, and preoccupied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Mrs. Twiss, I am grateful for your good intentions,” Mr. Ashdown said with a courteousness that was gentle, decisive, and entirely terrifying, “nevertheless, my child cannot be given to you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Mrs. Twiss’s expression was uncomprehending. His refusal was something she had not ever imagined.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Why, Mr. Ashdown,” she uttered, amazed. “You are surely cr—this cannot be your intention. It is necessary that you reconsider—reflect upon every benefit I am able to offer her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Mrs. Twiss, thinking it over is unnecessary. The matter is completely impossible. Whatever earthly benefits you are capable of granting her could never make up for being deprived of a father’s affection and guidance. Once more, I offer my thanks—however, it cannot be considered.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Her customary self-restraint was overwhelmed by the rage of her letdown. Mrs. Twiss’s wide, ruddy visage flushed dark violet, and she spoke with a shaking tone.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “I assumed you would be more than happy to give her to me,” she sneered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “What made you believe that?” Mr. Ashdown inquired softly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Since no one ever believed you had any regard for any of your offspring,” Mrs. Twiss shot back disdainfully. “Your disregard of them is disgraceful. Everyone in town is talking about it. Their nourishment and attire are inadequate, and they receive zero discipline. A band of untamed savages possesses just as much politeness as they do. Performing your fatherly obligations never enters your mind. You permitted an unfamiliar youngster to stay with them for two weeks without paying her the slightest attention—a kid who used the language of a soldier from what I hear. It would not have bothered you if she had infected them with small-pox. Furthermore, Grace publicly humiliated herself by standing up to deliver a sermon and giving that address! On top of that, she traveled on a swine through the town—directly in front of your own face as I comprehend it. Their behavior exceeds credibility, yet you do not raise a hand to halt their conduct or attempt to instruct them in any way. Now, after I provide one of them with a fine residence and favorable future possibilities, you decline the proposal and affront me. What a splendid parent you are, speaking about cherishing and watching over your children!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “That will suffice, woman!” Mr. Ashdown said. Rising to his feet, he gazed at Mrs. Twiss with an expression that caused her to shrink back. “That will suffice,” he said again. “I wish to listen to nothing further, Mrs. Twiss. You have spoken excessively. Perhaps I have been negligent regarding certain aspects of my parental responsibility, yet you are not the one to bring it to my attention using the words you employed. We shall bid each other good afternoon.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Mrs. Twiss failed to utter anything even remotely as pleasant as good afternoon, yet she made her exit. While she moved grandly past the clergyman, a big, chubby toad, which Rupert had hidden beneath the couch, leaped forth right beneath her feet. Mrs. Twiss uttered a scream, and while attempting to keep from stepping upon the terrible creature, she surrendered her equilibrium and her sunshade. She failed to go down completely, yet she stumbled and swayed through the room in a most unseemly manner, coming to a halt against the door with a impact that shook her whole body. Mr. Ashdown, having missed seeing the toad, speculated whether she was suffering from some type of stroke or fit, and hurried in fright to help her. However, Mrs. Twiss, regaining her footing, angrily motioned for him to stay away.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “Do not presume to lay a finger on me,” she nearly yelled. “I assume this is yet another piece of your children’s mischief. No respectable woman belongs in a location like this. Hand over my umbrella and allow my departure. Never again will I step foot inside your church or your manse.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: Mr. Ashdown submissively gathered up the splendid parasol and handed it to her. Mrs. Twiss grabbed it and strode away outside. Tobias and Rupert had stopped sliding down the banister and were perched alongside Grace on the veranda's edge. Regrettably, the trio was belting out “There’ll be a hot time in the old town to-night” as loudly as their vigorous young lungs allowed. Mrs. Twiss convinced herself that the tune was directed exclusively at her. Pausing, she brandished her parasol toward them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “The father who raised you lacks any sense,” she remarked, “and the three of you are little scoundrels who deserve a thrashing that stops just short of killing you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “He is not,” Grace exclaimed. “We are not,” exclaimed the boys. Mrs. Twiss, however, had departed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: “My word, she is certainly insane!” Tobias remarked. “Also, what does ‘varmint’ actually mean?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: For several minutes, John Ashdown walked back and forth in the parlour, after which he returned to his study to sit down. However, he failed to go back to his German theology. He was far too deeply troubled to do so. Mrs. Twiss had stirred him awake with a vengeance. Could he really be the negligent, heedless father she had charged him with being? Had he truly so shockingly disregarded the physical and spiritual well-being of the four young motherless children relying on him? Were his parishioners discussing the matter as severely as Mrs. Twiss had asserted? It had to be true, because Mrs. Twiss had arrived to request Ida under the complete and certain conviction that he would surrender the child to her just as indifferently and pleased as someone might surrender a wandering, unwanted kitten. And, if this was true, what was to follow?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: A groan escaped John Ashdown as he restarted his walking back and forth across the untidy, dust-covered room. What course was open to him? His affection for his children was as profound as that of any father, and no effort by Mrs. Twiss or others of her type could alter his certainty that their devotion to him was equally deep. Yet was he suited to be responsible for them? Nobody understood his own shortcomings and boundaries better than he did. The situation required the guidance, sensible nature, and attendance of a fine woman. Still, in what manner could this be brought about? Supposing he managed to hire that sort of housekeeper, Aunt Martha would be deeply hurt. In her own mind, she was still capable of performing every required and fitting task. He was unable to inflict such pain and offense upon the needy elderly woman who had shown such goodness to him and his family. Her devotion to Cecilia had been so great! Furthermore, Cecilia had requested that he show great thoughtfulness toward Aunt Martha. Indeed, a sudden recollection came to him that Aunt Martha had previously suggested he should take a second wife. He sensed that a wife would not offend her in the way a housekeeper would. Nevertheless, that remained impossible. Marriage was not his desire—he possessed no affection for anyone, nor could he develop it. What option remained for him then? The thought abruptly struck him to travel to Hollowmere so he could discuss his troubles with Mrs. Carrow. Mrs. Carrow belonged to that small group of women in whose company he never experienced shyness or a loss for words. Her nature was constantly so understanding and invigorating. There was a chance she might propose a remedy for his troubles. Even if that proved impossible, Mr. Ashdown was aware of his need for a bit of proper human company following his encounter with Mrs. Twiss—an experience to remove her lingering flavor from his spirit.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: He put on his clothes in a rush and consumed his evening meal with fewer distractions than he normally had. The thought struck him that the food was mediocre. He inspected his offspring; their complexions were rosy and they appeared sufficiently robust—with the exception of Ida, who had not possessed much strength even during her mother’s lifetime. The whole group was giggling and chatting—indubitably, they appeared joyful. Rupert felt particularly joyful on account of two exceedingly lovely spiders traversing the area around his dinner plate. Their tones were agreeable, their etiquette appeared acceptable, and they showed thoughtfulness and kindness toward each other. Nevertheless, Mrs. Twiss had stated that the way they acted was being discussed by the entire congregation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL
text: When Mr. Ashdown passed through his gate, Dr. Carrow and Mrs. Carrow rode by on the highway heading toward Kettlebridge. A disappointed look crossed the clergyman's face. Since Mrs. Carrow was leaving, traveling to Hollowmere would be pointless. Yet his desire for some company was stronger than ever. Looking out over the countryside with a feeling of despair, the rays of the setting sun caught a windowpane of the former Ainslie house situated on the hill. It gleamed with a rosy glow like a signal of optimism. Clementine and Harriet Ainslie came unexpectedly to his mind. He reflected that he would enjoy hearing a bit of Harriet's sharp talk. He reflected that it would be delightful to behold Clementine's gentle, unhurried smile and serene, celestial blue eyes once more. How did that ancient poem by Sir Philip Sidney go?—“continual comfort in a face”—those words described her perfectly. Furthermore, he was in need of solace. What reason was there not to pay them a visit? He recalled Harriet requesting that he drop by occasionally, plus he had Clementine's volume to return—it was proper to return it prior to forgetting. He possessed a troubling thought that his study contained numerous volumes he had taken on loan on various occasions and from different locations, failing to return them. It was certainly his obligation to ensure he avoided doing so on this occasion. Re-entering his study, he retrieved the volume, and descended into Fern Hollow.

Miss Winifred and Mary Stubbs journeyed to Hollowmere on the evening following the burial of Mrs. Myra Murray from the over-harbour section. Miss Winifred desired to relieve her spirit regarding various matters. Naturally, the complete details of the funeral required thorough discussion. Miss Winifred and Tabitha debated this topic back and forth; Nell found no pleasure in these gruesome dialogues and refrained from joining in. Sitting slightly separated from them, she observed the dahlias' fall glow throughout the garden, alongside the serene, enchanting harbor framed by the September sunset. Mary Stubbs was seated next to her, quietly engaged in knitting. Although Mary's thoughts were anchored down in the Fern Hollow, where gentle, muted echoes of laughing children drifted from, Miss Winifred kept watch over her hands. A set quantity of stocking rounds had to be completed prior to her departure for the valley. Mary continued her knitting and remained silent, though she listened attentively.

“No deceased person ever possessed a finer appearance,” stated Miss Winifred with expert judgment. “A lovely female was what Myra Murray had constantly been—her maiden name was Corey from Kettlebridge, a family famed for being handsome.”

“When I went by the body, I uttered to it, ‘poor woman. I wish you to be as joyous as you appear.’” Tabitha exhaled. “She was not greatly altered. The gown on her was the black satin acquired fourteen years back for the marriage of her daughter. At that time, her Aunt advised her to save it for her burial, yet Myra chuckled and replied, ‘I might be dressed in it for my burial, Aunty, but I shall enjoy myself in it beforehand.’ And it is fair to state she accomplished that. Myra Murray was not the type of person to go to her own burial prior to her death. On numerous occasions later on, observing her having a fine time among others, I reflected to myself, ‘You are a fine-looking woman, Myra Murray, and that gown suits you, yet it will probably end up as your burial clothes.’ And as you can observe, my statement has proven accurate, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr.”
Tabitha let out another deep sigh. She was having a wonderful time. Discussing a funeral was truly an enjoyable topic.

“I was always fond of seeing Myra,” Miss Winifred stated. “She possessed such constant gaiety and cheerfulness—her greeting alone sufficed to improve your spirits. Myra invariably turned everything to good account.”

“That is correct,” Tabitha affirmed. “I was informed by her sister-in-law that upon being finally notified by the physician that his efforts were futile and her confinement to that bed was permanent, Myra remarked with considerable cheer, ‘Well, if such is the case, I am grateful that all the preserving has been completed, and I am spared from undergoing the autumn house-cleaning. Spring house-cleaning was always to my liking,’ she remarks, ‘whereas I invariably despised doing it in the autumn. Thank goodness, I shall escape it this year.’ Certain individuals might label such a remark as lightmindedness, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, and it seemed to me that her sister-in-law felt somewhat embarrassed by it. She suggested that Myra’s illness might have rendered her somewhat delirious. However, I replied, ‘No, Mrs. Murray, let this not distress you. It was merely Myra’s manner of seeing the positive side.’”

“Her sister Luella was the exact reverse,” Miss Winifred said. “Luella saw no bright side—for her, only black and gray shades existed. Throughout many years, she was constantly asserting that her death would occur within about a week. ‘I won’t be here to burden you long,’ she was accustomed to telling her family while groaning. Furthermore, if a single one of them dared to speak of their modest upcoming plans, she would groan as well and utter, ‘Ah, I won’t be here then.’ Whenever I visited her, I invariably concurred with her statements, which infuriated her to the point that she became considerably improved for a number of days following. Her health is superior now, yet she possesses no additional cheerfulness. Myra differed greatly. Making somebody feel good through her actions or words was her constant habit. It may be that the husbands they wedded were partially responsible. Luella’s husband was a Tartar, take my word for it, whereas Saul Murray was respectable, as far as men are concerned. He appeared grief-stricken today. Feeling pity for a man during the burial of his wife is a rare thing for me, yet my sympathies truly went out to Saul Murray.”

“It is no surprise that he appeared mournful. A spouse such as Myra will not come his way again anytime soon,” Tabitha remarked. “Perhaps he will refrain from trying, given that his offspring are fully grown and Mirabel can manage the home. However, one cannot foresee the actions of a widower, and I, personally, shall not attempt to.”

“Myra will be terribly missed by us in church,” Miss Winifred remarked. “She was a true worker. She was never stumped by anything. Whenever a difficulty couldn’t be gotten over by her, she’d get around it, and whenever she couldn’t get around it, she’d act like it didn’t exist—and usually it didn’t. ‘I’ll keep a stiff upper lip to my journey’s end,’ she stated to me one time. Well, her journey has been ended by her.”

“Is that what you believe?” inquired Nell abruptly, returning from her daydream. “I am unable to imagine her travels having come to a close. Are you able to envision her seated with her hands folded—that earnest, inquiring soul she possessed, along with its splendid, daring perspective? No, it is my belief that when she died she simply unlocked a portal and passed across—forward—forward—toward fresh, brilliant quests.”

“Maybe—maybe,” Miss Winifred agreed. “Do you know, Nell dearie, I myself was never very drawn to this eternal rest doctrine—although I hope saying so isn’t heresy. In heaven, I want to bustle around just like here. And I hope pies and doughnuts will have a celestial equivalent—something that requires BEING MADE. Naturally, a person does grow terribly tired at times—and you grow tireder the older you get. But you would think the very tiredest could become rested in less time than eternity—except, perhaps, for a lazy man.”
“I want to see Myra Murray, when I encounter her once more,” Nell said, “approaching me in her usual brisk and laughing manner, exactly as she continually used to do in this place.”
“Oh, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked, sounding horrified, “you certainly cannot believe that Myra is going to be laughing in the next life?”
“What is the reason, Tabitha? Is it your belief that our tears will fall in that place?”
“No, no, Mrs. Dr. dear, do not misinterpret my meaning. It is my belief that we will neither be weeping nor laughing.”
“Then what?”
“Well,” said Tabitha, forced into speaking, “Mrs. Dr. dear, I believe that our only course is to appear devout and grave.”
“And do you truly believe, Tabitha,” inquired Nell, appearing sufficiently grave, “that either Myra Murray or myself could appear grave and pious constantly—constantly, Tabitha?”

“Well,” Tabitha conceded hesitantly, “I could perhaps agree that each of you would need to grin occasionally, yet I am unable to ever acknowledge that laughter exists in heaven. That notion appears truly disrespectful, Mrs. Dr. dear.”

“Well, returning to earth,” Miss Winifred said, “who is available for us to secure for Myra’s class in Sunday School? Since Myra fell ill, Julia Clow has been its teacher, but with her moving to town for the winter, we must acquire someone else.”
“I was told that Mrs. Laurie Jamieson was interested in it,” Nell remarked. “Since relocating to the Glen from Kettlebridge, the Jamiesons have attended church on a very regular basis.”
“Fresh sweepers!” expressed Miss Winifred with hesitation. “Hold off until they have attended consistently over twelve months.”

“Mrs. Dr. dear, Mrs. Jamieson is not someone you can rely on at all,” Tabitha remarked with gravity. “Having passed away on one occasion, she actually returned to life right when they were taking her measurements for a coffin, following a truly lovely laying out! So, Mrs. Dr. dear, it is clear that a woman of that sort is not to be depended upon.”

“It’s possible she could become a Methodist whenever,” Miss Winifred remarked. “I am informed that they attended the Methodist Church in Kettlebridge just as frequently as the Presbyterian one. So far, I haven't seen them doing so in this place, but allowing Mrs. Jamieson to join the Sunday School would not meet with my approval. Even so, causing them offense is something we cannot do. Too many of our members are being lost, either because they die or lose their tempers. Having departed from the church, Mrs. Hector Twiss left without anybody understanding the reason. The managers were informed by her that Mr. Ashdown’s salary would never receive another cent from her. Naturally, the majority of folks claim she was insulted by the children, yet I somehow doubt that. Although I attempted to elicit information from Grace, the only thing she revealed was that Mrs. Twiss arrived to visit her father, appearing in very pleasant spirits, and departed in a terrible fury, referring to every one of them as ‘varmints!’”

“Varmints, indeed!” Tabitha exclaimed in an angry manner. “Is Mrs. Hector Twiss forgetting that the uncle she had through her mother was believed to have poisoned his spouse? It was never actually proven, my dear Mrs. Dr., and one shouldn't trust everything one hears. Nevertheless, were I to possess an uncle whose spouse passed away with no clear cause, I wouldn't travel across the land referring to blameless youths as varmints.”

“It comes down to this,” Miss Winifred stated, “that a substantial subscription was provided by Mrs. Twiss, and covering that deficit presents a real difficulty. Furthermore, should she manage to influence the remaining Fairlies against Mr. Ashdown, which she undoubtedly will attempt, his departure will be inevitable.”
“I do not believe Mrs. Hector Twiss is particularly popular among the other members of the family,” Tabitha remarked. “She probably will not manage to affect their thinking.”

“However, those Fairlies are all so united. Should you affect one, you affect them all. It is beyond doubt that we cannot manage without them. One half of the salary comes from them. Whatever other accusations are made against them, they are not stingy. Before his departure long ago, Lionel Fairlie was accustomed to contribute a hundred every year.”
“Why did he depart?” inquired Nell.

“He stated that a deal involving a cow was cheated out of him by a member of the session. For twenty years, he has failed to attend church. While she was living, poor thing, his wife brought herself regularly, yet he insisted she never contribute anything beyond a single red cent each Sunday. She experienced terrible humiliation. I am not certain if his treatment of her as a husband was particularly good, even if no complaints were ever heard from her. However, her expression was invariably cowed. Thirty years ago, the woman desired by Lionel Fairlie was not the one he obtained, and second best was something the Fairlies never cared to tolerate.”
“Which woman was the one he actually desired.”

“Harriet Ainslie. Although they were not precisely engaged, if I am not mistaken, their companionship lasted for two years. Then their relationship abruptly ended—without anyone ever learning the reason. It was merely a foolish disagreement, in my opinion. Lionel then proceeded to marry Dinah Coyle prior to his anger subsiding—doing so solely to inflict hurt on Harriet, I am entirely convinced. Typical male behavior! While Dinah was a pleasant young woman, she lacked a strong will, and he crushed the slight resolve she possessed. Her docility was excessive for Lionel. A wife capable of confronting him was what he required. Harriet would have managed him splendidly, an arrangement he would have appreciated far more. The reality is that he held Dinah in contempt simply owing to her constant submission. Years ago, in his youth, I frequently overheard his declaration ‘Give me a spunky woman—spunk for me every time.’ Yet he subsequently chose a bride who lacked the courage to utter a word—just like a man. Every member of that Coyle family was a mere vegetable. Despite performing the routines of existence, they possessed no real vitality.”

“When Russell Coyle wed his second bride, he utilized the wedding-ring from his first,” Tabitha recalled. “In my judgment, Mrs. Dr. dear, that was overly frugal. Furthermore, John, who is his brother, erected his own gravestone in the graveyard over the harbour, complete with all details except his date of death, and he visits and gazes upon it each Sunday. While the majority of people would fail to see the pleasure in that, he clearly finds it enjoyable. Individuals certainly possess varied notions regarding what is fun. Turning to Lionel Fairlie, that man is a complete pagan. Upon being questioned by the previous minister about his complete absence from church, he answered ‘The women there are too unattractive, parson—far too unattractive!’ Mrs. Dr. dear, I would love to approach a person like that and gravely declare, ‘Hell truly exists!’”

“Oh, Lionel denies the existence of such a location,” stated Miss Winifred. “It is my hope that his error becomes clear to him as he approaches death. Now, Mary, having completed your three knitted inches, you are permitted to join the children at play for thirty minutes.”

No further encouragement was required for Mary. With her heart matching the swiftness of her feet, she hurried to Fern Hollow, where, during their talk, she imparted every detail regarding Mrs. Hector Twiss to Grace Ashdown.

“And Mrs. Kerr states that she will cause every Fairlie to oppose your father, forcing him to depart from the Glen due to his salary going unpaid,” Mary ended. “Honest to goodness, I am at a loss as to what should be done. Things would not be quite so terrible if old Lionel Fairlie would simply return to church and resume paying. However, he will refuse to do so—the Fairlies will depart—and every one of you will be compelled to leave.”

Grace retired for the night with a burden of sorrow weighing upon her. It was impossible to endure the idea of departing from the Glen. The Carrows were companions unmatched anywhere on earth. Her young heart had experienced deep agony during their departure from Juneford—numerous painful tears had been wept by her as she said goodbye to her friends in Juneford and the ancient manse situated there, where her mother had spent her life and passed away. The prospect of experiencing a similar and even more painful separation was something she could not peacefully consider. Departing from Glen St. Agnes, beloved Fern Hollow, and that delightful cemetery was simply beyond her.

“Being a minister’s family is terrible,” Grace lamented, her face buried in her pillow. “The moment you begin to love a location, you get uprooted. I will never, ever, ever wed a minister, regardless of how wonderful he might be.”

Upright in her bed, Grace gazed through the small, vine-draped window. Nothing disturbed the profound stillness of the night except the gentle sound of Ida’s breath, leaving Grace with a dreadful sense of loneliness. Below her lay Glen St. Agnes, resting beneath the star-filled, azure expanses of the autumn sky. Across the valley, a lamp glowed in the girls’ bedroom at Hollowmere, while a second light beamed from the chamber belonging to Edmund, prompting Grace to wonder whether toothache was plaguing poor Edmund once more. A brief, envious sigh escaped her as she thought of Bess and Izzy, who possessed both a mother and an established home, unlike herself, exposed to the whims of individuals who flew into unprovoked rages and branded one a varmint. Farther past the Glen, surrounded by sleeping, silent pastures, yet another lamp flickered, which Grace recognized as emanating from the residence of Lionel Fairlie. According to rumor, he remained awake reading until the late hours of the night. Mary had remarked that if he could merely be persuaded to rejoin the church, harmony would be restored. What reason was there to doubt it? As Grace observed a prominent, low-lying star hovering above the high, sharp-topped spruce standing by the entrance of the Methodist Church, a sudden idea struck her. Understanding the necessary course of action, Grace Ashdown resolved that she herself would undertake it to rectify the entire situation. Contentedly sighing, she shifted away from the desolate, pitch-black world outside and snuggled up beside Ida.

With Grace, coming to a decision meant taking immediate action. She wasted no time in executing her plan. Following her return from school the following day, she departed the manse and went down the Glen. Edmund Carrow fell in with her when she went by the post office.
“Mother sent me on an errand to Mrs. Kerr’s house,” he said. “Grace, where are you heading?”

“I am going somewhere on church business,” Grace stated haughtily. Because she offered no extra details, Edmund felt somewhat rejected. A short period of quiet followed as they continued walking. Warmth and wind filled the night, which possessed a pleasant, piney fragrance. Gray, gentle, and lovely waters lay past the sand dunes. Carrying a cargo of crimson and gold leaves, the Glen stream resembled magical boats. Within the buckwheat stubble-land belonging to Mr. James Coyle, which displayed lovely shades of brown and red, a crow parliament convened to conduct serious discussions concerning the well-being of crowland. Grace heartlessly disrupted the grand gathering when she scaled the fence and launched a fractured rail toward it. Right away, noisy caws and beating dark wings crowded the atmosphere.
“What made you do that?” Edmund asked accusingly. “They were enjoying themselves so much.”

“Oh, I detest crows,” Grace remarked breezily. “They have such dark feathers and sneaky ways that I am certain they are deceitful. You see, they rob the eggs of small birds right from their nests. I witnessed a crow doing that very thing on our lawn during the previous spring. Edmund, why is your face so pale today? Were you suffering from that toothache once more during the night?”
A shudder ran through Edmund.

“Indeed—it was terrible. Sleep was completely impossible for me—consequently, I simply walked back and forth across the room and pictured myself as a martyr from the early Christian era undergoing torment on Nero’s orders. For a period, that provided a great deal of relief—and after that, my condition deteriorated to the point where my imagination failed me entirely.”
“Were you crying?” Grace asked with concern.

“No—yet I stretched out on the floor and groaned,” Edmund admitted. “Thereupon the girls entered, and Bess placed cayenne pepper inside it—which aggravated it—Izzy forced me to keep a gulp of cold water inside my mouth—and I was unable to endure it, so they summoned Tabitha. Tabitha stated that it served me right because I sat up in the chilly garret yesterday composing poetry trash. However, she kindled the kitchen fire and fetched me a hot-water bottle, which halted the toothache. The moment I felt improved, I informed Tabitha that my poetry was not trash and that she was no judge. Then she remarked no, thank goodness she was not, and she possessed no knowledge concerning poetry other than it was largely a heap of lies. Now you are aware, Grace, that is not true. That represents one reason I enjoy composing poetry—you are able to state so many matters within it that are true within poetry but would not be true within prose. I informed Tabitha as much, yet she instructed me to cease my jawing and get to sleep before the water cooled down, or she would abandon me to discover whether rhyming would heal a toothache, and she trusted it would prove to be a lesson to me.”
“Why do you not head over to Kettlebridge to see the dentist and have that tooth removed?”
Edmund shivered again.
“They wish for me to—yet I am unable to. The pain would be immense.”
“Does a bit of hurt frighten you?” Grace inquired scornfully.
Edmund flushed.
“Being injured is something I despise, and it would cause great suffering. My decision to depart must be made by me first, as Father mentioned he would not force my leaving until then.”

“The pain would not endure for as great a duration as the toothache,” Grace contended, “Five bouts of toothache have afflicted you. Should you simply attend an appointment to possess it extracted, subsequent unpleasant nights would cease. A tooth was extracted from me on one occasion. My cries lasted for a brief instant, yet everything concluded thereafter—save for the hemorrhaging.”

“What’s most terrible is the bleeding—it is so hideous,” Edmund exclaimed. “Last summer, when Kit sliced his foot, it simply nauseated me. Tabitha mentioned that I appeared closer to passing out than Kit himself. Yet seeing Kit injured was something I could not endure, either. People are constantly being injured, Grace—and it is terrible. Seeing anything in pain is simply unbearable for me. It creates an urge in me to just run—and run—and run—until they are beyond my hearing or sight.”

“It is pointlessly dramatic to make a scene when someone suffers an injury,” Grace remarked, shaking her ringlets. “Naturally, you must cry out if your injury is severe—plus blood causes a mess—and I also dislike watching others suffer. However, running away holds no appeal for me—my wish is to proceed to work and assist them. On many occasions, your father must inflict pain on people so as to heal them. If he fled, what would become of them?”

“I never stated that I was going to run; I merely expressed a desire to do so, which is not the same. Assisting others is also something I wish to do. However, I truly desire a world free from hideous and terrible realities, where all things are instead joyful and lovely.”

“Well, let us not ponder things that do not exist,” Grace remarked. “When all is said and done, existing offers plenty of enjoyment. Being dead would mean no toothache for you, yet wouldn’t being alive be far preferable to being dead? For my part, I would choose it a hundredfold. Oh, Dan Coyle is approaching. His trip down to the harbour was to get fish.”
“I detest Dan Coyle,” Edmund stated.
“I feel the same way. Every one of us girls does. I intend to just stroll by without giving him any attention whatsoever. Keep your eyes on me!”
Grace therefore strutted by Dan, her chin thrust forward and her face wearing a disdainful look that deeply wounded his spirit. Turning around, he yelled toward her retreating back.
“Pig-girl! Pig-girl!! Pig-girl!!!” with a growing intensity of offense.

Grace continued forward, appearing unaware. Nevertheless, her lip shook just a bit from a feeling of indignation. She recognized that she could not compete with Dan Coyle in swapping insults. She desired that Kit Carrow had accompanied her rather than Edmund. Had Dan Coyle ventured to term her a pig-girl while Kit was listening, Kit would have knocked him into the dust. Yet Grace never thought to look to Edmund for that, or hold it against him for failing to do so. Edmund, as she was aware, did not engage in fights with other boys. Wilfred Clow from the north road was the same. The odd thing was, whereas she looked down on Wilfred as a coward, she never thought to look down on Edmund. It was merely that he appeared to her as a resident of his very own realm, where other customs ruled. Grace would just as readily have anticipated a starry-eyed young angel to beat up filthy, freckled Dan Coyle on her behalf as Edmund Carrow. She would have held nothing against the angel and she held nothing against Edmund Carrow. Yet she longed for robust Kit or Tobias to have been present and Dan’s affront kept stinging her spirit.

The paleness had left Edmund's face. A deep crimson flush covered him, and shame and fury dimmed his lovely eyes. That he should have taken revenge for Grace was clear to him. Kit would have jumped straight into the fray and forced Dan to swallow his statements with bitter seasoning. Ritchie Warren would have flooded Dan with even nastier "names" than those Dan had used against Grace. Yet Edmund was incapable—utterly incapable—of "calling names." He was certain that he would be defeated. The crude, lewd taunts that Dan Coyle wielded in endless supply were things he could neither imagine nor speak. Furthermore, regarding a combat with fists, Edmund had no ability to fight. The thought of it repelled him. It was violent and sore—and, most terrible of all, it was hideous. Kit’s joy in a periodic brawl remained totally incomprehensible to him. Even so, he longed to be able to beat Dan Coyle. Extreme humiliation consumed him because Grace Ashdown had suffered an insult while he stood by, and he had made no effort to avenge her. It seemed certain to him that she held him in contempt. She had refrained from addressing a single word to him after Dan had labeled her pig-girl. When the point arrived where their paths split, he experienced relief.

Grace also felt relief, but her reasons were not the same. Her desire for solitude stemmed from a sudden wave of apprehension regarding her mission. The initial spark had faded, particularly after Dan damaged her pride. Although she was bound to complete the task, her driving passion had vanished. Her purpose was to visit Lionel Fairlie and request his return to church, yet she was starting to dread him. The undertaking that appeared so straightforward and uncomplicated back at the Glen appeared quite otherwise in this location. Rumors about Lionel Fairlie had reached her ears, and she was aware that even the oldest students at school feared him. What if he insulted her with a cruel name—she understood he was prone to such behavior. Insults were unbearable to Grace—they broke her spirit much faster than a physical hit. Nevertheless, she was determined to proceed—Grace Ashdown never backed down. Failing to do so might force her father to depart from the Glen.

Reaching the conclusion of the lengthy lane, Grace arrived at the dwelling—a spacious, ancient-style residence flanked by a line of disciplined Lombardies. Lionel Fairlie sat in person upon the rear veranda, engaged in reading a newspaper. His large canine companion remained by his side. From the rear, within the kitchen, a noisy rattling of tableware echoed from where his housekeeper, Mrs. Wilson, prepared the evening meal—a furious rattling, because Lionel Fairlie had recently engaged in a dispute with Mrs. Wilson, leaving each of them in a dreadful mood as a result. As a consequence, the moment Grace walked onto the veranda and Lionel Fairlie dropped his newspaper, she encountered the fiery gaze of a deeply annoyed individual.

In his own manner, Lionel Fairlie was a somewhat handsome figure. Across his wide chest cascaded a long red beard, and his large head bore a thick mane of red hair that remained untouched by grey despite his age. No wrinkles marked his tall, pale forehead, and the intensity of his stormy youth could still ignite his blue eyes. Depending on his whim, he possessed the capacity to be exceedingly charming or exceptionally frightening. Intent with such worry on fixing the circumstance concerning the church, poor Grace had encountered him during one of these frightening states.

Because he was unaware of her identity, his look toward her was one of dislike. Girls possessing laughter, fire, and high spirits were what Lionel Fairlie preferred. Grace appeared extremely pale right now. Colour was vital to the kind of appearance she possessed. Without the red in her cheeks, she came across as humble and downright ordinary. Her demeanor was fearful and full of regret, which aroused the aggressive nature within Lionel Fairlie’s heart.
“Who on earth are you? And what brings you here?” he asked with a fierce frown, speaking in his deep, echoing voice.

Grace lacked any response, a rare moment in her life. Never had she imagined that Lionel Fairlie possessed such a nature. Horror of him left her completely immobilized. Noticing her reaction, he became even more intense.
“What is wrong with you?” he bellowed. “Your expression suggests you wish to speak but are afraid to do so. What is bothering you? Dammit, can you not speak out?”
Negative. Grace was unable to utter a sound. She could produce no speech. Her lips, however, started to shake.

“In heaven’s name, stop weeping,” Lionel yelled. “Sniffling is something I cannot tolerate. Speak up and finish it if you have something to tell me. Holy Kitty, does a mute demon hold this girl? Stop staring at me in that manner—I am a man—there is no tail on me! Who might you be—I demand to know, who are you?”

The sound of Lionel’s voice was loud enough to reach the harbour. All activity within the kitchen came to a halt. Listening intently, Mrs. Wilson kept her eyes and ears wide open. Placing his massive, tan hands upon his knees, Lionel bent ahead and fixed his gaze on the pale, cowering face of Grace. To her, he appeared to tower above like a wicked giant from a storybook. It seemed to her that he was about to consume her entirely, flesh and bones included.
“Grace—Ashdown—am—I,” she stated, speaking barely above a whisper.

“Ashdown, is it? One of the parson’s kids, is it? I’ve heard about you—I’ve heard about you! Pig-riding and Sabbath-breaking! A fine crowd! What are you after here, is it? What are you after from the old pagan, is it? I do not request favours from parsons—and I do not grant any. What are you after, I ask?”
Grace desired to be a thousand miles from that place. Hesitantly, she uttered her idea in all its plain directness.
“My purpose in coming—was to request that you—attend church—and contribute—toward the wage.”
Lionel stared angrily at her. After that, he erupted once more.
“You insolent baggage—you! Who instigated you to do this, jade? Who instigated you to do this?”
“No one,” answered unhappy Grace.

“That is untruthful. Do not utter falsehoods to me! Who directed you to this place? It was not your father—he lacks the courage of a flea—yet he would not dispatch you to perform what he dared not attempt on his own. I presume it was certain of those dratted elderly spinsters at the Glen, was it not—was it, eh?”
“No—I—I merely arrived on my own.”
“Have you pegged me as an idiot?” yelled Lionel.
“No—it was my belief that you were a gentleman,” Grace whispered softly, and she truly had no intention of sounding sarcastic.
Lionel sprang upward.

“Attend to your own affairs. Not a single additional word from you do I wish to listen to. Were you not so young, a lesson would be taught to you about meddling where you have no business. Only when I desire clergymen or doctors shall I summon them. Until that time comes, I shall have nothing to do with them. Is that clear to you? Go away now, pale-face.”

Grace exited. Blindly, she stumbled down the steps, went out of the yard gate, and entered the lane. Midway up the lane, the daze of fear that gripped her passed away, and a reaction of tingling anger took possession of her. When she reached the end of the lane, she was in a temper so furious that she had never experienced its like before. The insults of Lionel Fairlie burned in her soul, lighting a scorching flame. Go home! She would not! Straight back she would go to tell that old ogre precisely what she thought of him—she would show him—oh, wouldn’t she! Indeed, Cheese-face!

Without hesitation, she turned around and trod back. Nobody was on the veranda, and the kitchen door was closed. Without a knock, Grace opened the door and entered. Lionel Fairlie had only just taken his seat at the supper table, yet his newspaper remained in his grip. Grace walked unyieldingly across the space, snatched the paper out of his hand, tossed it onto the floor, and stepped heavily upon it. After that, she turned to face him, her eyes blazing and her cheeks flushed red. She was so stunning a young fury that Lionel Fairlie scarcely knew who she was.
“Why have you returned?” he barked, though his tone reflected confusion rather than anger.
Without flinching, she stared back into those furious eyes that so few individuals were able to withstand.

“I have returned to inform you precisely of my opinion regarding you,” Grace declared in distinct, resounding tones. “You do not frighten me. You are an ill-mannered, unfair, oppressive, unpleasant old man. Tabitha claims you are certain to end up in hell, and I felt pity for you, but that is no longer the case. A decade passed without your wife receiving a new hat—it is no surprise that she passed away. From now on, I intend to pull faces at you every time you are in my sight. Whenever I am positioned behind you, you will be aware of what I am doing. In his study, Father possesses a book containing an illustration of the devil, and my plan is to return home to scribble your name beneath it. You are an ancient vampire, and my wish is that you catch the Scotch fiddle!”

Grace was as ignorant of the definition of a vampire as she was of the meaning of the Scotch fiddle. Having heard Tabitha utter these terms, she inferred through her tone that each was a terrible matter. Lionel Fairlie, however, was acquainted with the meaning of at least the second phrase. He had given Grace’s outburst his undivided, silent attention. As she brought her foot down with a stamp and stopped to catch her breath, he abruptly erupted into boisterous laughter. Striking his knee forcefully with his hand, he cried out,
“I swear you possess grit, despite everything—grit appeals to me. Here, take a seat—take a seat!”

“I will not.” The fire in Grace’s eyes blazed with greater fury. It seemed to her that she was the target of mockery—handled with disdain. A fresh outburst of anger would have given her pleasure, yet this pierced her profoundly. “I refuse to sit down inside your home. I am returning home. Still, I am pleased that I returned to this place and declared my precise judgment of you.”

“I agree—I really do,” Lionel laughed quietly. “You appeal to me—you are wonderful—you are magnificent. What color in your cheeks—what energy! Was I the one who called her cheese-face? Indeed, a cheese is something she has never even been near. Have a seat. If only your appearance had been like this from the beginning, young woman! So you intend to put my signature beneath the image of the devil, do you? However, that creature is dark, young woman, he is dark—whereas my complexion is red. That is unacceptable—that simply will not work! Furthermore, you express a wish that I catch the scabies, do you? Goodness bless you, young woman, that afflicted me during my childhood. Do not desire its return to me. Have a seat—come sit beside me. We shall share a drink together.”
“No, thank you,” Grace declared with a lofty air.

“Oh, yes, you are going to. Come, come now, my apologies, girl—my apologies. I behaved like a fool and I am sorry. A man cannot speak more fairly. Forgive and forget. Shake my hand, girl—shake my hand. She refuses—no, she refuses! But it is necessary that she does! Look right here, girl, should you shake my hand and share a meal with me, I am going to pay the amount I formerly did toward the salary, and I am going to attend church on the initial Sunday of each month, and I am going to compel Kitty Hector to keep her mouth shut. I am the sole person among the clan capable of accomplishing it. Does that make it a deal, girl?”

A good deal appeared to have been struck. Grace was soon clasping hands with the giant, after which she took a place at his dining table. She was no longer angry—the fits of rage Grace experienced were always brief—yet her eyes continued to shimmer with the leftover thrill, and her face remained flushed red. Lionel Fairlie observed her with admiration.

“Wilson, fetch a few of your finest preserves,” he commanded, “and cease your pouting, woman, cease your pouting. Suppose we did exchange words, woman? The atmosphere is cleared and things are enlivened by a strong storm. However, let us have no subsequent mists and rain—no mists and rain, woman. That is something I am unable to endure. I tolerate anger in a female, yet I forbid weeping. Look here, girl, this is a plate of jumbled meat and potatoes for yourself. Start eating it. A sophisticated title is given to it by Wilson, though macanaccady is my name for it. Macanaccady is what I term any food I am unable to decipher while chewing, whereas shallamagouslem is my word for any bewildering liquid. Shallamagouslem describes Wilson’s tea. I am certain burdocks are used by her to brew it. Refuse that unholy dark drink—this milk is provided for you instead. What was the name you gave yourself?”
“Grace.”
“No title like that—no title like that! A name like that makes me sick. Do you have a different one?”
“No, sir.”

“I dislike the name, I truly dislike it. It lacks any vigor. On top of that, it reminds me of my Aunt Jinny. Grace, Hope, and Charity were the names she gave her three daughters. Nothing was believed by Grace—a natural pessimist was what Hope turned out to be—and a miser described Charity. Red Rose is what you should be named—a resemblance to one appears when anger takes you. Red Rose is what I shall call you. And have you tricked me into agreeing to attend church? Remember though, it is merely a single time each month—merely a single time each month. Come along now, girl, will you excuse me from this? A hundred to the salary was what I used to contribute annually while attending church. Will you excuse my church attendance if my word is given to contribute two hundred annually? Come along now!”
“No, no, sir,” Grace said, her dimples appearing mischievously. “I want you to attend church, as well.”

“Well, an agreement remains an agreement. I suppose I am able to endure it a dozen times annually. What a stir it will create that initial Sunday I attend! And aged Tabitha Pratt claims I am heading to hell, does she? Is it your belief that I will end up there—tell me, now, do you?”
“I hope not, sir,” Grace stammered, somewhat flustered.
“What makes you hope not? Come on, why do you feel that way? Explain it to us, girl—tell us why.”
“Sir, it—it has to be a extremely—disagreeable location.”
“Uncomfortable? That relies entirely on what you consider comfortable, girl. Angels would bore me before long. Just picture old Tabitha wearing a halo, now!”
Grace was indeed taken with the idea, which amused her to the point of laughter. Approvingly, Lionel looked at her.
“Do you catch the humor in it, huh? Ah, I am fond of you—you are fantastic. Now, concerning this matter of the church—is your father capable of preaching?”
“He preaches splendidly,” faithful Grace declared.

“Is he, really? I am going to check—I am going to keep an eye out for defects. He ought to watch what he utters in front of me. I am going to trap him—I am going to catch him in a mistake—I am going to track his reasoning. I am certain to get some amusement from this church-attendance affair. Does he ever deliver sermons on hell?”
“Na—a—ay—it does not seem that way to me.”

“What a shame. Discourses regarding that topic appeal to me. Inform him that should he desire to maintain my pleasant disposition, he ought to deliver a vigorous, resounding address about the infernal regions one time per half-year—and the greater the quantity of sulfur, the more desirable it is. I prefer them fiery. Furthermore, consider every bit of enjoyment he would provide for the unmarried women as well. Every one of them would continuously gaze toward elderly Lionel Fairlie while reflecting, ‘That is meant for you, you ancient scoundrel. That is the fate reserved for you!’ Every occasion you convince your father to deliver a sermon regarding the underworld, I shall contribute a ten-dollar bonus. At this moment, Wilson is arriving bearing the preserve. You enjoy that, do you not? This does not happen to be macanaccady. Sample it!”
Grace dutifully took the large spoonful that Lionel offered her into her mouth. Fortunately, the taste was pleasant.

“The world’s top plum jam,” Lionel stated, pouring a generous portion onto a deep dish and dropping it in front of her. “Happy it pleases you. A pair of pots will be yours to carry back. Stinginess isn't in my nature—it never was. In that regard, the devil has no hold on me. Dinah going a decade without a fresh bonnet wasn't caused by me. She was responsible—she economized on millinery so she could hand funds to yellow men across in China. Not one penny have I ever donated to missionary work—and I won't ever. Don't ever attempt to trick me into doing so! One hundred annually toward the stipend and attending service monthly—however, no ruining fine heathens just to create miserable Christians! Why, child, neither heaven nor hell would suit them—thoroughly ruined for both destinations—thoroughly ruined. Say, Wilson, is a smile still missing from your face? It's incredible how you females manage to brood! Brooding was never something I did—my way is simply a single grand burst and thunderclap, followed by—pouf—the tempest finishing and brightness returning, leaving you ready to feed right from my palm.”
Lionel made a point of taking Grace home in the buggy following supper, packing it full with jars of jam, pumpkins, potatoes, cabbages, and apples.
“Out in the barn is a nice little tom-pussy, which I will also bestow upon you if you want it, so just say the word,” he said.
“No, thank you,” Grace declared firmly. “Cats aren't my preference, and furthermore, I own a rooster.”
“Hear what she says. A rooster cannot be cuddled the way a kitten can. Who has ever heard of stroking a rooster? You had better take little Tom. I am looking to secure a good home for him.”
“Negative. Since my aunt’s cat resides with Aunt Martha, an unfamiliar kitten would be slain by him.”

Lionel surrendered the argument somewhat unwillingly. He provided Grace with a thrilling ride back to her house, pulled by his untamed two-year-old horse, and after he had helped her step down at the door to the manse's kitchen and unloaded his haul onto the rear porch, he steered his carriage off while calling out,
“Mind you, it is just one time each month—just one time each month!”

Grace retired to her room, experiencing a slight dizziness and shortness of breath, as though she had barely broken free from a friendly cyclone's hold. Joy and gratitude filled her. She no longer dreaded that departing from the Glen, the cemetery, and Fern Hollow would be necessary. Nevertheless, she drifted off to sleep bothered by an unpleasant lingering awareness that Dan Coyle had referred to her as pig-girl, and that, having discovered such an apt name, he would go on addressing her by it every time a chance arose.

On the initial Sunday of November, Lionel Fairlie attended church, creating every bit of the stir he wished for. Upon the steps of the church, Mr. Ashdown distractedly shook his hand, expressing a vague hope that Mrs. Fairlie was in good health.

“Though her condition was poor prior to her interment by me a decade back, her well-being has likely improved since,” roared Lionel, startling and entertaining all present save Mr. Ashdown, who was preoccupied with considering whether he had rendered his sermon's final point as lucidly as possible, remaining entirely unaware of what passed between himself and Lionel.
Lionel stopped Grace as she reached the gate.

“I maintained my promise, as you can observe—maintained my promise, Red Rose. From this moment until December's initial Sunday, I am liberated. Excellent discourse, young lady—excellent discourse. The thoughts within your father's mind surpass what his facial expression reveals. However, he made a single self-contradiction—inform him that he contradicted himself. Furthermore, inform him of my desire for that brimstone sermon come December. A marvelous method to conclude the former year—experiencing a flavor of hell, as you are aware. Plus, what would be wrong with a pleasing, savory message regarding heaven to begin the New Year? Even if it would lack half the interest of hell, young lady—not even half. Nevertheless, I would care to discover your father's perspective concerning heaven—he possesses the ability to think—the most unusual trait on earth—an individual possessing the capacity to think. Still, he truly did contradict himself. Ha, ha! This presents an inquiry you could pose to him at some point when he is not sleeping, young lady. ‘Can God make a stone so big He couldn’t lift it Himself?’ Avoid forgetting this moment. I desire to listen to his judgment regarding the matter. I have bewildered numerous clergymen using that very thought, young lady.”

Grace was pleased to break away from him and hurry back to her house. Dan Coyle, who was positioned in the midst of the gathering of boys near the gate, cast his eyes upon her and formed his lips into "pig-girl," though he did not venture to pronounce the words out loud in that particular spot. The following day at school proved to be a different story. During the midday break, Grace met Dan within the small grove of spruces located at the rear of the schoolhouse, and Dan yelled again,
“Pig-girl! Pig-girl! Rooster-girl!”

Rising abruptly from a mossy cushion behind a small cluster of fir trees, where he had been engrossed in reading, Edmund Carrow stood up. Although his face was extremely pale, a fiery light blazed in his eyes.
“You keep quiet, Dan Coyle!” he commanded.
“Oh, hello, Miss Edmund,” Dan answered back, completely unconcerned. He jumped lightly up onto the top of the rail fence and sang out mockingly,
“Mustard pot thief, Yellow-bellied coward, Mustard pot thief!”

“A coincidence is what you are!” Edmund exclaimed with disdain, his face growing even paler. Although he possessed merely a vague notion of a coincidence's definition, Dan was completely ignorant of the term and assumed it was an exceptionally insulting remark.

“Bah! Sissy!” he shouted once more. “The things your mother writes are untruths—untruths—untruths! Likewise, Grace Ashdown is a swine-girl—a—swine-girl—a swine-girl! Furthermore, she is a fowl-girl—a fowl-girl—a fowl-girl! Bah! Sissy—sissy—custard—”

Dan was unable to say anything more. Launching himself over the distance between them, Edmund delivered a single, precise hit that sent Dan tumbling backward off the fence. This abrupt, humiliating fall from Dan was met by Grace with an explosion of laughter and applauding hands. Turning red with fury, Dan leaped to his feet and started scaling the fence again. At that precise moment, however, the school bell sounded, and Dan was well aware of the consequences for pupils who arrived late under Mr. Hazard’s authority.
“This will be fought to the end,” he bellowed. “Yellow-belly!”
“Whenever you wish,” Edmund replied.
“Oh, no, no, Edmund,” Grace objected. “Do not battle him. What he states does not bother me—I would not stoop to care about someone such as him.”
“You were insulted by him, and my mother was insulted by him as well,” Edmund said, maintaining that very same lethal composure. “Dan, tonight following school.”
“Dad says I have to head straight back from school to gather potatoes behind the harrows,” Dan replied sullenly. “However, tomorrow evening will work.”
“Very well—in this place tomorrow evening,” Edmund concurred.
“And your effeminate face will be crushed by me,” Dan pledged.

Edmund trembled—less out of dread regarding the menace than from disgust at its grossness and crude nature. Even so, he kept his chin up and walked forward into the building. Grace walked behind him, her feelings torn. It pained her to imagine Edmund coming to blows with that petty worm, yet oh, how magnificent he had been! Furthermore, his battle was for her—Grace Ashdown—so that her defamer would be punished! Naturally, triumph would be his—those eyes guaranteed success.
By the time evening arrived, Grace felt somewhat less confident in her champion, though. Throughout the remainder of the school day, Edmund had appeared remarkably silent and uninteresting.

“Were Kit the sole concern,” she breathed in a sigh to Ida, while the two rested atop the tombstone of Hezekiah Pollock within the cemetery. “Being such a combatant—Dan would be dispatched by him quickly. Edmund, however, lacks expertise in combat.”
“I am terribly fearful that he will suffer injury,” Ida uttered with a sigh, as she detested conflict and was unable to comprehend the quiet, hidden delight that she sensed within Grace.
“He shouldn’t be,” Grace stated uneasily. “His size is completely equal to Dan’s.”
“However, Dan is a lot older,” Ida remarked. “Indeed, he is almost twelve months older.”

“When you actually add it all up, Dan hasn't fought very much,” Grace remarked. “I think he is actually a coward. He never expected Edmund to fight, otherwise he would not have resorted to name-calling in his presence. Oh, Ida, if you had only been able to see Edmund’s face as he glared at him! It gave me a shiver—a pleasant kind of shiver. He resembled Sir Galahad so much from the poem father read aloud to us this past Saturday.”
“The idea of their battle repulses me, and I would be glad if it could be prevented,” Ida remarked.

“Oh, now it must proceed,” exclaims Grace. “A point of honour is involved. Ida, do not you venture to inform a soul. Should you do so, I will refrain from ever sharing secrets with you in the future!”
“I will keep quiet,” Ida assented. “However, I am not remaining tomorrow to witness the brawl. My return home will be immediate.”

“Oh, very well. I must attend—it would be unkind to refrain, since Edmund is battling on my behalf. I shall fasten my colours upon his sleeve—that is the proper custom when he serves as my knight. What good fortune that Mrs. Carrow presented me with that lovely blue hair-ribbon on my birthday! Having been worn merely twice, it remains nearly fresh. However, I desire certainty regarding Edmund's victory. Should he lose, it will prove so—so embarrassing.”

Had Grace been able to behold her defender at that moment, her skepticism would have grown. Returning from school, Edmund found that his noble fury had dwindled, leaving a highly unpleasant sensation in its stead. The following evening held a match against Dan Coyle—an event he dreaded—as the mere idea filled him with aversion. Furthermore, the anticipation haunted him continuously. He was unable to escape the lingering thought for even a single second. Would the pain be severe? A dreadful fear possessed him that the agony would be great. Moreover, was he destined to suffer defeat and disgrace?

An inability to consume any notable amount of supper affected him. Although Tabitha had baked a large quantity of monkey-faces, which were his favorite, a single one was all he could force down his throat. Four were consumed by Kit. Such an appetite baffled Edmund. What allowed anyone to eat? Furthermore, in what way were they able to converse so cheerfully as they currently did? Mother was present, her cheeks pink and her eyes bright. That her son was required to fight on the following day remained unknown to her. Darkly, Edmund pondered whether her gaiety would persist if she were aware. Tabitha’s photograph had been captured by Kit using his new camera, and after the outcome was circulated around the table, Tabitha became intensely outraged by it.

“I am not attractive, Mrs. Dr. dear, and I am fully aware of it, and I have forever been aware of it,” she declared with a hurt expression, “yet I shall never, no, never accept that I am as unattractive as I appear in that image.”
Kit found humor in this, prompting Nell to join him in laughter once more. Unable to bear it any longer, Edmund stood up and ran away to his room.
“Mrs. Dr. dear, that child has something weighing on his mind,” Tabitha remarked. “Hardly anything has been eaten by him. Could he be planning yet another poem, do you think?”
At that moment, poor Edmund’s mind was completely detached from the celestial domain of poetry. He rested an elbow on the open sill of his window and let his head drop heavily into his hands.
“Edmund, come down to the shore with me,” shouted Kit, bursting inside. “To-night, the boys intend to burn the grass on the sand-hill. We have permission from Father to go. Come on.”

Under different circumstances, Edmund would have been thrilled, as he took great pleasure in the combustion of the sand-hill grass. On this occasion, however, he adamantly declined to attend, remaining steadfast against all persuasion and pleading. Disheartened, Kit disliked the prospect of making the lengthy, pitch-black trek to Seven Gulls Point by himself, so he withdrew to his museum located in the attic and became absorbed in a volume. His sense of letdown quickly evaporated while he delighted in the exploits of ancient romantic figures, periodically stopping to envision himself as a renowned commander guiding his soldiers to triumph upon a momentous battleground.

Edmund remained sitting by his window up to his bedtime. Izzy entered quietly, wishing to learn what was troubling him, but Edmund was unable to speak about the matter, even with Izzy. Discussing it appeared to lend it a truth that made him pull back. Merely pondering it brought sufficient agony. On the maple trees beyond his window, the dry, brittle leaves made a rustling sound. Within the sunken, silvery sky, the radiant rose and fiery colors had faded, and above Fern Hollow, the full moon mounted grandly. Far in the distance, past the hills, a glowing woodfire was creating a splendid display across the skyline. The night was crisp and luminous, allowing distant noises to be perceived clearly. Across the pond, a fox barked; down at the Glen station, an engine puffed; inside the maple grove, a blue-jay shrieked wildly; and over on the manse lawn, laughter could be heard. In what way could people laugh? In what way could foxes, blue-jays, and engines carry on as though the next day held no impending event?
“Oh, how I long for it to end,” Edmund moaned.

That night brought him very little sleep, and he struggled greatly to swallow his morning porridge. Tabitha had been quite generous with her servings. That day, Mr. Hazard discovered that he was an unpromising student. Grace Ashdown appeared to have her thoughts wandering as well. On his slate, Dan Coyle continually sketched covert drawings of girls featuring heads of pigs or roosters, displaying them for everyone's view. Word regarding the approaching fight had spread, leading the majority of the boys and a large number of the girls to gather in the spruce plantation by the time Dan and Edmund went there following school. Ida had departed for home, yet Grace remained present, after tying her blue ribbon about Edmund’s arm. Edmund felt grateful that Kit, Izzy, and Bess were not included in the group of onlookers. For some reason, they had failed to learn about the upcoming event and had likewise returned home. Edmund stood before Dan with complete courage at this point. In the final instant, his entire dread had disappeared, though he remained disgusted by the prospect of a brawl. It was observed that Dan was actually paler beneath his freckles than Edmund was. A command was issued by one of the elder boys, and Dan punched Edmund in the face.

Edmund staggered slightly. For an instant, the stinging hurt from the strike radiated across his entire delicate body. Afterwards, he ceased to feel any agony. An unfamiliar sensation, unlike anything he had previously known, appeared to wash over him in a great wave. A deep red glow covered his face, and his eyes blazed such as fire. The students at Glen St. Agnes school had never imagined that “Miss Edmund” was capable of appearing in such a manner. He threw his weight onward and engaged Dan in a fight like a youthful wildcat.

In the brawls of the boys at the Glen school, no specific regulations existed. One had to grab wherever possible and land punches by any means. Edmund engaged with a fierce rage and a delight in the clash that proved too much for Dan to maintain his footing against. The entire affair concluded extremely fast. Edmund possessed no lucid awareness of his actions until, all at once, the crimson fog vanished from his vision, revealing him on top of the lying form of Dan, whose nose—what a terrible thing!—was gushing blood.
“Have you had plenty?” asked Edmund with his teeth pressed together.
Dan glumly acknowledged that he had done so.
“Does my mother write what is not true?”
“No.”
“Is Grace Ashdown not a pig-girl?”
“No.”
“Or a rooster-girl?”
“No.”
“And am I no coward?”
“No.”
Edmund was about to inquire, “And you are a liar?” yet compassion stepped in, preventing him from causing Dan any more embarrassment. What is more, the sight of that blood was dreadful.
“You may leave, in that case,” he said scornfully.

A noisy applause came from the youths sitting atop the rail fence, yet a few of the girls wept. Fear had overtaken them. Schoolboy brawls were familiar to them, but none matched Edmund when he had wrestled Dan. An element of horror had surrounded him. They believed Dan would be slain by him. With everything concluded, their weeping grew hysterical—with the exception of Grace, who remained motionless, her cheeks flushed red.

Edmund did not linger to receive the reward of a victor. Leaping across the fence, he hurried down the spruce-covered hill toward Fern Hollow. No triumphant delight filled him, yet he experienced a quiet contentment from completing his duty and redeeming his honor—blended with a nauseating shudder whenever he recalled the bloody nose of Dan. Its appearance had been dreadful, and Edmund detested dreadful things.

Additionally, it started to dawn on him that his own body was rather bruised and aching. A cut caused his lip to swell, while a peculiar sensation affected one of his eyes. Within Fern Hollow, he met Mr. Ashdown, who was returning from a visit made that afternoon to the Miss Ainslies. Upon seeing him, that reverend gentleman gave him a serious look.
“You appear to have been in a fight, Edmund, do you not?”
“Yes, sir,” Edmund replied, anticipating a reprimand.
“What was the topic?”
“Dan Coyle claimed that my mother penned falsehoods and that Grace was nothing more than a swine-herd,” replied Edmund without hesitation.
“Oh—h! In that case, Edmund, your actions were unquestionably warranted.”
“Is it your opinion that fighting is proper, sir?” Edmund inquired with curiosity.

“Not constantly—and not frequently—yet on occasion—indeed, on occasion,” stated John Ashdown. “Whenever women are disrespected for example—like with you. My principle, Edmund, is, refrain from fighting until you are certain that you should, and after that apply every bit of your strength to it. Regardless of various bruises I gather that you emerged victorious.”
“Indeed, I forced him to retract everything he said.”
“Extremely well done—truly, extremely well done. It hadn't occurred to me that you possessed such a combative spirit, Edmund.”

“Prior to this, I had never engaged in combat—and until the very end, I wished to avoid it—and after that,” stated Edmund, resolved to confess everything fully, “I found enjoyment in it during the time I was doing it.”
A twinkle shone in the Rev. John’s eyes.
“Were you—initially—a bit scared?”

“I felt extremely scared,” sincere Edmund remarked. “However, I do not intend to feel scared again, sir. Experiencing fear about troubles is more unpleasant than those troubles are. I plan to request that father drive me to Kettlebridge tomorrow so I can have my tooth pulled.”

“You are correct once more. ‘Fear is more pain than is the pain it fears.’ Are you aware of who penned those words, Edmund? William Shakespeare was the author. Did that extraordinary individual fail to understand a single sentiment, feeling, or trial of the human soul? Upon your return home, inform your mother that I feel pride in you.”

Edmund refrained from informing her of that, nevertheless; yet he recounted everything else to her, and she felt for him and expressed her pleasure that he had defended her and Grace, and she applied ointment to his tender places and applied cologne to his throbbing head.
“Is every mother as kind as you are?” Edmund inquired, embracing her tightly. “Defending you is truly worth it.”
Nell descended the stairs to find Miss Winifred and Tabitha in the living room, where they took great pleasure in hearing the account. Tabitha was especially delighted.

“I am exceedingly pleased to learn he put up a fine struggle, dear Mrs. Dr. It might possibly strip him of those foolish poetic notions. Moreover, I never, no, never was able to stand that tiny viper known as Dan Coyle. Won't you move your seat closer to the hearth, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr? The nights in November are quite cold.”

“I appreciate it, Tabitha, but coldness isn't a problem for me. Prior to arriving here, I stopped by the manse and warmed up considerably—even if doing so required me to enter the kitchen, seeing as every other room lacked a fire. Take my word for it, that kitchen appeared to have been tossed around with a rod. Mr. Ashdown was absent from the house. Discovering his whereabouts proved impossible for me, yet I suspect he was visiting the Ainslies' place. Would you believe, my dear Nell, rumor has it that his visits there have occurred often throughout the entire autumn, leading folks to suspect his intentions involve courting Clementine.”

“If Clementine became his bride, he’d gain a truly wonderful partner,” remarked Nell, placing more driftwood upon the flames. “Among all the young women I have met, she is exceptionally lovely—a genuine member of Joseph’s lineage.”

“Ye—s—except she belongs to the Episcopal church,” Miss Winifred remarked with hesitation. “Naturally, that surpasses her being a Methodist—nevertheless, it seems to me Mr. Ashdown might discover a sufficiently suitable spouse within his own fold. Still, the rumor might well be groundless. Just one month back, I remarked to him, ‘It is time you took another wife, Mr. Ashdown.’ His expression grew as appalled as though my proposal had been indecent. ‘The woman I married rests in the cemetery, Mrs. Kerr,’ he replied, employing his usual mild and holy tone. ‘That is my assumption,’ I responded, ‘otherwise I should not be recommending another marriage to you.’ At that, his countenance appeared even more scandalized. Because of this, I question whether this Clementine account holds much truth. Whenever an unmarried clergyman visits a home containing an unmarried female on two occasions, every gossip claims he is pursuing her.”
“In my opinion—should I be bold enough to utter it—Mr. Ashdown possesses too much shyness to seek a second wife in courtship,” Tabitha stated gravely.
