“Trust me, he isn’t timid,” Miss Winifred fired back. “Yes, he is forgetful, but he is certainly not timid. Despite his daydreaming and preoccupation, he holds himself in high regard, as men do, and once he fully pays attention, he wouldn't consider it much trouble to propose to any lady. No, the problem stems from him fooling himself that his heart is in the grave, even though it continues to pump inside him as everyone else's does. Whether he holds a fancy for Clementine Ainslie remains uncertain. Should that be the case, we have to accept it gracefully. She possesses a sweet nature, manages a home well, and would be a splendid mother to those unfortunate, overlooked children. Besides,” Miss Winifred finished with a tone of resignation, “an Episcopalian was what my grandmother happened to be.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Mary Stubbs, having been dispatched to the manse on a chore by Mrs. Kerr, was walking lightly down Fern Hollow, heading to Hollowmere to pass the afternoon alongside Bess and Izzy for a Saturday reward. Grace and Ida had joined Bess and Izzy to gather spruce gum within the woods of the manse, and the quartet sat presently upon a collapsed pine alongside the stream, each one, it should be acknowledged, masticating quite energetically. Anywhere outside the privacy of Fern Hollow, the Hollowmere twins were forbidden from chewing spruce gum, whereas Grace and Ida remained unconstrained by those etiquette regulations and happily masticated it all over, both in the house and outside, causing the Glen to feel a most respectable dread. Indeed, Grace had masticated it during a church service on a single occasion; nevertheless, Tobias recognized how monstrous that was, administering a lecture in the manner of a big brother that proved so severe she refrained from ever repeating the act.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I felt such a need to chew on something because my hunger was so great,” she argued. “Tobias Ashdown, you are fully aware of the nature of our breakfast. Burnt porridge was impossible for me to consume, leaving my stomach feeling exceedingly odd and hollow. That gum was a great aid—plus I refrained from chewing forcefully. No sound came from me, and not a single time did I pop the gum.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Anyhow, chewing gum in church is something you mustn’t do,” Tobias insisted. “If I catch you doing it again, you’ll be sorry.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “During prayer-meeting last week, you chewed yourself,” Grace shouted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “That’s different,” Tobias stated haughtily. “Prayer-meeting isn’t on Sunday. Besides, I sat far in the rear in a shadowy pew and no one noticed me. You were seated right in the front where all the people noticed you. And I removed the gum from my mouth for the final hymn and attached it to the rear of the pew right in the front where all the people noticed you. Then I departed and left it behind. I returned to retrieve it the following morning, but it had vanished. I imagine Rod Warren stole it. And it was a dandy chew.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Mary Stubbs moved along the Valley with her head lifted proudly. She was wearing a fresh blue velvet cap that featured a scarlet rosette, a coat made of navy blue cloth, and a small muff of squirrel fur. She was extremely aware of her fresh garments and immensely satisfied with her appearance. Her hair had been meticulously crimped, her face appeared rather full, her cheeks were rosy, and her white eyes were gleaming. She bore little resemblance to the miserable and tattered stray whom the Ashdowns had discovered inside the old Taylor barn. Ida attempted to keep envy at bay. In this moment stood Mary wearing a fresh velvet cap, whereas she and Grace were required to put on their faded old gray tams once more this winter. No one ever considered purchasing new ones for them, and they feared requesting them from their father because he might be lacking funds, which would cause him to feel distressed. Mary had mentioned to them on one occasion that ministers were constantly lacking funds and found it “awful hard” to make ends meet. From that time on, Grace and Ida preferred wearing rags over requesting anything from their father if they could avoid doing so. They did not feel overly troubled by their worn appearance; nevertheless, it proved somewhat difficult to observe Mary Stubbs stepping out in such fashion and exhibiting such arrogance over it, as well. The fresh squirrel muff truly served as the final indignity. Neither Grace nor Ida had ever owned a muff, considering themselves fortunate if they managed to secure mittens devoid of holes. Aunt Martha lacked the eyesight required to mend holes, and even though Ida attempted the task, she produced clumsy mending. For some reason, they were unable to render their welcome to Mary particularly warm. However, Mary remained unbothered and unaware of this, as she was not excessively thin-skinned. She leaped nimbly onto a perch on the pine tree, placing the disagreeable muff upon a branch. Ida observed that its lining consisted of gathered red satin and it possessed red tassels. She stared down at her own somewhat purple, rough, tiny hands and pondered whether she would ever, ever have the chance to slide them inside a muff of that sort.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Give us a chew,” Mary requested in a friendly tone. Bess, Izzy and Grace each pulled one or two amber-colored lumps out of their pockets, handing them over to Mary. Ida did not move at all. Inside the pocket of her snug, worn-out small jacket rested four splendid, large lumps, yet she refused to hand even a single one over to Mary Stubbs—absolutely none. Mary could gather her own gum! Owners of squirrel muffs should not anticipate receiving every single thing in existence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Isn’t it a great day?” Mary remarked, dangling her legs, possibly to show off her new boots that featured quite stylish cloth tops. Ida pulled her own feet beneath herself. A hole was present in the toe of one boot, and numerous knots bound both of her laces. Nevertheless, she possessed no better pair. Oh, that Mary Stubbs! Why had she not been left behind in the old barn?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Ida was never made to feel unhappy because the Hollowmere twins had finer garments than Grace and she possessed. With an indifferent elegance, they bore their lovely attire, appearing never to bestow a thought upon it. In some manner, they refrained from causing those around them to feel dowdy. However, whenever Mary Stubbs was finely attired, she appeared almost to radiate garments—to move within an aura of garments—to force everyone else into feeling and thinking garments. As Ida remained seated in the golden warmth of the pleasant December afternoon, she was sharply and wretchedly aware of every single item she wore—the discolored tam, which remained her finest one nevertheless, the ill-fitting jacket that had served her across three winters, the frayed areas in her skirt and her footwear, and the chilly inadequacy of her meager little underclothing. Naturally, Mary was preparing to go visiting whereas she remained behind. Yet even had she been departing as well, no superior clothes were hers to wear, and the sharpness of her distress rested in this fact.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Hey, this gum is wonderful. Hear me popping it. Down at Seven Gulls, there aren't any gum spruces,” Mary stated. “At times, I simply crave a chew. If Mrs. Kerr spots me, she forbids me from chewing gum. She claims it isn't lady-like. I am confused by this lady-business. I am unable to understand all its quirks. Hey, Ida, what is wrong with you? Has the cat got your tongue?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “No,” uttered Ida, whose transfixed gaze remained glued to the squirrel muff. Reaching across her, Mary snatched the item up and shoved it directly into Ida’s hands.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Put your hands inside there for a moment,” she commanded. “They seem somewhat cold. Isn't that an exquisite muff? Mrs. Kerr presented it to me a week ago as a gift for my birthday. I will receive the collar when Christmas comes. I overheard her saying that to Mr. Kerr.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Grace remarked that Mrs. Kerr was extremely kind to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “You can be sure she is. Plus, I treat her well,” Mary shot back. “I labor tirelessly so things are simple for her and set up precisely to her taste. We were a perfect match. Not just anybody could manage to live with her the way I can. She is obsessively clean, but I am the same way, which makes us get on great.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I informed you that she was never going to whip you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “That is true. She has never attempted to put a finger on me, and I have never uttered a single falsehood to her—not a single one, as sure as you live. However, she scolds me with her tongue on occasion, but that merely slides off me like water off a duck’s back. Tell me, Ida, why did you not keep the muff?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Ida had restored it to the branch.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I do not have cold hands, thank you,” she stated frostily.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Well, if you are satisfied, I am. Tell me, old Kitty Hector has returned to church as humble as Moses and no one understands the reason. But everyone is claiming it was Grace who brought Lionel Fairlie out. His housekeeper states that you visited there and delivered a terrible tongue-lashing to him. Did you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I walked over and requested that he join us at church,” Grace mentioned uneasily.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Imagine having such nerve!” Mary remarked with admiration. “I wouldn’t have ventured to do that, and I’m hardly timid. Mrs. Wilson claims that both of you argued terribly, yet you emerged victorious, after which he simply pivoted and seemed ready to devour you. Tell me, will your father be preaching here tomorrow?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “No. His intention is to swap places with Mr. Perry from Port Marlow. Father traveled to town earlier today, and Mr. Perry will arrive this evening.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I suspected that something was going on, even if old Martha refused to tell me anything satisfactory. Nevertheless, I was certain she would not have slaughtered that rooster without a reason.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Which rooster? What are you talking about?” exclaimed Grace, her face losing its color.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “I am unaware of any rooster, as I never saw it. At the time she collected the butter sent by Mrs. Kerr, she mentioned having visited the barn to slaughter a rooster for tomorrow’s dinner.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Grace leaped from the pine tree down to the ground.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “It’s Adam—we don’t possess any other rooster—Adam has been killed by her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Now, don’t lose your temper. Martha mentioned that no meat was available from the butcher at the Glen this week, forcing her to find an alternative, and since the hens were all laying, they were too scrawny.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “In the event that she has murdered Adam—” Grace started rushing up the incline.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Mary gave a shrug of her shoulders.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “She will lose her mind now. Her affection for that Adam was immense. That bird should have been cooked a long time back—his meat will be as hard as sole leather. However, I would hate to be in Martha’s position. Grace has turned completely pale from anger; Ida, it would be wise for you to follow her and attempt to calm her down.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: Ida abruptly spun around and sprinted toward Mary just as she had walked a short distance alongside the Carrow girls.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Mary, here is some gum for you,” she said, her voice catching slightly in repentance, as she shoved every one of her four knots into Mary’s hands, “and it makes me happy that your muff is so pretty.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVIII. MARY BRINGS EVIL TIDINGS
text: “Why, thanks,” Mary said, feeling somewhat astonished. Once Ida had left, she remarked to the Carrow girls, “Ain’t she a queer little mite? But I’ve always said she had a good heart.”

Upon Ida’s arrival at the house, Grace remained face down across her mattress, completely declining any solace. Adam had been slain by Aunt Martha. At that exact moment, he lay upon a plate inside the pantry, bound and prepared for cooking, surrounded by his own gizzard, heart, and liver. Aunt Martha paid not the slightest attention to Grace’s overwhelming fury and sorrow.

“We needed to provide a meal for the unusual minister,” she stated. “You are far too grown-up to cause such a commotion about an aged rooster. You were aware that he would need to be slaughtered eventually.”
“When father gets back, I’m going to inform him of what you did,” Grace said through her tears.
“Do not go disturbing your unfortunate father, as his worries are already sufficient, and I serve as the housekeeper in this place.”
“Adam belonged to me—Mrs. Johnson presented him to me. You possessed no right to lay a finger on him,” Grace declared furiously.

“Refrain from being impudent now. The rooster has been slaughtered, concluding the matter. I refuse to serve an unfamiliar clergyman a meal consisting of cold boiled mutton. My upbringing taught me greater propriety than that, despite my reduced circumstances.”

Grace refused to head downstairs for supper on that evening, nor would she attend church on the following morning. Nevertheless, when dinner time arrived, she took her seat at the table, possessing puffy eyes from weeping and a moody expression.

Possessing a gleaming bald pate, thick white eyebrows, and a stubbly white moustache, the Rev. James Perry was a smooth, ruddy-faced man. Although he was undeniably unattractive and a most tedious, self-important individual, Grace would have harbored the exact same deep hatred for him even had his appearance matched the Archangel Michael and his speech possessed the eloquence of men and angels. Displaying his well-formed diamond ring and fleshy white hands, he skillfully sliced Adam into pieces. Furthermore, he offered cheerful observations throughout the entire process. While Tobias and Rupert chuckled, even Ida produced a faint smile, believing good manners required such a response. Grace, however, merely wore a deep frown. Her behavior struck the Rev. James as terribly rude. On one occasion, as he was making a self-righteous comment to Tobias, Grace abruptly interrupted him with a direct denial. The Rev. James knitted his thick eyebrows together as he looked at her.
“Young females must not interject,” he stated, “and it is improper for them to gainsay individuals possessing vastly superior knowledge to their own.”

This made Grace even more ill-tempered. Being addressed as “little girl” as though her size were no greater than plump Tessa Carrow’s over at Hollowmere! The indignity was unbearable. Furthermore, the way that dreadful Mr. Perry devoured his food! He went so far as to strip poor Adam’s bones bare. Grace and Ida both refused to consume a single bite, viewing the boys as barely distinguishable from cannibals. Grace believed that if the terrible meal did not finish shortly, she would terminate it herself by launching an object at Mr. Perry’s shiny head. Luckily, Mr. Perry discovered that Aunt Martha’s tough apple pie exceeded even his own chewing abilities, bringing the dinner to a close following an extended grace wherein Mr. Perry expressed pious gratitude for the sustenance and moderate delight provided by a benevolent and charitable Providence.
“Grace, under her breath, muttered rebelliously that God had not had anything at all to do with supplying Adam for you.”

The boys were happy to flee outside, Ida departed to assist Aunt Martha with the washing-up—even if that quite crabby old woman never appreciated her hesitant help—and Grace went into the study, in whose grate a bright wood fire burned. Her belief was that this would allow her to get away from the despised Mr. Perry, who had declared that he planned to sleep in his room for the afternoon. Grace had hardly made herself comfortable in a corner with a book, however, when he entered and, positioning himself in front of the fire, began to examine the untidy study with an expression of displeasure.
“Your father’s volumes appear to be in rather terrible disorder, my child,” he remarked sternly.
Lurking in her corner, Grace grew somber and remained completely silent. She refused to speak with this—this creature.

“Attempts ought to be made by you to arrange them,” Mr. Perry continued, fiddling with his attractive watch chain while offering a patronizing smile to Grace. “Your age is sufficient for you to manage tasks of this nature. A mere ten years old, my young daughter residing at home serves as an outstanding little housekeeper currently, offering her mother supreme assistance and solace. A truly sweet child describes her. The privilege of knowing her is something I wish was yours. Assistance could be provided to you by her in numerous manners. Unquestionably, the priceless benefit of being cared for and trained by a good mother has been denied to you. A sorrowful deficiency—a most sorrowful deficiency. On multiple occasions, I have conversed with your father regarding this matter, dutifully highlighting his obligation to him, yet up to now it has yielded no result. May he come to realize his obligation prior to the arrival of too late a moment, I hope. Currently, striving to fill the void left by your holy mother stands as your obligation and honor. A profound impact could be made by you upon your brothers and your young sister—a genuine mother to them is what you could become. A concern exists for me that these matters are not pondered by you as they ought to be. My dear child, permit me to enlighten your perception concerning them.”

Mr. Perry’s greasy, self-satisfied tone continued to flow. He felt completely in his element. To dictate, condescend, and urge others on was what suited him above all else. Having no intention of ceasing, he kept right on talking. Planted securely on the rug in front of the hearth, he emitted a torrent of grandiloquent truisms. Grace failed to catch a single word. In truth, she was paying him no attention whatsoever. She was, however, observing his lengthy black coat-tails, an amused mischief mounting in her brown eyes. Mr. Perry had positioned himself extremely close to the flames. His coat-tails started to singe—his coat-tails started to emit smoke. Enraptured by his own rhetoric, he persisted in his tedious speech. The smoke from the coat-tails grew thicker. A minuscule spark leaped from the ignited timber and landed right in the center of one tail. It attached itself, took hold, and expanded into a slow-burning fire. Unable to hold back any further, Grace burst into a suppressed laugh.

Mr. Perry halted abruptly, enraged by such impudence. All at once, he realized that the chamber was filled with the smell of scorched fabric. Turning rapidly, he perceived nothing. After that, he slapped his hands onto his coat-tails, hauling them forward. A considerable tear had already formed in one tail—and he was wearing his new suit. Grace trembled, unable to control her laughter at his posture and face.
“Was my coat-tail catching fire visible to you?” he inquired in a rage.
“Yes, sir,” Grace replied with a modest air.
“Why wasn’t I told?” he asked, staring at her with anger.
“You mentioned that interrupting was not good manners, sir,” Grace said, with even greater demureness.

“If—if I was your father, I would give you a spanking that you would remember all your life, Miss,” stated an exceedingly irate reverend gentleman, while he marched out of the study. Because the coat belonging to Mr. Ashdown’s second best suit proved the wrong size for Mr. Perry, he was forced to attend the evening service wearing his scorched coat-tail. However, he failed to process up the aisle possessing his accustomed awareness of the dignity he bestowed upon the edifice. He refused to ever consent to a pulpit swap with Mr. Ashdown in the future, and he proved scarcely polite to the gentleman when their paths crossed briefly at the station the following morning. Nevertheless, Grace experienced a degree of somber gratification. Adam had been avenged in part.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: At school the following day, Grace faced a difficult time. The story regarding Adam had been spread by Mary Stubbs, leading every scholar, with the exception of the Carrows, to view the matter as entirely humorous. Amidst giggles, the girls informed Grace that the situation was indeed unfortunate, while sarcastic messages of sympathy were written to her by the boys. Grace returned home from school in a miserable state, experiencing a deep sense of internal soreness and pain.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “I am heading across to Hollowmere so I can speak with Mrs. Carrow,” she wept. “Unlike all the others, she will not mock me. I simply must speak to someone who comprehends the depth of my distress.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: She made her way down through Fern Hollow. Magic had been active during the previous night. A dusting of snow had come down, and the powdered firs were imagining an approaching spring and a future delight. The extended hill farther away was deeply purple from leafless beeches. The pinkish glow of sunset rested upon the earth like a rose-colored kiss. Among all the delicate, magical spots, brimming with strange, fairy-like elegance, Fern Hollow on that winter evening was the loveliest. However, its entire dreamlike beauty was unappreciated by poor, heartbroken little Grace.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Beside the stream she unexpectedly met Clementine Ainslie, who occupied the old pine tree. Home was her destination after leaving Hollowmere, the place where she had just provided the music lesson to the girls. A fair amount of time had passed while she tarried in Fern Hollow, gazing over its pale loveliness and wandering down several paths of reverie. To judge by her facial expression, her reflections were agreeable. It was possible that the gentle, sporadic clinking of the bells on the Tree Lovers produced the subtle, hidden smile upon her mouth. Alternatively, it might have been created by the awareness that John Ashdown rarely missed spending Monday evening at the gray house situated on the white, wind-blown hill.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Grace Ashdown, overflowing with defiant resentment, rushed into Clementine’s dreams. Upon noticing Miss Ainslie, Grace came to a sudden halt. Her acquaintance with her was minimal—only sufficient to exchange greetings upon meeting. Furthermore, she wished to avoid everyone at that moment—save for Mrs. Carrow. Aware that her nose and eyes were crimson and puffy, she despised the thought of a unfamiliar person discovering she had wept.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Good evening, Miss Ainslie,” she uttered, feeling ill at ease.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: In a gentle tone, Clementine inquired, “What is the matter, Grace?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Nothing,” Grace replied, speaking somewhat abruptly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Ah!” Clementine gave a smile. “It is your inability to share anything with those from the outside that you are referring to, isn't it?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: A sudden interest stirred in Grace as she looked at Miss Ainslie. This individual possessed a true understanding of things. Furthermore, her beauty was striking! Beneath her plumy hat, her hair shone with such gold! Above her velvet coat, her cheeks showed such pinkness! Her eyes appeared so blue and friendly! It seemed to Grace that a lovely friend could be found in Miss Ainslie—if she were merely a friend rather than a stranger!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “I—I am heading upstairs to inform Mrs. Carrow,” Grace declared. “Her understanding is constant—we are never mocked by her. I habituate discussing matters with her. Assistance comes from it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “My dear girl, it grieves me to inform you that Mrs. Carrow is away,” Miss Ainslie remarked with sympathy. “Having departed for Brierley today, she will remain absent until the week ends.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: The lip of Grace trembled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “In that case, I may as well return home,” she stated with sorrow.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “I believe that is true—unless you feel able to discuss it with me instead,” Miss Clementine offered softly. “Discussing things provides so much relief. I am aware of that. I doubt I am capable of understanding as well as Mrs. Carrow—yet I assure you I will not laugh.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “You wouldn’t laugh on the exterior,” Grace demurred. “However, you could—within.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Neither would I chuckle internally. For what reason would I? You have been harmed by something—witnessing anyone in pain is never entertaining to me, regardless of the cause of their distress. Should you experience a desire to inform me about what has caused your pain, I will gladly pay attention. However, if you believe you would prefer to keep it to yourself—that is completely fine as well, my darling.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Grace gazed once more into the eyes of Miss Ainslie with a prolonged, sincere look. They appeared deeply earnest, containing not a trace of mirth, even in their furthest depths. Letting out a quiet sigh, she seated herself on the ancient pine near her recently made companion and recounted the entire story of Adam along with his harsh destiny.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Laughter was far from Clementine, nor did she have any inclination toward it. Comprehension and empathy filled her—in truth, her capacity nearly matched that of Mrs. Carrow—indeed, it fully equaled hers.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Although Mr. Perry serves as a minister, he ought to have worked as a butcher,” Grace remarked with bitterness. “Carving things up brings him so much pleasure. Taking poor Adam apart gave him genuine enjoyment. He simply carved into him precisely like he was some ordinary rooster.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Giggling slightly—though Grace realized this was directed at Mr. Perry rather than Adam—Clementine remarked, “Grace, speaking privately, I do not care much for Mr. Perry either.” “He was never a favorite of mine. My school days were spent alongside him—as you are aware, he hailed from Glen—and in those days he was an utterly insufferable young prig. My goodness, the female students thoroughly despised grasping his chubby, damp palms during ring-around games. Nevertheless, my dear, we ought to keep in mind that he was unaware Adam held special status as your cherished companion. He assumed the bird was merely an ordinary rooster. Even amidst immense grief, fairness is required of us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “I guess that’s true,” Grace conceded. “However, Miss Ainslie, why is it that everyone appears to find my great love for Adam so humorous? No one would have found it odd if the pet had been a miserable old cat. Everyone felt sympathy for Lottie Warren when the binder severed her kitten’s legs. She wept in school for two days without anyone mocking her, not even Dan Coyle. Furthermore, all her close friends attended the kitten’s burial service and assisted her in interring it—except they were unable to inter its unfortunate small paws alongside it, since they were impossible to locate. Naturally, that was a terrible event to occur, but to my mind it was not as horrific as witnessing your pet being devoured. Still, everyone makes fun of me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “My belief is that it stems from the word ‘rooster’ sounding somewhat amusing,” Clementine stated seriously. “A humorous quality exists within it. Conversely, ‘chicken’ is not the same. Speaking about being fond of a chicken does not strike one as nearly so amusing.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Adam was the sweetest tiny chick, Miss Ainslie. He was merely a small ball of gold. He used to rush toward me to eat from my hand. Furthermore, he was good-looking when he matured, as well—pure white, boasting a lovely, curved white tail, even if Mary Stubbs claimed it lacked length. He recognized his name and consistently appeared whenever I summoned him—he was an exceptionally smart rooster. Moreover, Aunt Martha possessed no right to slaughter him. He belonged to me. It was not just, was it, Miss Ainslie?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “No, it was not,” Clementine stated with conviction. “It was not fair at all. I recall owning a pet hen during my childhood. That creature was extremely pretty—completely golden brown with small spots. My love for her matched the affection I ever felt for any animal companion. Her life was not ended by slaughter—she passed away from advanced years. Mother refused to permit her to be slaughtered owing to her being my pet.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Had my mother still been alive, Adam’s death would not have been allowed by her,” Grace remarked. “And as for father, he would not have permitted it either, had he been back and aware of the situation. Of that I am certain, Miss Ainslie.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “I’m positive, as well,” stated Clementine. Her cheeks displayed a slight extra color. She appeared somewhat self-aware, yet Grace failed to observe any of it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Did I act very wrongly by keeping quiet about Mr. Perry’s coat-tails burning?” she inquired with concern.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Oh, terribly wicked,” replied Clementine, her eyes dancing. “However, I would have behaved just as badly, Grace—I wouldn’t have informed him that they were burning—and I do not think I would have ever felt the slightest remorse for my bad behavior, either.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Ida was of the opinion that I ought to have informed him on the grounds that he was a clergyman.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “My dear, should a minister fail to act like a gentleman, we have no obligation to honor his coat-tails. I am certain I would have simply adored watching Jimmy Perry’s coat-tails catch fire. That had to be entertaining.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: A laugh came from both of them, though a faint, resentful sigh marked the end of Grace's.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Well, regardless, Adam has passed away and I will not love anything ever again.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Avoid speaking like that, my dear. If we fail to love, we forfeit a great deal of life's value. Life grows wealthier in proportion to how much we love—even when the object is merely a tiny pet with fur or feathers. Is a canary something you would want, Grace—a small, golden creature of a canary? Should you desire it, I will present you with one. Up at our home, there are two.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Oh, I would like that,” Grace exclaimed. “Birds are a favorite of mine. Only—would Aunt Martha’s cat consume it? Having your pets consumed is extremely tragic. I doubt I could bear it once more.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Should you suspend the cage a sufficient distance from the wall, it seems unlikely to me that the cat would be able to hurt it. I am going to explain to you precisely how you ought to attend to it, and I am going to convey it to Hollowmere on your behalf the very next time I travel down.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Clementine was reflecting within her own mind,

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Every local busybody in the Glen will be provided with a topic of conversation by this, yet I shall be indifferent. I wish to bring solace to this unfortunate small heart.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: Grace found solace in these moments, finding the sympathy and understanding to be deeply comforting. Alongside Miss Clementine, she remained seated on the old pine as dusk gently descended across the white valley and the evening star began to glow above the gray maple grove. Grace shared her entire modest past and aspirations with Clementine, detailing her preferences and aversion, the intricacies of living at the manse, as well as the fluctuations of school life. Ultimately, when they separated, a strong friendship had been established.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: When the evening meal commenced, Mr. Ashdown was absorbed in his typical reveries, yet before long, a specific name penetrated his daydreaming and restored his attention to the present. Grace was recounting to Ida how she had encountered Clementine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “In my opinion, she is simply delightful,” Grace remarked. “Equally pleasant as Mrs. Carrow—though in another way. It made me want to embrace her. She actually embraced me—a wonderfully soft, velvety embrace. On top of that, she addressed me as ‘dearest.’ It gave me a wonderful thrill. I felt capable of confiding anything to her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “So Miss Ainslie met with your approval, Grace?” inquired Mr. Ashdown, using a somewhat strange tone.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Grace cried, “I love her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND
text: “Ah!” Mr. Ashdown said. “Ah!”

John Ashdown ambled lost in thought amidst the sharp, fresh air of a winter evening in Fern Hollow. Past the town, the hills sparkled with the cold, magnificent radiance of snow under the moon. Along the sprawling valley, each tiny fir tree chanted a unique, untamed melody to the music of frost and wind. Down the eastern incline and gliding across the ice-covered pond, his children alongside the Carrow boys and girls were sledding. A wonderful time was being had by them, and their cheerful shouts and even happier laughter rang throughout the valley, fading into tiny, magical tones among the timber. To the right, through the grove of maples, the lights of Hollowmere shone with the warm, welcoming attraction that continuously appears to shine from the lamps of a dwelling where one understands love, gladness, and a reception exist for every relative, whether related by blood or soul. Now and then, Mr. Ashdown greatly enjoyed passing an evening debating with the doctor beside the driftwood fire, where the renowned china dogs of Hollowmere maintained an eternal guard, just as hearth gods ought to do, yet he did not glance in that direction this evening. Far away on the western hill, a dimmer but more captivating light shone. Mr. Ashdown was traveling to visit Clementine Ainslie, and he intended to reveal a matter to her that had been gradually developing inside his heart ever since they initially met and had bloomed completely on the night Grace had so enthusiastically expressed her praise for Clementine.

He had come to understand that he had grown fond of Clementine. Naturally, it was not like his feelings for Cecilia. That was a totally distinct matter. He believed that particular love, filled with romance, dreams, and glamour, could never come back. Nevertheless, Clementine was lovely, sweet, and cherished—extremely cherished. A better companion could not be found. In her presence, he experienced more happiness than he had ever anticipated feeling again. For his house, she would make a perfect mistress, and for his children, a fine mother.

In the time following the death of his wife, Mr. Ashdown had been given countless suggestions—coming from fellow Presbytery members, from various church members who were above suspicion of self-interest, and from a few who were not—that taking a second wife was something he should do: However, such suggestions failed to leave an impact on him. The general consensus was that he failed to notice them. Yet his awareness of them was actually very sharp. Moreover, during those moments when common sense briefly struck him, he recognized that finding a wife was indeed the practical course of action. Nevertheless, practical judgment was not a prominent trait in John Ashdown, and selecting a "suitable" female in a calculated, unemotional manner—much like hiring a housekeeper or taking on a business partner—represented a task he was entirely unable to perform. He despised the term "suitable" immensely. It brought James Perry to his mind with great intensity. “A suit able woman of suit able age,” that overly smooth fellow clergyman had remarked when dropping his exceedingly blatant suggestion. At that instant, John Ashdown experienced a truly astonishing urge to bolt wildly off and offer his hand in marriage to the most youthful, improper female he could possibly find.

His good friend Mrs. Ambrose Kerr was liked by him. However, his feeling when she had directly informed him that he ought to remarry was like she had ripped off the curtain suspended in front of a holy altar of his deepest existence, and from that point onward he had been somewhat fearful of her. The existence of women “of suitable age” within his flock who would willingly wed him was known to him. Very early during his pastorate at Glen St. Agnes, that truth had penetrated through his complete detachment. Good, solid, tedious women they were, with a couple being reasonably attractive and the rest not quite that, and John Ashdown would have considered hanging himself just as willingly as wedding any single one of them. Unfaithful to certain ideals he possessed no apparent requirement could render him. No woman could be requested by him to take Cecilia’s spot within his house except if he was able to present her with a minimum portion of the devotion and reverence he had bestowed upon his young wife. Furthermore, where could such a female be located among the small number of women he knew?

Clementine Ainslie entered his existence on that evening in autumn, bearing a presence where his soul identified its true element. They joined hands in fellowship over the abyss of unfamiliarity. Within those ten minutes beside the concealed spring, he understood her more deeply than he understood Emmeline Drew or Elizabeth Kirk or Amy Annetta Fairlie over the course of a year, or ever could comprehend them throughout a hundred years. He had sought refuge with her for solace after Mrs. Hector Twiss offended his intellect and spirit, and he had received that comfort. From that moment forward, he frequently visited the dwelling atop the hill, moving along the darkened trails of evening in Fern Hollow with such skill that the chatter of the Glen was never able to confirm beyond doubt that his visits were to Clementine Ainslie. He had been discovered once or twice in the West living room by different guests; that comprised the sole evidence the Ladies’ Aid possessed. However, upon Elizabeth Kirk learning this, she discarded a quiet expectation she had permitted herself to hold, showing no transformation of look on her gentle, unpretentious visage, while Emmeline Drew decided that on her following encounter with a particular elderly unmarried man from Kettlebridge, she would refrain from dismissing him as she had during an earlier encounter. Naturally, should Clementine Ainslie set out to capture the clergyman, she was bound to capture him; her appearance seemed youthful for her age and gentlemen considered her attractive; furthermore, the Ainslie daughters possessed wealth!

“May he not prove so distracted that he accidentally asks Harriet to marry him,” represented the sole spiteful remark she permitted herself to utter to a compassionate sister Drew. Emmeline harbored no additional resentment toward Clementine. Ultimately, a single man without obligations was vastly superior to a widower possessing four offspring. It was merely the allure of the parsonage that had briefly obscured Emmeline’s vision regarding the superior choice.

Passing Mr. Ashdown, a sled carrying three yelling riders hurtled toward the pond. Grace’s hair was flowing in the breeze, her long curls trailing, and the sound of her laughing rose above the rest. John Ashdown watched the trio go with a kind, wistful expression. It pleased him that his youngsters were companions with the Carrows—he was pleased they possessed a confidante as intelligent, cheerful, and gentle as Mrs. Carrow. Yet they lacked a further element, one that would be provided once he brought Clementine Ainslie to the old manse to be his wife. Possessed by her was a nature fundamentally motherly.

Because it was Saturday evening, he rarely paid visits at that time, as those hours were meant for carefully reviewing his sermon for Sunday. Nevertheless, he had selected this particular evening after discovering that Harriet Ainslie would be out of town and Clementine would be by herself. Although he had frequently enjoyed agreeable evenings in the house on the hill, he had not, from the time of their initial encounter at the spring, ever found Clementine by herself. Harriet had invariably been present.

It was not that he genuinely disapproved of Harriet’s presence. His fondness for Harriet Ainslie was great, and their friendship was of the highest order. Harriet possessed a mind that was nearly masculine, alongside a sense of humour that accorded exceptionally well with his own reserved, concealed enjoyment of wit. Her engagement with politics and global affairs pleased him. Within the Glen, including Dr. Carrow, no man possessed a superior comprehension of these matters.

“I consider it just as good to maintain an interest in matters for the duration of your life,” she had stated. “If you fail to do so, it appears to me that little distinguishes the living from the deceased.”

His fondness extended to her agreeable, low, resonant voice, as well as the robust laughter that invariably concluded her cheerful, expertly narrated tales. Unlike the remaining females of Glen, she refrained from making sharp remarks concerning his offspring; she refrained from wearying him with neighborhood rumors; she possessed neither ill will nor small-mindedness. Her truthfulness was consistently grand. Adopting Miss Winifred’s method of categorizing individuals, Mr. Ashdown felt that Harriet was part of Joseph’s line. On the whole, she was an excellent person to have as a sister-in-law. Even so, a gentleman wished for the absence of even the finest females while he was offering marriage to a different lady. Yet Harriet remained constantly present. She refrained from demanding that Mr. Ashdown converse solely with her throughout the time. She allowed Clementine an equal portion of his attention. In fact, on numerous nights, Harriet withdrew almost completely, resting in the corner with St. Laurence held in her lap, while Mr. Ashdown and Clementine engaged in conversation, music, and joint reading. Occasionally, her existence slipped their minds entirely. Should their dialogue or duet selections display the slightest inclination toward what Harriet deemed flirty behavior, however, Harriet immediately crushed that inclination and sidelined Clementine for what remained of the night. Even the most stern among friendly guardians, however, cannot fully obstruct a particular delicate communication of glances, grins, and meaningful hushes; thus, the clergyman’s romantic pursuit advanced to a degree.

However, if a peak were ever to be attained, that peak had to occur during Harriet’s absence. And Harriet was rarely absent, particularly during the winter months. She declared that she considered her own hearth to be the most delightful spot on earth. Traveling about possessed no charm for her. She enjoyed society, yet she desired to have it in her own house. Mr. Ashdown had nearly reached the point of believing he would have to express his thoughts to Clementine in a letter, when Harriet nonchalantly mentioned one night that she intended to attend a silver wedding the following Saturday evening. She had served as a bridesmaid at the original wedding of the couple. Because the invitation was restricted to old guests, Clementine was not among those invited. Mr. Ashdown listened with somewhat heightened interest, and a spark shone in his dark, dreamlike eyes. Harriet and Clementine both observed this; and Harriet and Clementine each experienced, with a sharp thrill, the realization that Mr. Ashdown was sure to ascend the hill the coming Saturday night.

“We might just as well get this over with, St. Laurence,” Harriet firmly remarked to the black cat, once Mr. Ashdown had departed for home and Clementine had quietly headed upstairs. “He intends to propose to her, St. Laurence—I am completely certain of it. Therefore he ought to be given his opportunity to ask and discover that she is beyond his reach, Laurence. She would quite enjoy accepting him, Saint. I am aware of that—nevertheless she gave her word, and she must adhere to her word. I feel somewhat regretful in certain respects, St. Laurence. I am unaware of any man I would prefer more as a brother-in-law if having a brother-in-law were suitable. I have no objections to him, Saint—not a single objection other than his inability to recognize and be convinced that the Kaiser poses a threat to the peace of Europe. That constitutes his blind spot. Even so, he provides good companionship and I am fond of him. A female is able to speak whatever she desires to a male possessing a mouth such as John Ashdown’s and remain confident she will not be misconstrued. A gentleman of that sort is worth more than rubies, Saint—and far less common, Laurence. Even so, Clementine is not for him—and I imagine that once he learns she is unavailable to him he will abandon the two of us. And we will long for his presence, Saint—we will long for his presence to an extraordinary degree, Laurence. All the same, she gave her word, and I shall ensure she adheres to her word!”
Harriet’s expression appeared nearly unattractive due to its dark determination. On the upper floor, Clementine wept into her pillow.

Thus Mr. Ashdown discovered his lady by herself and appearing extremely gorgeous. Clementine had not prepared any particular attire for the meeting; she wished to, yet she considered it ridiculous to adorn oneself for a gentleman whom you intended to reject. Consequently she was clad in her simple dark afternoon gown and possessed the appearance of a queen in it. The excitement she kept hidden tinted her countenance to a radiant glow, while her enormous blue eyes formed basins of illumination that were less calm than ordinary.

She longed for the meeting to come to an end. All day long she had anticipated it with fear. She was entirely confident that John Ashdown held her in high regard in his own way—and she was equally convinced that he lacked the feeling for her that he had possessed for his initial love. She sensed that her rejection would cause him significant disappointment, though she doubted it would completely destroy him. Still, she detested delivering the rejection; she detested it for his sake and—Clementine admitted this candidly to herself—for her own. She was aware that she was capable of loving John Ashdown if—if she were allowed to do so. She was aware that her existence would become empty if, once turned down as a suitor, he declined to remain her friend. She was aware that she could find great joy with him and that she possessed the ability to bring him joy. However, blocking her path to joy was the immovable barrier formed by the vow she had given Harriet long in the past. Clementine had no recollection of her father. His death had occurred when her age was merely three. Harriet, being thirteen at the time, retained a memory of him, though without any particular affection. He had been a severe, aloof individual much senior to his attractive, comely spouse. Five years afterwards, their twelve-year-old brother passed away as well; following his passing, the pair of girls had continually resided solely alongside their mother. They had refrained from participating very openly in the societal activities of the Glen or Kettlebridge, even if, whenever they attended, the humor and vigor of Harriet together with the gentleness and charm of Clementine rendered them desired visitors. Each of them had experienced what people termed “a disappointment” during their youth. The ocean had failed to return Clementine’s beloved; while Lionel Fairlie, at that time a striking, red-haired youthful colossus, renowned for reckless driving along with boisterous yet innocent misdeeds, had engaged in a dispute with Harriet and deserted her in a sudden bout of resentment.

No shortage of suitors appeared for the positions of Martin and Lionel, yet not one appeared to gain approval from the Ainslie girls, as they gradually slipped out of their youth and status as belles with no apparent remorse. Their devotion belonged to their mother, an individual with a long-term illness. A small realm of domestic pursuits—comprising books, pets, and flowers—was shared by the three, leaving them joyful and satisfied.

A profound sorrow came upon them when Mrs. Ainslie died on the day Clementine turned twenty-five. Their initial state was one of unbearable isolation. Harriet’s mourning and despondency persisted with particular intensity, as prolonged, somber reflections were interrupted solely by outbursts of violent, fierce tears. Clementine was informed by the aged Kettlebridge physician that he worried about lasting desolation or an even darker outcome.
On one occasion, after Harriet had spent the entire day in silence and refused to consume any food, Clementine had dropped to her knees beside her sister.
“Oh, Harriet, I am still here with you,” she pleaded. “Do I mean nothing to you? Our love for one another has always been so strong.”

“You will not belong to me forever,” Harriet had uttered, shattering her quietness with severe force. “After getting married, you will go away from me. Only I will remain, entirely by myself. It is impossible for me to endure that idea—simply impossible. Passing away would be my preference.”
“Never will I take a husband,” declared Clementine, “never, Harriet.”
Leaning toward her, Harriet peered intently into the eyes of Clementine.
“Do you solemnly give me your promise on that?” she asked. “Swear it using mother’s Bible.”

Clementine agreed immediately, being perfectly happy to indulge Harriet. It made no difference to her. She was entirely aware that she would not ever wish to wed a soul. The depths of the ocean held her love, which had descended there alongside Martin Crawford; and lacking love, marriage to anyone was impossible for her. Consequently, she gave her word without hesitation, even if Harriet turned the affair into a somewhat terrifying ritual. In the empty room belonging to their mother, they held hands across the Bible, and each swore to the other a solemn oath that marriage was out of the question for them and that cohabitation would be their lifelong choice.

Harriet’s health got better from that moment on. Before long, her usual cheerful composure returned. Clementine and she resided in the old home contentedly for a decade, unbothered by any idea of wedlock or matrimony. They felt the burden of their vow very little. Whenever an available man encountered them, Harriet made a point to recall their agreement to her sister, yet she had not experienced genuine anxiety until Clementine brought John Ashdown home that evening. Regarding Clementine, Harriet’s fixation on that pledge had continually served as a minor source of amusement for her—up to recently. Currently, it was a ruthless chain, chosen by herself yet impossible to break free from. On account of it, she had to look away from joy this evening.

Indeed, the timid, gentle, youthful affection she had bestowed upon her boy-lover could never be offered to someone else. Nevertheless, she realized at present that the love she could bestow upon John Ashdown was richer and more mature. She recognized that he reached depths within her character that Martin had failed to reach—depths that, perchance, the seventeen-year-old girl had lacked. Yet she was required to dismiss him this evening—to dispatch him home to his solitary fireside, his vacant existence, and his agonizing troubles, all because she had sworn to Harriet, a decade earlier, upon their mother’s Bible, that she would refuse to ever wed.

John Ashdown failed to seize his chance right away. Instead, he spent two full hours discussing topics that were far from romantic. He went so far as to bring up politics, despite knowing that Clementine was always bored by the subject. She started to believe that she was completely wrong, and all at once her anxieties and hopes appeared absurd to her. A sense of flatness and foolishness came over her. Her face lost its warmth and her eyes lost their shine. John Ashdown was not planning to ask for her hand in marriage at all.

And then, all at once, he got up, walked to the other side of the room, and inquired it while standing beside her chair. The room had become dreadfully quiet. St. Laurence even stopped purring. Her own heart was heard beating by Clementine, who felt certain that John Ashdown had to hear it as well.

Gentle yet decisive, her refusal ought to have been spoken right then. For days, she had held her stiff, apologetic little speech in reserve. Yet in that moment, its phrasing was entirely erased from her memory. A negative answer was required of her—and all at once, she discovered an inability to utter it. The word was simply unutterable. That she did not merely possess the capacity to love John Ashdown, but truly loved him already, was now clear to her. Rejecting him from her existence felt like pure torment.
Compelled to speak, she raised her bent blonde head and falteringly requested that he grant her a short period to—to think it over.

A small amount of astonishment touched John Ashdown. Although his vanity did not exceed what is permissible for any man, his expectation had been that Clementine Ainslie would give her consent. That she possessed feelings for him had seemed fairly certain to him. What then accounted for this uncertainty—this pausing? Having passed the age of a school girl, she was not one to be doubtful regarding her own inclinations. A nasty jolt of letdown and alarm registered within him. Nevertheless, showing his ever-present mild politeness, he agreed to what she asked and departed without delay.
“In a handful of days, I shall inform you,” stated Clementine, her gaze directed downward and her cheeks flushed.
As soon as the door closed behind his exit, she returned to the interior of the room, wringing her hands together.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: When midnight arrived, Harriet Ainslie was returning on foot to her house from the silver wedding of the Pollocks. She had remained for a short time following the departure of the remaining guests, assisting the bride with gray hair as she washed dishes. Because the space separating the pair of homes was brief and the path was in good condition, Harriet was taking pleasure in her moonlight return journey to her house.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: The night had proved to be an enjoyable one. It was very enjoyable for Harriet, who had not attended a party in years. Every guest had belonged to her former circle, and no unwelcome young people were there to ruin the atmosphere, since the bride and groom’s only son was attending college far away and was unable to attend. Lionel Fairlie had attended, and it was the first time they had met in a social setting in years, even though she had spotted him one or two times in church during that winter. Their encounter did not stir the slightest bit of romance in Harriet’s heart. Whenever she pondered the matter at all, she was used to being amazed that she could have ever been attracted to him or been so deeply hurt by his abrupt wedding. Nevertheless, she had quite enjoyed seeing him once more. She had failed to remember how invigorating and inspiring he was able to be. An assembly was never dull whenever Lionel Fairlie was in attendance. Everyone was astonished when Lionel arrived. His habit of never going out was common knowledge. He had been asked by the Pollocks because he was among the original guests, yet they did not actually expect him to show up. He escorted his second cousin, Amy Annetta Fairlie, to supper and appeared quite attentive toward her. However, Harriet was seated opposite him at the table and engaged in a lively debate with him—a debate throughout which his entire shouting and teasing failed to fluster her, and from which she emerged victorious, defeating Lionel so calmly and thoroughly that he said nothing for ten minutes. When those minutes had passed, he growled into his reddish beard—“spunky as ever—spunky as ever”—and started picking on Amy Annetta, who laughed foolishly at his remarks where Harriet would have offered a sharp comeback.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: These matters were pondered by Harriet as she made her way back, savoring them with a backward-looking enjoyment. Frost made the night air, lit by the moon, glisten. Beneath her boots, the snow crunched. The Glen spread out beneath her, leading to the snowy harbor past it. A lamp burned inside the manse study. John Ashdown had returned home, then. Was Clementine asked by him to be his wife? And in what manner had her rejection been communicated? That she would never learn this was Harriet's feeling, despite her considerable inquisitiveness. That Clementine would refrain from ever sharing anything regarding the matter with her was a certainty to her, nor would she have the courage to inquire. The reality of the rejection simply had to satisfy her. Ultimately, nothing else was truly important.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I wish he possesses sufficient wisdom to return occasionally and act amicably,” she uttered inwardly. Her aversion to isolation was so strong that speaking her thoughts was a method she used to bypass unwanted loneliness. “It is terrible to lack a intelligent male figure to converse with on occasion. And it is quite probable he will refrain from approaching the dwelling forever. Lionel Fairlie exists as well—that individual appeals to me, and I would enjoy engaging in a spirited debate with him occasionally. However, he would not venture here lest folk suspect he was pursuing me anew—or perhaps lest I suspect it myself—even though he feels more unfamiliar to me at present than John Ashdown. The idea that we were once romantic partners resembles a fantasy. Yet that remains the reality—a mere two males in the Glen merit my conversation—and owing to rumors and this miserable romantic affair it is improbable I will behold either one henceforth. I was capable,” Harriet stated, directing her words toward the indifferent stars with bitter force, “of creating a superior world on my own.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: A sudden, indistinct sense of dread made her stop beside her gate. A light continued to shine in the living-room, where the silhouette of a woman paced back and forth, moving incessantly across the window-shades. Why had Clementine not gone to bed at such a late hour? And what reason did she have to march back and forth like a mad person?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Harriet stepped quietly inside. Clementine emerged from the room just as she unclosed the entrance to the hall. Her face was red, and she was out of breath. She was surrounded by an aura of strain and intensity as if wearing it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Clementine, what is the reason you are not sleeping?” Harriet asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Step inside,” Clementine said with intensity. “There is something I wish to tell you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Taking off her wraps and galoshes with composure, Harriet went after her sister into the room that was warm and lit by the fire. Remaining stationary with her hand upon the table, she waited. In her own stern, dark-eyebrowed manner, she was looking quite handsome. Designed by her specifically for the gathering, the new black velvet gown, featuring a V-neck and a train, suited her grand, large frame. Wrapped about her neck, she wore the opulent, weighty amber bead necklace that served as a family relic. Her face had been bitten to a radiant red by her stroll through the crisp air. Nevertheless, her steel-blue eyes remained just as frozen and rigid as the night sky in wintertime. She remained standing and waiting in a quietness that Clementine could disrupt solely through a spasmodic exertion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet, this evening Mr. Ashdown was here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Yes?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “And—and—he requested that I become his wife.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “That is what I anticipated. Naturally, you turned him down?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “No.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Clementine.” Harriet’s fists tightened as she unconsciously moved a step toward her. “Are you saying that you agreed to marry him?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “No—no.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Harriet regained control of her feelings.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “What was your next course of action?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I—I requested that he grant me several days to consider the matter.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I do not quite understand why that had to be done,” Harriet remarked, with aloof disdain, “since you can give him but a single response.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: In an imploring gesture, Clementine extended her hands.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet,” she pleaded, “John Ashdown has my heart—I desire to become his spouse. Would you release me from that vow?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “No,” Harriet replied, lacking any pity, since terror was making her ill.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet—Harriet—”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Listen,” Harriet broke in. “That promise was not requested by me. It was offered by you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I am aware—I am aware. However, back then, I failed to believe I might ever love somebody else.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “It was proffered by you,” Harriet continued without flinching. “Over the Bible belonging to our mother, your word was given. Rather than a mere promise, an oath was made. At present, you wish to go back on it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet, my sole request was for you to release me from it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I shall refrain from doing it. To me, a pledge remains a pledge. I shall refrain from doing it. Violate your own word—commit perjury if you so choose—yet it will occur without any agreement from me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet, you treat me with great severity.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “It is severe for you! But what about my situation? Did it ever cross your mind how isolated I would be in this place should you abandon me? That would be unbearable for me—my mind would break. Existing by myself is impossible for me. Has my sisterhood to you not been devoted? Was there ever a desire of yours that I stood against? Did I not yield to all your whims?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Yes—yes.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Why, then, is it your wish to abandon me for a man you were unacquainted with a year back?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Harriet, I am in love with him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Love! Your speech resembles that of a school miss rather than a middle-aged woman. His feeling for you is not love. What he desires is a housekeeper and a governess. Your feeling for him is not love. Your desire is to be ‘Mrs.’—you belong to that group of weak-minded women who consider it a disgrace to be categorized as an old maid. There is nothing more to it than that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Clementine trembled. Harriet was unable, or perhaps unwilling, to comprehend. It was futile to debate with her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “Then you refuse to set me free, Harriet?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “No, I will not. Nor will I speak about it any more. A promise was made by you, and you must hold to your word. Nothing else needs to be said. Retire to sleep. Observe the hour! Romantic excitement has overcome you. By to-morrow, your good sense will return. In any case, I am not to hear another word of this foolishness. Go.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Clementine departed in silence, her face drained of color and lacking energy. After pacing the room angrily for a short duration, Harriet stopped in front of the seat in which St. Laurence had slept peacefully all night long. An unwilling grin spread across her swarthy countenance. Harriet had failed to balance drama with humor on merely a single occasion in her existence—at the moment her mother died. Even during that distant period of grief, when Lionel Fairlie had jilted her to an extent, she had found reason to laugh at herself just as frequently as she had wept.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “I anticipate some pouting will occur, St. Laurence. Indeed, Saint, a period of disagreeable, misty days likely lies ahead for us. Nevertheless, we will ride them out, Laurence. Foolish youths have been managed by us in the past, Saint. Clementine will mope for a time—and afterwards she will recover from it—and everything will return to its previous state, Laurence. She gave her word—and she is required to fulfill her vow. And those are the final remarks regarding the matter that I shall utter to you, to her, or to any person, Saint.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: Yet till the arrival of morning, Harriet remained fiercely awake in her bed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: No brooding occurred, however. The following day, Clementine appeared pale and silent, yet Harriet noticed no other alteration in her behavior. Indeed, she appeared to harbor no resentment toward Harriet. Because the weather was tempestuous, no one spoke of attending church. During the afternoon, Clementine locked herself in her bedroom and composed a line to John Ashdown. She lacked the confidence to utter “no” face to face. She was entirely convinced that if he surmised her “no” was given unwillingly, he would refuse to accept it, and she lacked the fortitude for entreaties or supplications. She had to convince him that he meant absolute zero to her, a feat achievable solely through correspondence. She drafted the most formal, icy little rejection one could conceive. It was scarcely polite; it undeniably offered no faint ray of hope to even the most daring suitor—and John Ashdown was far from daring. He recoiled internally, wounded and humiliated, upon reading Clementine’s message the following day inside his dusty study. Yet beneath his humiliation, a terrible truth soon became apparent. He had believed his affection for Clementine was inferior to the love he had harbored for Cecilia. At present, having lost her, he recognized that he truly did. She represented all things to him—all things! And he was forced to remove her from his existence entirely. Even comradeship was now out of the question. Existence lay ahead of him in unbearable gloom. He was required to continue—he possessed his labor—his offspring—yet his spirit was utterly destroyed. He remained isolated the entire evening inside his dim, chilly, uninviting study, his head resting upon his hands. High on the hill, Clementine suffered from a headache and retired to bed early, whereas Harriet observed to St. Laurence, who purred his contempt for senseless humanity, who failed to realize that a plush cushion was the sole matter of genuine importance,

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT
text: “How would women manage had headaches not been created, St. Laurence? However, it does not matter, Saint. For a short time, we shall simply close an eye to it. I allow that I do not feel at ease myself, Laurence. My sensation is like having submerged a kitten. Nevertheless, she gave her word, Saint—and the proposal came from her, Laurence. Bismillah!”

Gentle, fine, and lovely spring rain had descended throughout the entire day, appearing to subtly suggest and murmur about emerging violets and mayflowers. Pearl-gray mists had obscured the low shore fields, the gulf, and the harbour. However, as night fell, the precipitation stopped, and the ocean winds swept the mists away. Small, flaming roses of clouds were scattered across the sky above the harbour. Past this, the hills appeared dark when set against an extravagant display of crimson and daffodil. Over the bar, a large, silver evening star kept vigil. A lively, leaping wind that had just arisen blew from Fern Hollow, filled with the resinous scents of wet mosses and fir. This breeze murmured among the ancient spruces encircling the cemetery and disturbed Grace’s magnificent curls as she rested upon Hezekiah Pollock’s tombstone, her arms encircling Ida and Mary Stubbs. Facing them on a different tombstone sat Tobias and Rupert, and everyone was feeling somewhat mischievous following a whole day of being confined indoors.
“The atmosphere simply glows this evening, doesn't it? You know, it has been cleansed so thoroughly,” Grace remarked with joy.

Grace appeared entirely too cheerful to Mary Stubbs, given the details she was aware of, or imagined she was aware of, causing her to gaze at her with a somber expression. There was a thought resting on Mary’s mind that she intended to voice prior to returning home. Having been dispatched to the manse by Mrs. Kerr to deliver a batch of fresh eggs, she had received instructions not to remain beyond thirty minutes. As that allotted time was almost exhausted, Mary unfolded her legs from beneath her where they had grown stiff, and remarked suddenly,

“Forget about the air. Simply hear what I have to say. You youths from the manse simply must conduct yourselves far better than you have been doing throughout this spring—it comes down to that alone. I came up this very evening with the sole intention of informing you of this. The manner in which folks are discussing you is dreadful.”

“What have we been doing now?” exclaimed Grace with surprise, wrenching her arm from Mary’s grasp. The lips of Ida quivered as her delicate little spirit cringed inside her. Mary never failed to be so savagely blunt. A whistle came from Tobias out of defiance. He intended to show Mary that her outbursts did not affect him. Regardless, the way they acted was none of her concern. By what authority was she scolding them about their behavior?

“You are doing it now, just like you are doing it all the time,” Mary snapped back. “The moment people stop discussing one of your shenanigans, you commit another to get them talking once more. It appears to me that you have no concept of how the children of a manse should conduct themselves!”
“It's possible you could inform us,” Tobias said, his tone dripping with sarcasm.
Mary completely failed to grasp sarcasm.

“I can inform you about the consequences if you fail to master proper behavior. Your father will be requested to resign by the session. So there, Master Tobias-know-it-all. Mrs. Hector Twiss uttered those words to Mrs. Kerr. They reached my ears. Whenever Mrs. Hector Twiss visits for tea, my ears are invariably alert. It was her statement that every one of you was deteriorating further, and even though such an outcome was anticipated given that you lacked anyone to raise you, the congregation nevertheless could not be required to tolerate it for much longer, meaning an action would need to be taken. Continuous laughter is directed at you by the Methodists, which damages feelings among the Presbyterians. According to her, a strong application of birch tonic is required by all of you. Lor’, were such a thing capable of making people righteous, a young saint is what I ought to be. My reason for sharing this with you is not a desire to wound your feelings. My sympathy goes out to you”—Mary was past mistress of the gentle art of condescension. “It is clear to me that given how things stand, your prospects are limited. Yet, the same level of allowance I make is not granted by others. According to Miss Drew, a frog was inside Rupert’s pocket during Sunday School this past Sunday, and during her recitation of the lesson, it leaped out. Her intention is to relinquish the class, so she says. What is the reason you fail to leave your insecks at home?”

“I put it right back inside,” Rupert said. “It was just a harmless little frog! I also hope that old Odette Drew stops teaching our class. She is awful. Her very own nephew carried a filthy wad of tobacco in his pocket and invited us boys to take a chew while Elder Clow was offering a prayer. That must be far worse than a frog.”

“No, on account of frogs being more out of the blue. A bigger stir is caused by them. Furthermore, he didn't get caught doing it. On top of that, a terrible scandal was created by that praying contest you held last week. It's the talk of everyone.”
“Why, the Carrows took part in that just like we did,” Grace shouted angrily. “Bess Carrow was actually the one who proposed it to begin with. And the prize was won by Edmund.”
“Well, regardless, you are given the credit for it. Had you not done it inside the graveyard, it would not have been quite so awful.”
“A graveyard would make a particularly fine location for praying, in my opinion,” Tobias fired back.

“When you were engaged in prayer, Deacon Hazard traveled by,” Mary remarked, “and after taking note of your hands resting across your belly and listening as you uttered a moan following each statement, he witnessed you. It appeared to him that you were mocking him.”

“Indeed I was,” announced unashamed Tobias. “Except I was unaware he was passing, naturally. It was merely a nasty coincidence. My prayers weren't truly sincere—I was aware I stood no likelihood of taking the award. Thus, I was simply deriving whatever amusement I was able to from the situation. Edmund Carrow is capable of praying fantastically. Why, his praying abilities match those of dad.”
“Ida is the sole person among US who truly enjoys prayer,” Grace remarked thoughtfully.
“Indeed, if our prayers cause such offense to others, we have to stop doing it,” Ida lamented.

“Well, you are allowed to pray as much as you like, just not within the cemetery—and do not turn it into a joke. It was that which caused such trouble—that, along with holding a tea-party atop the gravestones.”
“We had not.”

“Well, a soap-bubble gathering then. You possessed something. The folks from across the harbour insist you hosted a tea-party, though I am ready to believe you. And you made use of this tombstone for a table.”
“Indeed, Martha refused to allow us to blow bubbles indoors. On that day, her temper was dreadful,” Tobias clarified. “Furthermore, this ancient slab functioned as such a splendid table.”

“Were they not lovely?” exclaimed Grace, her eyes shining as she recalled the memory. “Like tiny magical realms, they showed the trees, the hills, and the harbour, and after we released them, they drifted off toward Fern Hollow.”
“Every single one except for a solitary one, which flew past and shattered against the steeple of the Methodist church,” Rupert remarked.
“I am happy that we accomplished it a single time, at least, prior to discovering that it was incorrect,” Grace stated.

“Blowing them on the lawn would not have been wrong,” Mary said with impatience. “It appears I am unable to knock sense into your heads. You have been informed frequently enough that playing in the graveyard is something you shouldn't do. About it, the Methodists are sensitive.”

“We forget,” Grace remarked in a mournful tone. “And the lawn is extremely tiny—and contains so many caterpillars—and is packed with bushes and such. It is impossible for us to remain in Fern Hollow perpetually—and where else can we head?”
