“It is your actions in the cemetery that cause trouble. Just sitting in this place and speaking softly, like we are doing this very moment, would not be an issue. Though I cannot say what the outcome will be, I am certain Elder Warren intends to talk to your pa regarding the matter. Deacon Hazard happens to be his cousin.”
“I wish they would leave father alone regarding us,” Ida remarked.

“Indeed, folks believe that he should pay you a bit more attention. I do not—I comprehend his nature. In certain respects, he is merely a youth himself—that is his true character, and he requires somebody to take care of him just as urgently as you require it. Indeed, maybe he will possess somebody in the near future, if every rumor proves accurate.”
“In what way do you mean?” Grace inquired.
“Do you really not have any notion—truthfully?” asked Mary.
“No, no. What is it that you mean?”
“Well, upon my word, you are all so naive. Why, the entire town is discussing the matter. Your father pays visits to Clementine Ainslie. She will soon become your stepmother.”
“It isn't true,” Ida exclaimed, turning bright red.

“Indeed, I am uncertain. My words merely reflect what people are saying. I am not presenting it as certainty. Still, it would prove beneficial. I am willing to wager a penny that Clementine Ainslie would force you to behave if she arrived here, despite her appearing so lovely and pleasant on the surface. That is how they always act until they have secured them. Nevertheless, you require somebody to discipline you. You bring shame upon your father, and my sympathies lie with him. My esteem for your father has been immense ever since he spoke to me so kindly that evening. Since that time, not one profanity has crossed my lips, nor have I uttered a falsehood. Furthermore, my desire is to behold him content and at ease, possessing his buttons and receiving proper food, alongside you youngsters being brought to order, while that old hag Martha gets relegated to her rightful position. Consider how she inspected the eggs I delivered to her this evening. ‘I hope they’re fresh,’ says she. My desire was that they were spoiled instead. However, you must ensure that she distributes one to each of you for breakfast, your father included. Cause a scene if she fails to do so. That was the purpose behind sending them up—yet Martha cannot be trusted. She is fully capable of giving them to her cat.”

Because Mary’s tongue was for the moment exhausted, a short quietness settled across the churchyard. The manse children had no desire to speak. They were mulling over the fresh and less than appetizing thoughts that Mary had put forward to them. Tobias and Rupert felt a bit shaken. Even so, what difference did it make in the end? Besides, it was improbable that any of it was true. Grace, taking everything into account, felt glad. It was only Ida who was deeply disturbed. She wished that she could go off somewhere and weep.
“In my crown, will any stars be present?” the choir of Methodists commenced singing, starting their rehearsal inside the church of the Methodists.

“Only three are what I want,” stated Mary, whose understanding of theology had grown significantly since she began living with Mrs. Kerr. “Only three—arranged atop my head, similar to a crown, with a large one situated in the center and a little one on either side.”
“Is there a variety of sizes when it comes to souls?” Rupert inquired.

“Naturally. Why, tiny infants require smaller ones than large grown men. Well, night is falling and I need to hurry back. Mrs. Kerr disapproves of my being outside past dusk. Goodness, during the time I resided with Mrs. Grimble the night was no different than daytime to me. It bothered me no more than it would a gray cat. Those times feel like a century back. Now, remember my words and endeavor to act properly, for your father's sake. I will constantly support you and stand up for you—you may be absolutely certain of that. Mrs. Kerr claims she has never encountered anyone quite like me when it comes to standing by my companions. I spoke quite impudently to Mrs. Hector Twiss regarding you and Mrs. Kerr gave me a scolding for it later. That lovely Winifred possesses a sharp tongue of her own and that's the truth. However, she was secretly delighted despite everything, because she detests old Kitty Hector and she is truly devoted to you. I can read people.”
Departing with a great deal of satisfaction, Mary voyaged away, abandoning a somewhat disheartened small party in her wake.
“Whenever Mary Stubbs walks up to us, she consistently utters remarks that upset us,” Ida stated with bitterness.
“I would have preferred it if we had abandoned her to go hungry in that former barn,” Tobias remarked with spite.
“Oh, that’s wicked, Tobias,” Ida rebuked.
“If our reputation is already so terrible, we might as well act the part,” replied Tobias without a shred of remorse. “We should just be evil if that is what everyone claims we are.”
“However, provided it doesn't cause pain to father,” Grace begged.

Tobias shifted about in discomfort. His father was someone he idolized. Mr. Ashdown was visible sitting by his desk through the uncurtained window of the study. Reading or writing did not appear to be what he was doing. Resting his head within his hands, his entire posture conveyed an impression of exhaustion and gloom. The children were abruptly aware of this.
“It seems likely that today someone has been bothering him regarding us,” Grace remarked. “I would prefer if we managed to get by without causing gossip. Oh—Kit Carrow! You frightened me so much!”

Kit Carrow had crept into the burial ground and taken a seat next to the girls. Having been roaming around Fern Hollow, he had managed to discover the initial small, star-white spray of arbutus for his mother. The children from the manse became somewhat quiet following his arrival. During this spring, Kit was starting to grow apart from them a bit. Preparing for the entrance examination at Regent’s Academy, he remained behind after school alongside the older students to receive extra instruction. Furthermore, because his evenings were so packed with study, he rarely came to Fern Hollow with the rest of them anymore. It appeared he was slipping away into the world of adults.
“What has come over everyone this evening?” he inquired. “You are no fun at all.”
“Not much,” Grace sorrowfully concurred. “You would not have much fun in you either if you were aware that you were bringing shame upon your father and causing people to gossip about you.”
“Who has been speaking of you this time?”

“All of us—according to Mary Stubbs,” Grace said, unburdening her anxieties to an understanding Kit. “The problem is,” she finished mournfully, “there is no one to raise us. Consequently, we end up in trouble and are considered bad by everyone.”

“Why do you not elevate yourselves?” Kit proposed. “I will offer a suggestion for what you should do. Establish a Good-Conduct Club and penalize yourselves whenever you commit an action that is improper.”

“I think that is a wonderful thought,” Grace remarked, impressed by the suggestion. “However,” she continued with hesitation, “actions that appear completely innocent to US are viewed as downright terrible by everyone else. What way is there for us to know? It is impossible to constantly trouble father—especially since his presence is frequently required elsewhere.”

“If you paused to consider an action beforehand and questioned what the congregation might remark regarding it, you would usually be able to judge,” Kit said. “Your problem stems from jumping straight into matters without giving them any thought whatsoever. According to Mother, every one of you acts far too impulsively, which reflects how she once behaved. Should you deal with your infractions justly and truthfully when enforcing penalties, The Good-Conduct Club would assist you in contemplating your actions. Your chosen punishment would need to inflict genuine discomfort, as it would prove useless otherwise.”
“Lash one another?”

“That is not quite it. Different methods of penalty would need to be devised by you so that they fit the individual. Each other would not be punished by you—yourselves would be the ones you punish. Information regarding that kind of club was something I read completely in a story-book. If you give it a try, you will observe the way it functions.”

“Let us,” Grace stated; and after Kit had left, they came to an agreement that they would. “If conditions are not proper, it is simply up to us to set them proper,” Grace remarked, with determination.

“As Kit mentions, our actions must be honest and just,” Tobias remarked. “Because there is no one else available to accomplish this task, our group exists to improve our own standing. Having numerous regulations serves no purpose. We should establish merely a single rule, and whoever among us violates it must receive severe chastisement.”
“But how.”

“We will devise that while we proceed. Every evening, we will gather for a club meeting right here in the cemetery to discuss our actions during the daytime, and if we determine that any of us performed an act that is improper or would dishonor dad, the person who committed it, or brought it about, has to receive punishment. Such is the requirement. Everyone will jointly determine the type of penalty—it has to match the offense, as Mr. Flagg states. Furthermore, the person who is at fault will be obligated to execute it without any dodging. This is going to be enjoyable,” Tobias ended, with satisfaction.
“The soap-bubble party was your idea,” Grace pointed out.
“However, our club had not been established back then,” Tobias quickly added. “To-night marks the beginning of everything.”

“However, what happens if we fail to reach an accord regarding what is correct, or what penalty should be imposed? Imagine two among us favored one idea while two held a different view. An organization of this nature really should have five members.”

“Kit Carrow can be asked to act as umpire, being the squarest boy in Glen St. Agnes,” I said. “Though I suppose we are able to manage our own business for the most part, since our desire is to maintain this as confidentially as possible. Avoid uttering a single word to Mary Stubbs, for she would demand to participate and handle the raising.”
“In my opinion,” Grace stated, “dragging punishments into every day serves no purpose other than to ruin it. A punishment day should be established instead.”
“Since school won't be in the way, Saturday would be our best choice,” Ida proposed.

“And ruin our single day off for the week,” exclaimed Grace. “Certainly not! Instead, let us choose Friday. It is fish day regardless, and fish is disliked by all of us. It makes sense to combine all the unpleasant matters into a single day. After that, we are free to proceed and enjoy ourselves on the remaining days.”

“Rubbish,” declared Tobias with authority. “That sort of plan would be entirely ineffective. We will simply impose penalties on ourselves as we progress to maintain a clean record. Everyone understands now, right? Our group is a Good-Conduct Club, formed to improve our own behavior. We consent to discipline ourselves for misdeeds, and invariably to pause prior to performing any action, regardless of what it is, to consider whether it might harm dad in any manner, while whoever avoids their duty will be expelled from the club and forbidden from ever playing with the others in Fern Hollow again. Kit Carrow will act as referee if arguments arise. Rupert, no further bringing of insects to Sunday School, and Miss Grace, kindly cease masticating gum in view of others.”
“There will be no further mocking of older people at prayer or attending the Methodist prayer service,” Grace shot back.
“Well, attending the Methodist prayer meeting does no damage,” Tobias objected, utterly astonished.
“Mrs. Kerr claims that is the case, stating that minister's kids ought to attend only Presbyterian events.”
“Darn it, going to the Methodist prayer meeting is something I won't give up,” Tobias exclaimed. “Ours isn't nearly as much fun as that one is.”
“A bad word was spoken by you,” Grace exclaimed. “You must discipline yourself now.”

“Only when everything is put in black and white. Our discussion is merely about the club. Its actual formation doesn't happen until it is set down in writing and endorsed by us. A constitution as well as by-laws must be created. Besides, you are aware that attending a prayer meeting is not wrong.”
“However, we are required to chastise ourselves not merely for our misdeeds, but for whatever could potentially cause harm to father.”

“No one is going to be harmed by it. You are aware that Mrs. Kerr holds crazy views regarding Methodists. Aside from her, my going causes no stir with anyone. My behavior is always proper. Query Kit or Mrs. Carrow to discover their thoughts on the matter. Whatever they decide, I will accept. Now I am leaving to fetch the paper, after which I will carry out the lantern so everyone can sign.”

A quarter of an hour afterwards, the paper was gravely endorsed upon the gravestone of Hezekiah Pollock, in the middle of which the dim manse lantern had been placed, with the children kneeling in a circle about it. Mrs. Elder Clow happened to be walking by right then, and by the following day the whole of the Glen was told that the youngsters from the manse had engaged in yet another contest of prayer, finishing it off by pursuing one another through the tombstones with a lantern. It was likely that this added detail had been inspired because, once the signing and sealing had been finished, Rupert had picked up the lantern and paced carefully over to the small depression so he could inspect his ant-hill. The remaining children had walked silently into the manse and gone to sleep.
“Is it real, do you suppose, that Miss Ainslie will be married to father?” was the trembling query Ida had put to Grace, once they had finished saying their prayers.
“I am not sure, yet I would enjoy it,” Grace said.

“Oh, I wouldn’t,” Ida uttered, gasping. “She is nice as she currently is. Mary Stubbs, however, asserts that becoming stepmothers transforms individuals completely. At that point, they become terribly ill-tempered, stingy, and spiteful, and they estrange your father from you. She claims that they always do so. In not one instance has she known this to fail.”
“I doubt Miss Ainslie would ever attempt such a thing,” Grace exclaimed.

“Mary claims that everyone would think so. Grace, she understands everything regarding stepmothers—she claims to have encountered hundreds of them—while you have not encountered a single one. Oh, the horrifying stories Mary has related to me concerning them. She claims she was aware of a stepmother who lashed her husband’s young daughters upon their naked shoulders until blood flowed, and afterwards locked them inside a freezing, unlit coal cellar for the entire night. She claims every one of them is desperate to perform actions such as those.”

“Miss Ainslie wouldn't, in my opinion. Ida, your knowledge of her isn't as deep as mine. Consider that lovely small bird she gave me as a present. My affection for it is much greater, even, than what I feel for Adam.”
“Step-parenting simply alters their nature. Mary claims it is beyond their control. Father’s hatred toward us would be far worse than the beatings.”

“You are aware that no circumstance could cause father to despise us. Stop being foolish, Ida. It is quite probable that we have no reason for concern. It is likely that if we manage our club correctly and raise ourselves in a suitable manner, father will not consider taking another wife. Should he do so, however, I am certain that Miss Ainslie will treat us wonderfully.”
However, Ida lacked any such assurance, and she wept until she fell asleep.

For two weeks matters proceeded without a hitch in the Good-Conduct Club. It appeared to function wonderfully. Kit Carrow was not summoned as arbiter even one time. Not a single time did any of the manse youngsters stir up the Glen gossips. Regarding their smaller home offenses, they monitored one another strictly and bravely endured their self-assigned penalties—usually choosing not to attend some lively Friday evening gathering in Fern Hollow, or remaining in bed during some spring night when every youthful body longed to be outside roaming. Grace, because she whispered in Sunday School, sentenced herself to spend an entire day without uttering a solitary word, except if it was completely required, and carried it out. It was somewhat unlucky that Mr. Pratt from over-harbour selected that particular night to visit the manse, and that Grace chanced to answer the door. She did not answer a single word to his friendly welcome, but departed without a sound to fetch her father concisely. Mr. Pratt felt a bit insulted and informed his wife upon returning home that the eldest Ashdown girl appeared to be a remarkably timid, moody young person, lacking sufficient manners to reply when addressed. However, no greater trouble resulted from it, and usually their punishments caused no damage to themselves or anyone else. Every one of them was starting to feel utterly confident that, as it turned out, raising yourself was a remarkably simple task.

“I suppose everyone will shortly realize that we are capable of conducting ourselves just as appropriately as anyone else,” Grace declared exultantly. “It is not difficult once we set our focus on it.”

Ida and she were perched upon the Pollock tombstone. Fern Hollow was far too unsuitable for girls due to the cold, raw, wet conditions of a spring storm, even though the boys from the manse and Hollowmere had gone down there to fish. Although the rain had paused, a brutal east wind swept in from the sea, piercing straight to the bone and marrow. Despite its initial promise, spring was tardy, and a firm drift of old ice and snow remained even now in the northern corner of the graveyard. Shivering, Zilla Marsh, who had walked up to deliver a mess of herring to the manse, slipped through the gate. She came from the fishing village situated at the harbour mouth, and for thirty years, her father had maintained the habit of sending a mess to the manse from his initial spring catch. Never entering a church door, he was a heavy drinker and a wild man; nevertheless, provided he dispatched those herring to the manse each spring, just as his father had done prior to him, he felt pleasantly certain that his standing with the Powers That Govern was settled for the year. Had he failed to send the season's first fruits in this manner, he would not have anticipated a profitable mackerel catch.

Though Zilla had reached a decade of age, her tiny, shriveled frame made her appear even younger. She crept toward the manse girls with a certain bravery this evening, looking as though warmth had eluded her during her entire existence. A purple hue covered her visage, while her pale-blue, audacious little eyes appeared red and filled with tears. Dressed in a torn print garment, she had a frayed woolen comforter fastened over her skinny shoulders and beneath her arms. The journey of three miles from the harbour mouth had been made on her bare feet, along a path still covered in snow, slush, and mud. A purple tone, matching her face, marked her feet and legs. Yet Zilla was not greatly bothered by these conditions. Coldness was familiar to her, and her bare feet had already endured a month of exposure, just like the rest of the teeming young offspring in the fishing village. Pitying herself was far from her thoughts when she placed herself upon the tombstone and offered a bright smile to Grace and Ida. Grace and Ida responded with cheerful smiles of their own. Their acquaintance with Zilla was slight, rooted in a couple of encounters during the previous summer when a trip down the harbour had been taken with the Carrows.
“Hello!” said Zilla, “isn’t the night quite wild? It is not suitable for a dog to be outside, is it?”
“Then what brings you outside?” Grace inquired.

“Pa made me bring you up some herring,” Zilla answered back. She trembled, gave a cough, and extended her bare feet. Zilla was not dwelling on herself or her feet, nor was she attempting to gain any sympathy. She extended her feet purely by instinct so they would not touch the damp grass surrounding the tombstone. However, Grace and Ida were immediately overwhelmed by a surge of compassion for her. She appeared so cold—so unhappy.
“Oh, on a night so cold, why are you barefoot?” Grace exclaimed. “Almost frozen, your feet must be.”
“Almost,” Zilla declared with pride. “I’m telling you, trekking up that harbour road was brutal.”
“Why didn’t you put your shoes and stockings on?” Ida asked.
“There isn’t any to wear. Everything I owned was completely worn out when winter ended,” Zilla remarked with indifference.

Grace stared in horror for a moment. It was terrible. A little girl, who was almost a neighbour, was half frozen in this cruel spring weather because she lacked shoes or stockings. Impulsive Grace could think of nothing except how dreadful it was. She was pulling off her own shoes and stockings in a moment.
“Here, put these on immediately,” she urged, shoving the garments upon the bewildered Zilla. “Hurry up. A fatal chill will come over you. More are in my possession. Put these on right now.”

Regaining her senses, Zilla grabbed the presented present, a gleam appearing in her lifeless eyes. Certainly she intended to wear them, and exceedingly fast, prior to the arrival of anybody with the power to take them back. Within sixty seconds, she had drawn the stockings across her thin small legs and slid the shoes of Grace over her stout small ankles.
“I am grateful to you,” she remarked, “however will your people not be angry?”

“No—and their identity doesn't matter to me,” Grace stated. “Is it possible you believe I could watch a person freeze to death and not assist them if it were in my power? Doing so would be wrong, particularly since a minister is what my father is.”
“Will you need them returned? Down at the harbour mouth, it is terribly cold—well after this place has warmed up,” Zilla noted cunningly.
“No, you are supposed to retain them, naturally. My intention when presenting them was precisely that. Another pair of shoes and a large quantity of stockings belong to me.”

Zilla had intended to remain for a time to discuss numerous topics with the girls. Nevertheless, she currently felt it was wiser to depart prior to anyone arriving to force her to surrender her spoils. Consequently, she moved away through the freezing dusk using the same quiet, elusive manner in which she had arrived. Once the manse was no longer within view, she seated herself, removed the shoes and stockings, and placed them inside her herring basket. Wearing them along that filthy harbour road was not something she planned to do. Their purpose was to be preserved in good condition for special events. No other young girl near the harbour mouth possessed such splendid black cashmere stockings and such stylish, barely worn shoes. Zilla was fully equipped for the summer season. She experienced no feelings of guilt regarding the situation. To her mind, the individuals at the manse possessed immense wealth, and those girls unquestionably owned an abundance of shoes and stockings. Afterward, Zilla hurried down to the Glen village where she engaged in play for an hour with the boys in front of Mr. Flagg’s store, wading through a puddle of slush alongside the wilder children, right up to the moment Mrs. Kerr arrived and ordered her to go home.

“Grace, I do not believe you ought to have performed that action,” Ida remarked with mild reproof once Zilla had departed. “Now it will be necessary for you to put on your fine boots daily, and before long they will become scuffed.”

“I don’t care,” exclaimed Grace, who was yet experiencing the wonderful warmth that comes from performing a good deed for someone else. “It is not right for me to possess two pairs of shoes while poor little Zilla Marsh does not own even one. We each possess a pair now. You are well aware, Ida, of what father stated during his sermon this past Sunday concerning how genuine joy is never found in acquiring or possessing things—it comes solely through giving. That is absolute truth. At this moment, I am conscious of a much greater happiness than I have ever experienced at any previous time in my life. Imagine Zilla traveling toward home at this exact second, her unfortunate small feet now feeling completely comfortable, cozy, and warm.”

“You are aware that you do not own a second pair of black cashmere stockings,” Ida stated. “Aunt Martha declared that your alternate pair had too many holes for her to mend again, so she sliced the legs into stove dusters. All you possess are those couple of pairs of striped stockings that you despise.”

Grace lost every bit of her radiance and inspiration. The joy she felt deflated just like a punctured balloon. For several gloomy minutes, she remained seated without speaking, confronting the repercussions of her hasty deed.
“Oh, Ida, that had not occurred to me,” she remarked mournfully. “I failed to pause and reflect whatsoever.”

Aunt Martha had knitted blue and red striped stockings for Grace during the winter, which were thick, heavy, coarse, and ribbed. Unquestionably, they were hideous. Grace's hatred for them surpassed any dislike she had ever felt previously. She was determined not to wear them under any circumstances. In her bureau drawer, they remained completely unused.

“After this, wearing the striped stockings will be necessary for you,” Ida said. “Only imagine how much you will be laughed at by the boys at school. The way they make fun of Mamie Warren because of her striped stockings and nickname her barber pole is familiar to you, and the ones you have are much worse.”
“I refuse to put them on,” Grace declared. “Despite the chill, I’d rather go without shoes.”
“Tomorrow, you are unable to attend church without shoes. Consider what folks would think.”
“I will remain at home then.”
“It is impossible for you to refrain. You are fully aware that Aunt Martha is going to force your attendance.”

Grace was aware of this. Aunt Martha made a point of demanding only one thing: everyone had to attend church, regardless of the weather. She was indifferent to how they were attired, or whether they had clothes on at all. Nevertheless, their attendance was mandatory. Seven decades in the past, Aunt Martha was raised in this exact manner, and she intended to raise them in the very same way.
“Can you not lend me a pair, Ida?” asked poor Grace in a piteous manner.

Shaking her head, Ida responded, “No, you are aware that I possess just a single black pair. Moreover, because they are exceedingly tight, I struggle to put them on. They would fail to fit you. My gray ones would not fit either. Furthermore, their legs are covered in repeated darning.”

“I will not put on those striped stockings,” Grace declared obstinately. “How they feel is still worse than how they look. They give me the sensation that my legs have grown as large as barrels, plus they are extremely scratchy.”
“Well, I am unaware of what your plans are.”

“Were father at home, I would head over and request that he purchase a fresh pair for me prior to the shop’s shutting. However, he will not return until it is far too late. My request will have to wait until Monday—and I am not attending church tomorrow. Feigning illness will be my strategy, leaving Aunt Martha with no choice but to permit me to remain at home.”

“To do that would be living a falsehood, Grace,” Ida exclaimed. “It is impossible for you to do so. You are aware of how terrible it would be. How would father react if he found out? Have you forgotten his words to us following mother's death, when he instructed us to remain truthful above all other shortcomings? He stated that we must never speak or live a falsehood—he mentioned he was counting on us to refrain from it. You cannot proceed with this, Grace. Simply put on the striped stockings. The situation will last for just one occasion. No one is going to observe them during the service. The setting is different from school. Furthermore, they will hardly be visible beneath your long new brown dress. Wasn't it fortunate that Aunt Martha crafted it large to allow space for your growth, despite how much you disliked it upon its completion?”

“Those stockings are something I will not wear,” Grace said once more. After unwinding her pale, unclothed legs from the gravestone, she intentionally strode across the damp, icy turf toward the snowbank. Clenching her jaw, she placed her feet on the snow and remained standing.
“What are you doing?” Ida exclaimed, horrified. “Grace Ashdown, you’ll catch your death of cold.”

“I am attempting to do so,” Grace replied. “My wish is that I contract a terrible cold and become terribly ill on the following day. If that happens, my behavior will not be deceitful. My plan is to remain standing in this spot for as long as I am able to endure it.”

“However, Grace, your life could actually be in danger. Pneumonia could catch you. Grace, I beg you, do not do this. We ought to step inside and find a remedy for your feet. Ah, Tobias has arrived. My gratitude is immense. Tobias, compel Grace to step away from the snow. Observe her feet.”
“Holy cats! Grace, what are you doing?” Tobias demanded. “Are you crazy?”
“No. Go away!” Grace snapped.
“Are you, in that case, inflicting punishment on yourself for a reason? Should you be doing so, it is not correct. You will become ill.”
“I desire to throw up. Punishing myself is not what I am doing. Leave.”
“Where are her stockings and shoes?” Tobias inquired of Ida.
“They were given to Zilla Marsh by her.”
“Zilla Marsh? Why?”

“Since Zilla possessed none—and her feet felt very freezing. Also, she desires to become ill at present to avoid attending church the next day and putting on her striped stockings. Nevertheless, Tobias, she might perish.”
“Grace,” Tobias said, “step away from that ice-bank, otherwise I will drag you off it.”
“Pull away,” Grace dared.

Tobias leaped toward her and seized her arms. As he tugged in one direction, Grace tugged in the opposite direction. Ida hurried up from behind Grace and shoved. Grace yelled furiously at Tobias to leave her alone. Tobias yelled right back at her not to be a dizzy idiot; and Ida began to weep. A great deal of clamor was made by them, and they were near the graveyard's road fence. Driving past, Henry Warren and his wife both heard them and saw them. It was not long before the Glen was told that a terrible brawl had occurred among the manse children in the graveyard, complete with the use of most improper language. In the meantime, Grace had permitted herself to be dragged off the ice, for her feet were hurting so intensely that she was willing to leave it by any means. All of them went inside amicably and retired to bed. Grace had the sleep of a cherub and awakened the next morning without the slightest sign of a cold. Recalling that long-ago conversation with her father, she felt unable to pretend to be ill and live a falsehood. Nevertheless, her resolve remained just as strong as it had ever been that those abominable stockings would not be worn by her to church.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Grace arrived at Sunday School early and sat down in the corner of her class pew before anybody else got there. Consequently, nobody realized the awful truth until Grace walked from the class pew beside the door up to the manse pew when Sunday School ended. The church was half full by that time, and everyone seated beside the aisle noticed that boots were on the minister’s daughter, but she had no stockings!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Aunt Martha had crafted Grace’s new brown dress using an old pattern, rendering it absurdly long for her, yet it still failed to reach her boot-tops. A clear two inches of bare white leg were plainly visible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Grace and Rupert were the sole occupants of the manse pew. Tobias had moved to the gallery so he could sit beside a friend, whereas Ida had been taken by the Carrow girls. It was the custom of the Ashdown children to be “sitting all over the church” like this, a practice that numerous people deemed highly inappropriate. In particular, the gallery—a gathering spot for careless boys who were heard whispering and believed to chew tobacco throughout the service—was considered unsuitable for a child of the manse. Tobias, however, despised the manse pew located at the church’s highest point, directly beneath the gaze of Elder Clow and his household. He fled from that spot every chance he got.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Rupert, who was completely engrossed in observing a spider weaving a web by the window, failed to observe Grace’s legs. As she journeyed back to her house beside her father following the church service, he failed to observe them as well. Prior to the arrival of Tobias and Ida, she put on the detested striped stockings, ensuring that none of the residents in the manse were aware of her actions for the moment. However, every other person in Glen St. Agnes was fully aware of the situation. Those rare individuals who had not witnessed it directly were informed shortly after. During the return trip from the church service, no other topic was discussed. Mrs. Hector Twiss remarked that it was merely what she had anticipated, and before long one would observe some of those youths arriving at church devoid of any garments whatsoever. It was resolved by the president of the Ladies’ Aid that she would introduce the issue during the subsequent Aid gathering, proposing that they visit the minister as a group to raise an objection. Miss Winifred declared that, as far as she was concerned, she surrendered. Continuing to fret over the manse fry served no purpose any further. A slight sense of shock was experienced even by Mrs. Dr. Carrow, although she laid the blame for the event entirely upon the forgetfulness of Grace. Because the day was Sunday, Tabitha was unable to start knitting stockings for Grace right away, yet she had a pair cast onto her needles prior to anyone else rising from bed at Hollowmere on the following morning.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Only that old Martha was to blame is all you need to inform me, Mrs. Dr. dear,” she said to Nell. “My guess is that the poor little girl lacked any proper stockings to put on. My guess is that holes were in every pair she owned, just as you are well aware is usually the case. And it is my opinion, Mrs. Dr. dear, that making some for those children would be a finer use of the Ladies’ Aid’s time than arguing about the fresh rug for the pulpit platform. Although I do not belong to the Ladies’ Aid, I will make Grace two pairs of stockings using this lovely black yarn as quickly as my hands can manage, and you can count on that. My feelings will never leave my memory, Mrs. Dr. dear, from the moment I observed a clergyman’s daughter stepping down the aisle of our church without stockings on her feet. Truly, I was at a loss as to where I should turn my eyes.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “And yesterday the church was simply packed with Methodists, as well,” moaned Miss Winifred, who had traveled up to the Glen for a bit of shopping and stopped by Hollowmere so she could discuss the matter. “I cannot explain why, but whenever those children from the manse commit a particularly terrible act, the church is bound to be filled with Methodists. Mrs. Deacon Hazard looked as though her eyes were going to pop right out of her head. Upon leaving the church, she remarked, ‘Well, that display was hardly proper. The Presbyterians have my sympathy.’ And we were forced to accept it. One was completely unable to offer any reply.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Had I overheard her, Mrs. Dr. dear, I might have offered a response,” Tabitha remarked with a stern expression. “To begin with, I would have declared my belief that clean, unclad legs were every bit as respectable as garments full of holes. Furthermore, I would have pointed out that the Presbyterians hardly required any sympathy, given that they possessed a minister capable of delivering a sermon while the Methodists lacked one. Mrs. Dr dear, I could have utterly silenced Mrs. Deacon Hazard, and you can be certain of that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I wish Mr. Ashdown preached a bit less effectively and took somewhat better care of his family,” Miss Winifred replied. “He might at minimum inspect his children prior to their departure for church to ensure their attire was entirely suitable. Trust me, I am weary of offering excuses on his behalf.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: In the meantime, Fern Hollow was the place where Grace’s soul was undergoing torment. Mary Stubbs had arrived, and, habitually, she was inclined to give a sermon. She made Grace comprehend that she had brought irredeemable dishonor upon herself as well as her father, and that she, Mary Stubbs, had washed her hands of her. “Everybody” was gossiping, and “everybody” uttered the identical sentiment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I just think that it is impossible for me to spend time with you from now on,” she finished.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “So we will be spending time with her,” Bess Carrow exclaimed. Although Bess privately believed that Grace had committed a terrible act, she refused to allow Mary Stubbs to control things so dictatorially. “Furthermore, Miss Stubbs, if you refuse to do so, you don’t need to visit Fern Hollow ever again.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Bess and Izzy each wrapped an arm around Grace, staring at Mary with fiercely protective eyes. Mary unexpectedly lost all her composure, collapsing onto a tree stump as tears started to fall.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I want to, truly,” she cried out. “However, staying on good terms with Grace will make folks claim I encouraged her behavior. Indeed, some people are making those claims right this minute. Having those rumors spread about me is something I can’t risk, now that I have a respectable position and am attempting to act like a lady. Besides, even during my wildest times, I never went into church bare-legged. Such an act would never have crossed my mind. Yet that dreadful old Kitty Hector claims Grace changed for the worse after the period I spent at the manse. According to her, Winifred Kerr is going to regret taking me into her home. It truly wounds my feelings. Nevertheless, the person I’m actually concerned about is Mr. Ashdown.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I feel you do not need to be concerned over him,” Izzy stated with contempt. “It is probably not required. At present, Grace darling, cease your weeping and inform us of your reason for doing it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Grace offered a weeping explanation. Her plight drew sympathy from the Carrow girls, and even Mary Stubbs concurred that her situation was difficult. Tobias, however, hit by the news like a bolt of thunder, would not be appeased. Thus, the cryptic clues he had picked up at school earlier that day were finally made clear! Instantly rushing Grace and Ida back to their house, he left the Good-Conduct Club to assemble right away in the cemetery, where they convened to evaluate Grace’s actions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I fail to perceive how it caused any damage,” Grace stated with defiance. “Hardly any of my legs were visible. It was not incorrect, nor did it injure anyone.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “It is going to cause Dad pain. You are aware that it will. You are aware that people place the blame on him every time we perform any strange action.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “That hadn't crossed my mind,” Grace mumbled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “That is precisely the problem. You failed to think when you ought to have thought. Our Club exists for that very purpose—to raise us properly and force us to think. Every one of us promised to constantly pause and think prior to acting. Because you failed to do so, Grace, you must receive punishment—and a truly severe one at that. As your penalty, you will have to wear those striped stockings to school for an entire week.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Oh, Tobias, can’t you make it just one day—or perhaps two days? Why must it be an entire week!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Indeed, an entire week,” uttered relentless Tobias. “It is just—inquire of Kit Carrow whether it is not.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Grace was inclined to yield instead of inquiring of Kit Carrow regarding a topic of that nature. It was starting to dawn on her that the transgression she committed was exceedingly disgraceful.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “In that case, I will,” she mumbled, somewhat sullenly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Your punishment is light,” Tobias said with sternness. “And our disciplining of you cannot undo the harm to father, regardless of what we do. It will constantly be viewed as mere trouble-making on your part, and father will be faulted for failing to prevent it. Making everyone understand will be impossible for us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Grace was troubled by this particular side of the matter. While she could endure her own dishonor, the thought of her father being held at fault agonized her. Should the actual circumstances of the situation become known to the public, he would be freed from fault. Yet, in what way was she to reveal them to everyone? Standing up during a church service to clarify the situation, just as she had formerly done, was completely impossible. Mary Stubbs had informed Grace about the way the churchgoers had viewed that spectacle, making her understand that it could not be done again. For three and a half days, Grace agonized over the dilemma. An idea then struck her, which she carried out without delay. That night was passed in the attic, illuminated by a lamp as she wrote feverishly in a notebook, her face red and her eyes gleaming. No better solution existed! She felt so smart for coming up with it! Everything would be corrected and clarified without creating any public outrage. By eleven o’clock, she completed the task to her liking and went quietly downstairs to sleep, feeling utterly exhausted yet thoroughly joyful.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: Within a handful of days, The Journal, which was the small weekly paper printed in the Glen, appeared as it always did, delivering yet another shock to the Glen. A piece of correspondence bearing the signature “Grace Ashdown” held a conspicuous spot on the first page, reading in this manner:—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “FOR THE ATTENTION OF THOSE AFFECTED:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “My goal is to make it clear to everyone why I ended up attending church bare-legged, which will prove that father does not deserve a single bit of fault, so those old gossips can stop making that untrue claim. After seeing Zilla Marsh barefoot with her poor little feet freezing, I felt so much pity that I handed over my sole pair of black stockings to her. In a Christian town, no kid should be forced to walk around lacking shoes and stockings until the snow has completely melted, so my opinion is that her stockings should have come from the W. F. M. S. naturally, sending supplies to the young heathen kids is fine and thoughtful, as I well understand. Nevertheless, those young heathen kids enjoy a great deal more warm weather than our climate offers, so Zilla ought to be cared for by the females of our congregation instead of putting everything on my shoulders. It slipped my mind when handing over my stockings that no other holeless black pair remained in my possession, yet making that gift makes me happy, since my conscience would plague me if I had withheld them. Following the departure of the poor little creature, who left filled with pride and joy, it struck me that my only remaining option was to put on those awful red and blue items Aunt Martha created for me previous winter using yarn that arrived from Mrs. Joseph Burr of Upper Glen. That yarn had terrible coarseness and constant knots, and none of Mrs. Burr’s own offspring were ever spotted by me in garments knitted from it. Mary Stubbs claims, however, that Mrs. Burr passes off unusable or inedible items to the minister, believing such offerings should count toward the salary pledged by her husband, which he constantly fails to pay.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “Putting on those horrible stockings was simply more than I could endure. They possessed such an unattractive, coarse appearance and caused such an unpleasant, prickly sensation. Every single person would have mocked me. Initially, my intention was to feign an illness so I could miss going to church the following morning, yet I concluded that was impossible for me, as it amounted to living a falsehood, something our father instructed us never, ever to engage in following mother's passing. Performing a deceitful deed is fully as wicked as uttering a untruth, even if I am aware of certain individuals, in this very Glen, who practice such deceptions without appearing to experience the slightest remorse. Although I refrain from naming anyone, their identities are known to me, as well as to father.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “After that, I made every effort to contract a cold and become truly ill by placing my unclad feet on the snowbank located in the Methodist cemetery until Tobias dragged me away. Nevertheless, it failed to harm me in the least, meaning I was unable to avoid attending church. Consequently, I simply made up my mind to slip on my boots and attend in that manner. I am unable to understand why it was such a terrible thing, especially since I took great care to scrub my legs until they were as spotless as my face, yet, in any case, my father should not be held responsible for what happened. He was inside the study reflecting on his sermon along with other divine matters, and I stayed out of his sight prior to leaving for Sunday School. Father avoids staring at the legs of congregation members during services, which naturally meant he failed to observe mine, whereas every gossip took notice and gossiped about the matter, and that reason explains my decision to write this letter to the Journal as a way of clarifying things. I imagine my actions were extremely improper, given that everyone claims they were, and I feel remorse and am donning those terrible stockings as a form of self-punishment, even though father purchased two pleasant new black pairs for me immediately after Mr. Flagg’s store commenced business on Monday morning. However, the blame rests entirely on me, and should anyone fault father regarding the incident once they have perused this, they lack Christian virtues and thus their remarks do not bother me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “I wish to clarify one more matter before I finish speaking. Mary Stubbs mentioned to me that Mr. Evan Garrick believes the Lew Baxters stole potatoes from his field this past autumn. His potatoes were not touched by them. Although they are extremely poor, they possess honesty. We were the ones responsible—Tobias, Rupert, and myself. Ida was absent from our group when it happened. It never crossed our minds that this was theft. Our only desire was a handful of potatoes to roast over a Fern Hollow campfire one night, accompanying the trout we fried. Situated right between the valley and the village, Mr. Garrick’s field happened to be closest, so we scaled his fence and uprooted several plants. Because Mr. Garrick failed to apply a sufficient amount of fertilizer, those potatoes were terribly tiny, forcing us to uproot numerous stalks to gather a decent quantity, and even then, their size barely surpassed marbles. Edmund and Izzy Carrow assisted us in consuming them, but their arrival occurred only after the cooking was finished, and they lacked any knowledge of our source, meaning they bear no fault whatsoever, only the three of us do. Harm was not our intention, yet should this count as stealing, our regrets are deep, and we shall reimburse Mr. Garrick for the crop if he allows us time to reach adulthood. At present, we possess no funds since our age prevents us from earning any, and Aunt Martha claims that maintaining this home consumes every single penny of poor father’s income, even on the rare occasions when it arrives on time. Nevertheless, Mr. Garrick has to stop accusing the Lew Baxters, who were completely faultless, and ruining their reputation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”
text: “With respect, “GRACE ASHDOWN.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Tabitha, once my life is over, my return to earth will happen whenever the daffodils bloom in this garden,” Nell remarked with great joy. “I might be invisible to everyone, yet this is where I will be. Should someone happen to be in the garden then—my arrival will likely occur on an evening identical to this one, though a gorgeous, pale-pinkish spring dawn is also a possibility—the daffodils will simply be seen swaying vigorously by them as though swept by a stronger burst of wind, but it will actually be me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “In truth, dear Mrs. Dr., after your passing, you won’t consider showing off secular items such as daffies,” Tabitha remarked. “Furthermore, ghosts, whether visible or invisible, are not something I believe in.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Oh, Tabitha, I will not become a ghost! The word sounds so dreadful. I will merely remain myself. Whether it be morning or evening, I will scamper about in the twilight and visit every place dear to me. Tabitha, do you recall how deeply grieved I was upon departing from our tiny House of Dreams? I believed I could never cherish Hollowmere to the same degree. Yet I do. Every single inch of this land, along with every stick and stone upon it, is precious to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “The location pleases me quite a bit,” stated Tabitha, whose life would have ended had she ever been taken away from it, “yet our hearts ought not to be excessively tied to worldly possessions, my dear Mrs. Dr. Disasters like fires and earthquakes do occur. Being ready at all times is our duty. Three nights back, the home of the Tom MacAllisters across the harbour was destroyed by fire. It is claimed by some that Tom MacAllister started the blaze on his own home to collect the insurance money. Whether that is true or false, I cannot say. Even so, my recommendation is that the doctor inspect our chimneys immediately. Preventing trouble takes far less effort than fixing it later. Look there, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr is walking through the gate, wearing an expression that suggests she was summoned but found herself unable to attend.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Has the Journal crossed your path today, my sweet Nell?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: Miss Winifred had a tremble in her voice, caused in part by her feelings, and in part because she had rushed up from the store so quickly that she had run out of breath.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: Nell leaned above the daffodils so that her smile would be concealed. That day, she and Hugh had chuckled loudly and unfeelingly about the front page of the Journal, yet she was aware that dear Miss Winifred regarded it as nearly a tragedy, so she had to avoid hurting her feelings through any show of lightheartedness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Is it not terrible? What can we do?” inquired Miss Winifred in despair. Although Miss Winifred had declared that she would no longer fret about the tricks of the children at the manse, she continued to fret all the same.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: Going first, Nell headed for the veranda, a spot where Tabitha sat engaged in her knitting, flanked by Harcourt and Tessa who were both studying their primers. At this point, Tabitha had already started working on a second pair of stockings intended for Grace. Worry over poor humanity was something Tabitha never experienced. Whatever she could manage for its improvement she accomplished, before peacefully entrusting everything else to the Higher Powers.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Winifred Kerr believes this world was created for her to manage, Mrs. Dr. dear,” she had remarked to Nell on one occasion, “which keeps her constantly agitated about one thing or another. I have never held that view about myself, allowing me to proceed peacefully. Though it has occasionally crossed my mind that affairs could perhaps be administered somewhat more efficiently than their current state. Still, it is improper for us miserable worms to entertain these ideas. Such notions merely cause us distress without achieving anything.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Now, I fail to see how any action can be taken,” remarked Nell, as she drew a comfortable, plush seat forward for Miss Winifred. “Yet in what possible way did Mr. Vickers permit the publication of that letter? He certainly ought to have possessed greater judgment.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Well, he is gone, Nell dearie—for a week now he has been away in New Brunswick. In his absence, that young scalawag Joe Vickers is editing the Journal. Mr. Vickers himself would certainly never have printed it, even though he is a Methodist, but Joe would merely consider it a fine joke. Just as you say, I do not imagine there is anything that can be done at this point, except live it down. However, if I ever catch Joe Vickers trapped in a corner somewhere, I will deliver a talking to that he will not quickly forget. I wished Ambrose to cancel our subscription to the Journal right away, but he did nothing but laugh and remark that the edition today was the single one containing anything readable for a year. Ambrose will not ever treat anything seriously—just like a man. As luck would have it, Evan Garrick resembles him in that way. He regards it as a joke and is laughing everywhere about it. Yet he is another Methodist! Regarding Mrs. Burr of Upper Glen, she will naturally be enraged and they will quit the church. Not that losing them will be a significant loss in any way. The Methodists are entirely welcome to have them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Mrs. Burr gets what she deserves,” remarked Tabitha, who harbored a long-standing grudge against that particular woman and had been greatly amused by the mention of her in the letter from Grace. “She is going to realize that she cannot swindle the Methodist minister out of his pay using inferior yarn.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “The worst part about it is that there is little chance of conditions improving,” Miss Winifred remarked despondently. “While Mr. Ashdown was still visiting Clementine Ainslie, I harbored a real hope that a proper mistress would shortly be at the manse. However, that has completely ended. It is my guess she refused him because of the children—or rather, that appears to be what everyone believes.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “It is my belief that he never made a proposal to her,” remarked Tabitha, as she was unable to imagine a person declining a minister.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Indeed, that remains a complete mystery to everyone. However, it is beyond doubt that his visits there have ceased. Furthermore, Clementine appeared unwell throughout the spring season. It is my hope that her time in Portmaris proves beneficial for her. She departed one month ago and, as I gather, intends to remain for one more month. I am unable to recall a previous occasion when Clementine was absent from home. She and Harriet were always completely inseparable. Nevertheless, my understanding is that Harriet demanded she take this trip. In the meantime, Harriet and Lionel Fairlie are reheating the old soup.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Does that actually hold true?” inquired Nell, with a chuckle. “Word of it reached my ears, yet it seemed scarcely believable to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Accept it as true! You can certainly take it as fact, Nell, my dear. No one lacks knowledge of this. Lionel Fairlie did not ever leave a single person uncertain about what he intended regarding any issue. The courting he engaged in was always done openly in front of everyone. He mentioned to Ambrose that Harriet hadn't entered his thoughts for years, yet during his initial visit to church last autumn, he caught sight of her and succumbed to love for her once more. He remarked that he had completely forgotten her great beauty. Two decades had passed since he last beheld her, if that seems credible to you. Naturally, he abstained from attending church services, whereas Harriet frequented no other places in these parts. Ah, every one of us understands Lionel's intentions, but the intentions of Harriet are an entirely separate issue. I will not assume the responsibility of forecasting if a wedding will result or not.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “It appears that being jilted by him once does not matter to certain individuals, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha observed in a somewhat bitter tone.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “He abandoned her during an angry outburst and regretted it for the rest of his days,” Miss Winifred remarked. “That is not like a calculating abandonment. As for me, Lionel was never an object of my hatred like he was for others. He was incapable of intimidating me. I really am curious about what prompted him to begin attending church. Mrs. Wilsons’s claim that Grace Ashdown visited him and intimidated him into going is something I could never credit. Asking Grace directly has always been my intention, yet the thought never crossed my mind on the occasions I met her. How could Grace Ashdown possibly sway Lionel Fairlie? When I departed, he was still inside the store, roaring with amusement about that disgraceful letter. His voice was loud enough to reach Seven Gulls Point. ‘The greatest girl in the world,’ he was yelling. ‘She’s so packed with spirit that it’s overflowing. And every single old biddy wants to subdue her, blast them. However, they will never manage it—never! It would be like attempting to submerge a fish. Garrick, ensure you apply additional fertilizer to your potato crop next season. Ho, ho, ho!’ Whereupon his laughter rattled the very roof.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Tabitha observed, “At any rate, the compensation Mr. Fairlie offers is generous.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Well, in certain respects Lionel lacks malice. A thousand would be handed over by him without fluttering an eyelid, yet he would bellow like a Bashan Bull should an overcharge of merely five cents be demanded of him. On top of that, Mr. Ashdown’s preaching pleases him, and Lionel Fairlie remained consistently ready to fork over money provided his intellect received a stimulating jolt. About him there exists no greater amount of Christianity than can be found in a dark, unclothed pagan within Africa, nor shall there ever be. Nevertheless, possessing intelligence and extensive reading, he evaluates sermons in the same manner he would speeches. In any case, his support for Mr. Ashdown and the young ones comes at a good time, since after these events their necessity for allies will be greater than before. Trust me, offering justifications on their behalf has exhausted me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “I wonder, dear Miss Winifred,” Nell remarked gravely, “if we have not all been fashioning far too many excuses. We are being extremely silly, and it is time for us to cease. Let me inform you of what I should love to do. Naturally, I shall refrain from doing it”—Nell had observed a flash of apprehension in Tabitha’s eye—“it would stray too far from convention, and once we attain what is deemed a dignified age, we are obliged to remain conventional or perish. Even so, I should love to do it. I should love to convene a gathering of the Ladies Aid, the W.M.S., and the Girls Sewing Society, while admitting into the audience every single Methodist who has been finding fault with the Ashdowns—though I truly believe that if we Presbyterians ceased our finding fault and excusing, we would discover that alternative denominations would bother themselves scarcely at all regarding the people in our manse. I would address them, ‘Dear Christian friends’—stressing ‘Christian’ with clear intent—‘I possess a message for you and I desire to deliver it firmly and forcefully, so that you may carry it back and reiterate it to your households. You Methodists have no occasion to feel sorry for us, nor do we Presbyterians need to feel sorry for ourselves. We intend to stop doing so immediately. Furthermore, we are going to declare, with courage and honesty, to every critic and sympathizer, “We take pride in our minister and his household. Mr. Ashdown stands as the finest preacher Glen St. Agnes church has ever possessed. In addition, he serves as a genuine, devoted instructor of truth and Christian charity. He proves to be a loyal friend, a wise pastor in every vital aspect, and a polished, learned, well-mannered gentleman. His household is deserving of him. Gerald Ashdown ranks as the brightest student in the Glen school, and Mr. Hazard asserts that he is bound for a splendid future. He represents a courageous, principled, truthful young boy. Grace Ashdown is a striking beauty, and she is just as uplifting and creative as she is gorgeous. There is not a single ordinary thing about her. The entirety of the remaining girls in the Glen combined do not possess the spirit, cleverness, cheerfulness, and ‘spunk’ that belong to her. She does not have a single adversary anywhere. Each person acquainted with her adores her. Regarding how many individuals, whether young ones or adults, can such a statement be made? Ida Ashdown embodies pure gentleness. She is bound to develop into an exceedingly endearing woman. Rupert Ashdown, owing to his fondness for ants, frogs, and spiders, will eventually become a naturalist whom the whole of Canada—indeed, the whole world—will take joy in honoring. Are you aware of any alternative family inside the Glen, or beyond it, regarding whom every one of these statements can be uttered? Banish all sheepish excuses and apologies. We exult in our minister along with his marvelous sons and daughters!”’

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: Nell came to a halt, influenced in part by the breathlessness that followed her impassioned utterance, and in part because the expression on Miss Winifred’s face warned her against risking any more words. The kindly woman was gazing powerlessly at Nell, seemingly overwhelmed by a sea of unfamiliar thoughts. Nevertheless, she surfaced with a gasp and bravely made her way toward land.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Nell Carrow, my wish is that you would convene that gathering and state precisely those words! As one individual, you have caused me to feel embarrassment for my actions, and I certainly will not decline to acknowledge it. Undoubtedly, that represents the manner in which we ought to have spoken—most of all to the Methodists. Furthermore, every single word of it is the truth—all of it. We have simply been closing our vision to the important, valuable matters and narrowing it upon the trivial details that are not worth a pin. Oh, dearie Nell, I am capable of recognizing a point once it has been driven into my mind. I will offer no further apologies for Winifred Ambrose! Following this, I am going to keep my head held high, you can be sure—even if I might still discuss matters with you as I normally do merely to vent my emotions in the event that the Ashdowns perform further shocking actions. Even regarding that letter that made me feel so terrible—well, it is nothing more than a fine jest when all is said, just as Lionel states. Few young women would possess the cleverness to conceive of composing it—with all the punctuation so well executed and without a single word spelled incorrectly. Simply permit me to listen to any Methodist utter a single comment concerning it—even if, despite everything, I am never going to pardon Joe Vickers—you may trust me! To-night, where are the remaining members of your young brood?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Fern Hollow is where Edmund and the twins are. As for Kit, the garret is where she is studying.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. MISS WINIFRED GETS A NEW POINT OF VIEW
text: “Fern Hollow has them all completely infatuated. Mary Stubbs considers it the sole place worth being in the universe. Were I to allow it, she would spend every single night up here. However, I refrain from fostering her roaming habits. Furthermore, Nell dearie, her absence leaves a void for me. I never anticipated developing such deep affection for her. That is not to say I am blind to her flaws and fail to amend them. Nevertheless, from the moment she entered my dwelling, not a single impudent word has passed her lips toward me, and her assistance is immense—because when everything is taken into account, Nell dearie, my youth has slipped away, and refusing to acknowledge it is useless. Fifty-nine was my age on my previous birthday. I fail to feel that old, yet disputing the Family Bible is impossible.”

Although Miss Winifred held a revised perspective, she was unable to prevent herself from feeling somewhat unsettled about what the children from the manse did subsequently. When out in public, she handled the matter admirably, repeating to every busybody the essence of what Nell had stated during the season of daffodils, conveying it with such sharpness and strength that those listening were left feeling somewhat ridiculous and commenced believing that, ultimately, they were overreacting to a piece of juvenile mischief. However, behind closed doors, Miss Winifred permitted herself the comfort of lamenting the incident to Nell.

“Nell dearie, a concert was held by them in the churchyard last Thursday night, at the same time the Methodist prayer meeting took place. Upon Hezekiah Pollock’s tombstone they sat, singing for an entire hour. Naturally, I realize the songs they sang were mainly hymns, which would not have been so terrible had they stopped there. However, I am informed that they concluded with the complete version of Polly Wolly Doodle—right as Deacon Baxter offered his prayer.”

“I was present on that evening,” Tabitha said, “and, even though I did not mention it to you, Mrs. Dr. dear, I was unable to stop myself from believing it was a terrible shame they selected that specific night. Hearing them sit in that dwelling of the deceased, screaming that lighthearted tune as loudly as possible, was genuinely chilling.”
“What you were doing at a Methodist prayer meeting is beyond me,” Miss Winifred remarked sharply.

“Methodism has never proven contagious in my experience,” Tabitha replied with rigidity. “And, continuing what I meant to state before the interruption occurred, despite my poor feelings, I refused to yield to the Methodists. Upon our exit, when Mrs. Deacon Baxter remarked, ‘What a disgraceful exhibition!’ my response, while meeting her gaze directly, was, ‘Every one of them sings beautifully, and it appears that not a single member of your choir, Mrs. Baxter, takes the trouble to attend your prayer meeting. Apparently, their voices are attuned solely for Sundays!’ This rendered her entirely submissive, giving me the impression of a well-deserved put-down. Nevertheless, my triumph would have been far more complete, Mrs. Dr. dear, had Polly Wolly Doodle simply been omitted. Hearing such a tune performed within a cemetery is a genuinely dreadful thought.”
“It may be that a few of those deceased individuals used to sing Polly Wolly Doodle while alive, Tabitha, and they might still enjoy listening to it,” Hugh put forward.

Miss Winifred cast a critical glance at him, resolving to suggest to Nell at a later date that the doctor ought to be warned against making those types of remarks. His business could suffer as a result. It might occur to folks that he lacked orthodoxy. Granted, Ambrose was in the habit of making far more outrageous statements, yet he did not hold a public role.

“I gather that their father remained in his study throughout the duration, with his windows unclosed, yet failed to observe them in any way. Naturally, he was absorbed in a book as he normally is. However, I discussed the matter with him yesterday, during his visit.”
“In what way did you have the courage, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr?” Tabitha inquired in a scolding manner.

“Dare! Someone needs to venture something at last. Look, people claim he is entirely unaware of Grace’s letter to the publication since everyone was afraid to bring it up with him. Naturally, he never reads a publication. Yet my feeling was that he should be made aware of it so that similar occurrences are avoided going forward. He mentioned that he intended to ‘discuss it with them.’ Naturally, though, the moment he passed beyond our gate, it would completely slip his mind. That man lacks any humor whatsoever, Nell, take my word for it. Last Sunday, his sermon was about ‘How to Bring up Children.’ Indeed, it was a lovely sermon—while every single person in the congregation was reflecting, ‘what a shame your own actions don't align with your teachings.’”

Mr. Ashdown was judged unfairly by Miss Winifred when she assumed he would quickly erase what she had imparted to his memory. The journey back to his house was taken in a state of great distress, and the moment the children returned from Fern Hollow that evening, having stayed out roaming in that spot far past the time they ought to have been, he summoned them to his study.

Feeling a bit intimidated, they stepped inside. Their father performing such an action was quite extraordinary. What might he intend to tell them? They searched their minds for any recent misdeed grave enough to warrant this, yet they drew a blank. Two nights earlier, Rupert had knocked a saucer of jam onto the silk gown of Mrs. Peter Flagg, who had remained for dinner following Aunt Martha’s request. However, Mr. Ashdown had failed to see the accident, and the good-natured Mrs. Flagg had refrained from causing a scene. Furthermore, Rupert had already suffered his penalty when he was forced to put on Ida’s dress for the remainder of that night.

A sudden thought struck Ida that her father might intend to announce his upcoming marriage to Miss Ainslie. Trembling in the legs, she felt her heart start to pound wildly. However, she then noticed the extremely stern and mournful expression on Mr. Ashdown's face. No, that was impossible.

“Children,” Mr. Ashdown said, “a piece of news has reached me that has caused me great pain. Did you really spend the entire previous Thursday evening sitting outside in the graveyard, singing lewd songs at the same time a prayer meeting was taking place inside the Methodist church?”
“By Great Caesar, Father, it completely slipped our minds that tonight was when they held their prayer meeting,” Tobias cried out with distress.
“Is it true, then—did you really commit this act?”

“Oh, Father, I am at a loss as to your meaning regarding vulgar tunes. Hymns were what we sang—as you are aware, it was a religious performance. Where was the wrongdoing in that? I assure you that the fact it was the evening for the Methodist prayer service never crossed our minds. Their gatherings used to be held on Tuesday evenings, and remembering the shift to Thursdays is difficult.”
“Was it nothing except hymns that you sang?”

“Why,” Tobias said, his face flushing, “at the end, Polly Wolly Doodle was sung by us. Grace remarked, ‘Let’s have something cheerful to wind up with.’ However, Father, no harm was intended by us—truly it wasn't.”

“It was I who thought of the concert, Father,” Grace said, fearing Mr. Ashdown would hold Tobias overly responsible. “You are aware that three Sunday evenings back, a sacred concert was held by the Methodists themselves inside their church. Getting one up to copy it seemed to me like it would be great fun. They included prayers at theirs, however, whereas we omitted that portion, since word reached us that folks considered our praying in a cemetery to be terrible. You remained seated in this room the entire duration,” she appended, “and did not speak a single word to us.”

“I failed to see what you were up to. Naturally, that does not excuse my behavior. The fault lies more with me than with you—I recognize that. However, what made you sing that silly tune at the conclusion?”

“It never occurred to us,” Tobias mumbled, sensing the weakness of his justification, given how severely he had scolded Grace during the Good-Conduct Club meetings regarding her own thoughtlessness. “We apologize, Father—really, we do. Lay into us severely—we warrant a thorough scolding.”

However, no pitching into or combing down was done by Mr. Ashdown. Sitting down, he pulled his little offenders near him and spoke to them briefly, with wisdom and tenderness. Remorse and shame completely overwhelmed them, and they believed that repeating such thoughtless silliness would be impossible for them.

“We must simply inflict a severe punishment upon ourselves for this,” Tobias murmured in a low voice while they stole up the stairs. “Our very first order of business tomorrow morning will be a meeting of the Club to determine our method. Father has never appeared so deeply distressed, to my knowledge. Even so, I sincerely wish the Methodists would restrict their prayer meeting to a single night instead of shifting it throughout the week.”
“At all events, I am happy it proved not to be the thing I had feared,” Ida muttered quietly to her own self.
In the study behind them, Mr. Ashdown had taken a seat at his desk, hiding his face inside his arms.
“May God assist me!” he uttered. “A terrible father am I. Ah, Clementine! Had you merely cared!”

Prior to the start of classes the following morning, a extraordinary meeting was held by the Good-Conduct Club. Once several ideas had been put forward, the members agreed that enduring a fast day would serve as a suitable penalty.
“For an entire day, not one thing will pass our lips,” Tobias declared. “Besides, I have a bit of curiosity about how fasting feels. We can discover it now through this opportunity.”

“Which day are we going to pick for this?” inquired Ida, who believed it was going to be an entirely simple penalty and felt somewhat surprised that Tobias and Grace had failed to invent a more difficult one.
“Monday would be a good choice,” Grace suggested. “Our Sunday evening meals are usually rather heavy, and what we eat on Mondays is never very substantial anyway.”

“But that’s just the point,” Tobias cried out. “We ought not to fast on the easiest day, but on the most difficult—and Sunday fits that description, since, as you mentioned, our meal that day is usually roast beef rather than cold ditto. Going without ditto would hardly be a punishment. Let us choose next Sunday. That day will work well, because father plans to trade morning service duties with the minister from Upper Kettlebridge. Father won't return until evening. Should Aunt Martha question our behavior, we will state plainly to her that our fasting is for our souls' benefit, pointing out that it appears in the Bible and telling her to leave us alone, which I expect she will.”

Aunt Martha failed to do so. She simply remarked in her irritable, muttered manner, “What foolishness are you young rips up to now?” and promptly dismissed it from her mind. Prior to anyone rising, Mr. Ashdown had departed early that morning. Furthermore, he left without eating his morning meal, though such an event was naturally a frequent happening. He omitted it half the time, and no person existed to bring it to his attention. Missing breakfast—the breakfast prepared by Aunt Martha—did not constitute a severe ordeal. Abstaining from the “lumpy porridge and blue milk” that had provoked the disdain of Mary Stubbs was not considered any major loss, even by the famished “young rips.” Nevertheless, the situation altered when dinner time arrived. Their hunger was ravenous by then, and the scent of roast beef that filled the manse—a scent entirely delicious, even though the meat was severely undercooked—proved nearly unbearable to them. Out of sheer despair, they hurried to the graveyard to escape the aroma. However, Ida was unable to avert her gaze from the dining room window, which revealed the Upper Kettlebridge minister calmly consuming his food.
“If I were merely able to obtain a tiny, little portion,” she uttered with a sigh.

“Now, cease doing that,” Tobias ordered. “It is obviously difficult—however, that constitutes the penalty. Right now, I am hungry enough to consume an idol, yet do you hear me grumbling? We should focus on a different topic. Superiority over our appetites is what we must achieve.”
When the hour for supper arrived, the intense pangs of hunger that had plagued them during the earlier part of the day were no longer felt by them.
