“It seems to me that we are becoming accustomed to the situation,” Grace remarked. “A remarkably strange, completely hollow sensation comes over me, yet I am unable to claim that I feel hunger.”
“My mind feels strange,” Ida stated. “At times, it spins and spins.”

Yet she attended church courageously alongside the rest. Had Mr. Ashdown not been so completely absorbed in and captivated by his topic, he perhaps would have observed the pallid small face and sunken eyes sitting in the manse pew below. However, he observed nothing at all, and the sermon he delivered went on somewhat longer than was typical. Subsequently, right before he announced the last hymn, Ida Ashdown fell from the manse pew's seat and remained unconscious on the floor.

The initial person to get to her was Mrs. Elder Clow. Taking the slender small frame out of the pale, frightened arms of Grace, she bore it inside the vestry. Mr. Ashdown, neglecting the hymn along with all other matters, hurried wildly behind her. By whatever means they managed, the congregation dispersed on its own.
“Oh, Mrs. Clow,” Grace gasped, “has Ida died? Is she dead because of us?”
“What is wrong with my child?” the pallid father inquired.
“I believe she has merely lost consciousness,” Mrs. Clow stated. “Oh, thank goodness, the doctor is here now.”

Reviving Ida proved to be quite a difficult task for Hugh. A considerable period elapsed while he tended to her before she unclosed her eyes. After that, he transported her to the manse, with Grace trailing behind, weeping uncontrollably out of relief.
“You see, she is merely hungry—she failed to eat any food today—no one among us did—all of us were fasting.”
“Fasting!” exclaimed Mr. Ashdown, and “Fasting?” queried the doctor.
“Indeed—as a penalty on ourselves because we sang Polly Wolly inside the graveyard,” Grace remarked.
“Do not make yourselves suffer for that, my child,” Mr. Ashdown said, upset. “You received your small reprimand from me—and every one of you showed remorse—and you were forgiven by me.”

“Yes, but punishment was necessary for us,” Grace clarified. “In our Good-Conduct Club—you know—it’s our rule that whenever we do something wrong, or something that might harm father in the congregation, self-punishment is required. We are raising ourselves, you know, since there isn’t anyone else to do it.”
A groan escaped Mr. Ashdown, yet the doctor, carrying a look of relief, rose from beside Ida.

“Therefore, this young girl merely collapsed because she lacked nourishment, meaning a hearty dish is all that she requires,” he stated. “Mrs. Clow, would you have the goodness to ensure she receives one? Furthermore, judging by what Grace told us, I believe every one of them could use a bite of food, lest additional people pass out.”
“I guess making Ida fast was a mistake,” Grace stated with regret. “Thinking about it, punishment should have fallen solely on Tobias and me. We organized the concert, plus we were the eldest.”
“The same as everyone else, I sang Polly Wolly,” Ida’s faint, small voice uttered, “which meant I needed to receive punishment, as well.”

Mrs. Clow arrived bearing a glass of milk, Grace along with Tobias and Rupert crept away to the pantry, and John Ashdown retired to his study, sitting in the dark for an extended period, solitary with his bitter reflections. Thus, his offspring were raising themselves owing to the fact that there was “nobody to do it”—laboring through their small confusions absent a guiding hand or a counseling voice. The phrase innocently spoken by Grace festered within her father’s thoughts like a barbed arrow. There was “nobody” to attend to them—to give solace to their little souls and tend to their small bodies. How delicate Ida had appeared, resting on the vestry sofa during that prolonged swoon! How slender were her tiny hands, how pale her small face! It seemed as though she could drift away from him in a single breath—sweet little Ida, whom Cecilia had pleaded with him to guard so carefully. Ever since his wife died, he had not experienced such a painful terror as when he had leaned over his small daughter during her state of unconsciousness. Action was required of him—yet what action? Ought he to request Elizabeth Kirk to be his wife? A good woman was she—she would show kindness to his offspring. He might force himself to take that step were it not for the affection he felt for Clementine Ainslie. However, until he had stamped that feeling out, he was unable to approach a different woman with a proposal of marriage. And stamping it out proved impossible—his attempts had failed. Clementine had attended church that very evening, marking her first appearance since coming back from Portmaris. A glimpse of her countenance at the rear of the packed sanctuary had met his eyes, precisely as he concluded his sermon. A wild pulse had surged in his heart. With bowed head and vibrant veins, he remained seated while the choir performed the “collection piece.” He had not laid eyes on her since the night he had requested her hand in marriage. On standing up to announce the hymn, his hands had been shaking and a flush had covered his pale face. Subsequently, Ida’s loss of consciousness had driven every thought from his memory for a while. At present, surrounded by the dark and isolation of the study, it returned forcefully. Clementine stood as the sole woman in existence for him. Attempting to wed any other was pointless for him. Even on behalf of his offspring, he could not perpetrate such a desecration. His load had to be carried by him alone—an effort had to be made to become a superior, more attentive father—his children had to be instructed not to fear approaching him regarding all their minor difficulties. Afterwards, he lit his lamp and picked up a thick recently published volume that was causing great controversy in the theological sphere. A single chapter would be read by him to quiet his thoughts. A mere five minutes afterward, he had become oblivious to the world and its attendant worries.

During an evening in early June, Fern Hollow proved to be a thoroughly enchanting spot, a fact the children recognized as they were seated in the unshaded glade where the bells produced an elfin ring on the Tree Lovers, and the green tresses of the White Lady swayed. Like a faithful, joyful companion, the wind laughed and whistled around them. A spicy fragrance rose from the young ferns in the hollow. Scattered across the valley amidst the dark firs, the wild cherry trees appeared mistily white. Over in the maples behind Hollowmere, the robins were whistling. Further off, upon the Glen's slopes, fruit-laden orchards bloomed in the dusk's veil, looking sweet, mystic, and wonderful. It was springtime, a season when youth is meant to be joyful. Everyone in Fern Hollow felt that joy that evening—up to the moment when Mary Stubbs chilled them to the bone by recounting the tale of Henry Warren’s ghost.

Kit was absent. Kit passed his evenings these days preparing for his entrance examination in the Hollowmere garret. Tobias was by the pond, fishing for trout. Edmund had read Longfellow’s sea poems to the rest of them, and they were filled with the beauty and mystery of the ships. Afterwards, they discussed what they would accomplish once they grew up—the places they would travel to—the distant, lovely shores they would behold. Bess and Izzy intended to travel to Europe. Edmund desired the Nile lamenting past its Egyptian sands, alongside a sight of the sphinx. Grace suggested somewhat gloomily that she imagined she would be forced to become a missionary—old Mrs. Taylor informed her she should be one—and in that way she would at least view India or China, those mysterious lands of the Orient. Rupert’s heart was determined on African jungles. Ida remained silent. She believed she would simply prefer to remain at home. This place was more beautiful than any other. It would be terrible when they had all grown up and were forced to disperse across the globe. The mere thought made Ida experience loneliness and homesickness. However, the others continued dreaming joyfully until Mary Stubbs showed up and dispelled poetry and dreams all at once.
“My goodness, I have lost my breath,” she cried out. “I hurried down the slope at top speed. Something gave me a terrible fright up at the former Bailey property.”
“What gave you a fright?” Izzy inquired.

“I’m not sure. I was searching beneath those lilacs in the former garden, attempting to check whether any lilies-of-the-valley had emerged so far. That spot was pitch black—and unexpectedly I noticed a moving and whispering noise on the far side of the garden, among those cherry bushes. A white thing was there. I assure you that I didn’t delay to look again. I rushed across the dyke as fast as possible. I felt certain that Henry Warren’s ghost was there.”
“Henry Warren was who?” Izzy inquired.
“And for what reason ought he to possess a phantom?” Bess inquired.
“Laws, were you never told the tale? And you raised in the Glen. Well, hold on a moment until I regain my full breath and I will inform you.”

Edmund felt a delightful shiver run through him. Ghost stories were something he adored. He derived a frightening, wonderful enjoyment from their strangeness, their tense endings, and their uncanny nature. Longfellow lost all its appeal and became mundane at once. Tossing the volume to the side, he extended his body, leaning up on his elbows so he could give his full attention, and trained his large, glowing eyes directly on Mary’s face. Mary preferred that he not stare at her in that manner. It seemed to her that she would perform the ghost story more effectively if Edmund’s gaze was turned away. She would be able to include various embellishments and make up some creative elements to heighten the terror. Given the circumstances, however, she was forced to adhere strictly to the plain truth—or to what she had received as the truth.

“Well,” she commenced, “you are aware that ancient Tom Bailey and his spouse resided in that dwelling up there three decades back. He was a terrible old scoundrel, according to rumor, and his spouse was not much superior. They possessed no offspring of their own, but a sibling of old Tom passed away and left behind a young lad—this Henry Warren—and they accepted him. He was roughly twelve upon his arrival to them, and somewhat small and frail. People claim Tom and his spouse treated him terribly from the beginning—lashed him and deprived him of food. People remarked they desired his death so that they might obtain the modest sum of money his mother had bequeathed to him. Henry did not perish immediately, but he commenced having seizures—epileps, as they termed them—and he developed into a somewhat simple youth, until he reached roughly eighteen. His uncle was accustomed to beating him in that garden up there because it was situated behind the dwelling where nobody could observe him. Nevertheless people could listen, and they claim it was terrible on occasion listening to poor Henry beg his uncle not to slay him. Yet no one ventured to intervene because old Tom was such a villain he would certainly have retaliated against them in some fashion. He set fire to the barns of an individual at Harbour Head who angered him. Finally Henry passed away and his uncle and aunt announced he perished during one of his seizures and that was everything anyone ever learned, yet everyone asserted Tom had simply up and murdered him permanently in the end. And before long word spread that Henry walked. That ancient garden was haunted. He was detected there during evenings, groaning and weeping. Old Tom and his spouse departed—relocated out West and never returned. The property acquired such an ill reputation no person would purchase or lease it. That is the reason it has completely fallen into decay. That occurred three decades back, yet Henry Warren’s spirit haunts it still.”
“Is that something you believe?” Bess inquired with disdain. “It’s not something I do.”

“Well, decent folk have observed him—and listened to him,” Mary answered back. “They claim he shows himself and crawls on the dirt and grips you around the legs and jabbers and laments the way he used to when he lived. I remembered that the moment I spotted that pale object in the shrubs and figured if it seized me in that manner and lamented I’d fall down dead right there. Therefore I bolted and fled. It may not have been his phantom, but I didn't intend to risk anything with a spectre.”
“Old Mrs. Stimson’s white calf was probably what it was,” Izzy laughed. “That garden is where it grazes—I’ve noticed it there.”

“That could be true. However, I will no longer take the path through the Bailey garden to go home. Tobias has arrived carrying a large catch of trout, and the responsibility to cook them now falls on me. According to both Kit and Tobias, my cooking surpasses everyone else's in the Glen. Additionally, Winifred permitted me to carry this collection of cookies up here. I nearly spilled them the moment I spotted Henry’s ghost.”

Tobias let out a hoot upon hearing the tale of the ghost—a story Mary iterated while she cooked the fish, embellishing it slightly, given that Edmund had left to assist Grace with laying the table. Tobias remained entirely unaffected by it, yet Grace, Ida, and Rupert were inwardly terrified, even if they refused to admit as much. Everything was fine while the rest of the group accompanied them in the valley; however, once the meal concluded and darkness began to descend, the memory made them tremble. Tobias ascended to Hollowmere alongside the Carrows to consult Kit regarding a matter, and Mary Stubbs took that route on her journey back. Consequently, Grace, Ida, and Rupert were forced to return to the manse by themselves. Walking in tight formation, they steered well clear of the old Bailey garden. Naturally, they didn't think it was haunted, but they refused to approach it nonetheless.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: In some way, the story of Henry Warren’s ghost had seized the imaginations of Grace and Rupert and Ida, and they were unable to free themselves from its grip. Belief in ghosts was something they had never held. They had listened to ghost tales in abundance—Mary Stubbs had recounted several that were significantly more terrifying than this one; yet those stories all concerned locations and individuals and specters that were distant and unfamiliar. Once the initial sensation of awe and dread—a feeling both somewhat fearful and somewhat enjoyable—had passed, they gave them no further thought. This narrative, however, struck close to home. Almost at their own doorway—nearly within their cherished Fern Hollow—lay the old Bailey garden. Frequently they had walked past it again and again; they had searched for flowers inside it; they had used it as a shortcut whenever they desired to travel directly to the valley from the village. Yet they would do so no longer! Following the evening on which Mary Stubbs shared its ghastly account with them, they would have refused to walk through it or approach it even if threatened with death. Death! Indeed, what was death when set against the terrifying chance of being seized by the grovelling ghost of Henry Warren?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: It was a warm evening in July when the three of them sat beneath the Tree Lovers, experiencing a slight sense of loneliness. That evening, no other person had approached the valley. Writing his entrance examinations, Kit Carrow was away in Port Marlow. Tobias and Edmund Carrow had gone out for a sail on the harbour alongside old Captain Crawford. Down the harbour road, Bess, Izzy, Tessa, and Harcourt had traveled to pay a visit to Julian and Damaris Treleaven, who had arrived with their parents to make a flying visit to the small, old House of Dreams. Although Bess had invited Grace to join them, Grace had refused. While she would not have acknowledged it to anyone, she harbored a quiet, private jealousy toward Damaris Treleaven, having heard much about her stunning beauty and city sophistication. No, she refused to travel down there and take a back seat to anyone. Accompanied by Ida, she brought her story books to Fern Hollow to read, as Rupert examined insects beside the brook's banks, and the three of them remained content until they abruptly noticed that dusk had arrived and the old Bailey garden was unsettlingly close. Rupert moved over and seated himself right beside the girls. Every one of them wished they had departed for home somewhat earlier, yet no one uttered a word.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Enormous, plush, violet clouds piled together in the west and stretched across the valley. No breeze blew, and all became abruptly, oddly, horribly quiet. Thousands of fire-flies filled the marsh. Undoubtedly, a parliament of fairies was assembling that evening. In all respects, Fern Hollow was no safe spot right at that moment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Grace gazed in terror up the valley toward the old Bailey garden. At that precise instant, if the blood of any human being ever froze, Grace Ashdown’s undoubtedly did. The eyes of Rupert and Ida went where her captivated look led, and shivering dread started racing up and down their backbones as well. Positioned there beneath the large tamarack tree, upon the ruined and weed-covered embankment of the Bailey garden, rested a white object—an indistinctly white form amidst the deepening darkness. Transfixed like statues, the three Ashdowns remained seated and stared.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “It’s—it’s the—calf,” Ida finally whispered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “For—the—calf, it is—too—big,” Grace whispered. Her lips and mouth had become so dry that articulating the words was nearly impossible for her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: All at once, Rupert drew in a sharp breath,

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “It’s coming here.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: The girls cast a final, anguished look. Indeed, it was crawling downward across the dyke in a manner no calf ever performed or was capable of performing. Sudden, overwhelming terror drove away all reason. At that instant, all three individuals were absolutely certain that the sight before them was the ghost of Henry Warren. Rupert jumped up and fled without direction. Screaming together, the girls pursued him. Like frantic beings, they sprinted up the slope, traversed the road, and entered the manse. They had abandoned Aunt Martha sitting in the kitchen at her sewing. She was absent. They hurried into the study. It was black and empty. Moving as if guided by a single thought, they turned about and headed toward Hollowmere—yet not by way of Fern Hollow. Descending the hill and passing along the Glen street, they sped as fast as their intense fright could carry them, with Rupert leading the way and Ida coming last. No person attempted to halt their flight, even if all who observed them marveled at the new mischief those manse children were engaged in this time. However, upon reaching the gate of Hollowmere, they collided with Clementine Ainslie, who had merely stepped inside briefly to yield back a few borrowed books.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Her eyes took in their pale, horrified features and wide-open gaze. It dawned on her that a genuine, terrible dread, regardless of its origin, was tormenting their frail young spirits. Pulling Rupert to her side with one arm, she gathered Grace using the other. Ida lost her footing, bumping into her, and clung on with all her strength.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “What is the matter, dear children?” she inquired. “Why are you scared?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “Henry Warren’s ghost,” Rupert replied, his teeth chattering as he spoke.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “Henry—Warren’s—ghost!” uttered bewildered Clementine, to whom the tale had never been told.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “Yes,” Grace cried out amidst her hysteria. “It is over there—upon the Bailey embankment—we spotted it—and it began to—pursue us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Clementine ushered the three inattentive beasts toward the veranda at Hollowmere. Hugh along with Nell had left as well, having likewise departed for the House of Dreams, yet Tabitha emerged at the threshold, scrawny, sensible, and not at all like a ghost.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “What is the cause of all this commotion?” she asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Once more the children stammered through their dreadful story, as Clementine pressed them near to herself and calmed them with comforting sounds that contained no words.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “It was probably an owl,” Tabitha remarked, completely unbothered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: A bird of the night! From that moment on, the Ashdown kids held no respect whatsoever for the cleverness of Tabitha!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “It exceeded a million owls in size,” Rupert stated, weeping—oh, how embarrassed Rupert felt about that weeping in later times—“and it—it crept along precisely as Mary described—and it was slithering down across the embankment toward us. Is crawling something owls do?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Clementine turned her gaze toward Tabitha.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “Something must have scared them for them to be this frightened,” she observed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “I am going to check,” Tabitha remarked calmly. “Now, children, compose yourselves. It was certainly not a ghost, regardless of what you witnessed. Regarding poor Henry Warren, I am certain he would want nothing more than to repose peacefully in his tranquil grave after reaching it. He will definitely not dare to return, and you can rely on that. If you are able to persuade them to be logical, Miss Ainslie, I shall discover what is actually happening.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Tabitha set off toward Fern Hollow, courageously holding a pitchfork that she discovered propped against the rear fence in the spot where the doctor had been laboring in his small hay-field. Although a pitchfork could prove ineffective against “ha’nts,” it provided a reassuring kind of protection. Upon Tabitha's arrival at Fern Hollow, there was nothing visible. No pale specters seemed to be hiding in the dark, overgrown old Bailey garden. Tabitha strode courageously across it and past it, using her pitchfork to knock on the door of the small cottage situated on the far side, the residence of Mrs. Stimson and her two daughters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: Over at Hollowmere, Clementine was able to quiet the youngsters. They continued to weep slightly because of the fright, yet a creeping, beneficial doubt that they had behaved like utter fools was starting to take root in them. Once Tabitha at last came back, this doubt turned into a conviction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “I have discovered what your phantom turned out to be,” she remarked, wearing a stern grin as she sat in a rocking chair and fanned herself. “For seven days, old Mrs. Stimson had been bleaching two factory cotton sheets inside the Bailey garden. Because the turf was tidy and brief in that spot, she laid them across the embankment beneath the tamarack tree. She ventured outside to retrieve them tonight. Carrying her knitting in her hands, she draped the sheets across her shoulders to transport them. Subsequently, she must have lost one of her needles, which she was unable to locate and still has not found. Nevertheless, she got down on her knees and crawled around searching for it, and that was her exact occupation when she heard terrible screams down in the valley and observed the three children racing up the slope right by her. Believing something had bitten them, her frail old heart suffered such a shock that she was incapable of moving or uttering a word, merely remaining stooped there until they went out of sight. Afterwards, she stumbled back to her house where they have been administering remedies to her continually, and her heart remains in a dreadful state, with her declaring that this scare will affect her for the rest of the summer.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: The Ashdowns remained seated, red with a humiliation that not even the compassionate understanding of Clementine was able to dispel. They crept away toward their house, encountered Tobias by the gate of the manse, and offered a penitent confession. For the following morning, a meeting of the Good-Conduct Club was set up.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: From her bed, Grace softly asked, “Didn’t Miss Ainslie treat us so kindly this evening?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “Yes,” Ida acknowledged. “The transformation that people undergo upon becoming stepmothers is truly unfortunate.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE
text: “I do not think it does,” Grace replied with loyalty.

“I fail to understand why any punishment should be given to us,” Grace remarked, appearing quite cross. “No wrongdoing was committed by us. Our fear was something we were unable to control. Furthermore, father will suffer no injury from it. What happened was merely an accident.”

“You proved to be cowards,” Tobias declared with the contempt of a judge, “and you succumbed to your fear. That is the reason you ought to be disciplined. Everyone is going to mock you over this, and the family is disgraced by it.”

“Were you aware of how terrible everything was,” Grace stated while shivering, “you’d believe our punishment was already sufficient. Nothing in the entire world could make me endure it a second time.”
“I think you’d have taken part in the run yourself had you been present,” Rupert grumbled.
“Coming from an elderly female wrapped in a piece of cotton fabric,” taunted Tobias. “Ho, ho, ho!”

“It failed to resemble an old woman in the least,” Grace exclaimed. “It was merely a huge, large, white object wriggling around in the grass precisely how Mary Stubbs stated Henry Warren did. Laughing is all well and good for you, Tobias Ashdown, but your laughter would have turned to distress had you been present. And in what manner will we receive punishment? Though I consider it unfair, inform us of what we must perform, Judge Ashdown!”

“In my opinion,” Tobias stated with a scowl, “Rupert holds the greatest responsibility. From what I gather, he was the first to run away. Furthermore, being a boy, he ought to have held his position so as to safeguard you girls, regardless of the peril. Isn’t that right, Rupert?”
“I guess so,” muttered Rupert with a look of shame.
“All right. Here is what your punishment will be. You will sit by yourself on the tombstone of Mr. Hezekiah Pollock in the cemetery tonight, up to twelve o’clock.”

Rupert trembled slightly. The old Bailey garden was located not particularly far from the cemetery. Although it promised to be a difficult test, Rupert eagerly desired to clear his dishonor and demonstrate that he was not, in fact, a faint-hearted person.
“Very well,” he replied with resolve. “However, in what way will I recognize the moment it reaches twelve?”

“You will hear the clock chime because the study windows are unclosed. And see to it that you do not move from that graveyard before the final chime ends. Regarding you girls, you must abstain from jam at supper for seven days.”

Grace and Ida wore somewhat bewildered expressions. They tended to believe that Rupert's relatively brief, albeit intense, suffering was a less severe penalty than this extended, lingering trial. An entire seven days of damp bread lacking the redeeming presence of jam! Nevertheless, no evading of duties was allowed within the club. The girls embraced their fate with whatever stoicism they were able to muster.

When nine o'clock arrived that evening, every one of them retired to bed, with the exception of Rupert, who was at that moment already maintaining his watch upon the tombstone. Ida crept inside so that she could wish him a good night. The deep sympathy she felt caused her gentle heart to ache.
“Oh, Rupert, are you very frightened?” she murmured.
“By no means,” Rupert stated lightheartedly.

“Not a wink of sleep will I get until twelve has passed,” Ida stated. “Should you become lonely, simply gaze toward our window and keep in mind that I am in there, awake, and contemplating you. Will that not offer a bit of companionship?”
“Do not fret over my well-being, for I shall be fine,” Rupert remarked.

Yet regardless of his brave statement, Rupert felt quite isolated once the manse’s lights were extinguished. It had been his hope to find his father in the study, where he frequently spent his time. In that case, loneliness would not have touched him. However, Mr. Ashdown had been called away that evening to the harbour mouth's fishing village to visit a man who was dying. His return was unlikely to occur before midnight had passed. Rupert had to endure his fate by himself.

A man from the Glen walked by, holding a lantern in his hand. The bizarre shadows produced by the illumination of the lantern rushed wildly across the cemetery, resembling a dance of witches or demons. Afterwards, those passed by, and shade returned once more. Individually, the Glen’s lights ceased to shine. The night was exceedingly dark, featuring a sky full of clouds, alongside an unpleasantly cold east wind that felt chilly regardless of what the calendar indicated. Distant on the horizon lay the faint, muted glow belonging to the Port Marlow lights. Within the ancient fir-trees, the wind moaned and breathed softly. Through the darkness, the lofty monument of Mr. Hector Twiss shone pale. Beside it, the willow flung out lengthy, twisting branches like a ghost. Now and then, the spinning of its limbs created the illusion that the monument was likewise in motion.

Rupert drawn his legs beneath himself as he curled up on top of the tombstone. Letting them dangle over the side of the stone was not particularly agreeable. Imagine—just imagine—if skeletal hands were to extend upward from Mr. Pollock’s underlying grave and grab him around his ankles. When they had all been gathered in that spot on a past occasion, Mary Stubbs had offered that bright thought. The idea came back to torment Rupert in this moment. He gave no credit to such notions; he did not even truly credit the ghost of Henry Warren. Regarding Mr. Pollock, sixty years had passed since his death, making it improbable that he minded who perched on his tombstone at present. Nevertheless, an immense strangeness and dread accompany being conscious while everyone else in the world sleeps. In those moments, you stand by yourself, possessing merely your own weak personality to match against the vast principalities and powers of darkness. Rupert was merely ten, surrounded on every side by the deceased—and he wished, oh, how he wished the clock would chime twelve. Was it ever going to chime twelve? Aunt Martha had certainly neglected to wind it.

And subsequently the hour of eleven rang out—merely eleven! An additional hour had to be spent by him in that dreary location. If merely a handful of welcoming stars could be spotted! The gloom possessed such density that his face appeared to be pushed by it. An impression of quiet, roving footsteps echoed throughout the cemetery. Rupert shuddered, caused in part by tingling dread and in part by actual chilliness.

A cold, soaking drizzle then started to fall. The thin cotton blouse and shirt worn by Rupert were quickly soaked. A deep cold reached his bones. His physical misery caused him to forget his psychological fears. Nevertheless, he was bound to remain in that spot until twelve, as he was enforcing his own punishment and bound by his honor. Although rain had not been mentioned, that altered nothing. As the study clock at last chimed twelve, a soaking wet small form climbed stiffly off the tombstone of Mr. Pollock, walked into the manse, and went up to bed. The teeth in Rupert’s mouth were knocking together. It seemed to him that he would be cold forever.

By the time morning arrived, he had become warm enough. Tobias cast a single alarmed glance at his flushed face and subsequently hurried to summon his father. Mr. Ashdown arrived in haste, his personal countenance pale as ivory from the faintness caused by his night-long watch beside a deathbed. Daylight had already broken when he finally reached home. With great anxiety, he leaned down over his young boy.
“Are you ill, Rupert?” he asked.
“That—gravestone—right here,” Rupert said, “it’s—shifting—around—it’s advancing—toward—me—hold it—back—I beg you.”

Mr. Ashdown hurried over to the phone. Dr. Carrow reached the manse within ten minutes. A telegram requesting a trained nurse was dispatched to town thirty minutes afterward, and the entire Glen learned that Rupert Ashdown had fallen gravely sick with pneumonia, with Dr. Carrow having been observed shaking his head.

More than a single time during the two weeks that came next, Hugh moved his head side to side. Double pneumonia struck Rupert. Mr. Ashdown walked back and forth across his study floor during a particular night, while Grace and Ida drew close together weeping in their bedroom, and Tobias, frantic with guilt, would not move away from the hall floor just beyond Rupert’s door. Neither Dr. Carrow nor the nurse departed from the bedside. Until the crimson sunrise, they bravely battled death, and they achieved the win. Rupert gained strength and safely survived the critical moment. Throughout the expectant Glen, the update was telephoned, and folk discovered the true depth of affection they held for their minister and his children.

“Since learning about the child’s illness, a single good night of sleep has eluded me,” Miss Winifred said to Nell, “and the weeping of Mary Stubbs has continued until her peculiar eyes resembled singed openings in a blanket. Did Rupert really contract pneumonia because he wandered into the graveyard on that rain-soaked night to satisfy a dare?”

“No. His reason for remaining in that place was self-punishment due to his lack of courage regarding the Warren ghost incident. Apparently, they belong to a club dedicated to self-improvement, where members inflict penalties on themselves for misdeeds. The whole story was relayed by Tobias to Mr. Ashdown.”
“The poor little souls,” Miss Winifred said.

Rupert recovered quickly, because the members of the church brought a sufficient amount of nutritious items to the manse to stock a hospital. Lionel Fairlie came by in his vehicle each night carrying twelve newly laid eggs alongside a pot of Jersey cream. On occasion, he remained for sixty minutes to shout debates concerning predestination alongside Mr. Ashdown inside the study; more frequently, he continued driving up toward the hill that had a view over the Glen.

A unique celebration was held in his celebration upon Rupert’s return to Fern Hollow, where the doctor joined the group to assist with the pyrotechnics. Although Mary Stubbs also attended, she refrained from sharing ghost tales, having received a lecture on the matter from Miss Winifred that Mary was unlikely to soon forget.

Clementine Ainslie, while returning to her house after a music lesson at Hollowmere, veered off toward the concealed spring located in Fern Hollow. All summer long, she had avoided the place; that lovely small area had lost its charm for her. Nowadays, her young lover's spirit failed to appear at the meeting place; furthermore, the recollections associated with John Ashdown proved excessively painful and sharp. However, having chanced to look back up the valley, she had observed Lionel Fairlie leaping as lightly as a youth over the ancient stone dyke belonging to the Bailey garden, which made her think he was heading up the hill. Had he caught up to her, she would have been forced to accompany him home, an outcome she intended to avoid. Consequently, she ducked immediately behind the spring's maple trees, wishing he had failed to spot her and would continue past.

However, Lionel had spotted her, and beyond that, he was giving chase to her. For a while now, he had desired to converse with Clementine, yet it appeared that she had consistently evaded him. At no point had Clementine ever particularly cared for Lionel Fairlie. She had perpetually been repelled by his bluster, his temper, and his loud merriment. A long time back, she had frequently questioned how Harriet could conceivably find him appealing. Lionel Fairlie was fully conscious of her antipathy, and he laughed softly about it. People disliking Lionel never bothered him. It failed to even render him averse to them in response, because he viewed it as a sort of compelled tribute. He considered Clementine a splendid girl, and he intended to prove himself a superb, open-handed brother-in-law to her. Yet prior to becoming her brother-in-law, a conversation with her was necessary, so, upon catching sight of her departing Hollowmere while he remained in the entrance of a Glen shop, he had immediately charged into the valley to catch up to her.

Clementine was seated in a pensive mood on the maple bench that John Ashdown had occupied on that night almost twelve months prior. Underneath its border of ferns, the miniature spring glistened and rippled. Sunlight at dusk cast opal-red glints through the overhanging branches. Beside her blossomed a tall cluster of flawless asters. The small location was just as dreamlike, enchanting, and elusive as any sanctuary of fairies and dryads within primeval woods. Lionel Fairlie burst into this setting, instantly dispersing and destroying its magic. The environment appeared to be completely consumed by his presence. Nothing remained there except Lionel Fairlie, large, red-bearded, and self-satisfied.
“Good evening,” Clementine said in a cold tone as she rose to her feet.

“‘Good evening, girl. Take a seat once more—take a seat once more. It is my desire to speak with you. Bless the girl, why is she staring at me in that manner? I am not going to devour you—my supper has already been eaten. Take a seat and act politely.”
“From where I am, I can listen to what you need to tell me just as clearly,” Clementine remarked.

“Indeed you are able to, girl, provided you employ your hearing. My sole intention was for you to feel at ease. You appear so blame uncomfortable, remaining on your feet like that. Oh well, I shall take a seat regardless.”

Lionel therefore took a seat in the exact spot previously occupied by John Ashdown. Clementine feared she might burst into a fit of hysterical laughter because the comparison was so absurd. Throwing his hat to one side, Lionel rested his enormous, red hands upon his knees and peered at her with twinkling eyes.

“Don’t act so rigid, girl, come on,” he urged in an attempt to win me over. He possessed a great capacity to be charming whenever he chose to. “Let us engage in a friendly, sensible, and reasonable conversation. I need to inquire about a certain matter. Because Harriet refuses, the responsibility falls on me to ask.”
Clementine peered below toward the spring, a feature that appeared to have diminished until it was merely as large as a drop of dew. Lionel looked upon her, filled with hopelessness.
“Durn it all, you could assist a guy a little,” he suddenly exclaimed.
“What do you need my assistance to state?” Clementine inquired with disdain.

“Young woman, you are just as aware of this as I am. Stop behaving so dramatically. It is no surprise that Harriet was frightened to make her request to you. Pay attention, girl, Harriet and I intend to get married. Is that not clear enough language? Do you understand? Moreover, Harriet claims she is unable to do so unless you release her from a ridiculous vow she gave you. Now then, are you willing to do it? Are you willing to do it?”
“Yes,” Clementine said.
Lionel sprang upward and took hold of her unyielding hand.

“Good! I was certain you would—I mentioned to Harriet you would. I was aware it would require merely a minute. Now, girl, you head home and inform Harriet, and a fortnight from now we’ll hold a wedding and you’ll reside with us. We will not abandon you to perch on that hill-top such as a solitary crow—do not fret. I am aware you despise me, but, Lord, residing with somebody who despises me will be immense fun. Life will possess some flavor following this. Harriet is going to roast me and you are going to freeze me. A dull moment will not be had by me.”

Clementine refused to demean herself by informing him that no circumstance could force her to reside in his home. Letting him stride back toward the Glen, radiating happiness and self-satisfaction, she proceeded to walk leisurely up the hill toward her house. Ever since coming back from Portmaris and discovering that Lionel Fairlie had become a regular night visitor, she had anticipated this moment. Although she and Harriet never spoke his name, that deliberate silence spoke volumes. If Clementine had possessed a bitter temperament, she would have experienced great bitterness, but such feelings were foreign to her nature. She maintained a distant politeness toward Lionel, while treating Harriet precisely as she always had. Harriet, however, derived little joy from being courted a second time.

Clementine arrived back to find her in the garden, accompanied by St. Laurence. In the dahlia walk, the two sisters came together. St. Laurence positioned himself on the gravel path in their midst, neatly curling his shiny black tail around his white paws, displaying the total nonchalance of a cat that was properly fed, well-bred, and impeccably groomed.
“Have you ever laid eyes on such dahlias?” Harriet asked with pride. “They are easily the best we’ve ever grown.”

Dahlias had never been to Clementine's liking. It was purely to accommodate Harriet’s preference that she allowed them in the garden. Among them, a single gigantic, speckled blossom of red and yellow caught her eye as it dominated the rest.
“That dahlia,” she remarked, as she gestured toward it, “is the spitting image of Lionel Fairlie. It could seamlessly pass for his twin brother.”

Harriet’s sullen face grew red. While she held the dahlia in high regard, she was aware that Clementine held no such affection for it, meaning no praise was meant. Yet she lacked the courage to take offense at Clementine’s remark—the unfortunate Harriet lacked the courage to take offense at anything at that moment. Furthermore, Clementine had never brought up Lionel’s name to her before this moment. It struck her that this boded something.
“In the valley, I encountered Lionel Fairlie,” Clementine said, gazing directly toward her sister, “and he informed me that the two of you wished to wed—provided I granted you my consent.”

“Yes? What did you say?” Harriet inquired, attempting to sound casual and unconcerned, though she failed entirely. Clementine’s gaze was something she was unable to meet. Her eyes dropped to St. Laurence’s smooth back, and an overwhelming fear seized her. Clementine’s statement had been either an agreement or a refusal. Should it be an agreement, Harriet’s shame and regret would render her an exceedingly uneasy bride-to-be; yet should it be a refusal—well, living without Lionel Fairlie was something Harriet had managed in the past, but having forgotten how, she believed the lesson could not be mastered a second time.
“I mentioned that, as long as it depended on me, you had complete freedom to wed one another whenever you wished,” Clementine stated.
“I am grateful,” Harriet stated, her eyes remaining fixed on St. Laurence.
The expression on Clementine’s face grew gentler.
“I wish you happiness, Harriet,” she spoke with gentleness.
“Oh, Clementine,” Harriet raised her eyes in anguish, “I feel such shame—I am not worthy of it—following everything I told you—”
“That is a subject we will not discuss,” Clementine stated with haste and firmness.
“Yet—yet,” Harriet kept on, “you are likewise unbound at present—and there is still time—John Ashdown—”

“Harriet Ainslie!” Underneath all her sweetness, Clementine possessed a small spark of temper, and right now it flared out from her blue eyes. “Are you completely out of your mind in all regards? Do you imagine even for a moment that I will approach John Ashdown and say submissively, ‘Please, sir, I’ve changed my mind and please, sir, I hope you haven’t changed yours.’ Do you wish for me to do that?”
“No—no—but with just a bit of—encouragement—he’d return—”

“At no time. He holds me in contempt—and with good reason. Say nothing further about it, Harriet. I hold no resentment toward you—choose anyone you wish for a husband. However, do not interfere with my business.”
“You have to come live at my place then,” Harriet stated. “Leaving you here by yourself is not something I will do.”
“Is it your honest belief that I would take up residence in the home of Lionel Fairlie?”
“For what reason?” Harriet exclaimed, her humiliation notwithstanding, with a touch of anger.
Clementine started laughing.
“Harriet, I believed you possessed a sense of humour. Do you picture me performing it?”
“I do not understand what would stop you. The size of his house is sufficient—you would possess your own portion of it—he would not intrude.”
“Harriet, it cannot be considered at all. Do not mention it another time.”
“In that case,” Harriet stated with a cold, resolute tone, “he and I will not be wed. I refuse to abandon you in this place by yourself. The matter is completely settled.”
“Nonsense, Harriet.”

“This isn't foolishness. My mind is completely made up. You contemplating residing in this place alone—a mile away from all other homes—would be ridiculous. Should you refuse to accompany me, I am going to remain with you. At this point, we will not debate the issue, so do not attempt to.”
“I will permit Lionel to handle the debate,” Clementine remarked.

“Lionel will be handled by me, as I am capable of managing him. Never would I have requested the return of my promise from you—not ever—yet the reason I was unable to wed Lionel had to be explained to him, and he stated his intention to ask you himself. Stopping him was beyond my power. It is unnecessary for you to assume that self-respect belongs solely to you in this world. The idea of getting married and deserting you here by yourself never entered my mind. Furthermore, you will discover that my determination equals your own.”
Shrugging her shoulders, Clementine turned around and walked into the dwelling. Harriet glanced toward St. Laurence, who had not moved a whisker or blinked an eyelash throughout the entire encounter.

“St. Laurence, I’ll grant that this world would be dreary lacking the men, yet I am nearly inclined to desire that not a single one of ‘em existed in it. See the difficulty and fuss they have caused in this very place, Laurence—utterly uprooted our joyful former life, Saint. John Ashdown started it and Lionel Fairlie has completed it. And at present each of them must depart into limbo. Lionel stands as the sole man I have ever encountered who concurs with me that the Kaiser of Germany is the most perilous being living upon this earth—and I am unable to wed this reasonable individual because my sister is unyielding and I am more unyielding. Take note of what I say, St. Laurence, the minister would return if she lifted her pinky. However she will not Laurence—she will under no circumstances do so—she will not so much as bend it—and I dare not interfere, Saint. I shall not brood, Laurence; Clementine refrained from brooding, therefore I am set on not doing so either, Saint; Lionel will throw a fury, yet the bottom line is, St. Laurence, that every one of us aged fools has to simply cease contemplating marriage. Ah well, ‘despair is a free man, hope is a slave,’ Saint. Therefore come inside the house now, Laurence, and I will comfort you using a small bowl filled with cream. At that point there shall be at least one joyful and satisfied being upon this hill.”
“I believe there is a matter I should disclose to you,” Mary Stubbs remarked with an air of mystery.

She was strolling arm in arm with Grace and Ida through the village, after they had met up at Mr. Flagg’s store. Ida and Grace traded glances that communicated, “Now something disagreeable is coming.” Little joy was ever found in listening when Mary Stubbs felt she should share things with them. They frequently questioned why their fondness for Mary Stubbs persisted—because they truly did like her, regardless of all else. Certainly, she proved to be an invigorating and pleasant friend as a rule. If merely she did not harbor those beliefs regarding her obligation to share things with them!
“Are you aware Clementine Ainslie refuses to wed your father due to her belief that you are all so untamed? Fearing her own inability to raise you properly, she rejected his proposal.”
A hidden feeling of triumph made Ida’s heart leap. Hearing that Miss Ainslie was not going to wed her father brought her great joy. Grace, on the other hand, felt a bit let down.
“In what way are you aware of this?” she inquired.

“Oh, it is being said by everyone. I overheard Mrs. Kerr discussing it with Mrs. Doctor. Although they believed I was beyond hearing distance, my ears are as sharp as a cat’s. Mrs. Kerr mentioned she felt certain Clementine feared attempting to be a stepmother to you on account of the reputation you have acquired. Your pa no longer walks up the hill. Lionel Fairlie does not either. People claim Harriet jilted him simply to even the score because he jilted her a long time back. Nevertheless, Lionel is walking around swearing he will win her in the end. Furthermore, I believe you should realize you ruined your pa’s romantic prospects and I consider it a shame, since he is certain to take a wife soon, and Clementine Ainslie is the finest wife for him I can think of.”
“It was your claim that all stepmothers were evil and mean,” Ida remarked.

“Oh—well,” Mary said, feeling somewhat flustered, “I am aware that the majority of them are terribly ill-tempered. However, Clementine Ainslie is incapable of being particularly unkind to anybody. Mark my words, should your pa change his mind and take Emmeline Drew as his wife, you will regret not having conducted yourselves properly instead of scaring Clementine away. It is terrible that your bad name prevents any respectable lady from wedding your pa because of you. Naturally, I realize that fifty percent of the stories circulating regarding you are false. Still, give a dog a bad name. Indeed, certain people claim that Tobias and Rupert were the ones who hurled stones through Mrs. Stimson’s window a few evenings ago, whereas those two Garrick boys were actually responsible. Nevertheless, I suspect Rupert was indeed the person who placed the eel inside old Mrs. Carr’s buggy, even if I initially stated that I refused to credit it without stronger evidence than old Kitty Hector’s statement. I stated as much to Mrs. Kerr directly to her face.”
“Grace exclaimed, “What was it that Rupert did?”

“Listen, they claim—remember, I’m merely repeating what others are saying—so you shouldn't get mad at me over it—that one night last week Rupert along with several other lads was catching eels off the bridge. Mrs. Carr went by in her rickety old buggy that has an open back. And Rupert simply went ahead and tossed a huge eel into that rear area. As the poor old lady Mrs. Carr was going up the hill near Hollowmere, that very eel crawled out right around her feet. Believing it to be a snake, she uttered a single terrible scream, stood right up, and leapt completely over the wheels. Though the horse ran off, it made its way home without any harm being done. However, Mrs. Carr hurt her legs awfully bad, and she has suffered nervous fits ever since each time she recalls the eel. Look, playing that lousy stunt on the poor old creature was terrible. She is a good person, even if she happens to be as odd as Rufus’s hat band.”
An exchange of glances passed between Grace and Ida once more. The Good-Conduct Club was the appropriate entity to address this affair. A discussion regarding it would not be held with Mary.

“There goes your pa,” Mary remarked when Mr. Ashdown went by them, “and he didn't notice us any more than if we were absent. Well, I'm reaching a point where it doesn't bother me. However, some people are affected by it.”

Although Mr. Ashdown had failed to spot them, he was not strolling with his customary dreamy and preoccupied air. He marched up the hill, filled with turmoil and grief. The account of Rupert and the eel had just been imparted to him by Mrs. Hector Twiss. Her reaction to it had been one of great outrage. A third cousin of hers was old Mrs. Carr. Beyond being outraged, Mr. Ashdown felt wounded and appalled. That Rupert would act in such a manner had never crossed his mind. He was not disposed to judge strictly any mischievous acts born of carelessness or memory lapses, yet this proved otherwise. There was an unpleasant quality to this. Upon arriving home, he discovered Rupert on the lawn, quietly observing how a community of wasps lived and behaved. Summoning him inside the study, Mr. Ashdown stood before him, wearing a look more severe than any his offspring had previously witnessed, and inquired whether the report was accurate.
“Indeed,” Rupert uttered, his face reddening, yet he boldly returned his father’s gaze.
Mr. Ashdown uttered a groan, having wished that the situation had been, at the very least, magnified beyond the truth.
“Relate the entire situation to me,” he requested.

“Over the bridge, the boys were angling for eels,” Rupert remarked. “Link Drew had taken a giant—that is, an extremely large one—the largest eel that ever met my eyes. Having landed it right at the beginning, he had kept it in his basket for a lengthy duration, remaining utterly motionless. Honest I did, I believed it was dead. Old Mrs. Carr then crossed the bridge in her carriage, labeling all of us young varmints and instructing us to head home. Truly, father, we had not uttered a single word to her. Therefore, once she returned from her trip to the store and drove past again, I was dared by the boys to place Link’s eel inside her buggy. Believing it was far too dead to harm her, I cast it inside. On the hill, however, the eel revived, and after hearing her screech, we watched her leap out. I felt terrible about it. Father, that is everything.”
Though the situation did not reach the full severity of Mr. Ashdown’s fears, its gravity remained undeniable. “I must punish you, Rupert,” he said sorrowfully.
“Indeed, I am aware, father.”
“I—I have to lash you.”
Rupert flinched. Being beaten was something he had never experienced. Next, recognizing the extent of his father's distress, he remarked brightly,
“All right, father.”

Mistaking his bright spirits for a lack of feeling, Mr. Ashdown instructed Rupert to join him in the study once supper was finished, and as soon as the youth had departed, he dropped into his seat with another groan. His dread of the upcoming night was seven times greater than Rupert's. The unfortunate clergyman lacked any idea of what instrument he ought to employ for the boy's whipping. Which items served to whip boys? Was it rods? Was it canes? No, such things would be overly cruel. Would a wooden switch do, then? Furthermore, he, John Ashdown, was obligated to hasten toward the forest to sever one from a tree. The notion was revolting. At that moment, an image forced its way into his thoughts without invitation. The shriveled, nut-cracker-like visage of Mrs. Carr upon the reanimation of that eel came into his view—he envisioned her flying like a witch over the wheels of the buggy. Prior to catching himself, the clergyman chuckled. Next, self-directed anger seized him, followed by an even deeper rage toward Rupert. He decided to procure that switch immediately—and it ought to possess a certain firmness, when all was said and done.

In the graveyard, Rupert discussed the situation with Grace and Ida, who had returned home recently. The thought of him being beaten—and by father, who had never performed such an action—appalled them! Nevertheless, they concurred solemnly that the punishment was fair.
“It was a terrible action, as you are aware,” Grace sighed. “Furthermore, you failed to confess while at the club.”
“I forgot,” Rupert said. “Moreover, it did not seem to me that any damage resulted. That her legs were jarred was unknown to me. However, my upcoming whipping will settle the matter.”
“Is it going to be very painful?” asked Ida, putting her hand in Rupert’s.

“Oh, I suppose it isn’t that bad,” Rupert uttered courageously. “Regardless, I refuse to weep, regardless of the severity of the pain. Doing so would cause father immense distress. He is already deeply upset. I only desire that I could administer a severe enough beating to myself so he wouldn't have to do it.”

Once supper concluded—a meal where Rupert consumed very little and Mr. Ashdown ate absolutely nothing—the two of them walked without a word into the study. Positioned on the table was the switch. Selecting an acceptable switch had proven difficult for Mr. Ashdown. Having severed a initial one, he deemed it excessively thin. What Rupert had committed was truly beyond justification. Subsequently, he severed a second one, which turned out much too stout. At any rate, Rupert believed the eel lacked life. A third attempt proved more satisfactory; yet, when he retrieved it from the tabletop, it felt exceedingly dense and weighty, resembling a club more than a switch.
“Extend your palm,” he instructed Rupert.

Rupert flung back his head and extended his hand without flinching. Nevertheless, because he was not particularly old, he was unable to fully hide a small amount of dread in his eyes. Mr. Ashdown gazed down into those eyes—indeed, they were Cecilia’s eyes—her exact eyes—and they held the identical look he had formerly observed in Cecilia’s eyes when she had approached him to disclose something she was somewhat fearful of disclosing to him. Her eyes were present here in Rupert’s small, pale face—and a month and a half earlier he had believed, during a single interminable, dreadful night, that his young boy was dying.
The switch was thrown down by John Ashdown.
“Depart,” he uttered, “I am unable to lash you.”
Rupert escaped toward the cemetery, sensing that the expression his father wore was far more painful than a thrashing.
“Is it ended already?” Grace inquired. She and Ida had stayed clasping hands and clenching their teeth upon the grave marker of Pollock.
“He—he refrained from whipping me entirely,” Rupert uttered while sobbing, “and—I would rather he had—and he remains inside, experiencing pure misery.”

Ida slipped away, for her heart yearned to comfort her father. Opening the study door as noiselessly as a little gray mouse, she crept in. Twilight made the room dark. Sitting at his desk, her father had his back towards her and his head in his hands. Broken, anguished words were being spoken as he talked to himself; nevertheless, Ida heard—heard and understood through the sudden illumination that comes to sensitive, unmothered children. She slipped out and closed the door just as silently as she had come in. In what he deemed his undisturbed solitude, John Ashdown went on talking out his pain.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Ida moved to the upper floor. Rupert and Grace were currently walking toward Fern Hollow under the nascent moon, since the fairy-like music of Tobias’s jews-harp had reached them from that direction, leading them to suspect the Carrows' presence and the start of amusement. Ida lacked the desire to join them. Heading to her private chamber initially, she seated herself upon the bed to weep briefly. Having someone replace her beloved mother was against her wishes. She detested the thought of a stepmother who would despise her and cause her father to despise her as well. Nevertheless, her father suffered such profound sorrow—and she was obligated to perform whatever action might increase his happiness. Only a single course of action was open to her—and from the instant she departed the study, she recognized her obligation to execute it. Yet it presented an extremely difficult task.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Once Ida had finished weeping copiously, she dried her tears and proceeded to the spare room. Because the blind had been left down and the window kept closed for an extended period, the room was pitch-black and somewhat stale. Fresh air was not something Aunt Martha cared for. However, since no one ever considered closing a door inside the manse, this was less of an issue, except on occasions when an unlucky minister stayed overnight and had no choice but to inhale the air of the spare room.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Inside the spare room sat a closet, and hanging deep within its depths was a gray silk dress. After stepping inside the closet and closing the door, Ida dropped to her knees and buried her face in the soft folds of silk. Her mother had worn it as a wedding-dress. A faint, sweet, and haunting scent, resembling a love that lingers, still filled it. Being in that spot always made Ida feel extremely near to her mother—just like she was kneeling at her feet with her head resting on her lap. Whenever life became excessively difficult, she would go there once in a great while.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Mother,” she murmured toward the dress of gray silk, “you will never be forgotten by me, mother, and my love for you will forever be the greatest. Yet this must be done by me, mother, since father suffers such great unhappiness. It is certain to me that his unhappiness would not be desired by you. Also, my behavior toward her will be exceptionally good, mother, as I endeavor to love her, notwithstanding her potential resemblance to what stepmothers always were according to Mary Stubbs.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Some splendid, soul-deep power was borne away from her hidden altar by Ida. On that night, with the marks of tears yet shining upon her dear, grave, small face, she drifted off to sleep in peace.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: During the following afternoon, she dressed in her finest hat and gown. They were quite worn out. With the exception of Grace and Ida, all the other young girls in the Glen possessed new garments that summer. Mary Stubbs possessed a beautiful gown made of white embroidered lawn, accompanied by shoulder bows and a sash of scarlet silk. However, Ida was unbothered by her worn appearance on this day. Being extremely tidy was her sole desire. Her face was washed with care. Her black hair was brushed by her until it reached a satiny smoothness. After mending a pair of runs in her single set of decent stockings, she neatly fastened her shoelaces. Polishing her shoes was something she wished to do, yet finding any blacking proved impossible for her. At last, she quietly left the manse, traveling down through Fern Hollow, ascending through the whispering woods, and emerging onto the road passing by the house on the hill. Because the journey was rather lengthy, Ida felt fatigued and heated upon her arrival.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Her eyes caught Clementine Ainslie positioned beneath a tree within the garden, prompting her to creep by the dahlia beds toward her. A book rested upon Clementine’s lap, yet her eyes were fixed on the far distance over the harbour, accompanied by rather mournful thoughts. Lately, living in the house on the hill had lacked pleasantness. Harriet had refrained from sulking—Harriet had acted like a brick. Nevertheless, unuttered feelings remain palpable, making the silence that fell between the two women intolerably expressive on occasion. Every single familiar element that used to render life sweet had acquired a bitter taste currently. Furthermore, Lionel Fairlie carried out recurring intrusions, alternating between bullying and coaxing Harriet. Clementine held the belief that this situation would conclude with his hauling Harriet away alongside him eventually, an outcome Clementine felt she would welcome almost gladly. While life would become dreadfully solitary at that point, it would cease to be filled with dynamite.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: A gentle, hesitant pat upon her shoulder awakened her from her disagreeable musings. Looking back, Ida Ashdown met her gaze.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “My goodness, dear Ida, was it on foot that you made the journey up here through such intense heat?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Indeed,” Ida remarked, “I arrived in order to—I arrived in order to—”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Yet accomplishing the task she had arrived for proved exceedingly difficult for her to voice. Her speech deserted her, and tears welled up in her eyes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “What is wrong, Ida, my little girl? You should not fear sharing it with me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Clementine placed her arm about the slender small figure and pulled the youngster near herself. Her eyes possessed great beauty—her contact was so gentle that Ida gathered bravery.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I arrived—to request that you—wed father,” she panted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: For a brief instant, Clementine said nothing because she was completely astonished. Her gaze rested uncomprehendingly on Ida.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Oh, please do not be mad, sweet Miss Ainslie,” Ida begged. “You know, it is being said by everyone that your refusal to marry father is due to our being so terrible. He feels very miserable concerning it. Therefore, I decided to come and inform you that our misbehavior is never intentional. And provided you just marry father, every one of us will attempt to be well-behaved and execute exactly what you command. I am certain that we will not cause you any difficulty. Please, Miss Ainslie.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Clementine’s thoughts had been racing. It was clear to her that idle speculation had planted this false notion in Ida’s head. With the girl, she needed to be completely candid and genuine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Ida, dear,” she murmured gently. “My inability to become the wife of your father is not on account of you poor little souls. Such an idea never entered my mind. You are not bad—I never imagined you were. There—Ida, there was a completely different reason.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Do you not like father?” Ida inquired, raising eyes filled with reproach. “Oh, Miss Ainslie, you have no idea how nice he is. I am certain he would be a good husband to you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Despite her confusion and suffering, Clementine was unable to suppress a faint, wry smile.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Oh, do not poke fun, Miss Ainslie,” Ida exclaimed with intense feeling. “Father is deeply upset over the matter.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I believe you are in error, my love,” Clementine remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I am not. I am certain I am not. Oh, Miss Ainslie, Rupert had been bad, so father was intending to whip him yesterday—and father was unable to accomplish it since, as you know, he lacked practice in whipping. Thus, once Rupert emerged and informed us that father felt extremely upset, I crept into the study to discover whether I might assist him—he prefers me to soothe him, Miss Ainslie—and he failed to hear me enter, allowing me to overhear his words. I will inform you, Miss Ainslie, provided you permit me to whisper it into your ear.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Ida spoke in a urgent whisper. A deep blush covered Clementine’s face. Therefore, John Ashdown continued to hold her in his heart. His feelings remained unaltered. Furthermore, his devotion had to be remarkably deep for him to have uttered those words—deeper than she had ever imagined it to be. For a brief pause, she remained seated without moving, running her fingers through Ida’s hair. After that, she remarked,

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Ida, would you carry a short note to your father for me?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Oh, will you be marrying him, Miss Ainslie?” Ida inquired with enthusiasm.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Maybe—if he genuinely desires me to do so,” Clementine answered, turning red once more.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I’m happy—I’m happy,” Ida uttered courageously. Afterwards, her lips trembling, she gazed upward. “Oh, Miss Ainslie, you will not cause father to oppose us—you will not cause him to despise us, will you?” she asked imploringly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Clementine gave another gaze.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Ida Ashdown! Is it your belief that I would commit such an act? What on earth made you think of that?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “According to Mary Stubbs, every stepmother behaved in that manner—hating their stepchildren and driving their fathers to hate them as well—because simply being a stepmother compelled them to act that way”—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “My poor child! Even so, you traveled up here and requested that I wed your father since you desired his happiness? You are a sweetheart—a heroine—or a brick, to use Harriet's phrase. Listen to what I am telling you, dearest, with great care. Mary Stubbs is an unwise young girl lacking extensive knowledge, and regarding certain matters, she is terribly incorrect. Turning your father against you is something I would not ever contemplate. Every one of you would be dearly loved by me. Taking the place of your own mother is not my desire—in your hearts, that must forever belong to her. However, becoming a stepmother is also not my plan. My wish is to serve as your friend, helper, and pal. Wouldn't that be pleasant, Ida—were you, Grace, Rupert, and Tobias able to simply view me as a fine, cheerful pal—a tall elder sister?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Oh, it would be lovely,” Ida shouted, her face completely altered. Impulsively, her arms wrapped around Clementine’s neck. Her happiness was so immense that she felt capable of taking flight on wings.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Are the rest of them—are Grace and the boys of one mind with you regarding stepmothers?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “No. Mary Stubbs was never believed by Grace. It was dreadfully foolish of me to believe her as well. You are loved by Grace already—ever since poor Adam was eaten, she has loved you. And it will be thought jolly by Tobias and Rupert. Oh, Miss Ainslie, when you come to live with us, will you—could you—teach me to cook—a little—and sew—and—and—and do things? Nothing is known by me. Much trouble I won't be—fast is how I'll try to learn.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “My dear, I will instruct you and render whatever assistance I am able to. Now, you will not utter a single thing to anyone regarding this, will you—not even to Grace, until your father himself informs you that you are permitted? And you will remain to take tea with me?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Oh, I appreciate it—however—however—I believe I should return immediately to give father the letter,” stammered Ida. “You understand, it will make him happy that much earlier, Miss Ainslie.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I understand,” Clementine remarked. Proceeding to the dwelling, she composed a message and handed it to Ida. As soon as that little maiden had scampered away, a quivering package of delight, Clementine moved toward Harriet, who happened to be podding peas upon the rear veranda.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “Harriet,” she stated, “Ida Ashdown was recently at this place requesting that I become her father's wife.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Harriet raised her eyes, studying what was written across her sister’s features.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “And what do you intend to do?” she asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “It’s highly probable.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Harriet continued to shell peas for a short time. After that, she abruptly raised her hands to her face. Her dark-browed eyes were filled with tears.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: “I—I hope happiness lies ahead for everyone,” she uttered, half laughing and half sobbing.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXIV. IDA VISITS THE HILL
text: Farther down at the vicarage, Ida Ashdown, glowing, flushed, and victorious, stepped courageously into the study of her father and placed a letter on his desk. The pale skin of his face reddened when his eyes caught the neat, delicate penmanship that was so familiar to him. Unsealing the letter, he found it to be brief—yet reading its contents stripped two decades from his age. In it, Clementine requested that he meet her by the spring in Fern Hollow at dusk that very night.
“And so,” Miss Winifred stated, “the two couples will be married at some point near the middle of this month.”

A slight coldness hung in the air during the early September evening, which led Nell to ignite her constantly prepared driftwood fire inside the large living room, where she and Miss Winifred took comfort in its magical glow.

“Particularly concerning Mr. Ashdown and Clementine, it is truly wonderful,” Nell remarked. “Thinking about it makes me just as joyful as I felt during my own wedding. Up on the hill yesterday night while I examined Clementine’s trousseau, I experienced the precise sensation of being a bride once more.”

“It has been mentioned to me that what she owns would suit a princess,” stated Tabitha out of a dark nook in which she held her brown boy close. “I was asked to go up and look at the items too, a trip I plan to make one night. Word has reached me that Clementine plans to wear a veil and white silk, whereas navy blue is chosen for Harriet's wedding. Mrs. Dr. dear, I do not question that her decision is quite practical, yet personally I have constantly held the opinion that should I ever get wed, I would choose the veil and white to feel more like a bride.”
An image of Tabitha dressed in “white and a veil” appeared to the mind’s eye of Nell, nearly overwhelming her.

“Regarding Mr. Ashdown,” Miss Winifred remarked, “his upcoming marriage alone has transformed him completely. Trust me, his dreaminess and preoccupation have been reduced by half. It was such a comfort to learn he had chosen to lock up the manse and allow the youngsters to stay with various people during his wedding trip. Had he permitted them and elderly Aunt Martha to remain in the house by themselves for four weeks, I would have anticipated waking up each day to find the building reduced to ashes.”
“Aunt Martha and Tobias will be arriving,” declared Nell. “Rupert’s destination is Elder Clow’s house. Their plans for the girls remain unknown to me.”

“Oh, I’m going to take them,” said Miss Winifred. “Naturally, I was happy to, though Mary would have bothered me endlessly until I asked them regardless. The manse will be cleaned from top to bottom by the Ladies’ Aid before the bride and groom return, and the cellar will be filled with vegetables through Lionel Fairlie's arrangements. Believe me, nobody has ever seen or heard anything remotely like Lionel Fairlie lately. Having desired Harriet Ainslie all his life, he is so thrilled that he is finally going to marry her. If I were Harriet—however, I’m not, and if it contents her, it can certainly content me. Years ago, when she was a schoolgirl, I overheard her state that a tame puppy was not what she wanted in a husband. Believe me, there’s nothing tame about Lionel.”

As dusk arrived above Fern Hollow, the pond sported a marvellous expanse of green, purple, crimson, and gold. Resting upon the eastern hill was a light blue mist, above which an enormous, round, pale moon was simply drifting upward in the manner of a silver bubble.

Every one of them was present, crouching in the small uncovered clearing—Grace and Ida, Tobias and Rupert, Kit and Edmund, Bess and Izzy, and Mary Stubbs. A particular party had been underway, because it was going to be the final night Kit spent in Fern Hollow. The next day he was set to depart for Port Marlow so he could go to Regent’s Academy. The group’s spellbound ring was going to be shattered; and, regardless of the lightheartedness of their small gathering, a trace of grief existed within each cheerful youthful soul.

“Look—over there in the sunset stands a massive golden palace,” Edmund said, pointing. “Gaze upon the gleaming tower—and the crimson banners floating from them. Maybe a victor returns home from war—and they hang them outside in his honour.”

“Oh, how I desire the return of the past,” Kit cried out. “It would be wonderful to serve as a soldier—to be a famous, victorious general. For the chance to witness a grand battle, I would sacrifice all I possess.”

Well, Kit was slated to enter the military and experience a fight larger than any previous one on earth; however, that remained a long time away; meanwhile, his mother, to whom he was the eldest boy, used to gaze at her sons while expressing gratitude to God that those “brave days of old” desired by Kit had ended permanently, meaning Canadian sons would not ever have to gallop away to war “for the ashes of their fathers and the temples of their gods.”

No icy harbinger of the Great Conflict's shadow had been experienced as of yet. Schoolboys, full of mischief and anticipating a good future, were what the young men who would do battle, and maybe perish, in the landscapes of France and Flanders, Gallipoli and Palestine then were; lovely young girls, glowing with expectations and fantasies, were what the young women whose spirits would be broken then were.

Gradually, the crimson and gold of the sunset city's banners were surrendered, and the conqueror’s pageant vanished at a slow pace. As twilight slid across the valley, silence descended upon the small gathered group. Edmund, who had spent time reading from his treasured book of myths earlier that day, recalled a former notion he had held about the Pied Piper descending into the valley during a dusk precisely such as this one.

He commenced speaking in a dreamy manner, in part due to his desire to give his companions a small thrill, and in part because an entity distinct from himself appeared to be utilizing his lips to speak.

“The Piper is drawing closer,” he said, “he is closer than he was on the evening I previously saw him. He has his long, shadowy cloak blowing about him. He pipes—he pipes—and we are forced to follow—Kit and Rupert and Tobias and I—around and around the globe. Listen—listen—are you unable to hear his wild music?”
A shudder passed through the girls.

“You are fully aware that you are merely playing a part,” Mary Stubbs objected, “and I would prefer that you stopped. Your performance is far too convincing. That ancient Piper of yours is something I despise.”

However, laughing merrily, Kit leaped to his feet. Upon a small mound he stood, magnificent and lofty, possessing an unclouded forehead alongside his brave gaze. Throughout the country of the maple, there existed thousands similar to him.
“May the Piper arrive and be welcomed,” he exclaimed, making a gesture with his hand. “With joy, I will pursue him all over the earth.”
